records.title: About focusChrist
records.text: Our purpose Help people turn toward Jesus Christ focusChrist exists to make sincere study easier: ask a question, explore scripture, follow sources, learn from faithful history, and continue into authoritative Church resources when deeper verification is needed. What we believe Jesus Christ is the center Content is presented from a Latter-day Saint perspective that worships Jesus Christ as Savior and Redeemer, accepts His Atonement and Resurrection, and believes His gospel and priesthood authority were restored. “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son...” (John 3:16) How the site works Study with clarity and source awareness Ask The Q&A experience combines curated material with AI-assisted responses when needed. Conversation is designed to support study, not replace scripture or official Church teaching. Verify Scripture and official Church resources are linked whenever available. AI-assisted responses are study aids and may contain errors; they should be checked against authoritative sources for doctrine, policy, and history. Continue Permanent Answers, Art & Study, Pioneer history, Watch & Study, Gospel Library, and other official resources provide natural next steps after a question is answered. Independent website. focusChrist is not an official website of, sponsored by, or endorsed by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. It presents material from a Latter-day Saint perspective and links to official Church resources when appropriate. Ask a Question Browse Answers Official Church Website Watch, read, and reflect Explore the faith behind this resource These official Church messages offer a starting point for learning about Jesus Christ and sharing faith. Church video Finding Hope Through the Resurrection of Christ Begin with the Savior’s Resurrection and the eternal hope it offers every family. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church video Love—the Essence of the Gospel Consider how Christlike love shapes both service and the way faith is shared. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Explore beliefs about Jesus Christ What you can expect from a study here focusChrist offers a Latter-day Saint perspective while welcoming readers who believe differently or are still deciding what they believe. Clear explanations should help you understand a teaching without asking you to pretend that differences or difficult questions do not exist. Scripture links take you to the passages being discussed. Official Church resources explain Church teachings and practices. Historical records support claims about the past. Original reflection offers a way to think or act; artwork offers a visual interpretation. Those purposes overlap, but they are not interchangeable kinds of evidence. See a respectful comparison in practice Explore shared Christian commitments and real doctrinal differences, with sources for the traditions being described. See how a historical question is studied Compare the setting, date, and purpose of accounts before drawing a conclusion. See scripture, image, and reflection work together Read John 10 and Psalm 23, distinguish the artist’s choices from the text, and consider a personal application. You remain free to question an explanation, check the source, or leave a matter unresolved. The purpose of these connections is to make careful learning easier and to treat the person doing that learning with respect.

records.text: The heart of our faith The Atonement of Jesus Christ Follow His love from the beginning. Linger with the artwork, read the scriptures, and explore His sacrifice, Resurrection, repentance, grace, and healing. Explore the Atonement Study Choose a Chapter Follow the record Explore Book of Mormon Evidences Study the translation, Royal Skousen’s manuscript research, witness accounts, chiasmus, stylometry, and ancient context. Explore the Evidences Study Begin with the Translation focusChrist is independent and does not speak for the Church. Each page links directly to official Church or scripture resources so visitors can verify teachings and continue studying from authoritative sources. What Do Latter-day Saints Believe About Jesus Christ? Jesus Christ as Son of God, Savior and Redeemer, His Atonement, Resurrection, premortal role, and promised return. The Birth of Jesus Christ Follow the scriptural promises, Mary and Joseph, the birth in Bethlehem, and the witnesses who received the Savior. Are Latter-day Saints Christian? Why Latter-day Saints identify as Christians, what they share with other Christians, and where important doctrinal differences remain. The Atonement of Jesus Christ Explore the Savior’s sacrifice and Resurrection through scripture, artwork, and a guided study of repentance, grace, and healing. What Is the Book of Mormon? What the Book of Mormon claims to be, why it is called another testament of Jesus Christ, and why it does not replace the Bible. Why Do Latter-day Saints Build Temples? Sacred worship, covenants, ordinances, eternal families, and service for those who have died. What Happens After Death? The spirit world, resurrection through Jesus Christ, judgment, and the hope of eternal life. Who Was Joseph Smith? The First Vision, Book of Mormon, Restoration, prophetic role, and a responsible approach to his complex history. Come unto Christ Bring every honest question You do not need to have everything settled to begin. Bring your curiosity, your doubts, and what matters to you. Take time with the scriptures and sources, and return to the questions that need more thought. How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work? Prayer, the Holy Ghost, personal guidance, discernment, and what it can mean when an answer does not come immediately. Why Are Families Important? Divine identity, marriage and parenting, temple sealing, imperfect family realities, and eternal hope. What Is Eternal Marriage? Temple sealing, Christ-centered equal partnership, covenant faithfulness, tender questions, eight scriptures, and a guided seven-day study. Who Is God Our Heavenly Father? Study the Father’s character, His relationship to Jesus Christ, prayer, the Godhead, and our identity as His children. How Can Faith Meet Grief? Read about lament, Christ’s compassion, practical support, and hope that does not require sorrow to disappear on a schedule. What Is the Restored Church of Jesus Christ? Explore restoration, scripture, priesthood, ordinances, prophets, and the purpose of the Church in leading people to Jesus Christ. How Can I Stand Forever in Christ? Study faith, courage, covenant discipleship, and the Savior’s invitation to remain steady when life is uncertain. Look Unto Me in Every Thought Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:32–37 in context, then follow a guided study of looking to Christ, remembering, sharing what you learn, rejoicing, and acting. Quiet Prayer Prayer and personal revelation Quiet Prayer Finding words for prayer can be difficult when you are tired or unsure. James invites us to ask God for wisdom. Start with what is honest today, then give yourself time for study, quiet thought, and one next step you can manage. Read James 1:5-6 Pause and reflect What question could I bring honestly to God today? What is one faithful step I can take while I continue seeking? Explore Prayer and Revelation Jesus Christ receives each child with love and dignity. How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together? How two different scriptural records can function as complementary witnesses of Jesus Christ. How Can Faith in Jesus Christ Help During Trials? Trusting Christ through adversity without denying pain, practical needs, or the complexity of suffering. Comfort in Grief Hope through Jesus Christ Comfort in Grief When someone you love is gone, even ordinary days can feel unfamiliar. Alma teaches that the Savior knows our pain and how to help us. The embrace in this artwork points to His compassion. You can seek His comfort while still missing the person you love. Read Alma 7:11-13 Pause and reflect What comfort do I need today? Who could sit with me, listen, or help carry a practical burden? records.title: Aaronic Priesthood
records.text: Answers / Aaronic Priesthood Follow Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery from their question about baptism to John the Baptist’s message and the baptisms that followed. Read the scriptural account alongside its historical sources, then consider how preparation, repentance, and service point toward Jesus Christ. A question, a messenger, and the waters of baptism The story begins with a question raised while translating the Book of Mormon. In Joseph Smith—History 1:68–69 , Joseph and Oliver go into the woods to pray about baptism. Their account connects reading with asking and receiving a responsibility to act. Read the passage slowly before looking at the artwork. Notice what led them to pray, how the messenger is introduced, and which words describe the authority he conferred. The opening artwork shows contemporary preparation at a sacrament table. As you study the restoration account, consider how authority and reverent preparation lead to service today. Explore and study Bring the question to scripture An open book and a quiet place give this reader time to consider his question. This imagined contemporary scene invites patient study before deciding what a passage means. Joseph and Oliver’s account also begins with a question awakened while reading. Read Joseph Smith—History 1:68–69 John the Baptist and the authority to baptize Explore and study Called to prepare the way Joseph and Oliver bow their heads beneath the messenger’s hands. Their account connects a question about baptism with a call to serve. Read John the Baptist’s words and think about how repentance and baptism turn a heart toward Jesus Christ. Read Doctrine and Covenants 13 Read Joseph Smith—History 1:68–73 Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery dated John the Baptist's visit to May 15, 1829, near Harmony, Pennsylvania. Their question about baptism arose during the translation of the Book of Mormon. They went apart to pray, and their accounts describe a heavenly messenger conferring authority by laying his hands upon them. The Church's history traces these reports, including Oliver's detailed account published in 1834. Read the history and its documentary sources . Into the waters of baptism Explore and study Joseph baptizes Oliver Joseph raises his hand as Oliver prepares for immersion. Following John the Baptist’s direction, Joseph baptized Oliver first. Their account places this beginning on May 15, 1829. Read Joseph Smith—History 1:70–73 Explore and study Oliver baptizes Joseph Oliver steadies Joseph as he lowers toward the water. Oliver then baptized Joseph. The two men afterward ordained one another as John had directed. Joseph’s history describes the spiritual joy that followed their baptisms. Read Joseph Smith—History 1:71–73 These artistic scenes follow the order in Joseph’s account. Clothing, gestures, and the precise riverbank are interpreted. Explore the account: baptism and the ordinations that followed In Joseph Smith—History 1:68–73 , the messenger identifies himself as John the Baptist and explains that further authority will follow. Joseph and Oliver then baptize each other. Doctrine and Covenants 13 preserves the words concerning the priesthood of Aaron, repentance, baptism, and the ministering of angels. The detailed narratives were recorded after the event. Reading their dates and source notes helps us distinguish the remembered experience from the later work of writing Church history. The artwork accompanying this study offers an interpretation of that testimony, not an authenticated view of John's face or the exact clearing where they prayed. After the baptisms, Joseph and Oliver ordained each other to the Aaronic Priesthood as commanded. Read Joseph Smith—History 1:71. Consider the movement from reading to asking, and from receiving an answer to acting upon it. What question has scripture awakened in you? What faithful next step can you take? Return to the translation study , or continue to Peter, James, and John and the unfolding restoration of priesthood authority. Read the scriptures in context Doctrine and Covenants 13 preserves John the Baptist’s words about the keys of the ministering of angels, the gospel of repentance, and baptism by immersion for the remission of sins. Keep those words beside Joseph Smith—History 1:70–72 , where the messenger explains the bounds of this authority and the greater authority that would follow. The account distinguishes John’s conferral from Joseph and Oliver’s later actions. They baptized each other, then ordained each other as directed. Reading that sequence carefully is more useful than combining every event into one scene. Compare the promise of preparation with John’s earlier witness in Mark 1:1–8 . In each setting, his ministry turns attention toward Jesus Christ. The accounts belong to different times; this comparison concerns the purpose of his witness, not an assertion that every circumstance was the same. Church video Restoration of the Aaronic Priesthood Watch this Church reenactment, then return to Joseph’s account and notice the instruction that led him and Oliver into the water. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Authority and a life of service John’s message speaks of repentance and baptism. Mosiah 18:8–10 describes a people willing to bear one another’s burdens and stand as witnesses of God. Read the whole setting around Alma’s invitation. How does belonging to Christ shape the way people treat one another? Explore and study Carry a burden together Two young men bring groceries to a woman at her doorway. This imagined moment of care invites us to consider Alma’s call to bear one another’s burdens and ask what would help someone near us. Read Mosiah 18:8–10 Church video Restoration of the Priesthood Church members share how restored priesthood has blessed their lives. Listen to their experiences, then consider the blessings and responsibilities described in the scriptures. Consider a small act of service, ask what would actually help, and respect the person’s wishes. records.title: Are Latter-day Saints Christian?
records.text: Answers / Christian identity Yes. Members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints identify themselves as Christians because they worship Jesus Christ, believe salvation comes through Him, and seek to follow His teachings. focusChrist is independent and does not speak for the Church. Official Church sources are linked below so readers can examine the Church’s own explanation. Watch and study Hear a Convert Explain His Christian Faith In Are We Christians? , Elder Gary J. Coleman discusses his conversion, the Godhead, additional scripture and revelation, and priesthood authority. His account offers a personal introduction to several beliefs that make this question important to people from different Christian traditions. Church video Are We Christians? The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints As you watch, distinguish his experience from the doctrinal claims you want to examine. Then read Articles of Faith 1:1, 3-4 . These statements name the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, place salvation through Christ's Atonement, and describe faith, repentance, baptism, and the gift of the Holy Ghost. Which belief would you like to understand in its own terms before comparing it with another tradition? Why Latter-day Saints Use the Word Christian For Latter-day Saints, Christianity is centered on Jesus Christ. They believe He is the Son of God, the promised Messiah, the Savior of humanity, and the risen Lord. They pray to Heavenly Father in Christ’s name, take the sacrament in remembrance of Christ, are baptized in His name, and organize worship around His gospel. Beliefs Shared with Other Christians Latter-day Saints believe Jesus was born of Mary, ministered in the Holy Land, taught the way of salvation, suffered and died on the cross, and rose bodily from the dead. They accept the Bible as scripture and affirm that redemption from sin and death comes through the Atonement and Resurrection of Jesus Christ. Why Some Christians Disagree Some Christian traditions do not classify Latter-day Saints as Christian because Latter-day Saint teachings differ from historic creeds formulated after the New Testament period. One important difference concerns the nature of God. Latter-day Saints understand the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost as distinct divine beings perfectly united in purpose. Nicene Christianity teaches one God in three distinct persons who share one divine nature. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 253-254 explains that belief in its own terms. Latter-day Saints also accept additional scripture and believe priesthood authority and the organization of Christ’s Church were restored through Joseph Smith. Difference Does Not Remove Christ from the Center These differences matter deeply to people on both sides of the conversation. Respectful discussion allows each tradition to explain its beliefs fairly. Latter-day Saints understand their restored doctrines as teachings about Christ and His work. The Church’s own name places Jesus Christ at the center, and its first Article of Faith begins with belief in God the Eternal Father, His Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost. A Fair Way to Evaluate the Question Rather than relying only on labels, a seeker can ask what a faith actually teaches about Jesus Christ, how its members worship, what its scriptures testify, and whether its disciples are trying to follow Him. Latter-day Saints answer the question of Christian identity by pointing to their faith in the living Christ and their dependence on His grace. Having the Conversation with Respect If this question comes up with a friend, it helps to ask what each of you means by Christian. One person may be speaking about faith in Jesus; another may be asking about agreement with a particular creed. Understanding that difference can make the conversation clearer without requiring either person to set aside convictions. John 13:34-35 records Jesus teaching His disciples to love one another. Consider that passage alongside the doctrinal sources below. It offers a way to approach the conversation with care, even where agreement is not possible. Watch and study What Does Christian Belief Ask of a Disciple? In Believers in the Book of Mormon , Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin connects belief in the Savior with conduct that follows His teachings. Use this message to explore a further question: How should a confession of faith shape the way a person lives? Church video Believers in the Book of Mormon The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Return to John 13:34-35 , where Jesus teaches His disciples to love one another. Consider how that teaching might shape a conversation with someone who disagrees with you. Christian conduct and theological definitions are both worth examining. A kind encounter can help people understand one another while leaving room to discuss real doctrinal differences. Study the Question Through Scripture Explore and study Learn from Christ, then practice His teaching Jesus Christ teaches two attentive disciples. His commandment to love one another places recognizable Christian discipleship in the patience, honesty and charity shown across differences in belief. John 13:34-35 The word Christian can name a commitment to Jesus Christ, membership in a historical tradition, or agreement with a creed. Those meanings overlap, but they are not identical. The readings below help separate the questions: Who is Jesus? How does salvation come through Him? What does following Him ask of us? Read the passages before drawing a conclusion about a community. Begin with the death and Resurrection of Jesus 1 Corinthians 15:1-8, 12-22 records Paul teaching the Corinthians about Christ dying for sins, being buried, rising again, and appearing to witnesses. He then explains why resurrection is essential to Christian hope. This is foundational to the Latter-day Saint confession of Christ as Savior, and to the faith of many other Christians. Ask what would be lost from the gospel Paul describes if Christ were only a moral teacher. Explore and study Grace that leads to discipleship A hand rests beside an open Bible and handwritten notes, lingering over Paul's promise of grace. The gift comes through Jesus Christ, and the life that follows is shaped by love and good works. Read Ephesians 2 Read what Latter-day Saint scripture says about salvation 2 Nephi 31:13-21 describes repentance, baptism, receiving the Holy Ghost, and continuing with faith, hope, and love. Its conclusion places salvation in the name of Christ. This passage helps explain why Latter-day Saints connect discipleship and ordinances to dependence on the Savior. It is a statement of their scriptural belief, not a demand that a visitor already accept the Book of Mormon. Consider grace and the life of a disciple together Read Ephesians 2:8-10 alongside James 2:14-18 . Paul describes salvation as God's gift and then speaks of a life of good works. James asks what faith means when a person in need is left without help. These passages should not be reduced to a contest between grace and kindness. They invite careful study of how trust in Christ shapes action. Christian traditions differ in how they explain faith, sacraments, works, and justification; this brief comparison does not resolve all of those differences. Look closely at the Father and the Son In John 17:1-5, 20-23 , Jesus prays to the Father and asks for unity among His disciples. Latter-day Saints read this in harmony with their belief in distinct members of the Godhead united perfectly. Nicene Christians also recognize the distinction of Father and Son, while affirming one divine being. The disagreement is not whether Jesus prayed to the Father, but how the whole scriptural witness is understood. Read each tradition's explanation on its own terms rather than expecting this chapter alone to settle the question. Questions Worth Taking Time With Explore and study Bring your question into the light Beside a sunlit window, a woman studies with her book and notebook open. She gives the question time, trusting that honest understanding begins by listening carefully and seeking truth in the light. Read Articles of Faith Does Christian identity mean all beliefs are the same? No. Acknowledging that Latter-day Saints identify as followers of Jesus does not erase disagreements about God, authority, scripture, or salvation. You can describe their self-understanding accurately while also explaining why your own tradition reaches a different theological judgment. Why does additional scripture matter to this discussion? The question involves authority as well as belief in Jesus. Latter-day Saints receive the Bible and additional scripture, while many other Christians do not accept those additional books as authoritative. The Book of Mormon study explains the book's claims, content, and invitation to read, so you can consider that question directly. What could I reflect on after reading? Write down one belief you understand more clearly, one difference you want to examine fairly, and one question you would ask a friend without trying to win an argument. Distinguish what a source actually says from what you previously heard about it. Explore and study Listen while discussing belief Three friends gather around an open Bible and listen without interrupting. Their patience shows how Christ's command to love one another can guide even a difficult conversation about belief. Read John 13 1. Make the question specific Ask your conversation partner whether they want to understand Latter-day Saint worship, compare beliefs about God, or discuss the authority of scripture. Choose one question for this conversation. Give each other time to state a belief before evaluating it. Try writing a sentence beginning, “What I understand you to believe is...” Invite a correction. This simple practice can reveal that two people have been answering different questions while using the same religious vocabulary. 2. Read a confession in its own words Open the Articles of Faith linked above. For each statement you discuss, distinguish the wording from your interpretation of it. Ask which words carry a different meaning in your own tradition. Follow the sources in the section on creeds to explore the theological difference more carefully. You can acknowledge a real disagreement and still describe the other person's conviction accurately. A conversation becomes more useful when a participant recognizes their own belief in your account of it. 3. Let conscience and care shape the exchange Article of Faith 11 affirms religious liberty for others as well as for Latter-day Saints. As a personal application, give your partner freedom to reach a conclusion without demanding a profession of agreement. Consider a way to practice the love taught in John 13 after the conversation: remember a concern they shared, offer help they would welcome, or simply keep the friendship open. Respectful conduct matters whether the theological discussion ends in agreement or remains unresolved. How can I explain my conviction without turning it into an argument? Describe what you believe about Jesus, identify a source that helps explain it, and speak honestly about why it matters to you. Ask whether your friend wants to share their own understanding. The study of Latter-day Saint beliefs about Jesus Christ can help you move from a label to specific teachings. records.title: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.pageTitle: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.keywords: bible and book of mormon together
records.text: Answers / Scripture Latter-day Saints read the Bible and Book of Mormon as distinct records that testify together of Jesus Christ. The point is not that one book makes the other unnecessary, but that multiple scriptural witnesses can deepen understanding of the same Savior and gospel. Explore the histories through the prophets’ experiences, then choose a paired reading. Tap a picture to study its passages or see the full scene. Watch and study Why Read Two Witnesses of Jesus Christ? In the short message Bible and Book of Mormon , Elder Russell M. Nelson discusses both books as witnesses of Jesus Christ. Listen for what a second witness contributes, then choose a pair of passages you can actually read and compare. Church video Bible and Book of Mormon The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Begin with John 20:1-18 . The account moves from an empty tomb to Mary Magdalene recognizing Jesus when He addresses her. Her encounter leads to her report to the disciples. Record one detail from this particular witness before turning to the Book of Mormon account. A comparison becomes clearer when you first understand each text on its own. The Bible’s history and witness Words preserved across generations Begin with two scenes the Book of Mormon invites us to revisit: Isaiah’s call and Moses’ raised serpent. They show how later prophets return to earlier scripture. Explore and study Isaiah answers the call In Isaiah’s vision, a seraph brings a live coal to his lips. After the assurance that his sin is purged, Isaiah offers himself for the Lord’s work. Isaiah 6:5–8 2 Nephi 16:5–8 A directly preserved prophetic vision The same commissioning vision in both records Second Nephi preserves Isaiah’s account of his call. Read the movement from awareness of unclean lips to cleansing and willingness to serve. This is a direct textual connection, rather than two prophets having the same vision. The picture focuses on the coal and Isaiah’s response; the fuller chapter describes the seraphim and the Lord’s glory. A library of sacred writings The Bible took shape across centuries. The Old Testament preserves Israel’s law, history, poetry, wisdom and prophecy, chiefly in Hebrew with some Aramaic. The New Testament’s Gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation come from the early Christian world and survive in Greek. They witness of Jesus Christ and the life of His Church. Explore the Bible’s history . Isaiah is one prophetic voice within that larger library. His words also became part of the record Nephi preserved. Explore and study Moses raises the brass serpent In the wilderness, the people are invited to look toward the serpent Moses has raised. Alma later recalls this act as a witness pointing to the Son of God. Numbers 21:6–9 Alma 33:19–22 John 3:14–15 An event recalled and interpreted An earlier event becomes a witness of Christ Numbers records the danger among Israel and the command to look and live. Alma explicitly recalls Moses and interprets the raised sign in relation to belief in the Son of God. John also preserves Jesus’ comparison with Moses’ act. Follow the connection from the wilderness event to its later explanations; the bronze serpent itself is not the Savior. How biblical writings reached later readers Texts were copied by hand before printing. The fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus contains the earliest complete surviving Christian New Testament; it is a later witness to the text, not an Apostle’s original manuscript. Explore Codex Sinaiticus . Wycliffe-associated English translations drew on Latin. Tyndale’s printed New Testament appeared in 1526; the King James Version followed in 1611. Translation brought the writings into readers’ own language. Read the history of the English Bible . The Book of Mormon’s history and witness Reading, preserving and bringing forth a record Follow the ancient narrative within the book, then the nineteenth-century account of its coming forth. Latter-day Saints receive the ancient account as scripture; surviving manuscripts also document the later translation and publication. Explore and study Nephi reads Isaiah to his brothers Nephi turns to the writings on the brass plates and reads Isaiah to his brothers, seeking to help them believe in the Lord their Redeemer. 1 Nephi 19:22–24 1 Nephi 20 Isaiah 48 An explicit reading and a quoted chapter The Book of Mormon invites us back into Isaiah Nephi names his source and explains why he reads it: to persuade his people to believe in the Redeemer and apply scripture to their lives. The following chapter preserves material corresponding to Isaiah’s words to the house of Israel. Read the two chapters closely, noting differences as well as shared language. The act of reading is explicit; the exact room and arrangement of the gathering are not. A scriptural heritage from Jerusalem The Book of Mormon’s narrative begins with Lehi’s family around 600 BC. The brass plates contain the books of Moses, prophetic writings, a record of the Jews and a genealogy, as described in 1 Nephi 5:10–16 . They connect the family to Israel’s scripture; they are not a complete modern Bible. Explore and study Alma keeps Abinadi’s words After escaping the king’s servants, young Alma writes the testimony he has heard. Abinadi’s teaching includes Isaiah’s prophecy of the suffering servant. Mosiah 17:2–4 Mosiah 14 Isaiah 53 Direct quotation within a preserved testimony Isaiah’s words are quoted, heard and preserved Mosiah presents Abinadi quoting Isaiah before explaining Christ’s redeeming work. Alma believes, speaks in Abinadi’s defense, flees and records his words while concealed. This passage connects biblical prophecy with a Book of Mormon witness and shows why preservation matters. The young man here is Alma the Elder, not his son Alma the Younger. From individual records to an abridgment Preservation continues across generations. Words of Mormon 1:1–11 describes Mormon selecting and joining records. Mormon 8:1–5 presents Moroni continuing after his father’s death. Distinct voices remain within the larger book. Explore and study Moroni brings Malachi’s words to Joseph In his account of the 1823 visit, Joseph remembers Moroni speaking of an ancient record and quoting biblical prophecies, including Malachi. The coming forth of the Book of Mormon is introduced within that scriptural setting. Joseph Smith—History 1:30–39 Malachi 3 Malachi 4:5–6 A reported biblical quotation in Restoration history An ancient prophet in the Restoration’s beginning This is Joseph’s later account of Moroni’s visit, recorded in the Pearl of Great Price. He reports that Moroni quoted Malachi and gave different wording for part of the Elijah prophecy. Compare the passages rather than calling them identical. The scene belongs to the 1823 bedroom visit, when Joseph was seventeen, not the 1827 delivery of the plates. 1829–1830: translation and publication Joseph Smith dictated most of the surviving text between April and June 1829. He described translating by God’s gift and power. Witness accounts discuss interpreters and a seer stone, including use of a hat to exclude light. The Church’s translation essay presents those accounts. A printer’s manuscript was prepared, and E. B. Grandin’s Palmyra shop printed the first edition. It went on sale March 26, 1830. Explore the Joseph Smith Papers’ manuscript history . These publication records are distinct from the ancient history narrated within the book. How the records work together Joined witnesses, distinct voices A quotation, a remembered event and an interpretation make different kinds of connections. These three scenes help us recognize the difference. Explore and study Ezekiel brings two sticks together Ezekiel holds the two pieces together before his people. The sign belongs to a promise that divided Israel will be gathered and become one under the Lord. Ezekiel 37:15–23 2 Nephi 3:12 A sign and a Latter-day Saint interpretation One people and joined witnesses Ezekiel explains the joining of Judah and Joseph as the reunion of a divided people. Latter-day Saints also understand the sign in connection with the Bible and Book of Mormon, as reflected in the Church’s chapter heading and cross-references. Lehi’s account speaks of writings from Joseph’s and Judah’s descendants growing together. This is an interpretive pairing; it does not mean Ezekiel names the Book of Mormon or quotes Lehi. Articles of Faith 1:8 affirms both books. Their shared witness of Jesus Christ invites readers to keep both open, while respecting each passage’s own speaker and setting. Explore and study Lehi counsels his son Joseph Near the end of his life, Lehi speaks to his youngest son about Joseph in Egypt and the Lord’s covenants. The family’s future is placed within a much older story. 2 Nephi 3:1–15 2 Nephi 3:22–25 Genesis 50:24–25 An ancestor’s covenant and additional recorded prophecy A covenant remembered across generations Genesis preserves Joseph’s assurance that God will visit his people and bring them to the promised land. Lehi identifies himself as Joseph’s descendant and attributes a longer prophecy to that ancestor, including future writings and a seer. That longer prophecy is supplied by the Book of Mormon; it is not the wording of the Genesis verses. The boy in the picture is Lehi’s son Joseph, distinct from Joseph in Egypt and Joseph Smith. Shared teachings about faith, repentance, baptism, resurrection and charity can bring one passage into conversation with another. A connection should help us notice what each writer contributes. Explore and study Mosiah interprets the engraved stone A large stone bearing engravings is brought to Mosiah. Omni says its account concerns Coriantumr and a people whose ancestors came from the tower when languages were confounded. Omni 1:20–22 Genesis 11:1–9 A shared narrative reference A record that reaches back to the tower Genesis tells of Babel and the confusion of language. Omni describes a stone record that connects an earlier people with that event. The relationship is a shared narrative reference, not a quotation of Genesis. This Mosiah is Benjamin’s father, often called Mosiah I, not Benjamin’s son of the same name. The picture illustrates the account; it does not present an identified archaeological artifact. For your own comparison, name the speaker, audience and setting before drawing a conclusion. Read the surrounding verses and keep questions that the passages leave unanswered. The Savior at the heart of both books His actions and His words illuminate one another Read five moments from Christ’s mortal ministry alongside Book of Mormon prophecy and teaching. Each pair invites us to understand Him more fully while keeping the events and speakers clear. Explore and study Christ opens Isaiah in Nazareth Standing in the synagogue, Jesus reads Isaiah’s words about good news, healing and deliverance. He then declares the scripture fulfilled in His listeners’ hearing. Luke 4:16–21 3 Nephi 23:1–5 Isaiah 61:1–2 Christ’s shared invitation to hear Isaiah Isaiah’s witness matters in both records Luke presents Jesus reading Isaiah and identifying His mission with the prophecy. In Third Nephi, Christ directs His hearers to search Isaiah’s words diligently. These are different occasions: Third Nephi does not repeat the Isaiah 61 quotation recorded in Luke. Read them together to consider why Christ turns His listeners toward the prophets and how their words help us recognize His work. Explore and study Christ answers temptation with scripture Hungry after His fast, Jesus refuses the temptation to turn stones into bread. He answers with the words of Moses, trusting the Father rather than yielding. Matthew 4:1–4 Mosiah 15:5 Deuteronomy 8:3 A Gospel event and Abinadi’s teaching Tempted, yet faithful to the Father Matthew records a particular temptation and Jesus’ answer from Deuteronomy. Abinadi teaches that Christ suffers temptation without yielding to it. The Gospel event gives us a moment to consider beside that prophetic teaching. Mosiah does not narrate this wilderness encounter. Notice both the Savior’s hunger and His resolve, then consider how scripture can guide a difficult choice. Explore and study A man is lowered through the roof Unable to reach Jesus through the crowd, four people open the roof and lower the bed carrying a man who cannot walk. Jesus receives him, speaks forgiveness and commands him to rise. Mark 2:1–12 Mosiah 3:5 A prophetic description and a Gospel encounter Benjamin’s prophecy beside a healing in Capernaum Benjamin describes the Lord coming among people with power to heal, including enabling the lame to walk. Mark gives a particular account of Christ’s healing and authority to forgive sins. Benjamin’s words are a prophetic description, not a second telling of this roof-top event. Read both passages, attending to the man’s need, his helpers’ faith and the Savior’s response. Explore and study Christ answers in the grainfield As His disciples pluck ears of grain, Jesus answers a question about the Sabbath. He recalls David’s experience and teaches His authority as Lord of the Sabbath. Mark 2:23–28 3 Nephi 15:2–10 Related teaching in distinct settings The Lord who gave and fulfilled the law The grainfield conversation concerns the Sabbath and Christ’s authority. After His Resurrection, Third Nephi records Him explaining that He gave the law of Moses and fulfilled it. These passages belong to different moments in His ministry. The grainfield dispute does not itself end the law; the later explanation helps readers consider the law in relation to the Savior who gave it. Explore and study Mercy in the moment of arrest During His arrest, Jesus touches and heals the servant’s right ear. Amid fear and confrontation, His response is an act of mercy. Luke 22:47–51 John 18:10 3 Nephi 12:43–45 Christ’s action beside His teaching Love for enemies, taught and lived Luke records the healing; John identifies the servant as Malchus and the disciple with the sword as Peter. Third Nephi records Christ’s teaching to love enemies and pray for those who persecute. Malchus does not appear in the Book of Mormon. Reading the teaching beside this Gospel action lets us consider what mercy looks like when a person faces hostility. Choose a paired reading Twelve paths between the books Choose a topic to reveal the two passages and a question to carry into your reading. The suffering servant Direct quotation Isaiah 53 Mosiah 14 Abinadi quotes Isaiah; read his surrounding explanation in the next chapter to see how he applies the prophecy to Christ. Malachi’s message Direct quotation Malachi 3 3 Nephi 24 Third Nephi presents Jesus giving Malachi’s words to His listeners. Notice the account’s instruction to record them. Other sheep Explicit connection John 10:14–16 3 Nephi 15:16–24 Third Nephi explicitly connects its people with Jesus’ statement about other sheep. That identification is supplied by the Book of Mormon; John’s passage alone does not name the Americas. Records and gathering Latter-day Saint reading Ezekiel 37:15–23 2 Nephi 3:12 Ezekiel’s immediate explanation concerns Judah and Joseph becoming one people. Latter-day Saints also connect the joined sticks with joined scriptural witnesses; Second Nephi speaks of writings growing together. Keep the original national-gathering context visible. The Beatitudes Parallel teaching Matthew 5:1–12 3 Nephi 12:1–12 Compare the promises to the meek, merciful and peacemakers. Notice the different openings and the post-Resurrection setting in Third Nephi. Following Christ in baptism Account and explanation Matthew 3:13–17 2 Nephi 31:4–12 Matthew records Jesus’ baptism. Nephi reflects on why the Holy One was baptized and what His example asks of His followers. The pattern of prayer Parallel teaching Matthew 6:9–13 3 Nephi 13:9–13 Read the prayers closely, including wording that differs. Both direct disciples toward the Father, His will, forgiveness and deliverance. Bread and remembrance Distinct covenant settings Luke 22:19–20 3 Nephi 18:1–11 Follow the movement from Christ’s body and covenant to remembrance, obedience and the companionship of His Spirit. Welcoming children Distinct encounters Mark 10:13–16 3 Nephi 17:21–24 Mark preserves His welcome and blessing; Third Nephi describes His personal blessing, prayer and tears. Neither account needs to erase the other’s details. The Resurrection Shared doctrine 1 Corinthians 15:20–22 Alma 11:42–45 Paul connects resurrection with Christ. Amulek explains the reunion of body and spirit and judgment before God. Distinguish resurrection from the further question of how we live before Him. Charity Closely related teaching 1 Corinthians 13:4–8 Moroni 7:45–48 Compare the descriptions of charity, then notice Moroni’s preservation of Mormon’s invitation to pray for this love. The shared wording is a textual observation, not by itself proof of a historical relationship. Blessing all families Covenant connection Genesis 12:1–3 3 Nephi 20:25–27 Read the promise to Abraham beside Christ’s teaching about the covenant’s children. Both place blessing beyond one household; Third Nephi connects blessing with turning from iniquity. How cross-references became easier to follow The Church’s 1979 English Bible and 1981 triple combination added expanded cross-references and study helps. These editorial tools help readers move among the standard works; they are distinct from the ancient text. Explore the scripture editions . Watch and study Does Additional Scripture Diminish the Bible? Explore and study Consider the witness at Bountiful At Bountiful, Jesus Christ teaches people who have come forward to know Him. His words stand beside the New Testament witness, joining both records in testimony of the risen Savior. Read 3 Nephi 11 In his April 2008 conference message My Words ... Then turn to 3 Nephi 11:10-17 . Compare this encounter with Mary's witness in John 20 . Keep the question of scriptural authority distinct from your observations about the two texts, and preserve any unresolved questions for further study. A Guided Comparison: Grace and Discipleship Explore and study Compare the accounts with care Two open books rest side by side, each bearing its own witness of the risen Jesus Christ. John and Third Nephi lead readers toward the same hope: to know the Savior and believe in Him. John 20:30-31 3 Nephi 11:10-17 Begin with Ephesians 2:8-10 and 2 Nephi 31:19-21 . Read the surrounding paragraphs rather than extracting a single phrase. Paul emphasizes salvation as a gift and speaks of good works; Nephi directs continuing disciples to rely on Christ while living with hope and love. Keep two columns in a notebook: what this passage says, and what I infer from it. Ask what each writer emphasizes and what problem or invitation the passage addresses. The two accounts do not need to use identical vocabulary to be compared thoughtfully. Where their wording raises a question, preserve the question instead of forcing a quick agreement. Explore and study Read first, then compare A woman compares two open books and records notes at a library desk. Ephesians joins salvation by grace with a life created in Christ Jesus for good works. Read Ephesians 2 Let the next passage answer a real question If you wonder what faith looks like in daily life, James 2:14-18 examines the response to a person without adequate food or clothing. As a reflection, consider whether your study is changing how you notice other people. That application grows from the passage's example; it is not a measure by which to judge someone else's private faith. What if I accept the Bible but am unsure about the Book of Mormon? You can compare the texts without pretending the question of authority is settled. Read each as it presents itself, identify shared and differing teachings, and then investigate the reasons Latter-day Saints accept the additional record. Respectful study leaves room for a reader to reach their own conclusion. Three Study Sessions That Keep Both Books Open Explore and study Discover what another reader sees On a park bench, an older woman and a younger man compare what they have read. Each book adds another witness, and their conversation keeps returning to Jesus Christ. 2 Nephi 29:7-8 These focusChrist study suggestions offer a way to explore the sources at your own pace. Explore and study Let charity guide the conversation A man repairs a wooden gate while an older woman steadies the tools. Working side by side, they show the patient, practical kindness Paul describes as charity. Read 1 Corinthians 13 Session 1: Scripture opens understanding Read Luke 24:13-35 . On the road to Emmaus, two disciples describe their disappointed hopes. Jesus interprets scripture concerning Himself, and they later recognize Him as He breaks bread. Then read 3 Nephi 17:1-3 , where listeners are given time to ponder and pray for understanding. Compare the role of scripture, conversation, reflection, and time. Write one question that would benefit from a slower second reading. Session 2: Love gives study a direction Read 1 Corinthians 13:1-13 and Moroni 7:43-48 . Both describe charity through qualities such as patience and kindness. Paul weighs spiritual gifts and knowledge against love; Mormon's teaching, recorded by Moroni, invites prayer to be filled with Christ's love. Choose one quality to practice during a real interaction. Afterwards, record what was difficult and what you want to learn. Allow the passages to question your habits as well as inform your beliefs. Session 3: Review without forcing a conclusion Look back over your notes. Name a teaching both passages emphasize, a detail that belongs to only one account, and a question you still cannot answer. Read the verses around that question before searching for another cross-reference. If studying with someone from another Christian tradition, ask which text they would add and why. You can learn from their reasoning while being clear about which books each of you accepts as scripture. The aim of this session is careful understanding and an honest next question. He opens the scriptures along the way Jesus walks with two disciples and explains the scriptures concerning Himself. Return to their conversation slowly, and notice how understanding grows before recognition. Luke 24:13–32 Does a shared teaching establish the authority of both books? A textual comparison can show a shared teaching. Deciding that a book is divinely authoritative involves further questions. Keep those questions visible as you study. The Book of Mormon introduction discusses the invitation to read, ponder, and pray, alongside the need to distinguish historical and spiritual inquiries. Let two witnesses shape one act of discipleship 1 Corinthians 13 invites a reader to weigh knowledge and spiritual gifts alongside charity. Return to the comparison you have made and consider how learning about Christ might change a real conversation. What did each witness help you notice? Choose one passage from each book already studied above. Write one sentence about what each says of Jesus Christ. Which detail would have been missing if you had read only one? Keep each speaker and setting beside your notes. How will charity shape the discussion? Think of someone who understands these books differently. What could you ask to understand their reading before explaining yours? Choose one quality from Paul’s description of charity to practice when a question becomes difficult. What will you return to? Save a pair of passages and one unresolved question. Read the surrounding chapters on your next visit. What new context would cause you to revise your first impression? A patient second reading can become part of your worship. records.title: Why Read Two Witnesses of Jesus Christ?
records.pageTitle: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.text: Watch and study Why Read Two Witnesses of Jesus Christ? In the short message Bible and Book of Mormon , Elder Russell M. Nelson discusses both books as witnesses of Jesus Christ. Listen for what a second witness contributes, then choose a pair of passages you can actually read and compare. Church video Bible and Book of Mormon The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Begin with John 20:1-18 . The account moves from an empty tomb to Mary Magdalene recognizing Jesus when He addresses her. Her encounter leads to her report to the disciples. Record one detail from this particular witness before turning to the Book of Mormon account. A comparison becomes clearer when you first understand each text on its own.

records.title: Words preserved across generations
records.pageTitle: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.text: The Bible’s history and witness Words preserved across generations Begin with two scenes the Book of Mormon invites us to revisit: Isaiah’s call and Moses’ raised serpent. They show how later prophets return to earlier scripture. Explore and study Isaiah answers the call In Isaiah’s vision, a seraph brings a live coal to his lips. After the assurance that his sin is purged, Isaiah offers himself for the Lord’s work. Isaiah 6:5–8 2 Nephi 16:5–8 A directly preserved prophetic vision The same commissioning vision in both records Second Nephi preserves Isaiah’s account of his call. Read the movement from awareness of unclean lips to cleansing and willingness to serve. This is a direct textual connection, rather than two prophets having the same vision. The picture focuses on the coal and Isaiah’s response; the fuller chapter describes the seraphim and the Lord’s glory. A library of sacred writings The Bible took shape across centuries. The Old Testament preserves Israel’s law, history, poetry, wisdom and prophecy, chiefly in Hebrew with some Aramaic. The New Testament’s Gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation come from the early Christian world and survive in Greek. They witness of Jesus Christ and the life of His Church. Explore the Bible’s history . Isaiah is one prophetic voice within that larger library. His words also became part of the record Nephi preserved. Explore and study Moses raises the brass serpent In the wilderness, the people are invited to look toward the serpent Moses has raised. Alma later recalls this act as a witness pointing to the Son of God. Numbers 21:6–9 Alma 33:19–22 John 3:14–15 An event recalled and interpreted An earlier event becomes a witness of Christ Numbers records the danger among Israel and the command to look and live. Alma explicitly recalls Moses and interprets the raised sign in relation to belief in the Son of God. John also preserves Jesus’ comparison with Moses’ act. Follow the connection from the wilderness event to its later explanations; the bronze serpent itself is not the Savior. How biblical writings reached later readers Texts were copied by hand before printing. The fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus contains the earliest complete surviving Christian New Testament; it is a later witness to the text, not an Apostle’s original manuscript. Explore Codex Sinaiticus . Wycliffe-associated English translations drew on Latin. Tyndale’s printed New Testament appeared in 1526; the King James Version followed in 1611. Translation brought the writings into readers’ own language. Read the history of the English Bible .

records.title: Reading, preserving and bringing forth a record
records.pageTitle: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.text: The Book of Mormon’s history and witness Reading, preserving and bringing forth a record Follow the ancient narrative within the book, then the nineteenth-century account of its coming forth. Latter-day Saints receive the ancient account as scripture; surviving manuscripts also document the later translation and publication. Explore and study Nephi reads Isaiah to his brothers Nephi turns to the writings on the brass plates and reads Isaiah to his brothers, seeking to help them believe in the Lord their Redeemer. 1 Nephi 19:22–24 1 Nephi 20 Isaiah 48 An explicit reading and a quoted chapter The Book of Mormon invites us back into Isaiah Nephi names his source and explains why he reads it: to persuade his people to believe in the Redeemer and apply scripture to their lives. The following chapter preserves material corresponding to Isaiah’s words to the house of Israel. Read the two chapters closely, noting differences as well as shared language. The act of reading is explicit; the exact room and arrangement of the gathering are not. A scriptural heritage from Jerusalem The Book of Mormon’s narrative begins with Lehi’s family around 600 BC. The brass plates contain the books of Moses, prophetic writings, a record of the Jews and a genealogy, as described in 1 Nephi 5:10–16 . They connect the family to Israel’s scripture; they are not a complete modern Bible. Explore and study Alma keeps Abinadi’s words After escaping the king’s servants, young Alma writes the testimony he has heard. Abinadi’s teaching includes Isaiah’s prophecy of the suffering servant. Mosiah 17:2–4 Mosiah 14 Isaiah 53 Direct quotation within a preserved testimony Isaiah’s words are quoted, heard and preserved Mosiah presents Abinadi quoting Isaiah before explaining Christ’s redeeming work. Alma believes, speaks in Abinadi’s defense, flees and records his words while concealed. This passage connects biblical prophecy with a Book of Mormon witness and shows why preservation matters. The young man here is Alma the Elder, not his son Alma the Younger. From individual records to an abridgment Preservation continues across generations. Words of Mormon 1:1–11 describes Mormon selecting and joining records. Mormon 8:1–5 presents Moroni continuing after his father’s death. Distinct voices remain within the larger book. Explore and study Moroni brings Malachi’s words to Joseph In his account of the 1823 visit, Joseph remembers Moroni speaking of an ancient record and quoting biblical prophecies, including Malachi. The coming forth of the Book of Mormon is introduced within that scriptural setting. Joseph Smith—History 1:30–39 Malachi 3 Malachi 4:5–6 A reported biblical quotation in Restoration history An ancient prophet in the Restoration’s beginning This is Joseph’s later account of Moroni’s visit, recorded in the Pearl of Great Price. He reports that Moroni quoted Malachi and gave different wording for part of the Elijah prophecy. Compare the passages rather than calling them identical. The scene belongs to the 1823 bedroom visit, when Joseph was seventeen, not the 1827 delivery of the plates. 1829–1830: translation and publication Joseph Smith dictated most of the surviving text between April and June 1829. He described translating by God’s gift and power. Witness accounts discuss interpreters and a seer stone, including use of a hat to exclude light. The Church’s translation essay presents those accounts. A printer’s manuscript was prepared, and E. B. Grandin’s Palmyra shop printed the first edition. It went on sale March 26, 1830. Explore the Joseph Smith Papers’ manuscript history . These publication records are distinct from the ancient history narrated within the book.

records.title: Joined witnesses, distinct voices
records.pageTitle: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.text: How the records work together Joined witnesses, distinct voices A quotation, a remembered event and an interpretation make different kinds of connections. These three scenes help us recognize the difference. Explore and study Ezekiel brings two sticks together Ezekiel holds the two pieces together before his people. The sign belongs to a promise that divided Israel will be gathered and become one under the Lord. Ezekiel 37:15–23 2 Nephi 3:12 A sign and a Latter-day Saint interpretation One people and joined witnesses Ezekiel explains the joining of Judah and Joseph as the reunion of a divided people. Latter-day Saints also understand the sign in connection with the Bible and Book of Mormon, as reflected in the Church’s chapter heading and cross-references. Lehi’s account speaks of writings from Joseph’s and Judah’s descendants growing together. This is an interpretive pairing; it does not mean Ezekiel names the Book of Mormon or quotes Lehi. Articles of Faith 1:8 affirms both books. Their shared witness of Jesus Christ invites readers to keep both open, while respecting each passage’s own speaker and setting. Explore and study Lehi counsels his son Joseph Near the end of his life, Lehi speaks to his youngest son about Joseph in Egypt and the Lord’s covenants. The family’s future is placed within a much older story. 2 Nephi 3:1–15 2 Nephi 3:22–25 Genesis 50:24–25 An ancestor’s covenant and additional recorded prophecy A covenant remembered across generations Genesis preserves Joseph’s assurance that God will visit his people and bring them to the promised land. Lehi identifies himself as Joseph’s descendant and attributes a longer prophecy to that ancestor, including future writings and a seer. That longer prophecy is supplied by the Book of Mormon; it is not the wording of the Genesis verses. The boy in the picture is Lehi’s son Joseph, distinct from Joseph in Egypt and Joseph Smith. Shared teachings about faith, repentance, baptism, resurrection and charity can bring one passage into conversation with another. A connection should help us notice what each writer contributes. Explore and study Mosiah interprets the engraved stone A large stone bearing engravings is brought to Mosiah. Omni says its account concerns Coriantumr and a people whose ancestors came from the tower when languages were confounded. Omni 1:20–22 Genesis 11:1–9 A shared narrative reference A record that reaches back to the tower Genesis tells of Babel and the confusion of language. Omni describes a stone record that connects an earlier people with that event. The relationship is a shared narrative reference, not a quotation of Genesis. This Mosiah is Benjamin’s father, often called Mosiah I, not Benjamin’s son of the same name. The picture illustrates the account; it does not present an identified archaeological artifact. For your own comparison, name the speaker, audience and setting before drawing a conclusion. Read the surrounding verses and keep questions that the passages leave unanswered.

records.title: His actions and His words illuminate one another
records.pageTitle: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.text: The Savior at the heart of both books His actions and His words illuminate one another Read five moments from Christ’s mortal ministry alongside Book of Mormon prophecy and teaching. Each pair invites us to understand Him more fully while keeping the events and speakers clear. Explore and study Christ opens Isaiah in Nazareth Standing in the synagogue, Jesus reads Isaiah’s words about good news, healing and deliverance. He then declares the scripture fulfilled in His listeners’ hearing. Luke 4:16–21 3 Nephi 23:1–5 Isaiah 61:1–2 Christ’s shared invitation to hear Isaiah Isaiah’s witness matters in both records Luke presents Jesus reading Isaiah and identifying His mission with the prophecy. In Third Nephi, Christ directs His hearers to search Isaiah’s words diligently. These are different occasions: Third Nephi does not repeat the Isaiah 61 quotation recorded in Luke. Read them together to consider why Christ turns His listeners toward the prophets and how their words help us recognize His work. Explore and study Christ answers temptation with scripture Hungry after His fast, Jesus refuses the temptation to turn stones into bread. He answers with the words of Moses, trusting the Father rather than yielding. Matthew 4:1–4 Mosiah 15:5 Deuteronomy 8:3 A Gospel event and Abinadi’s teaching Tempted, yet faithful to the Father Matthew records a particular temptation and Jesus’ answer from Deuteronomy. Abinadi teaches that Christ suffers temptation without yielding to it. The Gospel event gives us a moment to consider beside that prophetic teaching. Mosiah does not narrate this wilderness encounter. Notice both the Savior’s hunger and His resolve, then consider how scripture can guide a difficult choice. Explore and study A man is lowered through the roof Unable to reach Jesus through the crowd, four people open the roof and lower the bed carrying a man who cannot walk. Jesus receives him, speaks forgiveness and commands him to rise. Mark 2:1–12 Mosiah 3:5 A prophetic description and a Gospel encounter Benjamin’s prophecy beside a healing in Capernaum Benjamin describes the Lord coming among people with power to heal, including enabling the lame to walk. Mark gives a particular account of Christ’s healing and authority to forgive sins. Benjamin’s words are a prophetic description, not a second telling of this roof-top event. Read both passages, attending to the man’s need, his helpers’ faith and the Savior’s response. Explore and study Christ answers in the grainfield As His disciples pluck ears of grain, Jesus answers a question about the Sabbath. He recalls David’s experience and teaches His authority as Lord of the Sabbath. Mark 2:23–28 3 Nephi 15:2–10 Related teaching in distinct settings The Lord who gave and fulfilled the law The grainfield conversation concerns the Sabbath and Christ’s authority. After His Resurrection, Third Nephi records Him explaining that He gave the law of Moses and fulfilled it. These passages belong to different moments in His ministry. The grainfield dispute does not itself end the law; the later explanation helps readers consider the law in relation to the Savior who gave it. Explore and study Mercy in the moment of arrest During His arrest, Jesus touches and heals the servant’s right ear. Amid fear and confrontation, His response is an act of mercy. Luke 22:47–51 John 18:10 3 Nephi 12:43–45 Christ’s action beside His teaching Love for enemies, taught and lived Luke records the healing; John identifies the servant as Malchus and the disciple with the sword as Peter. Third Nephi records Christ’s teaching to love enemies and pray for those who persecute. Malchus does not appear in the Book of Mormon. Reading the teaching beside this Gospel action lets us consider what mercy looks like when a person faces hostility.

records.title: Twelve paths between the books
records.pageTitle: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.text: Choose a paired reading Twelve paths between the books Choose a topic to reveal the two passages and a question to carry into your reading. The suffering servant Direct quotation Isaiah 53 Mosiah 14 Abinadi quotes Isaiah; read his surrounding explanation in the next chapter to see how he applies the prophecy to Christ. Malachi’s message Direct quotation Malachi 3 3 Nephi 24 Third Nephi presents Jesus giving Malachi’s words to His listeners. Notice the account’s instruction to record them. Other sheep Explicit connection John 10:14–16 3 Nephi 15:16–24 Third Nephi explicitly connects its people with Jesus’ statement about other sheep. That identification is supplied by the Book of Mormon; John’s passage alone does not name the Americas. Records and gathering Latter-day Saint reading Ezekiel 37:15–23 2 Nephi 3:12 Ezekiel’s immediate explanation concerns Judah and Joseph becoming one people. Latter-day Saints also connect the joined sticks with joined scriptural witnesses; Second Nephi speaks of writings growing together. Keep the original national-gathering context visible. The Beatitudes Parallel teaching Matthew 5:1–12 3 Nephi 12:1–12 Compare the promises to the meek, merciful and peacemakers. Notice the different openings and the post-Resurrection setting in Third Nephi. Following Christ in baptism Account and explanation Matthew 3:13–17 2 Nephi 31:4–12 Matthew records Jesus’ baptism. Nephi reflects on why the Holy One was baptized and what His example asks of His followers. The pattern of prayer Parallel teaching Matthew 6:9–13 3 Nephi 13:9–13 Read the prayers closely, including wording that differs. Both direct disciples toward the Father, His will, forgiveness and deliverance. Bread and remembrance Distinct covenant settings Luke 22:19–20 3 Nephi 18:1–11 Follow the movement from Christ’s body and covenant to remembrance, obedience and the companionship of His Spirit. Welcoming children Distinct encounters Mark 10:13–16 3 Nephi 17:21–24 Mark preserves His welcome and blessing; Third Nephi describes His personal blessing, prayer and tears. Neither account needs to erase the other’s details. The Resurrection Shared doctrine 1 Corinthians 15:20–22 Alma 11:42–45 Paul connects resurrection with Christ. Amulek explains the reunion of body and spirit and judgment before God. Distinguish resurrection from the further question of how we live before Him. Charity Closely related teaching 1 Corinthians 13:4–8 Moroni 7:45–48 Compare the descriptions of charity, then notice Moroni’s preservation of Mormon’s invitation to pray for this love. The shared wording is a textual observation, not by itself proof of a historical relationship. Blessing all families Covenant connection Genesis 12:1–3 3 Nephi 20:25–27 Read the promise to Abraham beside Christ’s teaching about the covenant’s children. Both place blessing beyond one household; Third Nephi connects blessing with turning from iniquity. How cross-references became easier to follow The Church’s 1979 English Bible and 1981 triple combination added expanded cross-references and study helps. These editorial tools help readers move among the standard works; they are distinct from the ancient text. Explore the scripture editions .

records.pageTitle: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.text: Explore and study Compare the accounts with care Two open books rest side by side, each bearing its own witness of the risen Jesus Christ. John and Third Nephi lead readers toward the same hope: to know the Savior and believe in Him. John 20:30-31 3 Nephi 11:10-17 Begin with Ephesians 2:8-10 and 2 Nephi 31:19-21 . Read the surrounding paragraphs rather than extracting a single phrase. Paul emphasizes salvation as a gift and speaks of good works; Nephi directs continuing disciples to rely on Christ while living with hope and love. Keep two columns in a notebook: what this passage says, and what I infer from it. Ask what each writer emphasizes and what problem or invitation the passage addresses. The two accounts do not need to use identical vocabulary to be compared thoughtfully. Where their wording raises a question, preserve the question instead of forcing a quick agreement. Explore and study Read first, then compare A woman compares two open books and records notes at a library desk. Ephesians joins salvation by grace with a life created in Christ Jesus for good works. Read Ephesians 2 Let the next passage answer a real question If you wonder what faith looks like in daily life, James 2:14-18 examines the response to a person without adequate food or clothing. As a reflection, consider whether your study is changing how you notice other people. That application grows from the passage's example; it is not a measure by which to judge someone else's private faith. What if I accept the Bible but am unsure about the Book of Mormon? You can compare the texts without pretending the question of authority is settled. Read each as it presents itself, identify shared and differing teachings, and then investigate the reasons Latter-day Saints accept the additional record. Respectful study leaves room for a reader to reach their own conclusion.

records.title: Three Study Sessions That Keep Both Books Open
records.pageTitle: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.text: Explore and study Discover what another reader sees On a park bench, an older woman and a younger man compare what they have read. Each book adds another witness, and their conversation keeps returning to Jesus Christ. 2 Nephi 29:7-8 These focusChrist study suggestions offer a way to explore the sources at your own pace. Explore and study Let charity guide the conversation A man repairs a wooden gate while an older woman steadies the tools. Working side by side, they show the patient, practical kindness Paul describes as charity. Read 1 Corinthians 13 Session 1: Scripture opens understanding Read Luke 24:13-35 . On the road to Emmaus, two disciples describe their disappointed hopes. Jesus interprets scripture concerning Himself, and they later recognize Him as He breaks bread. Then read 3 Nephi 17:1-3 , where listeners are given time to ponder and pray for understanding. Compare the role of scripture, conversation, reflection, and time. Write one question that would benefit from a slower second reading. Session 2: Love gives study a direction Read 1 Corinthians 13:1-13 and Moroni 7:43-48 . Both describe charity through qualities such as patience and kindness. Paul weighs spiritual gifts and knowledge against love; Mormon's teaching, recorded by Moroni, invites prayer to be filled with Christ's love. Choose one quality to practice during a real interaction. Afterwards, record what was difficult and what you want to learn. Allow the passages to question your habits as well as inform your beliefs. Session 3: Review without forcing a conclusion Look back over your notes. Name a teaching both passages emphasize, a detail that belongs to only one account, and a question you still cannot answer. Read the verses around that question before searching for another cross-reference. If studying with someone from another Christian tradition, ask which text they would add and why. You can learn from their reasoning while being clear about which books each of you accepts as scripture. The aim of this session is careful understanding and an honest next question. He opens the scriptures along the way Jesus walks with two disciples and explains the scriptures concerning Himself. Return to their conversation slowly, and notice how understanding grows before recognition. Luke 24:13–32 Does a shared teaching establish the authority of both books? A textual comparison can show a shared teaching. Deciding that a book is divinely authoritative involves further questions. Keep those questions visible as you study. The Book of Mormon introduction discusses the invitation to read, ponder, and pray, alongside the need to distinguish historical and spiritual inquiries.

records.title: Let two witnesses shape one act of discipleship
records.pageTitle: How Do the Bible and Book of Mormon Work Together?
records.text: 1 Corinthians 13 invites a reader to weigh knowledge and spiritual gifts alongside charity. Return to the comparison you have made and consider how learning about Christ might change a real conversation. What did each witness help you notice? Choose one passage from each book already studied above. Write one sentence about what each says of Jesus Christ. Which detail would have been missing if you had read only one? Keep each speaker and setting beside your notes. How will charity shape the discussion? Think of someone who understands these books differently. What could you ask to understand their reading before explaining yours? Choose one quality from Paul’s description of charity to practice when a question becomes difficult. What will you return to? Save a pair of passages and one unresolved question. Read the surrounding chapters on your next visit. What new context would cause you to revise your first impression? A patient second reading can become part of your worship.
