records.title: Finding Hope After the Death of a Child
records.pageTitle: Finding Hope After the Death of a Child
records.text: Answers / Death of a child If you are grieving a child, we are sorry for your loss. No short answer can hold everything your child means to you. Here you can read about the Savior's compassion and the scriptural promises concerning little children, with room for sorrow and questions that remain. Watch and study A Father Speaks About Losing a Child In Because I Live, Ye Shall Live Also , Elder Shayne M. Bowen speaks directly to parents who have lost a child. He describes the death of his infant son and his own sorrow, guilt, and eventual hope in Jesus Christ. The account includes details of the death. You can choose the transcript, skip those details, or leave the message for another day. General conference video and text Because I Live, Ye Shall Live Also The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2012 He also recalls teaching Moroni 8 to a mother grieving a child who died without baptism. Read that passage with the study below: the teaching about little children addresses Christ's mercy and salvation. It does not supply an explanation for your own child's death. Elder Bowen distinguishes his experience from what his wife felt and describes love that continued after loss. His account is one father's testimony. You do not need to experience the same feelings, draw the same personal conclusions, or follow the same course of grieving to be welcome here. This independent study draws on Latter-day Saint scripture. It does not claim to know why a particular child died or prescribe how a family should grieve. Explore and study Compassion for a grieving father The Savior stays close to a grieving father who still holds a beloved reminder of his child. Nothing in the moment rushes his sorrow; Christ meets him there with tenderness and hope. What Scripture Says About Little Children Moroni 8:8-12, 19 teaches that little children are alive in Christ through His mercy and do not need baptism or repentance. Their salvation is not lost because they died without baptism. Doctrine and Covenants 137:10 teaches that children who die before the age of accountability are saved in the celestial kingdom. The promise concerns their salvation; it does not explain why a child died or ask a family to feel less sorrow. When the Child You Lost Was Older A parent's love does not end at a particular birthday. If your child was a teenager or adult, the verses about little children do not directly answer every question you may have about their eternal future. Doctrine and Covenants 137:7-9 also teaches that God considers people's works and the desires of their hearts. You do not have to settle your child's eternal future yourself. These verses invite trust in God's judgment, which takes account of more than any of us can see. Christ's Compassion Is a Place to Begin Alma 7:11-13 describes the Savior bearing pains, sicknesses, and infirmities so He would know how to help His people. This teaching offers a foundation for turning toward Him with sorrow as well as trust. These promises need not become a demand to feel better immediately. You can bring a prayer of gratitude, a question, or simply the words that today is hard. You do not need to meet a timetable for grief or accept an explanation for the death that these scriptures do not give. For Someone Supporting the Family Consider asking what would help this week: a meal, an errand, quiet company, or space. Let the family lead when speaking about their child. Avoid making the death into a lesson they are expected to accept. Offer help you can follow through on, and ask before sharing their story with others. Explore and study Companionship in grief The Savior sits close to grieving parents and gathers them into His compassion. Their sorrow is neither hurried nor explained away; they are simply held and loved. When Hope and Tears Come Together In John 11:17-36 , Martha speaks to Jesus about her brother's death, and Jesus later weeps with those who are grieving. The account holds His promise of resurrection alongside real sorrow. As you read, notice that the people He loves are able to speak their hurt aloud. This story does not promise that a family's loss will be reversed in this life. It offers a way to think about compassion: being present with someone matters, even when you cannot explain what happened. Watch and study When a Sibling Is Grieving Too Explore and study Listen with patience Two women sit together in a garden after loss, one speaking while the other listens. Patient attention honors the different ways family members remember and grieve. Read John 11 In The Grave Has No Victory , Sister Reyna I. Aburto remembers losing her older brother in an earthquake when she was nine. She describes the questions and longing she carried and how she later understood her hope through Jesus Christ's Resurrection. Her message may be meaningful when a family is also trying to understand the sorrow of surviving siblings. General conference video and text The Grave Has No Victory The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2021 She places her memories alongside Mary Magdalene's grief and witness of the risen Savior. As you read, allow both parts of the message to stand: missing someone deeply and believing in resurrection. Her remembered experience does not prescribe what another child should imagine or feel. The Church's Grief and Loss guidance encourages listening and continued support. A surviving sibling may want to talk, remember quietly, or return to ordinary activities. Ask what would help, and seek qualified support when needed. Explore and study Listen to a child’s memories A boy holds a small wooden truck while a caring adult gives him her full attention. For a child grieving a sibling, patient company offers time to share a memory, ask a question, or sit quietly together. Grief and Loss Mosiah 18:8–9 A gentle invitation to remember If welcome, ask whether someone would like to share a memory, look at a photograph, or have quiet company. There is no required activity or public expression. Adults can make room for different responses without asking children to reassure them or explain the loss. Resources for the Days Ahead Grief and Loss : Church counseling guidance for people offering support. It encourages listening, respect for individual grieving, and continued care after the first days of loss. Mosiah 18:8-10 : a covenant to share burdens and mourn with others. A useful passage to read with someone who wants to help but does not know what to say. 1 Corinthians 15:20-22, 42-44 : Paul's teaching about resurrection through Christ, for a day when you want to study the hope behind this belief. A Gentle Study for Parents and Those Beside Them Let the passages answer their own questions The passages about little children above address salvation and Christ's mercy. The account of Lazarus addresses sorrow and the Savior's power over death. They do not explain the cause of a particular loss. Keeping those distinctions can protect a grieving family from explanations that scripture itself does not give. When two people grieve differently The companion artworks show both an individual father and parents together. As an invitation for reflection, consider that shared loss does not require identical words, feelings, or ways of remembering. You might ask whether the person beside you wants company, conversation, or quiet, and be willing to hear a different answer tomorrow. Explore and study Carry one small burden A neighbor helps a parent load groceries into a car. Taking on an ordinary burden can offer real comfort when a grieving family chooses what help feels welcome. Read Mosiah 18 If you would like to explore prayer, remembrance, and receiving help at your own pace, continue with Grief and Faith . Remembering without pressure If it feels welcome, a family might keep a photograph, tell a story, or mark a meaningful day in a way that honors their child. There is no obligation to make grief public or to turn remembrance into a testimony for others. Friends can ask permission before offering a memorial gesture or sharing a story. If I can only read a little today Choose one of the short passages already linked, or simply read the opening paragraph. You do not need to finish the study. The resources remain here for another day, and seeking company or practical support may be the more useful next step. Questions for Quiet Reflection What do I need today? Would it help to be heard, to rest, to remember my child, or to ask someone for a specific kind of support? I do not need to resolve every question today. Which promise can I return to? Read one of the passages above slowly. What does it actually teach, and what questions does it leave unanswered? Allow both to be part of honest prayer. Ask a Question Life After Death Faith During Trials Where would you like to go next? Explore and study Hope waits beside sorrow Morning light enters the empty tomb. Sorrow is still real, but because Jesus Christ rose, grief is no longer the end of the story. Read 1 Corinthians 15 Explore resurrection when you feel ready Study the broader teaching without requiring yourself to feel comfort immediately. Receive support while carrying grief Consider spiritual hope and practical help together; there is no deadline to continue.

records.title: How Can I Find Hope in Christ During Divorce?
records.pageTitle: How Can I Find Hope in Christ During Divorce?
records.text: Answers / Divorce and faith Divorce can unsettle your sense of home, belonging, and the future you expected. You can bring that pain to Jesus Christ. A marriage ending does not, by itself, tell anyone the story of your faith, your effort, or the choices another person made. Watch and study Read the Teaching with Your Circumstances in View This conference message addresses divorce directly. You can read the transcript, watch the video, or return when the subject feels less difficult. In his April 2007 address Divorce , Elder Dallin H. Oaks speaks to several audiences: people who have divorced, married couples considering divorce, and people contemplating marriage. Notice those changes of audience as you read. Advice addressed to one group should not become a judgment on every person's circumstances. General conference video and text Divorce The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2007 In section II, he recognizes people who have experienced betrayal, abandonment, or abuse and points them and their children toward the healing and hope of Christ's Atonement. Later, he acknowledges that attempts to help a spouse do not always bring change and that we cannot control or take responsibility for another person's choices. Read this historical conference address alongside the Church's Divorce resource , which recommends trusted leaders and professionals and says no one should feel a need to remain in an abusive relationship. As you study, consider which audience a passage addresses and what support your own circumstances require. Explore and study Support Through Divorce A father and friend sit together on a quiet balcony. The friend's attentive posture suggests the compassion and steady companionship that can help someone feel less alone during a difficult season. Begin with Your Actual Circumstances The Church's Life Help resource on divorce recognizes that circumstances vary and there is no simple answer for every marriage. It upholds marriage covenants while encouraging careful, prayerful decisions and counsel from trusted leaders and professionals. It also makes clear that a person does not need to remain in an abusive relationship. Read Divorce in Life Help . Decisions about staying, separating, or divorcing deserve time and support that take your circumstances seriously. You do not have to prove your faith by accepting harm, and your effort alone cannot determine another person's choices. Christ Can Meet You in the Loss Alma 7:11-13 teaches that the Savior took upon Himself human pain and infirmity so He would know how to help His people. His compassion is a reason to seek Him with your real feelings, including disappointment, uncertainty, and exhaustion. You do not need a polished explanation before you pray. Study Alma 7:11-13 . A small beginning might be a brief prayer, one passage of scripture, or asking a trusted person to sit with you. Choose what you have room for today. A difficult day afterward does not make that effort meaningless. Safety and Support Matter The Church's teaching on abuse calls for protecting victims and taking reports seriously. It states that victims are not responsible for another person's abusive behavior and recognizes the need for help from professionals and civil authorities. Seeking safety is consistent with these teachings. Read the Church's guidance on abuse . If there is immediate danger, seek emergency help. For ongoing abuse, a qualified local support service can help you consider safety and practical needs. Spiritual counsel can accompany professional help; it does not replace it. Questions about legal rights, finances, or parenting arrangements need advice suited to your location and circumstances. Children Need Reassurance The Church's divorce resource specifically teaches that children should understand that their parents' decision is neither their fault nor their responsibility. A child should not have to repair an adult relationship. Read the guidance for families . Consider what reassurance your children need to hear again and which trusted adults can help you care for them. When family circumstances are complicated, seek qualified support rather than expecting a child to carry your worries. Explore and study Let a child know you are listening A mother pauses at the kitchen table to listen to her daughter, their hands resting together. During family changes, moments of steady attention can help a child feel heard and remind her that her questions and feelings matter. Divorce: Life Help Mosiah 18:8–9 You Still Need Friendship and Belonging In an Ensign account, Brian Duncan describes the loneliness and practical demands he faced after divorce, and the difference made by people who offered friendship, help with his children, and a place to talk. His account may offer ideas for friends and congregations who want to help and are unsure where to begin. Read Ministering to Members Who Are Divorced . For someone offering support, Mosiah 18:8-9 directs disciples toward sharing burdens and comforting people who mourn. Ask what would help, respect privacy, and keep extending friendship without demanding details. Practical kindness can make belonging tangible. Study Mosiah 18:8-9 . A Next Step for Today You do not have to resolve every question about your future at once. Consider one need you can name and one trustworthy person or resource you can approach. Your next step may be spiritual, practical, or both. What can I bring to God honestly? Name what feels hardest today. What would you ask if you did not feel you had to sound strong? Where do I need support? Consider safety, companionship, caring for children, or an appointment with a qualified professional. Which need can you ask someone to help with this week? For a Friend Who Wants to Help Ask what the person wants shared and what should remain private. An invitation to dinner, help with an errand, or steady friendship may be more useful than questions about why the marriage ended. Keep including the person without expecting them to explain their circumstances each time. Mosiah 18:8-10 describes bearing burdens and offering comfort. Applied here, that can mean listening without taking over decisions, respecting boundaries, and following through on the help you offer. Avoid using an invitation to forgive as pressure to resume an unsafe relationship. Rebuilding Daily Life Without Rushing the Heart Distinguish responsibility from blame You can reflect honestly on your own choices without taking responsibility for another person's abuse, dishonesty, or decisions. A study page cannot judge the history of a marriage. Use the Church's divorce and abuse resources above alongside qualified help that understands your situation. Explore and study Walk beside someone who is rebuilding A companion matches the pace of a friend who uses a cane. Walking side by side offers a gentle picture of patience, care and shared burdens. Read Romans 12 What does seeking peace ask of me? Romans 12:18 speaks of living peaceably as far as it depends on you. Read it with the surrounding counsel about sincere care. As an application, consider respectful communication and boundaries that protect safety. The verse does not require one person to make another person cooperate, nor does it replace legal or professional guidance. Care for children without drawing them into the conflict The Life Help resource linked above discusses the needs of children. Consider asking a qualified family professional how to respond to questions in an age-appropriate way. A child should not have to become a messenger, investigator, or source of emotional support for an adult. When safety or custody is involved, seek guidance suited to the actual circumstances. What could a new routine make room for? Think of one small source of steadiness: a regular meal with someone you trust, a moment to pray, a walk, or getting help with an unfinished task. These are suggestions to consider, not a checklist for recovery or a promise that grief will disappear. Watch and study When the Relationship Has Included Abuse Explore and study Listen before offering answers Two women sit facing one another in a quiet conversation. Their attentive posture offers a picture of the care it takes to listen before offering answers. Read Matthew 11:28–30 Explore and study Begin again, one morning at a time A woman finds a quiet place to read while life around her still feels unsettled. Returning to Christ's words can bring a little steadiness to a morning that asks her to begin again. Matthew 11:28-30 In He Is Risen with Healing in His Wings: We Can Be More Than Conquerors , Elder Patrick Kearon speaks directly to people harmed by abuse, neglect, and domestic violence. He teaches that victims are not responsible for another person's abuse and that what happened does not reduce their worth or God's love for them. He recognizes that the effects can persist for years and can make seeking help difficult. General conference video and text He Is Risen with Healing in His Wings: We Can Be More Than Conquerors The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2022 This message is particularly relevant if abuse is part of your story. It does not assume that every divorce involves abuse. You may read or watch at your own pace, with a trusted person if that would help. Read that teaching alongside the Church guidance on abuse , which calls for protecting victims, taking reports seriously, and helping people obtain appropriate professional care. A desire to follow Christ can coexist with a decision to maintain distance and seek protection. A private reflection, without a deadline You might consider three separate questions: What pain do I want to bring to Christ? What boundaries or practical needs require attention? Who is qualified to help me with those needs? You do not need to answer all three today. This reflection does not decide whether you should reconcile, separate, or take any particular legal step. If you are supporting someone else, ask whether they want a resource before sending it. A message about forgiveness should never become a way to demand access, silence a report of harm, or set a recovery deadline. Official Sources and Further Study Divorce: Life Help Abuse: Topics and Questions Alma 7:11-13 Mosiah 18:8-9 Ministering to Members Who Are Divorced Ask a Question Prayer and Personal Revelation Faith During Trials Where would you like to go next? Explore and study Help with what matters today Friends help arrange belongings in a new apartment after a difficult change. A box carried, a room made ready and a friend who stays can bring comfort when words are not enough. Read Mosiah 18:8–9 Revisit belonging and family Read about dignity and care across different family circumstances. Seek prayer and wise decisions Explore responsible action and counsel while answers remain uncertain.

The verse does not require one person to make another person cooperate, nor does it replace legal or professional guidance. Care for children without drawing them into the conflict The Life Help resource linked above discusses the needs of children. Consider asking a qualified family professional how to respond to questions in an age-appropriate way. A child should not have to become a messenger, investigator, or source of emotional support for an adult. When safety or custody is involved, seek guidance suited to the actual circumstances. What could a new routine make room for? Think of one small source of steadiness: a regular meal with someone you trust, a moment to pray, a walk, or getting help with an unfinished task. These are suggestions to consider, not a checklist for recovery or a promise that grief will disappear.

records.title: When the Relationship Has Included Abuse
records.pageTitle: How Can I Find Hope in Christ During Divorce?
records.text: Watch and study When the Relationship Has Included Abuse Explore and study Listen before offering answers Two women sit facing one another in a quiet conversation. Their attentive posture offers a picture of the care it takes to listen before offering answers. Read Matthew 11:28–30 Explore and study Begin again, one morning at a time A woman finds a quiet place to read while life around her still feels unsettled. Returning to Christ's words can bring a little steadiness to a morning that asks her to begin again. Matthew 11:28-30 In He Is Risen with Healing in His Wings: We Can Be More Than Conquerors , Elder Patrick Kearon speaks directly to people harmed by abuse, neglect, and domestic violence. He teaches that victims are not responsible for another person's abuse and that what happened does not reduce their worth or God's love for them. He recognizes that the effects can persist for years and can make seeking help difficult. General conference video and text He Is Risen with Healing in His Wings: We Can Be More Than Conquerors The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2022 This message is particularly relevant if abuse is part of your story. It does not assume that every divorce involves abuse. You may read or watch at your own pace, with a trusted person if that would help. Read that teaching alongside the Church guidance on abuse , which calls for protecting victims, taking reports seriously, and helping people obtain appropriate professional care. A desire to follow Christ can coexist with a decision to maintain distance and seek protection. A private reflection, without a deadline You might consider three separate questions: What pain do I want to bring to Christ? What boundaries or practical needs require attention? Who is qualified to help me with those needs? You do not need to answer all three today. This reflection does not decide whether you should reconcile, separate, or take any particular legal step. If you are supporting someone else, ask whether they want a resource before sending it. A message about forgiveness should never become a way to demand access, silence a report of harm, or set a recovery deadline.

records.title: How Can Faith in Jesus Christ Help During Trials?
records.pageTitle: How Can Faith in Jesus Christ Help During Trials?
records.keywords: faith in jesus christ during trials
records.text: Answers / Faith and adversity Latter-day Saint teaching does not promise that faith will remove every trial. It teaches that trusting Jesus Christ can give strength to endure, wisdom to act, power to change, and hope that suffering is not the final word. Spiritual support can coexist with practical help. Serious mental-health, medical, safety, legal, or abuse-related problems may require qualified professional or emergency assistance in addition to prayer and faith. Faith Can Include Honest Sorrow Faith in Jesus Christ includes belief in Him, but it goes further: it means relying on His power, wisdom, and love. A faithful person may still grieve, fear, question, or feel exhausted. Scripture is full of disciples who suffered while continuing to turn toward God. Christ Understands Suffering Latter-day Saints emphasize scriptural teachings that Jesus Christ took upon Himself pains, sicknesses, temptations, grief, and sin. Because of His Atonement, believers trust that He understands mortal suffering personally and can strengthen people in ways that are both spiritual and practical. Read Alma 7:11-13 slowly. Alma speaks of suffering, sickness, infirmity, death, and sin. He connects the Savior's experience of mortality with His knowledge of how to help His people. This passage gives a reason to bring Him the particular pain you carry, even when you cannot explain it neatly. Trials Have Different Causes Church teaching does not reduce every hardship to punishment from God. Some consequences follow personal choices; some suffering results from the choices of others; some comes through illness, accident, mortality, injustice, or conditions no individual caused. Different problems therefore require different responses. Taking One Step When Life Is Hard It is understandable to ask why, and you do not have to turn pain into a lesson before seeking help. When you have the capacity, consider one small question: Who could listen today? What practical need could someone help with? What might help me get through this afternoon? A next step can be small, and accepting help can be part of it. Hope Reaches Beyond the Present Moment Latter-day Saint hope is ultimately tied to Christ’s Resurrection. Loss, disability, injustice, and death are real, but they are not eternal victories over God’s children. Resurrection, judgment, healing, and eternal life place present suffering inside a larger story. When the Question Is Personal If your trial involves loss or changes in family life, you may find more specific support in Finding Hope After the Death of a Child , Divorce and Faith , or Prayer and Personal Revelation . Choose the subject that fits what you are carrying; there is no need to work through everything at once. Receiving Help Is Part of Being Cared For You may need a listening friend, help with daily responsibilities, or care from a qualified professional. It can be difficult to name a need when you are worn down. You might begin with something specific: asking someone to bring a meal, accompany you to an appointment, or check in tomorrow. In Mosiah 18:8-10 , those preparing for baptism commit to share burdens and comfort people who need comfort. This gives friends and congregations something concrete to do. The person suffering should not have to carry the whole responsibility for finding support. Like a Broken Vessel : Jeffrey R. Holland addresses mental and emotional suffering, including the importance of qualified care and compassion. Read or watch the talk if that is the kind of support you are seeking. Grief and Loss : guidance for supporting someone through loss, with attention to listening and differing experiences of grief. Compassion and Qualified Care Church video and transcript Like a Broken Vessel Elder Jeffrey R. Holland teaches compassion, patience, and the value of qualified care during mental and emotional suffering. The original artwork illustrates receiving attentive help; it does not portray a particular person from the talk. Jeffrey R. Holland · October 2013 · Official Church talk; original focusChrist artwork Read Suffering Without Simplifying It Explore and study Christ is present in the storm Wind and waves close in around the frightened disciples, yet Jesus is still in the boat with them. Mark's account bears witness that His presence and power remain real even before the storm grows quiet. Mark 4:35-41 A prayer from distress Doctrine and Covenants 121:1-9 begins with Joseph Smith pleading from imprisonment and then records words of comfort. Notice that the anguished question is part of the scripture. Do not rush past it to reach a reassuring line. A personal prayer can be honest about distress without becoming a polished lesson. Help before circumstances change Follow Mosiah 24:10-21 through the whole sequence. The people cry to God, face threats for praying aloud, and continue praying in their hearts. The Lord strengthens them under their burdens; later, He leads them out of bondage. The account includes help within hardship and deliverance from it. Their story does not establish when another person's circumstances will change. Conference video · 16:23 Bear Up Their Burdens with Ease The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Explore and study Strength while the burden remains The Lord strengthens Alma’s people to bear their burdens before He leads them out of bondage. Two neighbors sharing a heavy basket give that strength an everyday form. Their task and surroundings are an artistic interpretation of the passage. Mosiah 24:14–15 What kind of strength does this passage describe before deliverance? Ask about this part of the study . Watch and reflect: Elder David A. Bednar studies these same verses in Bear Up Their Burdens with Ease . He distinguishes receiving strength from having a difficulty immediately removed. What help within your circumstances could you ask for today? Explore and study Bring distress into prayer A man bows his head at a kitchen table, bringing distress honestly into prayer while hardship continues. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121 Hope when endurance feels small In Mountains to Climb , President Henry B. Eyring addresses people who fear that their faith is weakening under pressure. He describes a foundation built through patient acts of integrity and service. He also acknowledges that he cannot promise an end to adversity in this life. Listen for encouragement that fits your capacity today, with room for the sorrow you still carry. Conference video · 19:38 Mountains to Climb The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints In Matthew 14:27-33 , Peter's fear is followed by a cry for help and Christ's immediate reach. Read the rescue as carefully as the question Jesus asks him. The Savior remains central throughout the encounter. Explore and study Strength can arrive before relief A friend brings water to a woman whose wrist is wrapped, offering relief while the injury remains. Alma's people likewise receive strength to bear their burdens before deliverance comes. Read Mosiah 24 A personal reflection: Choose whichever question fits today: What do I wish someone understood? What help could I receive? What can I bring honestly to prayer? You can return to another question later, without a schedule or requirement to feel stronger first. Read for compassion, not comparison A story of endurance can encourage one person and feel heavy to another. Avoid comparing your capacity with a scriptural figure or treating someone's continuing suffering as proof of weak faith. Ask what the account actually says, what it does not promise, and what practical help is needed in your circumstances. What would support look like this week? Name a need that someone else could reasonably help meet. It might be a conversation, transport, childcare, or an appointment. You can pair that request with prayer without waiting to feel certain or strong. A quiet reflection for the strength you have today Mosiah 24:13–15 describes divine help while burdens remain. If you wish, choose the question that fits today and leave the others for another time. What do you wish someone understood? You may name a feeling, a practical difficulty, or something you cannot yet explain. What words would help a trusted person listen? Writing a sentence or asking someone to sit with you can be enough for this moment. What help would make the next step possible? Think about the next few hours rather than the whole future. Is there a task, appointment, meal, or conversation someone could share? You can receive care while the larger question remains unanswered. What can you bring honestly to Christ? Return to the passage on this page that feels closest to your experience. What would you say in prayer if you did not have to hide sorrow or sound strong? Allow the reflection to end where your capacity ends today. The burden has not disappeared, but shared strength makes the next step possible, much like the Lord's promise to Alma's people. Read Mosiah 24:14–15 Explore and study Keep pace with one another A companion keeps pace with a woman using a walking stick along a woodland path. Faithful progress may be slow, but patient company can make each step feel possible. Mosiah 24:14-15 Look to Christ amid fear Read D&C 6:36 beside the Savior's mercy and wounds. Explore an invitation to trust Him while difficult questions remain. Pray with unresolved questions Explore discernment without treating every feeling as an instruction. records.title: Is there a God who is our Father?
records.pageTitle: Is there a God who is our Father?
records.text: Answers / Stand Forever / God Is there a God who is our Father? Begin with what scripture says about His relationship with us, then make room for thoughtful inquiry, prayer, and lived experience. This study presents a Latter-day Saint approach to that foundational question. A question worth unhurried attention You can enter this study with conviction, uncertainty, or a mixture of both. Start by writing your question in your own words. Are you asking whether God exists, whether He knows you, or how to recognize an answer? These are related questions, but naming the one you are carrying makes your next step more useful. Choose a short reading below before starting a longer video. In a notebook, keep three spaces: what the passage teaches, what I understand, and what I still wonder. This simple distinction helps a meaningful impression become something you can revisit without turning every personal interpretation into a scriptural claim. The portrait in the opening is Jesus Christ, who directs disciples to the Father. It is not a depiction of Heavenly Father. The study focuses on the relationship described in the texts. Sunlight spreads across the landscape, awakening wonder at creation and at Paul's tender declaration that we are the offspring of God. Read Acts 17 1. Seek the God who gives life Acts 17 places Paul in Athens, speaking with people whose religious assumptions differ from his own. In verses 22–31, he describes God as the giver of life and speaks of humanity as His offspring. Paul moves from the world his listeners know toward an invitation to seek God and consider resurrection. Explore and study Paul invites Athens to seek God Paul speaks of God as the giver of life and invites his listeners to seek Him. Some believe, while others question or turn away. Read his words and their responses together. Acts 17:22–34 Read the address as a whole. Notice what Paul says about God, what he asks people to do, and the varied reactions afterward. The passage records religious teaching and a public encounter; it is not a modern scientific demonstration. Latter-day Saints read its language of offspring as part of their scriptural understanding of a relationship with Heavenly Father. Read Acts 17:22–34 in context Reflect on relationship Which description of God stands out to you? How might seeing another person as connected to God change the way you listen to or treat that person? For a longer exploration of this question, watch Corbridge’s discussion and return to Paul’s address with your own notes. Video · Original publisher thumbnail Stand Forever, Episode 29: Is There a God Who Is Our Father? Lawrence E. Corbridge considers belief in God and the roles of reason and spiritual witness. Compare his discussion with your notes from Acts 17 . Scripture Central · Lawrence E. Corbridge Read the full message 2. Learn prayer from Jesus Christ In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches His disciples to pray to the Father. Matthew 6:5–13 connects prayer with sincerity rather than public performance. The prayer includes reverence, daily need, forgiveness, and dependence on God. Its simplicity offers a starting place even when you do not know what to say. Explore and study Follow the Savior's example of prayer Beneath the open sky, Jesus kneels to speak with His Father. His example teaches that prayer can be personal, reverent and honest. Read Matthew 6 Read the surrounding teaching about giving and forgiveness. Jesus places prayer within a life turned toward God, not within a technique for controlling an outcome. You might begin by naming one gratitude, one need, and one question. This is a suggested practice, not a promise that a particular feeling or answer will arrive on your schedule. Read Matthew 6:5–15 Try an honest prayer What would I say to the Father if I did not need to sound certain or polished? What part of the Lord’s Prayer could help me begin? Continue into prayer and personal revelation → 3. Consider identity and divine purpose Moses 1 is part of the Pearl of Great Price, a book of scripture in the Latter-day Saint canon. The chapter presents Moses speaking with God and learning about his own relationship to Him. Near its conclusion, God explains His work in terms of the immortality and eternal life of humanity. Explore and study See the worth in one another An older man holds a bowl he made by hand while a volunteer listens with genuine interest. Being seen, heard and valued can help us recognize the divine worth God has given every person. Read Moses 1 Read verses 1–11 alongside verses 37–39. Hold the chapter’s sense of human limitation together with its attention to human worth. This text gives a theological account of purpose; it does not supply the cause of every experience a person has. Let its claims about God and His work lead your reflection before asking it to resolve a different question. Read Moses 1, especially verses 1–11 and 37–39 Connect purpose with daily life What kind of purpose does this chapter describe? What ordinary responsibility or relationship could I approach with greater care because of it? 4. Give growing faith thoughtful care Alma 32 addresses people who have been excluded from their place of worship. Alma discusses humility and faith, then uses a seed as a comparison for receiving and nourishing the word. His invitation includes beginning with a desire to believe and attending to what follows over time. Explore and study Nurture the faith that is growing Careful hands tend a small seedling in a greenhouse. Like Alma's seed of faith, new belief needs light, patience and steady nourishment before its strength can be known. Read Alma 32 Read verses 21–43 rather than isolating the seed image from its setting. Notice the difference between an initial response and continued nourishment. The passage invites participation, patience, and examination. A focusChrist application is to choose one teaching of Jesus, live it deliberately, and record what you notice without exaggerating either certainty or disappointment. Read Alma 32:21–43 Choose a small experiment in discipleship What teaching could I practice this week? What would I observe honestly, and when will I return to the passage to reflect? Watch, then return to the text Continue from Corbridge’s discussion above into Nelson’s teaching about following Jesus Christ through covenants. Pause to write one idea and its supporting passage before moving to another video. Video · Original publisher thumbnail Overcome the World and Find Rest Russell M. Nelson connects rest in Jesus Christ with covenant discipleship. Consider how a belief about God can shape a daily commitment. Official General Conference channel · October 2022 Read the full message Bring the study into one ordinary day Read: choose one passage and include its surrounding verses. Notice: record a specific teaching about God rather than a general impression alone. Respond: pray honestly, practice a teaching of Jesus, or care for someone. Return: revisit your notes and identify the question worth studying next. You do not need to complete every resource in one sitting. A family or study partner can choose one reading together, let each person describe what they noticed, and leave room for different questions. Keep the conversation curious and respectful; the purpose is to understand and grow, not to force identical responses. Explore and study Let divine love become personal A woman and an older man tend herbs together in a community garden. records.title: A question worth unhurried attention
records.pageTitle: Is there a God who is our Father?
records.text: You can enter this study with conviction, uncertainty, or a mixture of both. Start by writing your question in your own words. Are you asking whether God exists, whether He knows you, or how to recognize an answer? These are related questions, but naming the one you are carrying makes your next step more useful. Choose a short reading below before starting a longer video. In a notebook, keep three spaces: what the passage teaches, what I understand, and what I still wonder. This simple distinction helps a meaningful impression become something you can revisit without turning every personal interpretation into a scriptural claim. The portrait in the opening is Jesus Christ, who directs disciples to the Father. It is not a depiction of Heavenly Father. The study focuses on the relationship described in the texts.

records.title: 1. Seek the God who gives life
records.pageTitle: Is there a God who is our Father?
records.text: Acts 17 places Paul in Athens, speaking with people whose religious assumptions differ from his own. In verses 22–31, he describes God as the giver of life and speaks of humanity as His offspring. Paul moves from the world his listeners know toward an invitation to seek God and consider resurrection. Explore and study Paul invites Athens to seek God Paul speaks of God as the giver of life and invites his listeners to seek Him. Some believe, while others question or turn away. Read his words and their responses together. Acts 17:22–34 Read the address as a whole. Notice what Paul says about God, what he asks people to do, and the varied reactions afterward. The passage records religious teaching and a public encounter; it is not a modern scientific demonstration. Latter-day Saints read its language of offspring as part of their scriptural understanding of a relationship with Heavenly Father. Read Acts 17:22–34 in context Reflect on relationship Which description of God stands out to you? How might seeing another person as connected to God change the way you listen to or treat that person? For a longer exploration of this question, watch Corbridge’s discussion and return to Paul’s address with your own notes. Video · Original publisher thumbnail Stand Forever, Episode 29: Is There a God Who Is Our Father? Lawrence E. Corbridge considers belief in God and the roles of reason and spiritual witness. Compare his discussion with your notes from Acts 17 . Scripture Central · Lawrence E. Corbridge Read the full message

records.title: 2. Learn prayer from Jesus Christ
records.pageTitle: Is there a God who is our Father?
records.text: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches His disciples to pray to the Father. Matthew 6:5–13 connects prayer with sincerity rather than public performance. The prayer includes reverence, daily need, forgiveness, and dependence on God. Its simplicity offers a starting place even when you do not know what to say. Explore and study Follow the Savior's example of prayer Beneath the open sky, Jesus kneels to speak with His Father. His example teaches that prayer can be personal, reverent and honest. Read Matthew 6 Read the surrounding teaching about giving and forgiveness. Jesus places prayer within a life turned toward God, not within a technique for controlling an outcome. You might begin by naming one gratitude, one need, and one question. This is a suggested practice, not a promise that a particular feeling or answer will arrive on your schedule. Read Matthew 6:5–15 Try an honest prayer What would I say to the Father if I did not need to sound certain or polished? What part of the Lord’s Prayer could help me begin? Continue into prayer and personal revelation →

records.title: 3. Consider identity and divine purpose
records.pageTitle: Is there a God who is our Father?
records.text: Moses 1 is part of the Pearl of Great Price, a book of scripture in the Latter-day Saint canon. The chapter presents Moses speaking with God and learning about his own relationship to Him. Near its conclusion, God explains His work in terms of the immortality and eternal life of humanity. Explore and study See the worth in one another An older man holds a bowl he made by hand while a volunteer listens with genuine interest. Being seen, heard and valued can help us recognize the divine worth God has given every person. Read Moses 1 Read verses 1–11 alongside verses 37–39. Hold the chapter’s sense of human limitation together with its attention to human worth. This text gives a theological account of purpose; it does not supply the cause of every experience a person has. Let its claims about God and His work lead your reflection before asking it to resolve a different question. Read Moses 1, especially verses 1–11 and 37–39 Connect purpose with daily life What kind of purpose does this chapter describe? What ordinary responsibility or relationship could I approach with greater care because of it?

records.title: 4. Give growing faith thoughtful care
records.pageTitle: Is there a God who is our Father?
records.text: Alma 32 addresses people who have been excluded from their place of worship. Alma discusses humility and faith, then uses a seed as a comparison for receiving and nourishing the word. His invitation includes beginning with a desire to believe and attending to what follows over time. Explore and study Nurture the faith that is growing Careful hands tend a small seedling in a greenhouse. Like Alma's seed of faith, new belief needs light, patience and steady nourishment before its strength can be known. Read Alma 32 Read verses 21–43 rather than isolating the seed image from its setting. Notice the difference between an initial response and continued nourishment. The passage invites participation, patience, and examination. A focusChrist application is to choose one teaching of Jesus, live it deliberately, and record what you notice without exaggerating either certainty or disappointment. Read Alma 32:21–43 Choose a small experiment in discipleship What teaching could I practice this week? What would I observe honestly, and when will I return to the passage to reflect?

records.title: Watch, then return to the text
records.pageTitle: Is there a God who is our Father?
records.text: Continue from Corbridge’s discussion above into Nelson’s teaching about following Jesus Christ through covenants. Pause to write one idea and its supporting passage before moving to another video. Video · Original publisher thumbnail Overcome the World and Find Rest Russell M. records.title: Grief and Faith in Jesus Christ
records.pageTitle: Grief and Faith in Jesus Christ
records.text: Answers / Grief When someone you love is gone, even ordinary days can feel unfamiliar. Scripture makes room to mourn, to receive companionship, and to seek hope in Jesus Christ. You can seek His comfort while still missing the person you love. Begin with compassion Explore and study The Savior’s compassion in sorrow The Savior stays near in a moment of deep sorrow. His compassion does not erase the loss, but it assures the grieving heart that it is seen, loved and never abandoned. The image offers a place to pause before studying. Notice the Savior accompanying the grieving woman rather than searching for an explanation of the loss. The passages below offer different perspectives: the Savior’s response to mourning, His knowledge of suffering, and the responsibility to care for one another. These are invitations for reflection. They do not establish a timetable for sorrow or require you to describe a painful experience before you are ready. Jesus wept with those who mourned In John 11 , Martha and Mary speak to Jesus after their brother Lazarus has died. Martha expresses faith in resurrection, and Jesus identifies Himself as the resurrection and the life. Later, He sees Mary and the people with her weeping, and He also weeps. Explore and study Jesus weeps with those who mourn Mary comes to Jesus with the pain of losing her brother. He sees her tears and the sorrow of those with her, and He weeps. John 11:30–36 The account holds sorrow and hope together. Jesus’s knowledge of what He will do does not erase His compassionate response to the people before Him. Read the whole encounter, including the sisters’ words, rather than treating the shortest verse as the entire story. Read John 11:17–36 in context Pause with the passage What do you notice about the way Jesus receives sorrow? What would it mean to let hope and sadness be present in the same prayer? Scripture reading · Reflection artwork Read John 11 Read the exchange with Martha and Mary, then notice how Jesus responds to their sorrow. Official scripture text · ChurchofJesusChrist.org. Artwork: focusChrist reflection. Remembering someone you love In Sunday Will Come , Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin remembers his parents, sister, and wife. His memories are specific, and so is his sorrow. He speaks about resurrection while acknowledging how deeply he misses them. The message offers a way to hear Christian hope from someone who is also grieving. Explore and study Hold sorrow and resurrection hope together Light reaches into an empty tomb, holding sorrow and resurrection hope in the same view. Jesus's words to Martha place that hope in Him: the Resurrection and the Life. Read John 11:17–36 If you watch, pause wherever you need to. You might write a memory of your loved one, or simply notice the room he makes for affection and loss. His testimony looks toward resurrection and reunion. It does not set a deadline for when another person should stop feeling sorrow. General conference video and text Sunday Will Come Hear Elder Wirthlin remember loved ones and speak about the Resurrection. Notice how he speaks of missing them while expressing hope in Christ. Joseph B. Wirthlin · October 2006 · Official Church source and video preview A memory I want to keep Is there an ordinary moment, familiar saying, or small kindness I want to remember? I can keep it privately or share it with someone who would welcome it. The Savior knows suffering Alma 7:11–13 describes Jesus Christ taking upon Himself pain, sickness, death, and the infirmities of His people. Alma connects that experience with the Savior’s knowledge of how to help them. For Latter-day Saints, this passage is a source of confidence in Christ’s compassion. Its focus is His redeeming work and capacity to help; it does not explain the particular cause of every loss. When reading, distinguish what Alma promises about the Savior from an explanation you may wish the passage would provide. Read Alma 7:11–13 Name what you need today What comfort do I need today? What could I say to Heavenly Father without trying to make it sound polished or complete? Walk with Him as you are President Emily Belle Freeman teaches, “Jesus Christ will meet us where we are as we are.” Her message describes a covenant relationship with the Savior through the challenges of mortality. In grief, we can receive that invitation without waiting until we feel strong or have every answer. An honest prayer or a small step with someone who cares may be a beginning. General conference video and text Walking in Covenant Relationship with Christ President Freeman teaches that Christ accompanies us through mortal challenges and invites us into a covenant relationship with Him. Consider how His companionship can offer hope while you mourn. Emily Belle Freeman · October 2023 · Official Church source and video preview Grief can be met with companionship Explore and study Stay close and listen One woman speaks while another listens without hurry. Such presence honors the covenant to mourn with those who mourn and lets compassionate care be guided by the person who grieves. Mosiah 18:9 In Mosiah 18:8–10 , Alma describes a people willing to bear one another’s burdens, mourn with those who mourn, and comfort those needing comfort. He places this willingness within the commitments of baptism and service to God. The passage gives companions something concrete to consider: presence, shared burdens, and comfort. It does not ask them to supply an answer to every question. As an optional application, consider listening, bringing a meal, helping with an ordinary task, or remembering a meaningful date. Let the grieving person’s needs guide what you offer. Explore and study Care begins by listening A grieving woman welcomes a friend who gently arranges flowers nearby. Comfort becomes more compassionate when it respects the wishes and pace of the person who mourns. Read Mosiah 18:8–10 Read Mosiah 18:8–10 Consider one person Who could sit with me, listen, or help carry a practical burden? If I am supporting someone else, what could I ask instead of assuming what would help? Scripture reading · Reflection artwork Read Mosiah 18 Read verses 8–10 in context and consider what it means to mourn with and comfort another person. Official scripture text · ChurchofJesusChrist.org. Artwork: focusChrist reflection. Help that can be offered today President Camille N. Johnson’s Jesus Christ Is Relief distinguishes grief and other burdens of mortality from the burden of sin. She then describes care we can offer one another. Read this part of her message beside the covenant passage above. It gives a friend something useful to do without making the person who is grieving responsible for reassuring everyone else. General conference video and text Jesus Christ Is Relief Study President Johnson’s invitation to help carry another person’s burdens. Consider one practical form of care that the grieving person would welcome. Camille N. Johnson · April 2023 · Official Church source and video preview A specific offer can be easier to answer than a broad request to ask for anything. You might offer to bring dinner, accompany someone on an errand, or sit quietly together. Ask what would be welcome and accept the answer. These are optional applications of the passage, not a required way to grieve or help. Receiving comfort without having every answer In 2 Corinthians 1:3–7 , Paul blesses God as a source of comfort and connects receiving comfort with being able to comfort others. The passage acknowledges suffering within the community he addresses. It does not describe comfort as the absence of every painful feeling. Read the passage slowly, then consider what comfort might mean today: being listened to, having help with a task, remembering someone without being hurried, or finding words for prayer. You may have an unanswered question alongside something you are grateful to receive. Choose what would help Would I welcome conversation, practical help, or quiet company? Is there one person I could tell, in plain words, what I need today? A quiet practice for today This optional focusChrist practice can be done in a notebook, in prayer, or in conversation with someone you trust. Use only the parts that are helpful today. Explore and study Bring every memory and question An older man pauses beside a family photograph and an open notebook. Memory, sorrow and the need for comfort are all welcome in the presence of the God of consolation. Read 2 Corinthians 1:3–7 Choose one passage and read the surrounding verses. Write one thing the passage says about Christ or caring for another person. Write one memory, question, or need you want to acknowledge. Choose one small way to receive or offer companionship. Return without pressure What changed as I paused with this passage? What remains unresolved? I can return to both without pretending the loss no longer matters. Official sources The scripture explanations above are based on John 11:17–36 , Alma 7:11–13 , and Mosiah 18:8–10 . The additional study draws on 2 Corinthians 1:3–7 and the three linked general conference messages. Personal questions and practical suggestions are focusChrist study aids. records.title: Jesus Christ: Come to Know the Living Savior
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ: Come to Know the Living Savior
records.keywords: jesus christ latter day saint beliefs
records.text: Answers / Jesus Christ Latter-day Saints worship Jesus Christ as the divine Son of God, the Savior and Redeemer of the world. His life, Atonement, death, and Resurrection are at the center of their faith. One Savior · A connected journey Come to know Jesus Christ Before Bethlehem: the Son and Jehovah Explore His premortal identity, creation, covenant, deliverance, and the Old Testament witness of the Redeemer. Open study → Walk through His mortal ministry Follow His baptism, invitations, journeys, disciples, and the growing witness of who He is. Open study → His miracles and compassion Stay with the people He meets and discover how particular acts of healing reveal His character. Open study → Learn from the Master Teacher Study His commandments and explore the Gospel parables through six connected themes. Open study → The Redeemer and risen Lord Follow the final days of His mortal ministry, His sacrifice, and the witnesses of His Resurrection. Open study → The risen Savior in the Book of Mormon Read His ministry at Bountiful, His covenant teachings, and His care for the gathered people. Open study → Jesus Christ in the Restoration and today Explore restored witnesses of the living Savior, daily discipleship, and hope in His promised return. Open study → The birth of Jesus Christ Enter the complete companion study of the promises, Nativity accounts, and witnesses of His coming. Open study → In His prayer to the Father, Jesus connects eternal life with knowing the Father and Jesus Christ, whom the Father sent. John 17:3 gives this journey its purpose. We can learn what He taught, notice how He treated people, and consider how to respond to His invitation in our own lives. Follow the studies in order, or begin with a question you carry. Each path opens scripture in context and returns here, so you can move between His identity, His ministry, His saving mission, and His teachings without losing your place. John 17:3 The eternal Son His story begins before Bethlehem Study the witness before Bethlehem Read the passages about the Son, Jehovah, creation, and deliverance with their distinct settings and speakers. Open study → Continue to His coming into the world Follow the Nativity in its own full study, with the separate witnesses of Matthew, Luke, and the Book of Mormon. Open study → John begins with the Word who was with God, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh. John 1:1–5, 14 invites us to recognize the divine identity of the One who enters mortal life. His birth is a beginning within that mortal life; the scriptural witness reaches further back. In Moses 1:32–39 , the Father identifies His Only Begotten Son in the work of creation and declares His purpose for His children. Latter-day Saints also identify Jesus Christ as Jehovah, the God of Israel. Read the deliverance account in Exodus 3:7–14 and listen to the Lord's concern for the suffering of His people. Covenant and compassion belong together in this witness. John 1:1–5, 14 Moses 1:32–39 Exodus 3:7–14 An invitation to begin He invites people to come and see Explore and study Come and see Andrew and another disciple follow Jesus. His invitation gives them an opportunity to spend time with Him and begin to know Him. John 1:35–42 Two disciples hear John the Baptist testify of Jesus and follow Him. Jesus turns and asks what they seek. Their question about where He lives leads to an invitation to come and see. In John 1:35–42 , Andrew then brings his brother Simon. Learning of Christ becomes personal through listening, following, and sharing a discovery with someone else. Philip offers a similar invitation when Nathanael questions whether anything good can come from Nazareth. John 1:43–51 follows that exchange into Nathanael's encounter with Jesus. Jesus speaks of having seen him before Philip called him. Nathanael responds with recognition and faith, and Jesus points him toward greater things still to come. Explore and study Known before the meeting Philip brings Nathanael to Jesus. The conversation moves from Nathanael’s question to recognition of the Son of God. John 1:43–51 Pause and consider What would you want to ask Jesus if you could begin with a sincere question? Who has helped you take a first step toward knowing Him, and what did that person actually do? Follow the ministry that unfolds Continue into the calls, journeys, and encounters through which His disciples learned of Him. Open study → John 1:35–42 John 1:43–51 Compassion in an encounter He attends to particular people Explore and study A mother’s persistent plea A Syrophoenician mother asks Jesus to help her daughter. This illustration focuses on their conversation; Mark records that the daughter was healed at home. Mark 7:24–30 The woman in Mark 7:24–30 comes to Jesus because her daughter needs help. Mark identifies her as a Gentile, a Syrophenician by nation. Their exchange includes difficult words about children and bread; her answer persists within that comparison. Jesus tells her that the devil has gone out of her daughter, and she returns home to find the child well. The daughter's healing is reported at home, distinct from the mother's conversation with Him. In Mark 7:31–37 , Jesus takes a man who is deaf and has a speech difficulty aside from the crowd. The account describes His touch, His upward look and sigh, and the opening of the man's ears. Reading the sequence helps us notice personal attention as well as power. The man is a person being ministered to, not merely an example of a condition. Explore and study He took him aside Away from the crowd, Jesus gives the man His attention and looks toward heaven. Mark records the opening of his ears and the release of his speech. Mark 7:31–37 Ten men call to Jesus for mercy in Luke 17:11–19 . As they go in response to His instruction, they are cleansed. One returns, glorifies God, and falls at His feet in thanks. Luke identifies this man as a Samaritan. The account moves from shared need and healing to the gratitude of one person who turns back to the giver. Explore and study The one who returned One of the ten men who were cleansed returns to give thanks. Luke identifies him as a Samaritan. Luke 17:11–19 Pause and consider Which detail helps you see the person within one of these accounts? How could gratitude become a deliberate action in your life today? Stay with His miracles and compassion Study more encounters, their circumstances, and the difference between scriptural witness and assumptions about another person's suffering. Open study → Mark 7:24–30 Mark 7:31–37 Luke 17:11–19 Love, loyalty, and attention His teaching reaches the heart Explore and study Whose image is on the coin? John 20 records the risen Jesus Christ appearing to Mary Magdalene and later showing His wounds to His disciples. 3 Nephi 11 presents a second witness of the resurrected Savior teaching people gathered at Bountiful. Together, these accounts center the question on who Jesus declared Himself to be and how His Resurrection shapes Christian discipleship. Jesus Christ teaches with calm, undivided attention. His open expression draws us back to the scriptural witness of His words, His sacrifice and His Resurrection. Read John 20 Read a witness. Open John 20 and notice the people, their questions, and the stated purpose of the account. Read the whole encounter before drawing a conclusion from one sentence. Compare and study. Use the scripture study below to read 3 Nephi 11 alongside the New Testament. Record both shared testimony and differences in setting. Watch and respond. Choose one of this page’s reviewed messages, follow a scripture it cites, and write one question or faithful action to return to. Begin with scripture Watch and study focusChrist is an independent faith-based website. This page explains a Latter-day Saint perspective and links directly to official Church sources for authoritative teaching. Watch and study Begin with the living Savior What difference does it make to believe Jesus Christ lives? Watch Finding Faith in Christ as an introduction to that question, then give the scriptural witnesses room to speak in their own words. Church video Finding Faith in Christ The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints In John 20:11-18 , Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb grieving. She recognizes Jesus when He addresses her by name, then tells the disciples she has seen Him. The account brings the Resurrection into a personal encounter: the one she mourned speaks to her. Continue through verses 19-29 . The disciples see His hands and side; Thomas is later invited to examine His wounds. Notice the relationship between witness, belief, and the peace Jesus offers. Write one sentence about what this chapter says happened and a second about why it matters to you. Keep your response distinct from the scriptural account. Jesus Christ Is the Son of God Latter-day Saints believe in God the Eternal Father, His Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost. They understand the Father and the Son as distinct divine beings who are perfectly united in purpose. Jesus Christ is the Only Begotten Son of the Father in the flesh and the promised Messiah. He Is the Savior and Redeemer The central Christian claim of Latter-day Saint belief is that salvation is possible only through Jesus Christ. Through His atoning sacrifice, He took upon Himself sin, suffering, and death. His grace makes repentance, forgiveness, spiritual healing, and reconciliation with God possible. He Died and Rose Again Latter-day Saints believe Jesus was crucified, truly died, and rose bodily from the tomb. Because of His Resurrection, every person will be resurrected. Because of His Atonement, those who turn to Him in faith, repent, and receive and keep the covenants of His gospel can be cleansed from sin and receive eternal life. Explore and study Meet the risen Savior The risen Christ extends an open hand to a man at Bountiful. One by one, the people may come near, see the marks of His sacrifice and know for themselves that He lives. Read 3 Nephi 11:10-17 His Life Did Not Begin at Bethlehem Latter-day Saint scripture and apostolic teaching describe Jesus Christ as the premortal Jehovah, chosen before the creation of the world to be the Savior. Under the direction of the Father, He participated in the Creation. His mortal birth was therefore part of a divine mission that began before mortality. Follow the promises of His coming, Mary and Joseph’s journey, and the witnesses at Bethlehem in The Birth of Jesus Christ . He Leads His Church and Will Return Latter-day Saints believe the resurrected Jesus Christ lives, directs His work, and will return to the earth in glory. They also believe that His gospel and priesthood authority were restored through the Prophet Joseph Smith. Whatever is distinctive in Latter-day Saint doctrine is intended to lead back to Christ rather than replace Him. What Does Following Him Mean? Faith in Christ is more than acknowledging that He lived. It means trusting Him, repenting, trying to live His teachings, receiving His ordinances and covenants, serving others, and relying on His grace. Latter-day Saints see discipleship as a lifelong effort to become more like the Savior while depending on Him for the power to change. Explore and study Notice His pattern of prayer Jesus kneels beside an olive tree in quiet prayer. His repeated choice to withdraw and pray reveals communion with the Father as part of a life devoted to serving others. Read Luke 5:15-16 A Place to Begin Reading Start with Matthew 11:28-30 , where Jesus invites the weary to come to Him and learn of Him. Then read 3 Nephi 11:10-17 , the Book of Mormon account of the risen Savior inviting people to approach Him individually. What do His words and actions help you understand about Him? Learning About Christ Through His Encounters with People A summary of beliefs is a beginning. You can also get to know the scriptural accounts by paying attention to the people who come to Jesus. In John 11:17-36 , He listens to Martha and shares the sorrow around Lazarus's death. In 3 Nephi 11:10-17 , the risen Savior invites the gathered people to approach Him individually. Explore and study Welcome the children Jesus welcomes children and listens to them in a village courtyard. Mark's account shows the Savior defending their place near Him and receiving them with tenderness. Read Mark 10:13-16 As you read, consider what each encounter shows about His character. What question would you bring to Him? You can explore that question through the study on prayer , or turn to faith during trials if your concern is more immediate. The Savior, His Grace, and Our Response A risen person, not only a remembered teacher Luke 24:36-48 describes Jesus appearing to His disciples, showing His hands and feet, and teaching them about His suffering, Resurrection, and the preaching of repentance and forgiveness. Notice how the encounter connects who He is with what His followers are to share. Latter-day Saints read this as testimony of His bodily Resurrection. Why the Atonement matters Atonement names Christ's saving work of overcoming sin and death and reconciling people to God. In Mosiah 3:5-11, 17-19 , King Benjamin teaches of the Savior's coming, suffering, and power to save. Read the references to mercy and becoming receptive to God. The teaching calls for a changed heart grounded in Christ's power, not confidence that human effort can replace Him. What does it mean to follow Him? 2 Nephi 31:17-21 places faith, hope, love, and continued discipleship together. As a personal application, consider one teaching of Christ you could practice in a relationship today. Keep the action specific enough to be lived, while remembering that discipleship includes receiving help and beginning again. Explore and study Bring fear into the conversation Jesus listens to a frightened disciple as wind and waves surround their wooden boat. His calm attention meets the disciples' urgent fear before He stills the storm. Read Mark 4:35-41 Where could I begin if I do not yet know what I believe? Choose one encounter in Luke 24 and read it without rushing. Note what Jesus says, how people respond, and what remains a question for you. The purpose is attentive study, not producing a particular feeling on command. Watch and study His compassion in action Explore and study Give someone your full attention Jesus Christ gives an older man His full attention. At Bountiful, the Savior showed this same unhurried compassion when He stayed to heal, bless and care for the people before He departed. 3 Nephi 17:1-10 3 Nephi 17:1-10 slows the story down. Jesus recognizes that the people need time to understand His teaching. He invites them to ponder at home and pray for understanding. When He sees their tears, He stays to minister and calls for those who are afflicted. Church video What Has Our Savior Done for Us? The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints In the accompanying message, What Has Our Savior Done for Us? , President Dallin H. Oaks connects the Resurrection, forgiveness, Christ’s teachings, and His capacity to help us in affliction. Read the complete April 2021 address beside 3 Nephi 17 . Notice both minds that need time to learn and people who need compassionate care. As a personal application, consider someone whose needs you have been too hurried to notice. Listening, making room for a question, or offering practical assistance can become a way to practice Christlike care. The healing described here should not become a deadline you impose on someone else's suffering. A study you can carry into the week These focusChrist prompts are invitations for personal reflection. Read: identify His character Read John 20 alongside 3 Nephi 11:10-17 . List what Jesus says about Himself and what people are invited to do. Compare the witnesses without erasing the different settings of the two accounts. Remember: connect doctrine with hope Return to the sections on Atonement and Resurrection below the first video. Which question concerns you most: forgiveness, death, divine companionship, or becoming different? Follow its source link and write what you understand so far. Practice: make care concrete Choose one quiet act of attention for today. Ask a sincere question, follow through on a promise, or make time for someone who is hurting. Afterward, consider what you learned about the person you served. Discuss: give questions space With a willing friend, discuss which scriptural encounter has shaped your view of Jesus. You can explain your belief and listen to a different view with respect. An honest unanswered question belongs in the conversation too. Bring a passage and a specific question to Ask , then check the response against the linked original sources. Receive His welcome and extend it Mark 10:13–16 gives a particular glimpse of the Savior’s character: He welcomes and blesses children. Return to that encounter as you consider what following Him could mean today. What do His actions show you? Read the sequence slowly: people bring children, the disciples rebuke them, and Jesus responds. Which action helps you understand His welcome? Describe it before deciding how to apply it. Where do you need His care? Choose one teaching about Christ from this page that speaks to a need or question you carry. What would you like to say to Him in prayer? You may return to the same passage as understanding grows. Who could experience a warmer welcome? Think of someone who may feel overlooked. What would help that person feel listened to and included? Offer a specific act of attention that respects their wishes, then reflect on what you learned about Christlike care. records.text: The eternal Son His story begins before Bethlehem Study the witness before Bethlehem Read the passages about the Son, Jehovah, creation, and deliverance with their distinct settings and speakers. Open study → Continue to His coming into the world Follow the Nativity in its own full study, with the separate witnesses of Matthew, Luke, and the Book of Mormon. Open study → John begins with the Word who was with God, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh. John 1:1–5, 14 invites us to recognize the divine identity of the One who enters mortal life. His birth is a beginning within that mortal life; the scriptural witness reaches further back. In Moses 1:32–39 , the Father identifies His Only Begotten Son in the work of creation and declares His purpose for His children. Latter-day Saints also identify Jesus Christ as Jehovah, the God of Israel. Read the deliverance account in Exodus 3:7–14 and listen to the Lord's concern for the suffering of His people. Covenant and compassion belong together in this witness. John 1:1–5, 14 Moses 1:32–39 Exodus 3:7–14

records.title: He invites people to come and see
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ: Come to Know the Living Savior
records.text: An invitation to begin He invites people to come and see Explore and study Come and see Andrew and another disciple follow Jesus. His invitation gives them an opportunity to spend time with Him and begin to know Him. John 1:35–42 Two disciples hear John the Baptist testify of Jesus and follow Him. Jesus turns and asks what they seek. Their question about where He lives leads to an invitation to come and see. In John 1:35–42 , Andrew then brings his brother Simon. Learning of Christ becomes personal through listening, following, and sharing a discovery with someone else. Philip offers a similar invitation when Nathanael questions whether anything good can come from Nazareth. John 1:43–51 follows that exchange into Nathanael's encounter with Jesus. Jesus speaks of having seen him before Philip called him. Nathanael responds with recognition and faith, and Jesus points him toward greater things still to come. Explore and study Known before the meeting Philip brings Nathanael to Jesus. The conversation moves from Nathanael’s question to recognition of the Son of God. John 1:43–51 Pause and consider What would you want to ask Jesus if you could begin with a sincere question? Who has helped you take a first step toward knowing Him, and what did that person actually do? Follow the ministry that unfolds Continue into the calls, journeys, and encounters through which His disciples learned of Him. Open study → John 1:35–42 John 1:43–51

records.title: He attends to particular people
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ: Come to Know the Living Savior
records.text: Compassion in an encounter He attends to particular people Explore and study A mother’s persistent plea A Syrophoenician mother asks Jesus to help her daughter. This illustration focuses on their conversation; Mark records that the daughter was healed at home. Mark 7:24–30 The woman in Mark 7:24–30 comes to Jesus because her daughter needs help. Mark identifies her as a Gentile, a Syrophenician by nation. Their exchange includes difficult words about children and bread; her answer persists within that comparison. Jesus tells her that the devil has gone out of her daughter, and she returns home to find the child well. The daughter's healing is reported at home, distinct from the mother's conversation with Him. In Mark 7:31–37 , Jesus takes a man who is deaf and has a speech difficulty aside from the crowd. The account describes His touch, His upward look and sigh, and the opening of the man's ears. Reading the sequence helps us notice personal attention as well as power. The man is a person being ministered to, not merely an example of a condition. Explore and study He took him aside Away from the crowd, Jesus gives the man His attention and looks toward heaven. Mark records the opening of his ears and the release of his speech. Mark 7:31–37 Ten men call to Jesus for mercy in Luke 17:11–19 . As they go in response to His instruction, they are cleansed. One returns, glorifies God, and falls at His feet in thanks. Luke identifies this man as a Samaritan. The account moves from shared need and healing to the gratitude of one person who turns back to the giver. Explore and study The one who returned One of the ten men who were cleansed returns to give thanks. Luke identifies him as a Samaritan. Luke 17:11–19 Pause and consider Which detail helps you see the person within one of these accounts? How could gratitude become a deliberate action in your life today?
