records.text: Watch and study Begin with the living Savior What difference does it make to believe Jesus Christ lives? Watch Finding Faith in Christ as an introduction to that question, then give the scriptural witnesses room to speak in their own words. Church video Finding Faith in Christ The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints In John 20:11-18 , Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb grieving. She recognizes Jesus when He addresses her by name, then tells the disciples she has seen Him. The account brings the Resurrection into a personal encounter: the one she mourned speaks to her. Continue through verses 19-29 . The disciples see His hands and side; Thomas is later invited to examine His wounds. Notice the relationship between witness, belief, and the peace Jesus offers. Write one sentence about what this chapter says happened and a second about why it matters to you. Keep your response distinct from the scriptural account.

records.title: The Savior, His Grace, and Our Response
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ: Come to Know the Living Savior
records.text: A risen person, not only a remembered teacher Luke 24:36-48 describes Jesus appearing to His disciples, showing His hands and feet, and teaching them about His suffering, Resurrection, and the preaching of repentance and forgiveness. Notice how the encounter connects who He is with what His followers are to share. Latter-day Saints read this as testimony of His bodily Resurrection. Why the Atonement matters Atonement names Christ's saving work of overcoming sin and death and reconciling people to God. In Mosiah 3:5-11, 17-19 , King Benjamin teaches of the Savior's coming, suffering, and power to save. Read the references to mercy and becoming receptive to God. The teaching calls for a changed heart grounded in Christ's power, not confidence that human effort can replace Him. What does it mean to follow Him? 2 Nephi 31:17-21 places faith, hope, love, and continued discipleship together. As a personal application, consider one teaching of Christ you could practice in a relationship today. Keep the action specific enough to be lived, while remembering that discipleship includes receiving help and beginning again. Explore and study Bring fear into the conversation Jesus listens to a frightened disciple as wind and waves surround their wooden boat. His calm attention meets the disciples' urgent fear before He stills the storm. Read Mark 4:35-41 Where could I begin if I do not yet know what I believe? Choose one encounter in Luke 24 and read it without rushing. Note what Jesus says, how people respond, and what remains a question for you. The purpose is attentive study, not producing a particular feeling on command.

records.title: His compassion in action
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ: Come to Know the Living Savior
records.text: Watch and study His compassion in action Explore and study Give someone your full attention Jesus Christ gives an older man His full attention. At Bountiful, the Savior showed this same unhurried compassion when He stayed to heal, bless and care for the people before He departed. 3 Nephi 17:1-10 3 Nephi 17:1-10 slows the story down. Jesus recognizes that the people need time to understand His teaching. He invites them to ponder at home and pray for understanding. When He sees their tears, He stays to minister and calls for those who are afflicted. Church video What Has Our Savior Done for Us? The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints In the accompanying message, What Has Our Savior Done for Us? , President Dallin H. Oaks connects the Resurrection, forgiveness, Christ’s teachings, and His capacity to help us in affliction. Read the complete April 2021 address beside 3 Nephi 17 . Notice both minds that need time to learn and people who need compassionate care. As a personal application, consider someone whose needs you have been too hurried to notice. Listening, making room for a question, or offering practical assistance can become a way to practice Christlike care. The healing described here should not become a deadline you impose on someone else's suffering.

records.title: A study you can carry into the week
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ: Come to Know the Living Savior
records.text: These focusChrist prompts are invitations for personal reflection. Read: identify His character Read John 20 alongside 3 Nephi 11:10-17 . List what Jesus says about Himself and what people are invited to do. Compare the witnesses without erasing the different settings of the two accounts. Remember: connect doctrine with hope Return to the sections on Atonement and Resurrection below the first video. Which question concerns you most: forgiveness, death, divine companionship, or becoming different? Follow its source link and write what you understand so far. Practice: make care concrete Choose one quiet act of attention for today. Ask a sincere question, follow through on a promise, or make time for someone who is hurting. Afterward, consider what you learned about the person you served. Discuss: give questions space With a willing friend, discuss which scriptural encounter has shaped your view of Jesus. You can explain your belief and listen to a different view with respect. An honest unanswered question belongs in the conversation too. Bring a passage and a specific question to Ask , then check the response against the linked original sources.

records.title: Receive His welcome and extend it
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ: Come to Know the Living Savior
records.text: Mark 10:13–16 gives a particular glimpse of the Savior’s character: He welcomes and blesses children. Return to that encounter as you consider what following Him could mean today. What do His actions show you? Read the sequence slowly: people bring children, the disciples rebuke them, and Jesus responds. Which action helps you understand His welcome? Describe it before deciding how to apply it. Where do you need His care? Choose one teaching about Christ from this page that speaks to a need or question you carry. What would you like to say to Him in prayer? You may return to the same passage as understanding grows. Who could experience a warmer welcome? Think of someone who may feel overlooked. What would help that person feel listened to and included? Offer a specific act of attention that respects their wishes, then reflect on what you learned about Christlike care.

records.title: Look Unto Me in Every Thought
records.pageTitle: Look Unto Me in Every Thought
records.keywords: look unto me doctrine and covenants 6 36
records.text: Answers / Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 is not an isolated slogan. In context, the Lord directs Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery away from fear and toward Himself. The same Christ-centered movement appears across scripture: Paul tells disciples to rejoice in the Lord and rejoice in Christ Jesus, while Nephi declares, “we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ.” Together these passages form a study pattern for focusChrist: attention, remembrance, discipleship, and joy centered in the Savior. The revelation in context Explore and study Harmony, Pennsylvania: a setting of revelation A quiet lane leads toward an interpretive early nineteenth-century farmhouse. The scene recalls rural Harmony, Pennsylvania, where Oliver Cowdery sought assurance and received the Lord's tender command to look to Christ in every thought. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6 The Setting: Oliver Cowdery Comes to Harmony Oliver Cowdery arrived at Joseph and Emma Smith's home in Harmony, Pennsylvania, on April 5, 1829. He began writing as Joseph's scribe on April 7. Before their meeting, Oliver had boarded with Joseph's parents and prayed about what he learned of the plates. The Church's historical account describes a private experience of peace that he had not shared. Doctrine and Covenants 6 recalled that experience while addressing his participation in the work. Earlier in the revelation, the Lord reminds Oliver of an experience of peace: “Did I not speak peace to your mind concerning the matter?” ( D&C 6:23 ). That reminder gives verse 36 added depth. Looking to Christ includes remembering light already received rather than allowing present fear to erase it. Read Oliver Cowdery's Gift Study D&C 6, 8, and 9 Church video Christ Is Risen; Faith in Him Will Move Mountains Connect the invitation to look to Christ with faith that acts, grows, and keeps turning toward Him. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Study lesson Look Unto Me: D&C 6 Seminary Study Explore the lesson’s questions about doubts and fears, and read the Savior’s invitation in its scriptural setting. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Read the verses as a sequence Explore and study Turn attention toward Christ Christ meets the viewer with a calm, reassuring gaze. In the quiet light of the setting sun, His expression offers a simple invitation: look to Him, remember His words and keep walking with faith. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:32-37 Doctrine and Covenants 6:32-37 Read the complete passage first. The reflections below follow its movement from Christ's presence to faithful action and His promise of eternal life. Verse 32: Christ is in the midst Jesus recalls His promise to disciples gathered in His name and applies it to Joseph and Oliver. Their work begins with His presence. Before asking how strong their faith feels, notice who speaks and where He says He is. Verse 33: Fear not to do good The Lord joins courage to goodness through the image of sowing and reaping. Consider a good action fear has made difficult: offering help, telling the truth, or making amends. This is an invitation to act faithfully, not a timetable for a particular result. Verse 34: Build upon His rock The verse acknowledges opposition rather than promising its absence. Christ's rock is the foundation of the reassurance. Ask what supports your choices when approval, comfort, or circumstances change. Verse 35: Receive mercy and continue Christ's words of non-condemnation accompany a call to leave sin and perform the commanded work soberly. Mercy and responsibility belong together. A useful reflection is: what can I turn from, and what work can I return to with greater care? Verse 36: Look unto Me The invitation directs attention to a person, Jesus Christ. Read it with the verses on either side: His presence, goodness, mercy, and sacrifice give trust its substance. Looking to Him can shape what you choose even before every question is settled. Verse 37: Behold the wounds The final verse directs attention to the Savior's wounded side, hands, and feet, then invites faithfulness and obedience. The Church's student manual says it is not known whether verses 32 and 37 refer to a literal or figurative experience. We can study what His words teach without deciding whether a visitation occurred. Why do Christ's wounds follow the invitation to look? The Seminary lesson pairs these verses and invites students to consider His Atonement and Resurrection. Compare 3 Nephi 11:10-17 : the risen Lord identifies Himself and invites the people to feel His wounds, becoming witnesses for themselves. Then read Alma 7:11-13 . Alma teaches of Christ taking upon Himself suffering, infirmities, death, and sins, and knowing how to help His people. Together, these passages direct our attention to both His power to redeem and His knowledge of human suffering. The wounds invite trust in the Savior who suffered and lives. Reflect: When you pray about pain, guilt, or fear, how might remembering the living Redeemer change what you ask Him for? Give yourself room to seek forgiveness, strength, or companionship without demanding that grief disappear. Church video Wherefore Didst Thou Doubt? Watch the account of Peter and the Savior on the water. Read Matthew 14:22-33 and notice Peter’s appeal for help. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church video and transcript The Love of God Elder Benjamin M. Z. Tai connects Peter's appeal for rescue with looking to Christ in every thought. Watch for his invitations to remember God's love, pray for someone in need, and act. Which invitation could shape your next ordinary day? The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Bring the scripture into the day Explore and study Bring an honest question with you Beside the open scriptures, a woman pauses to write down a question she has not yet resolved. The wide ocean and quiet moment remind us that faith can keep growing even before every answer comes. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:22-23 Looking to Christ When Life Is Uncertain You can begin with the question you are carrying. These reflections are focusChrist study applications, offered alongside the scriptures and Church teachings linked here. What does “in every thought” mean? In Seek Christ in Every Thought , Elder Ulisses Soares describes bringing our minds and desires into harmony with Christ and choosing what is good each day. He also acknowledges that unwelcome thoughts can arise despite sincere effort. His teaching concerns how we respond and what we cultivate. Consider ordinary moments: preparing for work, listening to someone, or deciding how to answer a difficult message. A personal application is to pause and ask, “What would honesty, patience, and love require here?” Returning your attention to Christ can become a repeated practice. How does looking address doubt and fear? Read Matthew 14:27-33 all the way through. Peter becomes afraid and begins to sink, but he also calls for help. Jesus immediately reaches for him. The account includes rescue as well as correction. As a study application, distinguish a question you need to investigate from a fear that is preventing a good action. You can seek evidence, ask for help, and keep turning toward Christ. Do not use this passage to measure another person's faith by how calm they appear. Explore and study Immediately Jesus reached for him Peter sees the wind, becomes afraid, and cries for help. Matthew records that Jesus immediately reaches out and catches him. This scene invites us to notice the Savior’s response as carefully as Peter’s fear. Matthew 14:30–31 What does Christ’s immediate response help you notice in this account? Ask about this part of the study . October 2024 general conference O Youth of the Noble Birthright “You’ve got this because Jesus Christ has got you!” Brother Bradley R. Wilcox describes covenants as a relationship in which we hold more closely to Jesus Christ and receive His strength to live differently from the world. What would it mean to rely on His strength in the responsibility you are carrying today? Read the passage about holding to Christ Bradley R. Wilcox · The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints What if an answer has not come? Oliver's remembered peace concerned a particular question. Remembering it did not make every later question identical. The historical account continues through his desire to translate, his unsuccessful attempt, further counsel, and his return to serving as scribe. Try writing two short notes: what you have reason to trust, and what remains unresolved. Preserve earlier light without treating it as a prediction about a new outcome. Hebrews 12:1-3 places looking to Jesus within patient endurance. The next step may be continued study, a conversation, or a responsibility you can fulfill while waiting. What if I do not know what God wants? In Jesus Christ Is the Strength of Youth , Elder Dieter F. Uchtdorf explains that gospel principles guide decisions without providing a separate yes or no for every possible choice. Christ remains the guide, and the person still chooses. For a decision before you, identify the relevant teaching, gather needed information, consider who is affected, and pray. Distinguish what is clearly right from a preference about an uncertain outcome. Choose a responsible next step and remain willing to learn. The video below can deepen this reflection; Prayer and Personal Revelation continues the study. Alma 37:36-37 brings this attention into an ordinary day: actions, thoughts, affections, counsel with God, rest at night, and gratitude in the morning. Choose one of those moments as a reminder to turn toward Him. Questions, knowledge, and revelation Stand Forever Explore Elder Lawrence E. Corbridge’s devotional, its four primary questions, and a guided study of faith and revelation on the dedicated study page. Open the Stand Forever study → A practical way to study Guided Study: Look, Remember, Talk, Rejoice, Act 1. Look Read D&C 6:32-37 and mark every statement about Jesus Christ. Ask what the passage teaches about who He is and what He promises. 2. Remember Read D&C 6:22-23 . Record one experience of peace, truth, help, or spiritual clarity you do not want fear to erase. 3. Talk Read 2 Nephi 25:26 . Share one thing you are learning about Christ with someone willing to listen, or write it for yourself. Speak honestly about what you understand and what you are still seeking. Explore and study Talk about what you are learning A father and daughter share an unhurried conversation while washing dishes together. Faith becomes part of family life when we speak of Christ with warmth, listen to one another and learn side by side. Read 2 Nephi 25:26 4. Rejoice Read Philippians 4:4 and 2 Nephi 25:26 . Write one reason you rejoice in Christ Himself, not merely in a hoped-for outcome. 5. Act Choose one faithful action consistent with Christ's teachings. Continue praying and studying without forcing certainty that has not come. Journal prompts What thought most often pulls my attention away from Christ? What truth in D&C 6:32-37 answers it? What has Christ already done that gives me reason to rejoice? What good action am I postponing because of fear? What would one faithful next step look like today? 2027 Church theme connection Rejoice in Christ The Church's 2027 youth theme is “Rejoice in Christ.” Church leaders have connected the theme with Philippians 4:4 , and the same phrase is being used for the 2027 Salt Lake Temple Celebration. That creates a natural companion to D&C 6:36 : the Savior we are invited to look toward is also the Savior in whom disciples rejoice. Philippians 4:4 “Rejoice in the Lord alway.” Read the surrounding chapter and notice how rejoicing is linked with prayer, gratitude, peace, disciplined thought, and strength through Christ. Philippians 3:1-8 Paul says believers “rejoice in Christ Jesus” and place no confidence in the flesh. Compare that with D&C 6:36 : confidence shifts away from self and toward Christ. 2 Nephi 25:23-26 Nephi explains why he writes and teaches so openly of the Savior: “we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ, we prophesy of Christ.” 2 Nephi 11:4-8 Nephi explains that he includes Isaiah so readers can lift up their hearts and rejoice. Prophecy, covenant, gathering, and the Messiah all become reasons to rejoice in Christ. How does looking to Christ become rejoicing in Him? Philippians 4:4-13 develops the connection. Paul moves from rejoicing to prayer with thanksgiving, then to peace guarding hearts and minds through Christ. He names things worthy of attention and urges disciples to practice what they have learned. His testimony of strength follows his account of both abundance and hunger. Joy in Christ does not depend on calling every circumstance pleasant. In Philippians 3:7-14 , Paul places knowing Christ above his former advantages and continues pressing forward. In 2 Nephi 11:4-8 , Nephi delights in the Redeemer, God's covenants, grace, and plan of deliverance. These are reasons for rejoicing rooted in who Christ is and what God provides. Read the purpose at the end of 2 Nephi 25:23-26 . Nephi's speaking, writing, and rejoicing help his children know where to look for forgiveness. Talking of Christ is therefore part of helping someone else turn toward Him. It can be a quiet conversation, a shared scripture, or an honest account of something you are learning. Reflect: What about the Savior gives you reason for gratitude today? How could you speak of that without minimizing someone else's pain? These scriptures create a simple Focus pattern: look unto Christ, remember Christ, talk of Christ, rejoice in Christ, and act through Christ. D&C 6:36 gives the direction of our attention. Philippians and 2 Nephi show what can grow from that attention: confidence in Him, peace, gratitude, testimony, and joy. Explore the 2027 Youth Theme Rejoice in Christ Temple Celebration Study lesson We Rejoice in Christ Study 2 Nephi 20 , 2 Nephi 21 , 2 Nephi 22 , 2 Nephi 23 , 2 Nephi 24 , 2 Nephi 25 with Come, Follow Me. Look for what Nephi wants the next generation to know about the Savior. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Study lesson Strength and Joy in Christ The 2027 Come, Follow Me lesson on Philippians and Colossians offers a companion study of peace, endurance, and strength through Christ. Preview artwork: Light of the World, by Walter Rane. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Scripture picture quote We Talk of Christ: 2 Nephi 25:26 Open the Church’s picture quote, then read the complete verse. Notice how speaking of Christ points the next generation toward Him. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church announcement Rejoice in Christ: The 2027 Celebration Read the Church’s announcement and invitation to participate. Connect the celebration’s theme with your study of Philippians 4 . The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Trace the theme through scripture Cross-References for Deeper Study Matthew 14:22-33 Peter walks toward Jesus, then begins to sink as fear overtakes his attention. Compare his experience with D&C 6:36 . Numbers 21:4-9 Israel is invited to look and live. Scripture repeatedly connects faithful looking with trust in God's provided deliverance. Alma 37:36-37 Alma teaches that thoughts should be directed unto the Lord and that disciples should counsel with Him in all their doings. Hebrews 12:1-3 Disciples run with patience while “looking unto Jesus.” Compare the language of attention, endurance, and joy. Turn attention into discipleship Watch, Listen, and Take a Faithful Step Let each message lead back to the Savior’s words. Choose one question to carry into the seven-day study below. Church video Jesus Christ Is the Strength of Youth Hear Elder Dieter F. Uchtdorf’s teaching about choosing with Jesus Christ as your guide. What makes a decision Christ-centered? Official Church talk; original focusChrist artwork Church video and transcript Look to God and Live Elder D. Todd Christofferson connects D&C 6:36 with Alma 37 and daily decisions. His message also addresses grief. Consider what it would mean to seek God's counsel while some questions remain unanswered. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Resource collection Rejoice in Christ: Youth Resources Visit the official youth resource hub for the theme and available materials. This is a growing collection, not a single video. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church music video Look Unto Christ: Youth Music Festival Listen to the 2025 Youth Music Festival performance, then return to Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 with one thought to reflect on. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Listen to Look Unto Christ on the Church website Read Rejoice in Christ: testimonies of the Savior A seven-day Christ-centered study Seven Days of Looking and Rejoicing Day 1: D&C 6:22-23 . Remember peace already received. Day 2: D&C 6:32-37 . Mark what Christ says, promises, and commands. Day 3: Matthew 14:22-33 . Notice what changes when Peter's attention shifts. Day 4: Philippians 3:1-8 . Ask where you place confidence. Day 5: Philippians 4:4-13 . Trace rejoicing, prayer, peace, thought, and strength. Day 6: 2 Nephi 25:23-26 . Write why you talk of Christ and rejoice in Christ. Day 7: Hebrews 12:1-3 . Choose one burden, one faithful action, and one reason to keep looking unto Jesus. Explore and study Let study lead to something good A neighbor kneels to repair a small garden gate. The work is ordinary, but willing hands can answer the Lord's simple invitation to do good right where we are. Corbridge: Stand Forever Doctrine and Covenants 9:7–9 Doctrine and Covenants 50:23–24 Doctrine and Covenants 93:24 Alma 32:27–28 Moroni 10:4–5 Matthew 16:15–18 Jeffrey R. Holland: “Lord, I Believe” Neil L. Andersen: Faith Is Not by Chance, but by Choice Russell M. Nelson: The Power of Spiritual Momentum The Meaning of 636 at @theRisen636 The “636” in @theRisen636 points to Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 . The expanded study gives that name a fuller scriptural frame: look unto Christ, speak of Christ, rejoice in Christ, and help others turn toward Him. Ask a Question Prayer and Personal Revelation Continue studying Remember Him in the next ordinary day . Continue with two practical invitations from Elder Andersen: think more often of the Savior and read the Book of Mormon again. When guidance is not immediate Study prayer, personal revelation, discernment, and faithful decisions while a question remains open. When fear grows during a trial Explore faith in Jesus Christ without measuring faith by how quickly circumstances improve. Be still and remember Him Continue with Psalm 46 and a visual study about quiet attention, trust, and agency.

Remembering it did not make every later question identical. The historical account continues through his desire to translate, his unsuccessful attempt, further counsel, and his return to serving as scribe. Try writing two short notes: what you have reason to trust, and what remains unresolved. Preserve earlier light without treating it as a prediction about a new outcome. Hebrews 12:1-3 places looking to Jesus within patient endurance. The next step may be continued study, a conversation, or a responsibility you can fulfill while waiting. What if I do not know what God wants? In Jesus Christ Is the Strength of Youth , Elder Dieter F. Uchtdorf explains that gospel principles guide decisions without providing a separate yes or no for every possible choice. Christ remains the guide, and the person still chooses. For a decision before you, identify the relevant teaching, gather needed information, consider who is affected, and pray. Distinguish what is clearly right from a preference about an uncertain outcome. Choose a responsible next step and remain willing to learn. The video below can deepen this reflection; Prayer and Personal Revelation continues the study. Alma 37:36-37 brings this attention into an ordinary day: actions, thoughts, affections, counsel with God, rest at night, and gratitude in the morning. Choose one of those moments as a reminder to turn toward Him.

records.title: Guided Study: Look, Remember, Talk, Rejoice, Act
records.pageTitle: Look Unto Me in Every Thought
records.text: A practical way to study Guided Study: Look, Remember, Talk, Rejoice, Act 1. Look Read D&C 6:32-37 and mark every statement about Jesus Christ. Ask what the passage teaches about who He is and what He promises. 2. Remember Read D&C 6:22-23 . Record one experience of peace, truth, help, or spiritual clarity you do not want fear to erase. 3. Talk Read 2 Nephi 25:26 . Share one thing you are learning about Christ with someone willing to listen, or write it for yourself. Speak honestly about what you understand and what you are still seeking. Explore and study Talk about what you are learning A father and daughter share an unhurried conversation while washing dishes together. Faith becomes part of family life when we speak of Christ with warmth, listen to one another and learn side by side. Read 2 Nephi 25:26 4. Rejoice Read Philippians 4:4 and 2 Nephi 25:26 . Write one reason you rejoice in Christ Himself, not merely in a hoped-for outcome. 5. Act Choose one faithful action consistent with Christ's teachings. Continue praying and studying without forcing certainty that has not come. Journal prompts What thought most often pulls my attention away from Christ? What truth in D&C 6:32-37 answers it? What has Christ already done that gives me reason to rejoice? What good action am I postponing because of fear? What would one faithful next step look like today?

records.title: Rejoice in Christ
records.pageTitle: Look Unto Me in Every Thought
records.text: 2027 Church theme connection Rejoice in Christ The Church's 2027 youth theme is “Rejoice in Christ.” Church leaders have connected the theme with Philippians 4:4 , and the same phrase is being used for the 2027 Salt Lake Temple Celebration. That creates a natural companion to D&C 6:36 : the Savior we are invited to look toward is also the Savior in whom disciples rejoice. Philippians 4:4 “Rejoice in the Lord alway.” Read the surrounding chapter and notice how rejoicing is linked with prayer, gratitude, peace, disciplined thought, and strength through Christ. Philippians 3:1-8 Paul says believers “rejoice in Christ Jesus” and place no confidence in the flesh. Compare that with D&C 6:36 : confidence shifts away from self and toward Christ. 2 Nephi 25:23-26 Nephi explains why he writes and teaches so openly of the Savior: “we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ, we prophesy of Christ.” 2 Nephi 11:4-8 Nephi explains that he includes Isaiah so readers can lift up their hearts and rejoice. Prophecy, covenant, gathering, and the Messiah all become reasons to rejoice in Christ. How does looking to Christ become rejoicing in Him? Philippians 4:4-13 develops the connection. Paul moves from rejoicing to prayer with thanksgiving, then to peace guarding hearts and minds through Christ. He names things worthy of attention and urges disciples to practice what they have learned. His testimony of strength follows his account of both abundance and hunger. Joy in Christ does not depend on calling every circumstance pleasant. In Philippians 3:7-14 , Paul places knowing Christ above his former advantages and continues pressing forward. In 2 Nephi 11:4-8 , Nephi delights in the Redeemer, God's covenants, grace, and plan of deliverance. These are reasons for rejoicing rooted in who Christ is and what God provides. Read the purpose at the end of 2 Nephi 25:23-26 . Nephi's speaking, writing, and rejoicing help his children know where to look for forgiveness. Talking of Christ is therefore part of helping someone else turn toward Him. It can be a quiet conversation, a shared scripture, or an honest account of something you are learning. Reflect: What about the Savior gives you reason for gratitude today? How could you speak of that without minimizing someone else's pain? These scriptures create a simple Focus pattern: look unto Christ, remember Christ, talk of Christ, rejoice in Christ, and act through Christ. D&C 6:36 gives the direction of our attention. Philippians and 2 Nephi show what can grow from that attention: confidence in Him, peace, gratitude, testimony, and joy. Look for what Nephi wants the next generation to know about the Savior. records.title: Melchizedek Priesthood
records.text: Answers / Melchizedek Priesthood Study the testimony of Peter, James, and John’s ministry to Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery. Follow the surviving scriptural and historical witnesses, keep the unanswered questions visible, and consider the Lord’s teaching about how priesthood authority should be exercised. Authority received, understanding unfolded, people served Doctrine and Covenants 27:12–13 names Peter, James, and John and connects their ministry with apostolic authority and keys. Doctrine and Covenants 128:20 remembers their voices in the wilderness between Harmony and Colesville, along the Susquehanna River. Begin with those witnesses and the questions they actually answer. The opening artwork shows an imagined contemporary priesthood blessing. The historical account below traces a different moment: the restoration of authority through Peter, James, and John. The surviving sources do not establish a precise date for the conferral. Explore and study Read the witnesses carefully Books and notes rest together on a quiet desk in this imagined study scene. Take time with the witnesses: notice when each account was written, whose words it preserves, and what it helps you understand. Read Doctrine and Covenants 128:20 Peter, James, and John: authority and unfolding understanding Explore and study Authority to serve in Christ’s name Beside the river, Joseph and Oliver receive a solemn charge. Their later accounts remember Peter, James, and John as heavenly messengers. Read those accounts alongside the Lord’s teaching about gentle influence: authority in His name calls for persuasion, patience, and love. Read Doctrine and Covenants 27:12–13 Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–42 Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery testified that Peter, James, and John conferred greater priesthood authority upon them. The Church's historical account explains that surviving sources do not establish the exact date. Estimates differ, and the restoration should not be assigned a precise day simply to complete a timeline. Many detailed accounts were written later; earlier references are less specific. Study the evidence and the dating question . A ministry received by both men Explore and study Joseph receives the apostles’ ministry Joseph bows his head as Peter, James, and John place their hands upon him. The scene invites a closer look at the testimony that these messengers conferred priesthood authority in Jesus Christ’s name. Read Doctrine and Covenants 27:12–13 Explore and study Oliver receives the apostles’ ministry Oliver kneels beneath the three apostles’ hands while Joseph stands nearby. Oliver’s later accounts remember receiving greater priesthood authority. The paired pictures show each man receiving; they do not establish who came first. Read the Church’s historical account The three apostles participate in each artistic scene. Their faces, hand placement, and the order pictured are interpretations; the accounts do not describe that arrangement. Explore the evidence: the place, the date, and unfolding understanding Joseph's 1842 letter, now Doctrine and Covenants 128:20 , places their voices in the wilderness between Harmony and Colesville, along the Susquehanna. Doctrine and Covenants 27:12–13 connects these messengers with apostolic authority and the keys of ministry. These passages preserve the central claim without providing a complete scene description. Understanding also developed over time. The Church's account follows later revelations that clarified priesthood offices and terminology, and subsequent restoration of keys and temple ordinances. It presents the restoration as a sequence of events rather than a single moment containing every later organizational detail. Keeping these developments in view helps us read early records in their own setting. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–42 alongside this history. How should patience, gentleness, and sincere love shape the use of authority? The invitation is to serve people, not merely admire an office. Continue with careful source study or return to the artwork gallery . Read the scriptures in context Read Doctrine and Covenants 107:1–8 for the later explanation of the two priesthoods, the name associated with Melchizedek, and the presiding and spiritual responsibilities described there. Then return to the earlier historical account. A later explanation can clarify a teaching without proving that every term or organizational detail was already expressed in the same way in the earliest accounts. Doctrine and Covenants 84:19–22 connects priesthood ordinances with the power of godliness and coming to know God. Study these verses within the revelation’s wider treatment of priesthood and covenant rather than treating authority as a personal distinction. Keep a short record of what each source contributes: the testimony of the messengers, the named place, the later explanation of offices, and the spiritual purpose of ordinances. Leave an unanswered date as unanswered. Church video The Melchizedek Priesthood and the Keys President Dallin H. Oaks explains priesthood authority and keys in the Church and at home. Listen for how authority serves God’s children and how its blessings reach women and men. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Authority and a life of service Doctrine and Covenants 121:34–46 places the exercise of priesthood within a demanding moral teaching. Persuasion, long-suffering, gentleness, meekness, love unfeigned, kindness, and pure knowledge are part of the passage’s language. Read its warnings as well as its promises. These verses do not excuse pressure or mistreatment in the name of authority. They invite examination of how people are actually treated. In daily relationships, listening patiently and serving without seeking control are useful places to begin reflecting on the passage. Explore and study Listen with patience Two men sit together in a garden, one speaking while the other listens. This imagined moment invites us to consider how patience and gentleness can shape the way we serve someone. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–42 Church video The Restoration of the Priesthood Authority and Organization Matthew C. Godfrey and Spencer McBride discuss how Church leaders’ understanding of priesthood developed after authority was restored. Follow their account of changes in organization and duties. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Pause and reflect These questions are optional invitations for personal study. Take time with one before moving to the next. Separate witness from reconstruction Which details do the scriptural and historical sources establish? Which details in the pictures are an artist’s interpretation? Keep both lists so a familiar picture does not become your evidence. Read across time Compare the earlier witness with a later explanation of priesthood. What becomes clearer? What should you avoid projecting backward into the earlier account? Examine the way authority is used Choose one quality named in the passage on gentle influence. What would it change in a conversation where you are tempted to insist, hurry, or control? Official sources for further study Continue with the Church’s historical account and its documentary notes. Notice the dates of the records and follow the linked sources when a detail raises a question. Read the Church History Topics account and its source notes Continue your study Study the Aaronic Priesthood Read the related testimony while keeping the distinct accounts and responsibilities in view. The restored Church of Jesus Christ Connect priesthood, scripture, ordinances, and the purpose of the Church. Return to Church History Explore the wider history and its original sources. records.title: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.pageTitle: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.text: Answers / Prayer and revelation Latter-day Saints believe Heavenly Father hears sincere prayer and can give personal guidance through the Holy Ghost. They also believe spiritual impressions should be sought humbly, tested carefully, and kept within the responsibilities God has actually given a person. Personal revelation is a religious belief and spiritual practice, not a substitute for professional, legal, medical, or emergency help when those are needed. Prayer Is Communication with Heavenly Father Latter-day Saint prayer is directed to God the Father in the name of Jesus Christ. Prayer can include gratitude, confession, worship, requests for help, questions, and quiet listening. The purpose is not to force a preferred answer from God but to turn toward Him with sincerity and willingness to follow Him. What Is Personal Revelation? Personal revelation means divine guidance given to an individual for that person’s life, needs, relationships, and responsibilities. Latter-day Saints believe the Holy Ghost can bring peace, warning, understanding, remembrance, conviction, or quiet impressions. Revelation may come gradually rather than as a dramatic event. Recognize and remember Light Received Over Time Explore and study Step away and pray Jesus withdraws into the wilderness to pray alone. In the stillness, He shows the closeness, trust and renewal found in communion with the Father. Luke 5:16 In Using the Supernal Gift of Prayer , Elder Richard G. Scott describes seeking answers through prayer, thought, work, and patient action. He explains that understanding may arrive in portions. He also describes peace as a confirming witness in his own experience. Read his account as a personal testimony while making room for the questions you are still working through. Conference video · 14:58 Using the Supernal Gift of Prayer The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:22-23 alongside his teaching. The Lord reminds Oliver of peace connected with a particular question. As a personal reflection, write what you remember and what it helped you understand. Keep any unresolved question beside it. Remembering an experience does not require adding certainty about something it did not answer. Watch and reflect: What have I already received that deserves patient attention? How Can Someone Prepare to Receive Guidance? Official Church teaching emphasizes prayer, scripture study, repentance, obedience, worship, and patient effort. A person may study a question, make a thoughtful decision, ask God for confirmation or correction, and remain open to an answer that differs from the original preference. How Can Spiritual Impressions Be Discerned? Latter-day Saints are taught not to treat every feeling as revelation. Genuine guidance should be consistent with God’s revealed commandments and the teachings of Jesus Christ. It should not authorize a person to control someone else’s agency or claim revelation for responsibilities that belong to another. Time, scripture, wise counsel, repeated impressions, and the fruits produced by a decision can help with discernment. What If No Answer Comes? Explore and study Keep a question open together Two sisters walk together while one shares a question she has not resolved. They do not need to force an answer; patient companionship can help faith endure while understanding grows. Read Alma 32 Waiting for an answer can be lonely, especially when the question matters deeply. A quiet prayer or an uncertain feeling is not, by itself, a verdict on your faith. Latter-day Saint teaching makes room for guidance that comes gradually and for thoughtful decisions made without a detailed instruction. You can keep seeking, talk with someone you trust, and take time to gather what you need. Conference video · 12:41 A Framework for Personal Revelation Official Church talk; original focusChrist artwork Watch with a question: Elder Dale G. Renlund explains how personal revelation relates to scripture, commandments, and your own responsibility to choose. As you listen, identify what is yours to decide and what belongs to someone else. Use the discernment exercise below to consider a next step while remaining open to further guidance. A Simple Place to Start Read James 1:5-6 , which invites those seeking wisdom to ask God. Doctrine and Covenants 8:2-3 describes guidance through the Holy Ghost in the mind and heart. You might name one question in your own words, spend a little time with the passage, and write down what you still need to understand. This is an invitation to pray, not a test of whether you feel something immediately. When You Are Unsure Whether a Feeling Is Guidance You can take an impression seriously while still considering it carefully. What does scripture teach about the decision? What information is missing? Does the choice respect another person's freedom? An urgent feeling alone does not settle those questions. In A Framework for Personal Revelation , Dale G. Renlund discusses scripture, personal responsibility, God's commandments, and openness to further guidance. His explanation is especially helpful when someone claims to know God's will for another person's major life decisions. Counsel can help you think; it does not remove your responsibility to choose. If your concern is that answers seem slow, the Church's Recognize That Revelation Is a Process offers further study. You might return to one question over time, without treating each prayer as a deadline for certainty. Discernment in an Ordinary Decision Explore and study Study, ask and keep a careful record A man writes beside an open book, placing prayer, thoughtful effort and a responsible next step together. The Lord's counsel to Oliver Cowdery joins seeking God's help with patient study. Doctrine and Covenants 9:7-9 Consider this everyday example as a focusChrist application: you feel drawn to contact a friend who has been distant. Elder Dale G. Renlund's framework directs attention to scripture, your responsibilities, God's commandments, and openness to further guidance. You can choose to offer a kind message. Your friend remains free to respond, decline, or ask for space. An impression to care for someone does not give you authority to decide their life. Explore and study Seek counsel with an open heart Two women pause beside their bicycles for a thoughtful conversation. Wise counsel can broaden a decision while leaving prayer, agency and responsibility with the person who must choose. Read Doctrine and Covenants 9 Questions to consider before acting Is this kind? Is it mine to decide? What information or consent do I need? These questions are personal reflection aids. They do not certify an impression as revelation. You can act thoughtfully while remaining willing to learn and change. Three Passages for a More Thoughtful Prayer Life Prayer without performance Matthew 6:5-13 places Jesus's teaching on prayer beside cautions about public display and empty repetition. The prayer He teaches includes God's will, daily needs, forgiveness, and deliverance. Consider which part is closest to your concern. You may pray in ordinary words; a polished explanation is not a prerequisite for seeking God. Explore and study Prayer before the Father A man prays privately beside an open book, echoing Jesus's teaching in Matthew 6 that prayer is sincere communion with the Father rather than a public performance. Read Matthew 6 Study and responsibility Doctrine and Covenants 9:7-9 was addressed to Oliver Cowdery in connection with translation. It describes studying a matter and asking God. Keep that setting in view: the passage should not become a rule that every faithful person must experience the same physical sensation for every decision. Compare it with the broader discernment guidance linked above. Faith can begin before certainty Alma 32:21, 26-28 distinguishes faith from perfect knowledge and invites a willingness to begin. As a personal exercise, separate what you know, what you hope, and what you still need to learn. That can help you bring a more honest question to prayer without claiming certainty you do not have. What should I write down? Consider the question, information you have gathered, counsel you have received, and a possible next step within your responsibility. Revisit it as circumstances change. A journal can support reflection, but it does not turn every thought into revelation. Bring your own words to the Father Matthew 6:9–13 includes reverence, daily need, forgiveness, and God’s will. You can use these themes to consider what you want to bring into a sincere prayer. What do you need today? Name an ordinary need as plainly as you can. What part of it can you act on, and what help could you ask another person to provide? Bring the whole concern to prayer, including the part you do not know how to resolve. What would willingness sound like? Consider a decision where you strongly prefer one answer. What information or wise counsel would help you remain teachable? Write a prayerful question that leaves room to learn without handing your responsibility to someone else. What deserves another look? Return to a previous note about guidance. What remains clear, and what has changed as you learned more? Give thanks for what has helped, keep open questions visible, and choose a responsible next step within your own stewardship. records.title: Light Received Over Time
records.pageTitle: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.text: Recognize and remember Light Received Over Time Explore and study Step away and pray Jesus withdraws into the wilderness to pray alone. In the stillness, He shows the closeness, trust and renewal found in communion with the Father. Luke 5:16 In Using the Supernal Gift of Prayer , Elder Richard G. Scott describes seeking answers through prayer, thought, work, and patient action. He explains that understanding may arrive in portions. He also describes peace as a confirming witness in his own experience. Read his account as a personal testimony while making room for the questions you are still working through. Conference video · 14:58 Using the Supernal Gift of Prayer The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Read Doctrine and Covenants 6:22-23 alongside his teaching. The Lord reminds Oliver of peace connected with a particular question. As a personal reflection, write what you remember and what it helped you understand. Keep any unresolved question beside it. Remembering an experience does not require adding certainty about something it did not answer. Watch and reflect: What have I already received that deserves patient attention?

records.title: What If No Answer Comes?
records.pageTitle: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.text: Explore and study Keep a question open together Two sisters walk together while one shares a question she has not resolved. They do not need to force an answer; patient companionship can help faith endure while understanding grows. Read Alma 32 Waiting for an answer can be lonely, especially when the question matters deeply. A quiet prayer or an uncertain feeling is not, by itself, a verdict on your faith. Latter-day Saint teaching makes room for guidance that comes gradually and for thoughtful decisions made without a detailed instruction. You can keep seeking, talk with someone you trust, and take time to gather what you need. Conference video · 12:41 A Framework for Personal Revelation Official Church talk; original focusChrist artwork Watch with a question: Elder Dale G. Renlund explains how personal revelation relates to scripture, commandments, and your own responsibility to choose. As you listen, identify what is yours to decide and what belongs to someone else. Use the discernment exercise below to consider a next step while remaining open to further guidance.

records.title: Discernment in an Ordinary Decision
records.pageTitle: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.text: Explore and study Study, ask and keep a careful record A man writes beside an open book, placing prayer, thoughtful effort and a responsible next step together. The Lord's counsel to Oliver Cowdery joins seeking God's help with patient study. Doctrine and Covenants 9:7-9 Consider this everyday example as a focusChrist application: you feel drawn to contact a friend who has been distant. Elder Dale G. Renlund's framework directs attention to scripture, your responsibilities, God's commandments, and openness to further guidance. You can choose to offer a kind message. Your friend remains free to respond, decline, or ask for space. An impression to care for someone does not give you authority to decide their life. Explore and study Seek counsel with an open heart Two women pause beside their bicycles for a thoughtful conversation. Wise counsel can broaden a decision while leaving prayer, agency and responsibility with the person who must choose. Read Doctrine and Covenants 9 Questions to consider before acting Is this kind? Is it mine to decide? What information or consent do I need? These questions are personal reflection aids. They do not certify an impression as revelation. You can act thoughtfully while remaining willing to learn and change.

records.title: Three Passages for a More Thoughtful Prayer Life
records.pageTitle: How Do Prayer and Personal Revelation Work?
records.text: Prayer without performance Matthew 6:5-13 places Jesus's teaching on prayer beside cautions about public display and empty repetition. The prayer He teaches includes God's will, daily needs, forgiveness, and deliverance. Consider which part is closest to your concern. You may pray in ordinary words; a polished explanation is not a prerequisite for seeking God. Explore and study Prayer before the Father A man prays privately beside an open book, echoing Jesus's teaching in Matthew 6 that prayer is sincere communion with the Father rather than a public performance. Read Matthew 6 Study and responsibility Doctrine and Covenants 9:7-9 was addressed to Oliver Cowdery in connection with translation. It describes studying a matter and asking God. Keep that setting in view: the passage should not become a rule that every faithful person must experience the same physical sensation for every decision. Compare it with the broader discernment guidance linked above. Faith can begin before certainty Alma 32:21, 26-28 distinguishes faith from perfect knowledge and invites a willingness to begin. As a personal exercise, separate what you know, what you hope, and what you still need to learn. That can help you bring a more honest question to prayer without claiming certainty you do not have. What should I write down? Consider the question, information you have gathered, counsel you have received, and a possible next step within your responsibility. Revisit it as circumstances change. A journal can support reflection, but it does not turn every thought into revelation.

records.title: Is this the restored Church of Jesus Christ?
records.pageTitle: Is this the restored Church of Jesus Christ?
records.text: Answers / Stand Forever / The restored Church What does it mean to speak of the restored Church of Jesus Christ? Study its teachings about the Savior, authority, covenants, and service through primary sources, then connect those claims with thoughtful personal inquiry. Study the claim and the life it invites This is the fourth foundational question in the Stand Forever study. Latter-day Saints believe that Jesus Christ restored His Church through Joseph Smith, including priesthood authority and ordinances. Understanding that belief involves more than learning an organization’s name: it includes asking what the Church teaches about Christ and what its members covenant to do. Use two pages in your notebook. On one, record a claim and the source that makes it. On the other, record your questions and observations. A historical question, a doctrinal question, and a personal spiritual question may call for different kinds of inquiry. Keeping them distinct lets you examine each carefully without losing the relationship between them. Begin with one scripture section. The videos and linked companion studies give you places to continue, so this page can support several study sessions rather than a single quick visit. 1. Begin with Jesus Christ as the foundation Ephesians 2 describes reconciliation through Christ and a community whose members are no longer strangers. Verses 19–22 use the image of a household and a building, with apostles and prophets in the foundation and Jesus Christ as the chief cornerstone. The chapter places belonging within the redeeming work of Christ. Explore and study Keep Jesus Christ at the center Jesus Christ stands among attentive disciples as their teacher and sure foundation. Around Him, strangers can become fellow citizens in a covenant community built upon His peace. Read Ephesians 2:13–22 Read verses 13–22 together. Ask how the architectural image serves the chapter’s larger account of reconciliation. Latter-day Saints connect this language with their belief in a Church led through apostles and prophets. The passage itself does not narrate nineteenth-century events; studying that connection also requires the Restoration sources below. Read Ephesians 2:13–22 Keep Christ central What does this passage say brings people near? How should a community centered on Jesus Christ treat a person who feels like a stranger? Study the identity and redeeming work of Jesus Christ → 2. Read an early account of belief and order Doctrine and Covenants 20 combines an account of the Church’s beginnings with teachings, responsibilities, and ordinances. Its opening identifies the Church’s organization in 1830. Later passages describe faith in Jesus Christ, repentance, baptism, and the Holy Ghost, as well as responsibilities within the community. Explore and study Christ at the heart of the restored Church An open book, paper and inkwell bring the written revelation behind the Church's 1830 organization into view. Its doctrine, ordinances and community life all lead back to Jesus Christ. Read Doctrine and Covenants 20 For an initial reading, pair verses 1–12 with verses 17–37. Mark the difference between the historical statements and the theological claims. This is a primary religious text for what Latter-day Saints understand the restored Church to teach. Reading it carefully helps you ask more specific questions about authority, scripture, and the meaning of membership. Read Doctrine and Covenants 20 Make a source-based question Which claim would I like to understand more fully? What original account or passage would help me investigate it? Continue with Joseph Smith and the historical record → For a contemporary statement of these beliefs, watch the message below and read the Restoration proclamation within its transcript. Video · Reflection image Hear Him Russell M. Nelson teaches about hearing Jesus Christ and presents the 2020 Restoration proclamation. Read the proclamation within the full message. Official Church video · April 2020. Reflection image: Jesus Christ studying with two attentive listeners. Read the full message 3. See the responsibilities of belonging Explore and study Consider a covenant in practice A family arrives at an older neighbor's door with groceries and a warm meal. In that simple offering, the baptismal promise to bear burdens and give comfort becomes personal. Mosiah 18:8-10 In Mosiah 18 , Alma teaches people preparing for baptism. Verses 8–10 describe willingness to bear burdens, mourn with others, offer comfort, and stand as witnesses of God. These commitments give concrete meaning to a covenant community. Read through verse 16 to keep the invitation connected to the account of baptism. The passage helps you examine what discipleship asks of people in relation to one another. As an application, consider a place where you have received care and a person whose burden you could help carry. Service is worth practicing thoughtfully, without assuming you already know another person’s needs. Read Mosiah 18:8–16 Turn a covenant into care Who needs companionship, practical help, or patient listening? What small act could I offer respectfully this week? 4. Examine the gospel at the center In 3 Nephi 27 , the disciples ask Jesus about the name of the Church. His answer connects His name with His gospel. Verses 13–22 focus on His mission, His being lifted upon the cross, repentance, baptism, and sanctification through receiving the Holy Ghost. Explore and study Examine the gospel Christ describes Jesus Christ teaches a disciple who listens closely. His gospel is more than a statement of belief; it is a call to repent, follow Him and become changed through His grace. Read 3 Nephi 27 Read the chapter’s opening alongside that explanation. The name and the life of the community belong together in this account. When exploring the restored Church, look at what its sources teach about Jesus Christ, how ordinances point toward Him, and what discipleship asks people to become. Observations about a community can be meaningful while still leaving historical or doctrinal questions to investigate directly. Read 3 Nephi 27:1–22 Notice the connection How does Jesus describe His gospel here? Which part would you like to study or practice more intentionally? Explore temples and covenant worship → Watch with a question in mind Continue from the Restoration message above into the invitation to belong and serve. Keep the original transcript beside your notes. Identify a teaching, follow its scripture references, and separate the speaker’s words from your own application. Video · Original publisher thumbnail Come, Join with Us Dieter F. Uchtdorf speaks about belonging, discipleship, and making room for people with questions. Consider how an invitation becomes daily community life. Official Church YouTube channel · October 2013 Read the full message Connect careful study with lived discipleship Read: choose one original passage and summarize its claim in a sentence. Compare: follow a related reference or companion study instead of relying on a quotation alone. Reflect: record what is clearer and what remains a real question. Act: choose an appropriate step in prayer, service, conversation, or further research. If you study with others, give each person room to say what they understand without requiring a declaration of certainty. You can ask a Church member how a covenant shapes daily life, read a historical account together, or offer help in your own community. An encounter is one part of inquiry; it does not replace reading the sources. Explore and study Study a claim together Three friends gather around a source, listening carefully and giving each person room for a sincere question about belief or discipleship. Read Mosiah 18 Return to your notes after your chosen step. Which question became more specific? What source should come next? A coherent study grows through these connections, not through the number of tabs you open. Bring a source-based question to Ask , or explore General Conference for more messages. Check AI-assisted explanations against their original references. Read the original sources The scripture explanations above draw on Ephesians 2 , Doctrine and Covenants 20 , Mosiah 18 , and 3 Nephi 27 . The two videos link to official Church publications. Reading sequences and reflection prompts are focusChrist study aids, not additional Church doctrine. Ephesians 2: Reconciliation and the cornerstone Doctrine and Covenants 20: Organization, belief, and ordinances Mosiah 18: A covenant community 3 Nephi 27: The name of the Church and Christ’s gospel Continue the four-question study These studies belong together. Keep your notes as you move between them: what the sources teach, what you have experienced, what remains open, and what you want to do next. records.title: Settle This in Your Hearts
records.keywords: settle this in your hearts Settle Your Heart, Settle This in Your Hearts, Neil L. Andersen, settled faith
records.text: Answers / Settle Your Heart Give your heart to Jesus Christ, and keep learning to follow Him. Begin with Elder Neil L. Andersen’s September 15, 2026 BYU devotional, then explore scripture, related messages, and faithful choices in everyday life. A willing heart, a continuing journey Settling your heart on Christ is a deliberate commitment to follow Him. It can coexist with questions that need patient study. Elder Andersen’s devotional invites listeners to turn their thoughts more often toward the Savior and to embrace the Book of Mormon more fully. “To settle this in your heart is to courageously choose the road of discipleship, with a determination to never turn away.” Elder Neil L. Andersen · Hear this in the recording · 8:34 Use the original message as your starting point. The scripture connections below are a focusChrist companion study across the Latter-day Saint canon; they do not imply that Elder Andersen used every pictured story. His excerpts and the recording transcript below are identified separately. BYU devotional · September 15, 2026 Settle This in Your Hearts Listen to Elder Andersen’s invitation to give your heart to Jesus Christ. Notice his invitations to think more about the Savior and to read the Book of Mormon again. As you listen: What choice would help you respond to one of those invitations? Official BYU recording General conference · October 2015 Faith Is Not by Chance, but by Choice Elder Andersen connects faith with deliberate choices, seeking God, and continuing to follow Christ. Read his counsel with your own questions and daily habits in mind. As you listen: Which daily choice can nourish the faith you already have? Continue in the Stand Forever study Watch the BYU Devotional Open the BYU Source The devotional title draws on the Joseph Smith Translation of Luke 14 . Read the discipleship passage and its translation notes alongside the address. Read Luke 14:27–33 and its footnotes Begin with one honest reflection What do I already trust about Jesus Christ? What question am I still studying? What faithful action can I take while that study continues? Keep all three answers in view. Meet the Savior in the New Testament Bring questions, notice His compassion, and respond to His invitation. “Immerse yourself deeply into the divine mission, the perfect life, the life-changing teachings, the incomparable Atonement, and the breathtaking promises He offers you.” Elder Neil L. Andersen · Hear this in the recording · 17:10 Explore and study · Mark 9:20–27 Bring the faith you have Christ bends toward a boy with the boy’s father beside them. His attention rests on the child, and the father brings an honest appeal. The father does not pretend to possess an untroubled certainty. He asks for help with both his child’s suffering and his own belief. Jesus takes the boy by the hand and lifts him. A settled heart can still speak honestly about what it needs. Read Mark 9:20–27 Consider: What would it sound like to bring your real question to Christ, rather than the question you think you ought to have? Explore and study · Luke 13:10–17 Stand upright in His care An older woman stands upright before Jesus in the synagogue. Their eyes meet, and the people around them watch. Jesus notices a woman who has suffered for eighteen years, calls her forward, and frees her from her infirmity. He identifies her as a daughter of Abraham. Read beyond the healing to His answer when someone objects: His care gives a person’s dignity priority over the complaint. Read Luke 13:10–17 Consider: Whose needs might you notice more carefully as you turn your thoughts toward the Savior? Explore and study · John 5:5–9 Respond to His invitation A man holds his rolled bed near the pool of Bethesda and looks into Christ’s face. The conversation has led to a new beginning. The man describes a difficulty he has not been able to overcome. Jesus then gives a specific invitation: rise, take up the bed, and walk. This account witnesses the Savior’s power; it does not promise that every present illness will end immediately. Consider the next faithful action you can take while continuing to seek His help. Read John 5:5–9 Consider: What is one concrete response you can make to a teaching of Jesus this week? Choose faith in the Old Testament Read commitment in its setting of grief, pressure, and an uncertain future. “For many of us, this is not something that suddenly falls upon us. Rather, it comes as our faith in Christ and spiritual sensitivity grow step by step, while at the same time experiencing the distastefulness and emptiness of the world’s allure.” Elder Neil L. Andersen · Hear this in the recording · 4:33 Explore and study · Ruth 1:14–18 Choose faithful companionship Ruth rests her hand on Naomi’s arm beside the road. Both women carry loss into the conversation, and Ruth chooses to remain with her. Ruth’s commitment includes a people, a place, and God. The journey ahead is still uncertain when she makes that choice. Read her words beside Naomi’s grief, then follow their arrival in Bethlehem. Faithfulness can begin with staying close to someone who needs you. Read Ruth 1:14–18 Consider: Which relationship calls for patient loyalty rather than a quick answer? Explore and study · Daniel 3:16–18 Trust before the outcome is known Three men stand before the king and answer him together. Their expressions are serious; their decision comes before the rescue. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego believe God can deliver them. They also state that their worship will not depend on receiving the outcome they desire. Their answer helps distinguish trust in God from an attempt to bargain with Him. Read the whole chapter without overlooking the risk at this moment. Read Daniel 3:16–18 Consider: Which commitment can you keep while the outcome of a difficult situation remains unknown? Come closer through the Book of Mormon Attend to Christ’s trust, His love for praying disciples, and His care for children. “Second, embrace more completely the Book of Mormon. When was the last time you read the Book of Mormon from the first page until the last? Was it when you were on your mission? If so, it is time to read it again.” Elder Neil L. Andersen · Hear this in the recording · 17:58 Explore and study · 3 Nephi 18:36–37 Receive a responsibility to serve Christ rests a hand on an older disciple’s shoulder and meets his eyes. Other disciples attend to the exchange. Before departing, Jesus touches His chosen disciples one by one and gives them power to give the Holy Ghost. This moment follows His teaching about the sacrament, prayer, and welcoming others. The gift leads into service. The picture’s precise placement of His hand is an artistic choice; the passage records His touch and the authority He gives. Read 3 Nephi 18:36–37 Consider: How can a responsibility you have received become a more personal act of service? Explore and study · 3 Nephi 19:24–26 Continue in prayer Jesus looks warmly upon the praying disciples. Nephi’s face is lifted toward Him, and the others continue their prayer. After praying to the Father, Jesus returns to His disciples. The record describes His smile and the light upon His countenance as they continue praying. Linger over His relationship with the Father and His love for these disciples. Settled faith is nourished through that relationship, not simply through determination alone. Read 3 Nephi 19:24–26 Consider: What helps your prayers become an ongoing relationship rather than only a request in an emergency? Explore and study · 3 Nephi 26:14 Listen with humility A child speaks to attentive adults while Jesus stands beside him, listening. The adults give the child their full attention. Jesus ministers to the children and enables them to speak marvelous things to their fathers. The record does not give us those words to reproduce. It does invite us to notice that receiving truth requires humility, even from experienced adults. Read this moment with the surrounding account of Christ’s teaching and ministry. Read 3 Nephi 26:14 Consider: Whom might you hear more carefully if you expected to learn rather than only to teach? Remember willingness and seek wisdom Begin with the Son’s willing love, then follow a young seeker from scripture into prayer. Elder Andersen’s counsel about the heart and mind offers a way to approach these companion passages with commitment and honest questions. “To settle this in your heart does not mean you have to settle everything in your mind.” Elder Neil L. Andersen · Hear this in the recording · 10:46 Explore and study · Moses 4:1–2 Begin with the Savior’s willing love The Beloved Son stands with His hand over His heart, attentive to His Father. This devotional interpretation looks to His willing response before mortal life. Moses records the Son’s acceptance of the Father’s will and His desire that the glory belong to the Father. Read the contrast in these verses carefully. Our study of settled faith begins with the Redeemer’s love and willingness, not with a claim that human resolve saves us. The unseen setting is an artistic interpretation of the premortal account. Read Moses 4:1–2 Consider: What changes when you begin a difficult act of obedience by remembering the Savior’s willing love? Explore and study · Joseph Smith—History 1:11–13 Let scripture lead you to ask Young Joseph pauses over an open Bible. A passage has given him something to consider and a decision to make. In his history, Joseph recalls repeatedly reflecting on James’s invitation to ask God for wisdom. He describes confusion before describing his determination to pray. His account gives an important place to reading, reflection, and a sincere question. Continue into the following verses to read his testimony of what happened when he went to pray. Read Joseph Smith—History 1:11–13 Consider: Which passage deserves a second, slower reading before you decide what to do next? Live the covenant through work and hardship The Restoration’s history includes both building together and calling upon God in suffering. As you read these accounts, remember the spiritual experiences that have helped you choose to follow Christ. “The decision to permanently follow Jesus Christ is greatly bolstered by the impressions, promptings, and unforgettable spiritual moments you experience in your life.” Elder Neil L. Andersen · Hear this in the recording · 5:24 Explore and study · Doctrine and Covenants 95:8–11 Give faith the work of your hands Workers guide a stone into place while another watches with a trowel in hand. The work requires their attention and cooperation. The Lord’s instruction to build His house in Kirtland called for a real response from people with limited resources. The temple’s history includes labor, sacrifice, and shared effort. These unnamed workers are an illustration of that effort. Consider how a conviction becomes visible through patient work alongside other people. Read Doctrine and Covenants 95:8–11 Consider: What useful task can you begin, even if you cannot yet see the whole result? Explore and study · Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 Speak honestly in hardship Joseph sits in the confined jail interior and turns toward the window in prayer. His hands are clasped and his expression is earnest. The prayer from Liberty Jail asks where God is amid the Saints’ suffering. The answer speaks peace and endurance into that suffering. Read both the plea and the reassurance. Faith did not make the imprisonment unreal or erase its pain. Joseph was confined with companions; this close view concentrates on his personal appeal. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 Consider: What pain do you need to name honestly in prayer, and what source of support can you receive today? Read the Church’s history of the Kirtland Temple Practice settled faith today Let daily study and ordinary kindness give your commitment a place in everyday life. “Pray more in His name. Read His words. Apply His teachings. Speak His name in reverence and conviction. Believe in His power to forgive and refine you.” Elder Neil L. Andersen · Hear this in the recording · 17:25 Explore and study · Alma 37:6–7 Return to the word together Two women study an open scripture volume together. One points to a passage while the other pauses with a pencil and notebook. A settled pattern can be small enough to repeat: read a passage, ask what it says, write a question, and return the next day. Alma’s teaching about small and simple means offers a useful companion to that practice. This present-day scene illustrates shared study; the women are not people from a recorded historical event. Read Alma 37:6–7 Consider: What modest reading habit would you be willing to keep for the next seven days? Explore and study · Matthew 25:35–40 Carry belief into kindness Neighbors arrive with a meal and a bag of fruit. Their eyes meet at the doorway as the food changes hands. Jesus connects care for people in need with service to Him. A settled heart can take the shape of a visit, a meal, a patient conversation, or reliable help. Let this moment prompt a practical response to His teaching. Choose a kindness that respects the other person’s needs and dignity. Read Matthew 25:35–40 Consider: Who could receive a specific act of care from you this week? Continue with Elder Andersen These messages return to related concerns: receiving a witness, protecting faith through hardship, and remembering spiritual strength. Read each in its own setting, then consider what it adds to your study. General conference · October 2014 Joseph Smith Elder Andersen bears testimony of Joseph Smith and invites personal spiritual confirmation. Pair his message with Joseph’s own account and careful attention to the history and sources. As you listen: What do the original account and the speaker’s testimony each contribute to your study? Continue in the Joseph Smith study General conference · October 2012 Trial of Your Faith Elder Andersen speaks about protecting and strengthening faith through trials. Follow his counsel into prayer, scripture, worship, and the support of other disciples. As you listen: Which source of strength can you reach for in a present trial? Official Church video and text General conference · April 2020 Spiritually Defining Memories Elder Andersen invites listeners to remember and preserve experiences of spiritual strength. Consider what you have received and how recording it could help you return to it. As you listen: What experience of goodness, guidance, or peace do you want to remember? Official Church video and text For another Joseph Smith message, read the Church Newsroom report of Elder Andersen’s February 2025 Utah State University devotional . Continue with the Joseph Smith study for scripture, history, and further original sources. Carry one invitation into the week A seven-day reading practice Listen to the devotional and choose one of Elder Andersen’s two invitations: think more about the Savior or embrace the Book of Mormon more completely. This seven-day practice is a companion study, not a timetable he prescribed. Read one pictured New Testament account in full. Compare Ruth’s choice with the three men’s answer in Daniel. Read the Book of Mormon accounts and notice Christ’s attention to people. Read Joseph’s account of asking God for wisdom. Write a remembered experience of guidance, kindness, or peace. Choose and carry out one act of service. Record what you learned. Make room for a careful question Elder Andersen teaches that settling your heart does not require every question in your mind to be resolved. He also describes study and reason as part of spiritual learning. Write your question precisely. Separate the passage’s words, a speaker’s testimony, historical evidence, and your own interpretation. Use the linked original sources, speak with someone you trust, and bring the question to God. A sincere question deserves more than a hurried answer. Remember what strengthened you What helped you notice the Savior this week? Which passage will you return to? What remains unresolved? Record these honestly; a quiet experience does not need to become a dramatic story to be worth remembering. Original message and sources The original devotional was delivered September 15, 2026. At the time this study was prepared, BYU offered the video and audio while its edited transcript was forthcoming. The reporting below provides additional context; the linked scriptures are the source for each pictured account. Punctuation and paragraph breaks have been added for reading; brackets mark wording that remains uncertain. BYU’s edited text is the authoritative written version when available.
