records.excerpt: A source-grounded explanation of Latter-day Saint beliefs about death, the spirit world, resurrection, judgment, and eternal life through Jesus Christ.

records.title: Christ Meets Us in Grief
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: A Savior who knows sorrow Christ Meets Us in Grief Martha came to Jesus after her brother Lazarus had died. In John 11:21-27 , she speaks of her loss and her belief in a future resurrection. Jesus directs that hope to Himself. The promise of life rests in who He is and what He can do. Explore and study Christ listens to Martha Martha brings her loss and her belief to Jesus. His promise of resurrection begins with an invitation to trust Him. John 11:21–27 Later, when Mary and those with her are weeping, Jesus weeps too. Read John 11:32-36 beside His conversation with Martha. Confidence in resurrection and compassion for present sorrow belong in the same account. Tears do not disprove faith. The raising of Lazarus in John 11:38-44 witnesses Christ's power over death. Lazarus returned to mortal life; the Savior's Resurrection opens the way to immortal life. That distinction helps us read the miracle with hope while recognizing that loved ones are not ordinarily restored to us during mortality. Pause and reflect: a promise and a sorrow Notice what Martha believes and what still hurts. If you wish, name one promise you want to hold and one loss you need to speak about. Prayer can include both. If you are accompanying someone who mourns, begin by listening to what they want to share. If your question begins with a recent loss, the Grief and Faith study offers more room for sorrow, companionship, and practical support. You can begin there and return here when you want to explore the promises of resurrection. The Savior who weeps with those who mourn also overcomes death. Continue with Mary Magdalene at the empty tomb .

records.title: Mary Magdalene Sees the Living Lord
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: The foundation of Christian hope Mary Magdalene Sees the Living Lord Explore and study Morning at the empty tomb Morning light enters an open garden tomb, holding the astonishment and hope of the Resurrection. Mary's grief gives way when the risen Jesus calls her by name. John 20:1-18 The empty tomb is only the beginning of Mary's morning. In John 20:11-18 , she is still weeping and thinks Jesus' body has been taken. When He calls her by name, she recognizes Him. She then tells the disciples that she has seen the Lord. John presents a personal encounter with the risen Jesus. A witness that reaches into personal loss In And There Shall Be No More Death , Elder Paul V. Johnson reflects on resurrection after his adult daughter's death from cancer. He teaches that Christ makes the reunion of spirit and body permanent. Read his message beside Mary's witness: Christian hope rests in a living Savior. The message includes illness and bereavement. You may prefer to read a little at a time, beginning with the teaching about resurrection. General conference video and text And There Shall Be No More Death The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2016 Explore and study Mary recognizes the risen Savior Jesus calls Mary by name, and she recognizes Him. Her encounter turns the morning of sorrow toward the news that He lives. John 20:11–18 Pause and reflect: what changes when Christ is risen? Compare Mary's concern at the tomb with the message she carries to the disciples. What does Christ's Resurrection let you hope for? Write your own question beside the passage and return to it as the study continues. Mary's witness opens a larger question: what does Christ's Resurrection make possible for every person?

records.title: Everyone Will Be Resurrected
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: Christ's victory over physical death Everyone Will Be Resurrected When the risen Jesus comes among His disciples in Luke 24:36-43 , He offers peace and invites them to see His hands and feet. He distinguishes His resurrected body from a spirit and eats in their presence. Resurrection is more than the continued life of the spirit after death. Explore and study Peace among the disciples Christ comes among His disciples and offers peace. His hands and His presence testify that the One they mourned is alive. John 20:19–23 Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 15:20-22 that Christ's Resurrection makes resurrection possible for all. Later, in 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 and 1 Corinthians 15:51-57 , he describes mortality giving way to immortality and gives thanks to God for victory through Jesus Christ. This universal gift is not something we earn by being strong enough or by grieving in a particular way. Thomas and the witness we receive Explore and study An invitation to Thomas The Savior invites Thomas to witness for himself. John records Thomas’s answer of faith and Christ’s blessing on those who believe without seeing. John 20:24–29 Thomas was absent when Jesus first appeared to the assembled disciples. In John 20:24-29 , Jesus later invites Thomas to behold His hands and believe. The account also speaks to readers who have not seen Him. John explains his purpose in John 20:30-31 : his written witness invites belief in Jesus Christ and life through His name. Questions about resurrection can be brought to these witnesses patiently. Consider what they testify that Jesus did, then what His living reality means for the person you miss. Hope does not require you to invent details that scripture has not supplied. Knowing that body and spirit will be reunited helps us distinguish resurrection from the life of the spirit between death and resurrection .

records.title: What Happens Between Death and Resurrection?
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: The spirit continues to live What Happens Between Death and Resurrection? At death, body and spirit separate. Alma 40:11-14 describes spirits continuing to live while they await resurrection. Alma speaks of paradise as peace and rest for the righteous, and of a painful condition for the wicked. These are conditions in the spirit world, distinct from the final reunion of body and spirit. Explore and study Hope between death and resurrection In a quiet garden, an older man pauses over Alma's words about the life of the spirit after death. The promise of resurrection through Jesus Christ brings hope close to the memories he carries. Read Alma 40 Read on to Alma 40:21-23 . The body and spirit are to be reunited, and a person is brought before God. Keeping these teachings together helps us avoid treating the spirit world as the end of the story. The Church study guide on the spirit world offers further passages and questions for careful study. Christ's work reaches those who have died Doctrine and Covenants 138:12-19 describes faithful spirits awaiting the Savior's arrival and the redemption He makes possible. The vision then explains how His message reaches others: in Doctrine and Covenants 138:29-35 , Christ commissions messengers from among the righteous to teach those in darkness. They teach faith, repentance, and the ordinances of the gospel. The vision does not describe salvation as automatic. Doctrine and Covenants 138:58-59 connects redemption with repentance and the ordinances of God's house. Latter-day Saints perform proxy ordinances in temples because those who have died cannot perform these earthly ordinances for themselves. Each person remains free to accept or reject what is offered. Continue with the temple study to explore that connection. General conference video and text The Redemption of the Dead and the Testimony of Jesus The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2000 Elder Christofferson explains how temple service bears witness of Christ’s Resurrection and the reach of His Atonement. He makes clear that people who have died retain their agency: proxy ordinances take effect only if they accept them. General conference video and text The Vision of the Redemption of the Dead The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2018 President Ballard recalls the losses Joseph F. Smith endured and invites us to study the revelation he received. Doctrine and Covenants 138:29-35 describes Christ commissioning messengers to carry His gospel to the dead. Pause and reflect: hope with humility Find what the vision says Christ and His messengers do. Then separate those teachings from questions it does not answer about a loved one's daily experience. We can trust God's care without claiming to know where a particular person is or what they are doing. Christ's work reaches across death while honoring repentance and agency. Explore how this hope connects with judgment and eternal life with God .

records.title: Resurrection, Judgment, and Eternal Life
records.pageTitle: What Do Latter-day Saints Believe Happens After Death?
records.text: Mercy, agency, and our eternal future Resurrection, Judgment, and Eternal Life Living forever and receiving eternal life are related teachings with different meanings. Resurrection reunites body and spirit in immortality. Eternal life is life with God and the kind of life He lives, made possible through Jesus Christ. The Church study guide on eternal life explains this distinction. In John 17:3 , Jesus connects eternal life with knowing the Father and Himself. Judgment is God's work. Doctrine and Covenants 137:7-9 addresses people who died without knowledge of the gospel and teaches that the Lord considers both works and the desires of the heart. His knowledge of a person reaches beyond what family, neighbors, or observers can see. These verses invite trust in His justice and mercy, rather than conclusions about another person's eternal destiny. Latter-day Saints also believe that family relationships can endure through the Savior and temple covenants. That hope belongs within God's loving plan and respects each person's agency. The families and eternity study develops these promises with attention to the questions real families carry. What do the kingdoms of glory teach us? The restored gospel describes different kingdoms of glory and invites every person to come to Christ. President Oaks discusses these teachings in relation to our desires, choices, repentance, and the people we become. His message helps distinguish the gift of resurrection from exaltation with God. Read it as an invitation to follow the Savior. It does not give us a way to assign other people to a kingdom. General conference video and text Kingdoms of Glory The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · October 2023 President Oaks teaches about the celestial, terrestrial, and telestial kingdoms. He connects final judgment with our choices and what we become through Jesus Christ, repentance, and covenant faithfulness. Explore and study Bring questions to the reading together Three generations gather around the resurrection account and listen to one another. Shared hope in the risen Christ can hold both testimony and honest questions. Read John 20 Pause and reflect: leave judgment with the Lord What do these teachings tell you about God's understanding of His children? What remains unknown to you? Consider a way to speak of someone who has died that honors their life and leaves final judgment with the Savior. These promises invite trust in the Savior's character. His ministry in the Book of Mormon lets us study that character through individual encounters.

Christ’s knowledge of pain can sustain faith alongside medical care and the help of people who stay near. Alma 7:11–13 Alma 7:11-13 teaches that the Savior takes upon Himself pains, sicknesses, death, and infirmities, and knows how to help His people. The hope of resurrection is especially personal when the body is vulnerable. Prayer, medical care, and the help of loved ones can belong in the same day; needing treatment does not diminish faith. When loneliness makes life feel smaller Explore and study A conversation on the bench A shared bench becomes a place to speak and be heard. Hope in Christ can move us to notice someone, make time, and offer dependable companionship. Matthew 25:35–40 After a death or a difficult change, familiar routines can become quiet. The individual attention in 3 Nephi 11:14-17 invites reflection on each person's worth to Christ. As a practical response, consider one person you might call, sit beside, or invite for a walk. A small connection can be a way to give or receive care today. When you are carrying someone else's needs Explore and study Rest for the caregiver She pauses at the kitchen table and meets His eyes. His invitation to come and find rest can accompany the practical help, rest, and support a caregiver needs. Matthew 11:28–30 Caregiving can include devotion, exhaustion, and questions about what lies ahead. In Matthew 11:28-30 , Jesus invites the weary to come to Him and learn of Him. You can bring both love and fatigue into prayer. Letting another person share a task or sit with you can be one way to receive the burden-bearing care taught in Mosiah 18:8-10 . When the future is uncertain Explore and study Hope when the way is unclear The work on the desk can wait for a moment of attentive conversation. Trust in Christ’s living hope can support a next faithful step when the future remains uncertain. 1 Peter 1:3–5 Work, responsibilities, and unanswered questions can narrow our attention to what might go wrong. Moroni 7:41-48 grounds enduring hope in Christ's Atonement and Resurrection, and joins that hope to charity. Your worth and eternal possibilities reach beyond one result. You can take the next honest step, seek wise help, and continue caring for others while an answer is still unknown. A reflection for your own circumstances Which scene feels nearest to your life today? Read its linked passage and name what it actually teaches about Jesus Christ. Then choose one small response: a prayer, an honest conversation, an offer of help, or a request for support. You do not need to resolve every question about eternity before receiving or giving love today. Choose a question from your own circumstances and carry it into the official readings and messages below .

records.title: What Is Eternal Marriage?
records.text: Answers / Eternal marriage Latter-day Saints believe a husband and wife may be sealed in a temple by priesthood authority so their marriage can continue after death. The ceremony is sacred, but eternal marriage is more than a single day: it is a covenant life of faith in Jesus Christ, repentance, loyalty, service, and love. This teaching can touch deep hopes and deep wounds. Marital status does not measure a person’s worth or place in the Church. Covenants never require anyone to remain in danger or tolerate abuse. Christ at the center A sealing begins a covenant journey Jesus taught that God intends marriage to be a union, not a contest for power. Latter-day Saint teaching adds that the sealing authority Christ described can bind on earth and in heaven. In the temple, spouses covenant with God and with one another. Those promises are made possible through Jesus Christ and become a daily invitation to follow His way. Eternal does not mean that an unhealthy pattern should simply last forever. A Christ-centered marriage grows through agency, humility, equal counsel, forgiveness, fidelity, tenderness, and truth. Both spouses remain responsible for their own choices, and God’s judgment is perfectly just and merciful. Marriage through time One gospel ideal, lived in many circumstances These scenes move from Eden to the present, showing couples and families learning covenant love across different eras and circumstances. In every scene, Jesus Christ is the Savior and Teacher who calls His disciples to covenant love, equal partnership, fidelity, and mercy. 01 · Eden The beginning: companionship and shared stewardship Latter-day Saints read Adam and Eve’s union as marriage established by God. Their story begins with companionship, cleaving to one another, and becoming one while each remains a moral agent. Read Moses 3:18–24 02 · Ancient home Covenant character grows in ordinary life A lasting marriage is shaped in daily choices: loyalty, honest work, hospitality, patience, and care. The setting is symbolic; the principle is that sacred promises are lived at home. Read Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 03 · The Savior’s world Christ teaches unity without domination Jesus pointed marriage back to God’s intention that husband and wife become one. His gospel also rejects control and invites both disciples to lead through service, truth, repentance, and love. Read Matthew 19:4–6 04 · Restoration Sealing hope returns Latter-day Saints believe Elijah restored sealing keys in the Kirtland Temple. That authority joins family hope to Jesus Christ’s power over death and asks covenant keepers to live faithfully now. Read Doctrine and Covenants 110:13–16 05 · Dignity and belonging Divine worth is never a marital ranking A temple sealing is sacred in Latter-day Saint belief, but it is not a measure of human worth. People who are civilly married, single, divorced, widowed, in an interfaith family, or not yet sealed deserve full dignity, welcome, and Christlike care. Study belonging in the Church 06 · Today and onward A covenant journey, not a perfect photograph Temple sealing begins a life of discipleship. Husband and wife walk side by side as equal partners, relying on the Savior’s grace and choosing again and again to counsel, repent, forgive, protect, and serve. Study equal partnership with Elder Soares Every person is of infinite worth. Marriage and sealing status describe circumstances and covenants. They do not establish a hierarchy of souls. Jesus Christ’s invitation to come unto Him is extended to all. A scripture path Trace the doctrine, then bring it home Read one passage at a time. Ask what it teaches about God, covenant, agency, and the way two disciples should treat each other. Matthew 16:19 Christ speaks of authority to bind on earth and in heaven. Moses 3:18, 21–24 Companionship and becoming one without erasing either person. Doctrine and Covenants 42:22 Wholehearted marital loyalty. Doctrine and Covenants 131:1–4 Eternal marriage in the doctrine of exaltation. Doctrine and Covenants 132:19 Sealing, covenant conditions, and the Holy Spirit of Promise. Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–46 Influence through persuasion, gentleness, love, and integrity, without compulsion. Moroni 7:45–48 Charity as a gift from Christ and a daily way of loving. John 17:20–23 Unity patterned after the Father and the Son. A context note: Doctrine and Covenants 132 addresses more than marriage and includes historical questions about plural marriage. Read verse 19 in its full section and use the official sources below rather than making it carry every question by itself. Four voices, four study questions Watch, read, and reflect Conference talk · October 2008 Celestial Marriage President Russell M. Nelson explains temple marriage, individual discipleship, and covenant faithfulness. Ask: What makes Christ a partner in an eternal marriage? Russell M. Nelson Conference talk · April 2013 Marriage: Watch and Learn Elder L. Whitney Clayton describes commitment, faith, repentance, humility, respect, loyalty, and love. Ask: Which quiet habit would bring more light into a relationship? L. Whitney Clayton Conference talk · October 2022 In Partnership with the Lord Elder Ulisses Soares teaches full and equal partnership, walking side by side with Christ. Ask: Where could counsel replace control? Ulisses Soares Conference talk · April 2024 Fruit That Remains Elder Matthew L. Carpenter carefully distinguishes the covenant with God, the bond between spouses, personal faithfulness, and agency. Ask: What hope does God’s perfect justice offer? Matthew L. Carpenter Newest conference study: Eternal Marriage Is an Eternal Journey, Elder Neil L. Andersen, April 2026 Questions people carry Clear answers with room for individual circumstances Is a temple wedding automatically eternal? No. The sealing ordinance opens eternal promises, but scripture connects those promises with covenant faithfulness and ratification by the Holy Spirit of Promise. A ceremony should not be treated as a guarantee that makes choices or agency irrelevant. What is different from a civil marriage? A civil marriage establishes a legal union. A temple sealing is a priesthood ordinance in which husband and wife make sacred covenants with God and each other, with promises that can extend beyond death. Legal requirements still matter, and local practice varies. What if one spouse stops believing or breaks covenants? Each person retains agency and answers to God for individual choices. A faithful person is not mechanically stripped of every promised blessing by another person’s decisions. God will not force an unwilling or unworthy relationship to continue eternally, and individual outcomes belong to His perfect judgment. What about someone who is single, divorced, or widowed? They fully belong now. Church teaching promises every blessing of exaltation to faithful covenant keepers, but it is wise not to speculate about when, how, or with whom an individual promise will be fulfilled. Present marital status is not a spiritual ranking. Does forgiveness mean remaining in an unsafe marriage? No. Covenant language never requires tolerating abuse. Forgiveness, legal decisions, personal safety, Church membership, and the future of a marriage are related but distinct questions. Seek immediate safety and qualified local help when harm or threats are present. How can Christ be at the center today? Pray and worship together when both are willing; listen without preparing a defense; repent for your own conduct; share decisions; keep confidences and promises; serve in small ways; and invite help early. One spouse cannot do the agency-work of the other. Explore and study A Place in the Conversation An empty chair is drawn into the circle, and the arriving woman is met with warm attention. Welcoming participation begins with noticing someone and inviting them to join the conversation. Study belonging and participation A seven-day study pattern Move from doctrine to discipleship Authority Read Matthew 16:19 . Write what Christ’s sealing authority means to you. Covenant Read D&C 131:1–4 and 132:19 in context. Note every condition and promise. Charity Read Moroni 7:45–48 . Choose one quality to practice without keeping score. Equal partnership Watch Elder Soares. Ask where listening and shared counsel could deepen. Repentance Watch Elder Clayton. Name one change that belongs to you, not your spouse. Hope Read Elder Carpenter. Bring an unresolved sealing question to God without forcing an answer. Christ Read John 17:20–23 . Pray for unity founded in truth, love, and willing discipleship. A reflection to keep What does the Savior invite me to become in my closest relationships? Record one impression and one loving, safe action you can take. If you are studying alone, the same pattern can strengthen your preparation, healing, family relationships, and covenant discipleship. Official sources and further study Marriage: Gospel Study Guide What Happens in a Temple Sealing? Single Members of the Church In Crisis? Talk Now: Help for Victims of Abuse Ask a Question Families and Belonging Why Temples? Where would you like to go next? Build belonging in every family circumstance Continue from eternal marriage into divine identity, care, parenting, and family hope. When marriage includes separation or divorce Study dignity, boundaries, grief, faith, and support without an idealized story. Place eternal relationships beside Resurrection Explore the spirit world, universal resurrection through Christ, judgment, and eternal life.

records.title: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.keywords: what is the book of mormon
records.text: Answers / Book of Mormon Latter-day Saints accept the Book of Mormon as scripture and call it “Another Testament of Jesus Christ.” They do not see it as a replacement for the Bible, but as an additional witness of the Savior and His gospel. Explore the people and stories Follow the record Explore Book of Mormon Evidences Study the translation, Royal Skousen’s manuscript research, witness accounts, chiasmus, stylometry, and ancient context. Follow original sources, consider sincere questions, and return to the book’s witness of Jesus Christ. Explore the Evidences Study Begin with the Translation This is an independent Latter-day Saint study page. Official Church resources are linked for verification and further reading. Watch and study An Introduction Before You Begin Reading The official short explainer What Is the Book of Mormon? introduces the record, its setting, and its witness of Jesus Christ. Watch for the question that matters most to you: what the book contains, why Latter-day Saints read it, or how it relates to the Savior. Church video What Is the Book of Mormon? The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Then begin with the people gathered at Bountiful in 3 Nephi 11:1-17 . They hear a voice, turn their attention toward heaven, and encounter Jesus Christ. His introduction connects His identity with His suffering for the sins of the world. The people are invited to approach Him individually. How does reading this account add to the overview you just watched? What the Book Claims to Be The Book of Mormon presents itself as an ancient record of peoples in the Americas, written and abridged by prophets and translated by Joseph Smith through the gift and power of God. Its stated purpose is to persuade readers that Jesus is the Christ and to invite them to come unto Him. Why It Is Called Another Testament of Jesus Christ The book contains prophecies of Christ before His birth, teachings about His Atonement and Resurrection, and an account of the resurrected Savior appearing to people in the Americas. Jesus Christ is therefore not a side subject in the book; He is its central witness. Does It Replace the Bible? No. Latter-day Saints study the Old and New Testaments as scripture and cherish the Bible’s witness of Jesus Christ. The Book of Mormon is understood as a second scriptural witness that supports biblical teachings and can clarify or reinforce doctrines such as faith, repentance, baptism, resurrection, grace, and discipleship. Why Have More Than One Scriptural Witness? The Bible itself uses the principle that important truth can be established by multiple witnesses. Latter-day Saints see the Bible and Book of Mormon as separate records that converge on Jesus Christ. Their different histories and settings make the shared witness meaningful rather than redundant. How a Seeker Can Approach It The Church invites people to read the Book of Mormon, compare its teachings with the Bible, ponder its message, and pray for spiritual confirmation. The point is not simply to learn facts about a new book, but to test whether its teachings lead a reader toward Jesus Christ. Try Reading One Account If the book is unfamiliar, 3 Nephi 11:1-17 is a useful starting point. It tells of the resurrected Jesus appearing to a gathered people and inviting them to come forward individually. Read at your own pace, note what stands out, and keep track of your questions. You can also explore a short comparison with a Bible passage . What Does the Invitation to Pray Include? Moroni 10:3-5 invites readers to remember God's mercy, ponder, and ask sincerely in the name of Christ. Reading and reflection are part of that invitation. It need not become a demand to report a dramatic feeling after a single reading. If you are uncertain, keep track of the passage or claim you want to understand. A conversation can be more helpful when you can point to the actual words. The prayer and revelation study discusses discernment and questions that take time. Watch and study Why Nephi Keeps Returning to Jesus Christ Explore and study Follow Nephi’s stated purpose A reader pauses over an open book above a green valley. Nephi's stated purpose gives the study its center: persuading people to believe in Jesus Christ and be reconciled to God. Read 2 Nephi 25 In 2 Nephi 25:23-29 , Nephi explains why he writes and teaches about Christ. His concern includes the next generation: he wants children to understand where forgiveness is found. Read the verbs in verse 26 , then read the invitation to worship in verse 29 . Study lesson 2 Nephi 25: Saved by Jesus Christ The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The accompanying Seminary lesson explores salvation through Jesus Christ. After reading it, put Nephi's purpose into your own words. How would a family conversation change if it helped someone understand the Savior's mercy? You can begin with one experience of gratitude or one sincere question. A polished religious speech is unnecessary. Get to Know the Book by Reading It Meet the people behind its familiar passages in the Book of Mormon story journey , or begin with the Savior’s own words below. Explore and study Come forward and know The risen Jesus Christ extends His invitation to people gathered at Bountiful. Each person is welcomed to come forward and know for themselves that He is the God of Israel. 3 Nephi 11:10-17 Study a teaching, not only the book's description Alma 32:21-28, 37-43 uses the image of a seed to discuss faith and the patient care that follows an initial willingness to believe. The setting includes people who have been excluded from worship because of their poverty. Notice both the invitation to begin and the warning that growth requires continued nourishment. This is a religious account of developing faith; it is not a scientific experiment that establishes every historical claim about the book. Read the gospel invitation 2 Nephi 31:5-13, 17-21 connects Jesus's example with baptism and an ongoing life of faith, hope, and love. Read this beside the account of His ministry in 3 Nephi 11 already linked above. One explains a path of discipleship; the other portrays an encounter with the risen Savior. Together they show why the book matters in Latter-day Saint worship. Separate the questions you are asking You may be asking what the book teaches, how it came into print, whether its account is historical, or how to evaluate a spiritual conviction. Those are related but different inquiries. Reading a passage can illuminate its message; historical questions require historical evidence too. Keep a question list so one unresolved issue does not get quietly replaced by another. A reading note you can return to Record a passage, its speaker and setting, one teaching in your own words, and one question. On your next visit, start with that question rather than feeling you must begin the whole book again. People, promises, and the living Christ Walk through the stories. Come to know the Savior. The Book of Mormon carries us into homes and wilderness camps, royal courts and prisons, places of worship and fields of battle. We meet people who trust God, people who resist Him, and people who discover that repentance can change the direction of a life. Their experiences keep returning to Jesus Christ: His coming, His redeeming power, His ministry among the people, and His invitation to us. Begin with a person or moment that draws you. These stops follow the broad course of the record, beginning with the earlier Jaredite history. Some accounts overlap in time; the books sometimes return to an earlier event or follow another community. You can linger in one story and return to the journey later. About the story illustrations Each picture accompanies a passage you can open and read. The woodland landscapes, homes, clothing, and temple architecture are artistic interpretations inspired by Eastern Woodland settings, including Hopewell traditions; they do not establish where Book of Mormon events occurred. The scripture remains the source for what happens in each account. 01 · Before Lehi’s journey The brother of Jared brings his need to the Lord Long before Lehi’s family leaves Jerusalem, Jared asks his brother to pray for their families and friends. The Lord hears, preserves their language, and leads them toward a promised land. The journey begins with concern for other people, not only personal deliverance. Follow those widening prayers in Ether 1:33–43 . Preparing to cross the sea, the brother of Jared faces a practical difficulty: the vessels need light. He brings sixteen small stones to the Lord and asks Him to touch them. In Ether 3:1–16 , the Lord reveals Himself as Jesus Christ. This is an appearance of the premortal Savior in His spirit body, before His birth in mortality. His power to redeem does not begin at Bethlehem; His purpose already embraces the people who will trust Him. Explore and study Known by the Redeemer The brother of Jared comes to know the Redeemer who has spoken to him. Read how the Lord identifies Himself and explains why He has shown Himself. Read Ether 3:13–18 The ocean crossing still includes wind and waves. The people sing praises and give thanks while the Lord carries them toward shore in Ether 6:4–12 . Help has not removed the journey. It has given them light and a way forward within it. Bring a real need into your prayer What problem are you carrying? Describe it plainly. Notice how the brother of Jared combines preparation with dependence on the Lord. Consider one faithful step you can take while asking for the help you cannot provide yourself. 02 · A family leaves Jerusalem Lehi and Sariah’s family learns to follow Lehi’s call draws an entire household into the wilderness. In 1 Nephi 2:1–16 , their tents replace the familiar life they have left behind. Laman and Lemuel resist their father’s direction. Nephi also has something to work through: he cries to the Lord, and his heart is softened. Sam believes Nephi’s words in 1 Nephi 2:17–18 . These brothers share a family and a journey, but their responses are their own. Sariah’s voice becomes especially clear when her sons return safely from Jerusalem. She has feared that she has lost them. In 1 Nephi 5:1–9 , relief leads into a declaration of what she now knows about the Lord’s care. Her place in the account is more than standing beside Lehi: she speaks, struggles, rejoices, and bears witness. The wilderness story also includes hunger, a broken bow, the death of Ishmael, and a ship that must be built. Read 1 Nephi 16:18–35 and 1 Nephi 17:1–8 with those human needs in view. Nephi seeks direction and works; even Lehi needs correction. Faith is learned among imperfect people who still need food, guidance, forgiveness, and each other. At the seashore, Nephi does not simply wait for a ship to appear. The Lord teaches him, and he works the timbers. His brothers help, and the family sees that the completed vessel is good in 1 Nephi 18:1–4 . Guidance and patient work meet in a task the family could not accomplish through Nephi’s skill alone. Explore and study Learning to build, learning to trust Nephi describes work that grows out of repeated instruction from the Lord. His brothers help, and the finished ship exceeds their expectations. Consider how prayer, learning, and practical effort belong together in this account. Read 1 Nephi 18:1–4 A family takes the first step The Church’s illustrated story follows Lehi and Sariah as they leave Jerusalem with their family. Read or watch it alongside the opening chapters, noticing the Lord’s warning, the family’s departure, and the trust the journey will ask of them. Illustrated scripture story Lehi and Sariah Leave Jerusalem Book of Mormon Stories · The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Explore and study A family receives its sons again Sariah’s fear gives way to relief when her sons return. This family has not traveled without anxiety or disagreement. Their reunion brings gratitude and Sariah’s own testimony of the Lord’s care. Read 1 Nephi 5:1–10 03 · A vision centered in Christ Nephi wants his family to know where life is found Lehi’s dream begins with a man asking for mercy in darkness. When he reaches the tree and tastes its fruit, he wants his family to share it. Read his desire alongside the different responses of Sariah, Sam, Nephi, Laman, and Lemuel in 1 Nephi 8:5–18 . The dream speaks to the love and sorrow of someone who cannot choose for the people he loves. Nephi seeks to understand what his father has seen. His vision turns toward the Savior’s birth, ministry, and sacrifice. 1 Nephi 11:13–33 connects the love of God with the Son of God coming among His children. Nephi sees these events in vision; the passage is not an account of the mortal Jesus visiting Nephi’s wilderness camp. Explore and study A vision of the Savior’s compassion Nephi’s vision includes the Son of God ministering to people who suffer. This picture illustrates the mortal ministry he sees, rather than placing Nephi physically beside Jesus. What does that compassion add to Nephi’s understanding of the love of God? Read 1 Nephi 11:27–31 As a teacher, Nephi returns to Christ with remarkable steadiness. He wants the next generation to know where to look for remission of sins in 2 Nephi 25:23–29 . His final invitation is to follow the Savior through repentance, baptism, the Holy Ghost, and enduring discipleship in 2 Nephi 31:17–21 . The journey has a direction: forward with faith in Christ and love for God and all people. What do you want those you love to receive? Consider Lehi’s desire to share the fruit. Name one blessing of knowing Christ that you want someone else to experience. How could you offer an invitation with patience and respect for that person’s agency? 04 · The witness passes from hand to hand Jacob, Enos, and the quieter keepers of the record Jacob teaches about the Redeemer’s power over death and sin in 2 Nephi 9:6–23 . Later, as a leader among his own people, he challenges pride, the misuse of wealth, and conduct that wounds wives and children. Jacob 2:17–19 joins the desire for riches to the obligation to clothe, feed, and relieve others. Jacob 2:31–35 insists that God hears the pain of those who have been hurt. Covenant language never excuses cruelty at home. Jacob’s son Enos carries his father’s teaching into a long prayer. Forgiveness changes the reach of his concern: he prays for his own people and then for the Lamanites. Follow that movement in Enos 1:1–18 . The Lord’s assurance comes through faith in Christ, not through a claim that Enos has seen Him face to face. Jarom describes prophets patiently persuading the people to look forward to the Messiah in Jarom 1:10–12 . Omni, Amaron, Chemish, Abinadom, and Amaleki then preserve brief pieces of the record. Their entries remind us that preserving a record can be quiet work. At the close of Omni 1:25–26 , Amaleki invites us to bring our whole souls to Christ. Even a short record can leave a generous invitation. A prayer reaches beyond one person Follow Enos from his desire for forgiveness to his concern for other people. This illustrated story offers a clear way to revisit the account with a child, a friend, or someone meeting the Book of Mormon for the first time. Read Enos 1:2–12 05 · A people gather to hear Mosiah, Benjamin, and a kingdom of service The first Mosiah leads a people out of the land of Nephi and meets the people of Zarahemla. Omni 1:12–19 describes the bringing together of communities whose histories and languages have diverged. His son Benjamin later gathers families to hear his farewell teaching. His message then turns to Jesus Christ’s future mortal ministry, suffering, and Resurrection in Mosiah 3:5–11 . The king’s teaching rests on the Savior’s redeeming work, not on his own position. The gathered people plead for mercy and receive joy and peace through faith in Christ. Read Mosiah 4:1–4 together with Benjamin’s counsel to care for children and people in need in Mosiah 4:14–26 . As you read or watch, notice how remembering God’s goodness leads the people toward faith in Christ, service, and a changed heart. The anguish of remembering sin gives way to joy in Alma 36:12–21 . This deeply personal account does not make another person’s recovery follow the same timetable. It does show that past wrongdoing need not be the final word about a soul. Alma remembers that his strength returned and he stood again. He then told the people what he had experienced in Alma 36:17–23 . A sincere apology, a returned possession, or a promise kept may be a beginning. Keep the other person’s needs and freedom in view. 08 · Witnesses in a royal household Ammon, Aaron, Lamoni’s queen, and Abish Ammon enters King Lamoni’s service and earns an opportunity to teach. Write down one teaching worth carrying forward, then choose how you will make it your own. 12 · Leadership under pressure Captain Moroni defends; Pahoran answers with patience Moroni’s commitment to his people is tested by more than an opposing army. Their correspondence lets us see what happens when people working toward the same purpose understand a crisis differently. Pressure does not make Moroni’s judgments infallible. When supplies and support fail to arrive, he sends Pahoran a forceful accusation. Pahoran’s reply reveals circumstances Moroni did not know: rebellion has driven him from the judgment seat. In Alma 61:2–9 , he explains the crisis and chooses not to take offense at Moroni’s anger. Pahoran does not pretend there is no problem. He invites Moroni’s help and directs their effort toward deliverance in Alma 61:14–21 . Their exchange gives us a useful moment to pause: conviction can be strong while information is incomplete. Explore and study Remember Him in the bread Jesus blesses and breaks bread, gives it to His disciples, and asks them to give it to the multitude. He teaches them to remember His body and witness their willingness to do so. Read how this simple act joins remembrance and discipleship. Read 3 Nephi 18:1–7 He prays for those who will believe On the following day, the disciples teach and the people pray. Jesus withdraws a little distance and prays to the Father in 3 Nephi 19:19–23 . His prayer includes people who will believe the disciples’ words. Future listeners are already within the reach of His concern. He returns to the disciples, and His countenance shines upon them in 3 Nephi 19:24–25 . Explore and study A prayer for those who believe Jesus steps a little way from the disciples and prays for them and for those who will believe their words. This is His ministry among the people in Third Nephi. Read what He asks of the Father on their behalf. Read 3 Nephi 19:19–23 A missing witness is restored to the record The Savior commands the people to search the prophets, then asks Nephi to bring the record. Samuel had prophesied that many saints would rise and appear after Christ’s Resurrection, but the fulfillment had not been written. 3 Nephi 23:6–13 records the Lord’s direction to add it. Careful remembrance matters even among people who have seen Him. The witness is to remain available to readers who were not there. Explore and study The testimony is written down Jesus asks Nephi to bring the record and calls attention to a missing fulfillment of Samuel’s prophecy. The picture joins careful listening with careful keeping of testimony. Read 3 Nephi 23:6–13 A Church that bears His name and lives His gospel The disciples later pray about what to call the Church. Jesus answers in 3 Nephi 27:1–10 that it must bear His name and be built upon His gospel. He then teaches His Atonement and the invitation to repent and be sanctified in 3 Nephi 27:13–21 . The name belongs with a life shaped by Him. Explore and study Called by His name The disciples unite in prayer with a question about the name of the Church. Jesus answers and connects His name with His gospel. Read beyond the question of naming to what He says His Church must be built upon. Read 3 Nephi 27:1–10 His continuing ministry reaches children and future generations: children speak marvelous things in 3 Nephi 26:13–16 . He speaks personally with the twelve about their desires in 3 Nephi 28:1–10 . Three desire to remain and bring souls to Him. In 3 Nephi 28:4–10 , Jesus knows the desire they hesitate to voice and blesses them. His servants are prepared to keep ministering after the extraordinary gatherings end. Explore and study A desire to keep serving Three disciples hesitate to speak the desire of their hearts, but Jesus knows it. They wish to continue bringing souls to Him. Read His answer as an invitation to consider what you most want your own service to accomplish. Read 3 Nephi 28:4–10 19 · What happened after He came? The love of God becomes a way of living After the Savior’s ministry, the record describes a people converted to the Lord. They deal justly with one another and share so that there are no rich and poor among them. 4 Nephi 1:1–5 gives a glimpse of what a community can become when belonging to Christ reaches its ordinary arrangements. The account does not say that happiness comes from everyone having an identical personality or history. It locates the end of contention in the love of God dwelling in people’s hearts. 4 Nephi 1:15–18 describes a people whose inherited divisions no longer govern their life together. Their unity has moral substance: they are just, loving, and free from the violences the passage names. That peace is not permanent. Pride in costly clothing, division into classes, and the pursuit of gain return in 4 Nephi 1:24–29 . The change invites a searching question for any generation: what everyday habits help preserve love, and what habits quietly teach us to value ourselves above a neighbor? 20 · A witness kept through sorrow Mormon’s final words still offer hope in Christ Mormon receives responsibility for the records while young, then spends his life amid a society moving toward destruction. Mormon 1:1–5 introduces the observant child; Mormon 6:16–22 lets us hear the older man mourning his people. He has commanded armies and preserved their history, but he cannot make the people choose repentance. His sorrow comes through the record he leaves behind. At the end of that history, Mormon turns toward people who will live after him. In Mormon 7:1–10 , he asks them to remember who they are, lay down weapons of war, repent, and believe in Jesus Christ. The Savior has broken the power of death and opened the way to eternal life. These are words of hope from a man who has seen terrible loss. Explore and study Mormon’s last invitation Mormon’s sorrow for his people does not extinguish his hope for those who will read his words. His final appeal asks them to repent, lay down their weapons, and believe in Jesus Christ. Read the invitation he leaves for people he will never meet. Read Mormon 7:1–10 Mormon also joins the witness of this record with the witness that will come from the Jews. His hope reaches beyond the end of his own people’s story. Read his final counsel slowly, noticing what he chooses to place before a future reader: the Resurrection of Christ, reconciliation with God, and an invitation to follow the gospel. The life he cannot preserve through military strength can still be offered to the Redeemer. What witness would you want to leave? Think of someone who may need courage after you are no longer able to help directly. What have you learned about Christ that you would want that person to remember? Write it plainly and with kindness. 21 · A record preserved for those still to come Moroni leaves us a living invitation Moroni survives to finish his father’s record. He also abridges the much earlier Jaredite history, returning us to the world with which this journey began. Ether’s witness comes amid another society’s collapse. In Ether 12:2–6 , faith in God opens a future that present circumstances cannot supply. Moroni adds his own concern about weakness in writing and receives the Lord’s answer about grace in Ether 12:23–27 . Moroni preserves his father’s teaching that charity is the pure love of Christ and urges prayer for that gift in Moroni 7:45–48 . His final invitation asks us to remember God’s mercy, ponder, and ask with a sincere heart and real intent in Moroni 10:3–5 . Then he calls us to come to Christ in Moroni 10:32–33 . After so many generations and stories, the book still speaks to one reader willing to turn toward Him. Return to the story directory Continue with a guided study Carry Moroni’s invitation into your reading The Church’s illustrated story introduces Moroni’s care for the record and his invitation to future readers. After reading or watching, return to his final chapter and give yourself time to remember, ponder, and pray. Illustrated scripture story Moroni the Prophet Book of Mormon Stories · The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Explore and study Words kept for a future reader Moroni addresses people he will never meet in mortality. His invitation joins remembering God’s mercy, pondering, and asking with a sincere heart. Imagine receiving these words as a personal invitation to seek Jesus Christ. Read Moroni 10:1–5 22 · The record reaches another generation Moroni and Joseph Smith at the hill Joseph Smith’s history carries the story of the record into nineteenth-century New York. In Joseph Smith—History 1:51–54 , he describes finding the stone box in the hill near Manchester, seeing the plates, and learning from the messenger that he could not yet take them. He returns at the appointed time each year and receives instruction. The first visit and the eventual receiving of the plates are separate events, four years apart. On September 22, 1827, Joseph returns to the place where the plates have been deposited. Joseph Smith—History 1:59 records that the same heavenly messenger delivers them to him with a solemn charge to keep them safe. Joseph is twenty-one years old, based on the birth date he gives in Joseph Smith—History 1:3 . The responsibility before him is much larger than the physical act of receiving a record. Explore and study A record entrusted to Joseph Joseph receives the plates on September 22, 1827, after years of preparation. Moroni charges him to care for what has been entrusted to him. This scene imagines that moment of trust as the ancient record begins its journey toward new readers. Read Joseph Smith—History 1:59 The account helps us see the connection between a prophet preserving a witness for future readers and a young man entrusted with bringing that witness forth. The precise hand positions and arrangement of an illustrated meeting are an artist’s interpretation; the history centers on the record received and the responsibility attached to it. Continue with the Joseph Smith and Restoration study to follow that history, or return to the Book of Mormon’s invitation to come to Christ. A First Journey Through Three Kinds of Passage Explore and study Pause and ponder the promise A woman pauses beside a quiet lake with an open book in her lap. The still water and unhurried posture echo Moroni's invitation to remember, ponder and ask God with faith in Christ. Moroni 10:3-5 These focusChrist study suggestions offer a way to explore the sources at your own pace. Explore and study Let the words settle in the heart A grandmother listens as a teenage boy shares what he has found in an open book. Together they read, ponder and speak of Christ, letting understanding grow through a patient conversation. Read 3 Nephi 17 Explore and study Read a covenant through acts of care Neighbors load food and folded blankets into a car, making the covenant to bear one another's burdens visible through ordinary care. Read Mosiah 18 1. Notice Christ's care for individuals Read 3 Nephi 17:1-9, 21 . Jesus recognizes that His listeners need time to understand. He invites pondering and prayer, responds with compassion to their tears, heals those brought to Him, and blesses children individually. Write down a detail you might miss in a quick reading. As a personal application, make room for someone who needs time, attention, or help. Let the account deepen your understanding of compassion without turning its healings into a timetable for your own circumstances. 2. Follow belief into a community Read Mosiah 18:7-10, 21-29 . Alma connects baptism with caring for people who mourn or carry burdens. The community is also taught to share according to its members' resources and needs. Consider how belonging to Christ affects ordinary relationships. Who could use company, practical help, or a patient listener? Choose a specific, freely offered act of care. The passage gives a picture of covenant life you can discuss even while other questions about the book remain open. 3. Keep an honest record of your reading Return to one passage already studied. Write four short notes: what happens, what is taught about Christ, what you want to understand, and what you might do. Keep the chapter reference beside your notes so you can check your impressions against the text. On another day, revisit the question that mattered most. You may want to read a surrounding chapter, compare a Bible passage, pray, or ask someone to study with you. An ongoing conversation with the text can begin before you feel ready to make a final judgment about every claim. Where should I go when my question is historical? Use the Book of Mormon text to understand its message, then name the historical claim you want to investigate. The Joseph Smith and Restoration study offers a route into the history. Keep textual interpretation, historical evidence, and personal spiritual conviction distinct in your notes. Make room for the Savior’s words 3 Nephi 17 brings the reader close to a moment of compassion. Jesus notices His listeners’ limits and invites them to ponder and pray. Use these questions to return to the book itself. Which moment helps you know Him? Choose one action of Jesus in the chapter and describe it in your own words. What does it add to the introduction you read at the beginning of this page? Keep the verse nearby so you can distinguish the account from your response to it. What needs time to settle? Name a teaching you do not yet understand. How could pondering, prayer, or a conversation with a careful reader help you explore it? Give the question a place in your notes rather than expecting yourself to resolve the whole book at once. Who could receive your attention? Consider the people Jesus notices in this account. Who in your own life could use patient attention? Choose a small act of care that fits their needs, and ask what would help before deciding for them. Official Sources and Further Study The Book of Mormon: Another Testament of Jesus Christ How the Bible and the Book of Mormon Work Together Read the Book of Mormon in Gospel Library Ask a Question How the Two Books Work Together Where would you like to go next? Let another reading deepen your commitment . Explore three accounts of the Savior among the Nephites alongside Elder Andersen’s invitation to read the Book of Mormon again. Read the two books together Try a focused comparison while preserving the context of each passage. Explore prayer and discernment Consider how study, prayer, agency, and uncertainty can belong in the same inquiry. See the Savior's ministry in 3 Nephi Pair official Book of Mormon films with their chapters and continue into Christ's care for individuals.

records.title: An Introduction Before You Begin Reading
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Watch and study An Introduction Before You Begin Reading The official short explainer What Is the Book of Mormon? introduces the record, its setting, and its witness of Jesus Christ. Watch for the question that matters most to you: what the book contains, why Latter-day Saints read it, or how it relates to the Savior. Church video What Is the Book of Mormon? The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Then begin with the people gathered at Bountiful in 3 Nephi 11:1-17 . They hear a voice, turn their attention toward heaven, and encounter Jesus Christ. His introduction connects His identity with His suffering for the sins of the world. The people are invited to approach Him individually. How does reading this account add to the overview you just watched?

records.title: Why Nephi Keeps Returning to Jesus Christ
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Watch and study Why Nephi Keeps Returning to Jesus Christ Explore and study Follow Nephi’s stated purpose A reader pauses over an open book above a green valley. Nephi's stated purpose gives the study its center: persuading people to believe in Jesus Christ and be reconciled to God. Read 2 Nephi 25 In 2 Nephi 25:23-29 , Nephi explains why he writes and teaches about Christ. His concern includes the next generation: he wants children to understand where forgiveness is found. Read the verbs in verse 26 , then read the invitation to worship in verse 29 . Study lesson 2 Nephi 25: Saved by Jesus Christ The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The accompanying Seminary lesson explores salvation through Jesus Christ. After reading it, put Nephi's purpose into your own words. How would a family conversation change if it helped someone understand the Savior's mercy? You can begin with one experience of gratitude or one sincere question. A polished religious speech is unnecessary.

records.title: Get to Know the Book by Reading It
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Meet the people behind its familiar passages in the Book of Mormon story journey , or begin with the Savior’s own words below. Explore and study Come forward and know The risen Jesus Christ extends His invitation to people gathered at Bountiful. Each person is welcomed to come forward and know for themselves that He is the God of Israel. 3 Nephi 11:10-17 Study a teaching, not only the book's description Alma 32:21-28, 37-43 uses the image of a seed to discuss faith and the patient care that follows an initial willingness to believe. The setting includes people who have been excluded from worship because of their poverty. Notice both the invitation to begin and the warning that growth requires continued nourishment. This is a religious account of developing faith; it is not a scientific experiment that establishes every historical claim about the book. Read the gospel invitation 2 Nephi 31:5-13, 17-21 connects Jesus's example with baptism and an ongoing life of faith, hope, and love. Read this beside the account of His ministry in 3 Nephi 11 already linked above. One explains a path of discipleship; the other portrays an encounter with the risen Savior. Together they show why the book matters in Latter-day Saint worship. Separate the questions you are asking You may be asking what the book teaches, how it came into print, whether its account is historical, or how to evaluate a spiritual conviction. Those are related but different inquiries. Reading a passage can illuminate its message; historical questions require historical evidence too. Keep a question list so one unresolved issue does not get quietly replaced by another. A reading note you can return to Record a passage, its speaker and setting, one teaching in your own words, and one question. On your next visit, start with that question rather than feeling you must begin the whole book again.

records.title: Walk through the stories. Come to know the Savior.
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: The Book of Mormon carries us into homes and wilderness camps, royal courts and prisons, places of worship and fields of battle. We meet people who trust God, people who resist Him, and people who discover that repentance can change the direction of a life. Their experiences keep returning to Jesus Christ: His coming, His redeeming power, His ministry among the people, and His invitation to us. Begin with a person or moment that draws you. These stops follow the broad course of the record, beginning with the earlier Jaredite history. Some accounts overlap in time; the books sometimes return to an earlier event or follow another community. You can linger in one story and return to the journey later. About the story illustrations Each picture accompanies a passage you can open and read. The woodland landscapes, homes, clothing, and temple architecture are artistic interpretations inspired by Eastern Woodland settings, including Hopewell traditions; they do not establish where Book of Mormon events occurred. The scripture remains the source for what happens in each account.

records.title: The brother of Jared brings his need to the Lord
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Long before Lehi’s family leaves Jerusalem, Jared asks his brother to pray for their families and friends. The Lord hears, preserves their language, and leads them toward a promised land. The journey begins with concern for other people, not only personal deliverance. Follow those widening prayers in Ether 1:33–43 . Preparing to cross the sea, the brother of Jared faces a practical difficulty: the vessels need light. He brings sixteen small stones to the Lord and asks Him to touch them. In Ether 3:1–16 , the Lord reveals Himself as Jesus Christ. This is an appearance of the premortal Savior in His spirit body, before His birth in mortality. His power to redeem does not begin at Bethlehem; His purpose already embraces the people who will trust Him. Explore and study Known by the Redeemer The brother of Jared comes to know the Redeemer who has spoken to him. Read how the Lord identifies Himself and explains why He has shown Himself. Read Ether 3:13–18 The ocean crossing still includes wind and waves. The people sing praises and give thanks while the Lord carries them toward shore in Ether 6:4–12 . Help has not removed the journey. It has given them light and a way forward within it. Bring a real need into your prayer What problem are you carrying? Describe it plainly. Notice how the brother of Jared combines preparation with dependence on the Lord. Consider one faithful step you can take while asking for the help you cannot provide yourself.

records.title: Lehi and Sariah’s family learns to follow
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Lehi’s call draws an entire household into the wilderness. In 1 Nephi 2:1–16 , their tents replace the familiar life they have left behind. Laman and Lemuel resist their father’s direction. Nephi also has something to work through: he cries to the Lord, and his heart is softened. Sam believes Nephi’s words in 1 Nephi 2:17–18 . These brothers share a family and a journey, but their responses are their own. Sariah’s voice becomes especially clear when her sons return safely from Jerusalem. She has feared that she has lost them. In 1 Nephi 5:1–9 , relief leads into a declaration of what she now knows about the Lord’s care. Her place in the account is more than standing beside Lehi: she speaks, struggles, rejoices, and bears witness. The wilderness story also includes hunger, a broken bow, the death of Ishmael, and a ship that must be built. Read 1 Nephi 16:18–35 and 1 Nephi 17:1–8 with those human needs in view. Nephi seeks direction and works; even Lehi needs correction. Faith is learned among imperfect people who still need food, guidance, forgiveness, and each other. At the seashore, Nephi does not simply wait for a ship to appear. The Lord teaches him, and he works the timbers. His brothers help, and the family sees that the completed vessel is good in 1 Nephi 18:1–4 . Guidance and patient work meet in a task the family could not accomplish through Nephi’s skill alone. Explore and study Learning to build, learning to trust Nephi describes work that grows out of repeated instruction from the Lord. His brothers help, and the finished ship exceeds their expectations. Consider how prayer, learning, and practical effort belong together in this account. Read 1 Nephi 18:1–4 A family takes the first step The Church’s illustrated story follows Lehi and Sariah as they leave Jerusalem with their family. Read or watch it alongside the opening chapters, noticing the Lord’s warning, the family’s departure, and the trust the journey will ask of them. Illustrated scripture story Lehi and Sariah Leave Jerusalem Book of Mormon Stories · The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Explore and study A family receives its sons again Sariah’s fear gives way to relief when her sons return. This family has not traveled without anxiety or disagreement. Their reunion brings gratitude and Sariah’s own testimony of the Lord’s care. Read 1 Nephi 5:1–10

records.title: Nephi wants his family to know where life is found
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Lehi’s dream begins with a man asking for mercy in darkness. When he reaches the tree and tastes its fruit, he wants his family to share it. Read his desire alongside the different responses of Sariah, Sam, Nephi, Laman, and Lemuel in 1 Nephi 8:5–18 . The dream speaks to the love and sorrow of someone who cannot choose for the people he loves. Nephi seeks to understand what his father has seen. His vision turns toward the Savior’s birth, ministry, and sacrifice. 1 Nephi 11:13–33 connects the love of God with the Son of God coming among His children. Nephi sees these events in vision; the passage is not an account of the mortal Jesus visiting Nephi’s wilderness camp. Explore and study A vision of the Savior’s compassion Nephi’s vision includes the Son of God ministering to people who suffer. This picture illustrates the mortal ministry he sees, rather than placing Nephi physically beside Jesus. What does that compassion add to Nephi’s understanding of the love of God? Read 1 Nephi 11:27–31 As a teacher, Nephi returns to Christ with remarkable steadiness. He wants the next generation to know where to look for remission of sins in 2 Nephi 25:23–29 . His final invitation is to follow the Savior through repentance, baptism, the Holy Ghost, and enduring discipleship in 2 Nephi 31:17–21 . The journey has a direction: forward with faith in Christ and love for God and all people. What do you want those you love to receive? Consider Lehi’s desire to share the fruit. Name one blessing of knowing Christ that you want someone else to experience. How could you offer an invitation with patience and respect for that person’s agency?

records.title: Jacob, Enos, and the quieter keepers of the record
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Jacob teaches about the Redeemer’s power over death and sin in 2 Nephi 9:6–23 . Later, as a leader among his own people, he challenges pride, the misuse of wealth, and conduct that wounds wives and children. Jacob 2:17–19 joins the desire for riches to the obligation to clothe, feed, and relieve others. Jacob 2:31–35 insists that God hears the pain of those who have been hurt. Covenant language never excuses cruelty at home. Jacob’s son Enos carries his father’s teaching into a long prayer. Forgiveness changes the reach of his concern: he prays for his own people and then for the Lamanites. Follow that movement in Enos 1:1–18 . The Lord’s assurance comes through faith in Christ, not through a claim that Enos has seen Him face to face. Jarom describes prophets patiently persuading the people to look forward to the Messiah in Jarom 1:10–12 . Omni, Amaron, Chemish, Abinadom, and Amaleki then preserve brief pieces of the record. Their entries remind us that preserving a record can be quiet work. At the close of Omni 1:25–26 , Amaleki invites us to bring our whole souls to Christ. Even a short record can leave a generous invitation. A prayer reaches beyond one person Follow Enos from his desire for forgiveness to his concern for other people. This illustrated story offers a clear way to revisit the account with a child, a friend, or someone meeting the Book of Mormon for the first time. Illustrated scripture story Enos Book of Mormon Stories · The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Explore and study Prayer grows beyond one person Enos begins with the needs of his own soul. As he receives assurance, his concern widens to his people and then to the Lamanites. Follow that change in the direction of his prayers. Read Enos 1:2–12

records.title: A prayer reaches beyond one person
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?

Even a short record can leave a generous invitation. A prayer reaches beyond one person Follow Enos from his desire for forgiveness to his concern for other people. This illustrated story offers a clear way to revisit the account with a child, a friend, or someone meeting the Book of Mormon for the first time. Illustrated scripture story Enos Book of Mormon Stories · The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Explore and study Prayer grows beyond one person Enos begins with the needs of his own soul. As he receives assurance, his concern widens to his people and then to the Lamanites. Follow that change in the direction of his prayers. Read Enos 1:2–12

records.title: Mosiah, Benjamin, and a kingdom of service
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: The first Mosiah leads a people out of the land of Nephi and meets the people of Zarahemla. Omni 1:12–19 describes the bringing together of communities whose histories and languages have diverged. His son Benjamin later gathers families to hear his farewell teaching. The Mosiah who succeeds Benjamin is Benjamin’s son, a second king with the same name; Mosiah 1:9–16 helps keep the generations clear. Benjamin has worked alongside his people, and he asks them to see service to one another as service to God in Mosiah 2:10–19 . His message then turns to Jesus Christ’s future mortal ministry, suffering, and Resurrection in Mosiah 3:5–11 . The king’s teaching rests on the Savior’s redeeming work, not on his own position. The gathered people plead for mercy and receive joy and peace through faith in Christ. Read Mosiah 4:1–4 together with Benjamin’s counsel to care for children and people in need in Mosiah 4:14–26 . Their changed hearts take the form of a covenant in Mosiah 5:2–9 . The name of Christ is to shape daily life after the gathering ends. Let the gathering lead to service The illustrated story of King Benjamin brings the gathering and his teaching into focus. As you read or watch, notice how remembering God’s goodness leads the people toward faith in Christ, service, and a changed heart. Illustrated scripture story King Benjamin Book of Mormon Stories · The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Explore and study A king teaches the worth of service Benjamin speaks as a king who has labored alongside his people. He connects ordinary service with devotion to God. Look for what his example asks of a parent, neighbor, leader, or friend. Read Mosiah 2:5–18

records.title: Abinadi’s witness grows into a covenant community
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: The record now follows another community, descended from people who returned to the land of Nephi. Before King Noah and his priests, Abinadi teaches that salvation comes through Christ. One priest, Alma, believes and speaks in Abinadi’s defense. Forced to flee, he writes the prophet’s words. Abinadi is killed for his witness in Mosiah 17:1–20 . His death is terrible, but his testimony has not been silenced. This Alma, often called Alma the Elder to distinguish him from his son, teaches at the Waters of Mormon. Mosiah 18:7–17 links baptism with bearing burdens, mourning with others, comforting those who need comfort, and standing as witnesses of God. The people also share their resources in Mosiah 18:21–29 . Their covenant gives belonging a practical shape. Two deliverance stories follow. Limhi, Noah’s son, leads a people whose escape involves a plan, watchfulness, and a journey to Zarahemla in Mosiah 22:1–14 . Alma’s people receive strength to bear oppression before their eventual escape in Mosiah 24:8–22 . Read the stories separately, then consider what each teaches about turning toward God amid burdens that are not lifted immediately. Listen for the witness Alma remembers Return to Abinadi’s witness through the Church’s illustrated account. Notice the contrast between King Noah’s response and Alma’s willingness to believe, then return to the scripture to follow how that testimony reaches the people at the Waters of Mormon. Illustrated scripture story Abinadi and King Noah Book of Mormon Stories · The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Explore and study One listener chooses to believe Abinadi’s testimony reaches Alma even when the court rejects it. Alma speaks in his defense, then preserves his words after fleeing. This is Alma the Elder, whose son will later recount a different conversion. Read Mosiah 17:1–4

records.title: Alma the Younger and Mosiah’s sons choose to repair
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Alma the Younger and the sons of Mosiah begin by trying to destroy the Church. An angel confronts them in Mosiah 27:8–17 . The messenger is an angel; this is not a bodily appearance of Jesus. Alma’s father and the priests fast and pray while the younger Alma lies unable to speak. When he rises, his testimony is of being redeemed and changed through God in Mosiah 27:18–29 . Years later, Alma tells his son Helaman what happened within him. Remembering his father’s teaching about Jesus Christ, he cries inwardly for mercy. The anguish of remembering sin gives way to joy in Alma 36:12–21 . This deeply personal account does not make another person’s recovery follow the same timetable. It does show that past wrongdoing need not be the final word about a soul. Alma remembers that his strength returned and he stood again. He then told the people what he had experienced in Alma 36:17–23 . The account gives us a prayer that could not yet be spoken aloud: a plea made in the heart, heard by the Savior whose mercy Alma needed. Explore and study The memory that opened a way to joy Alma remembers his father’s teaching about Jesus Christ and cries inwardly for mercy. In his later account to Helaman, anguish gives way to joy and renewed strength. Read Alma 36:17–23 Repentance becomes visible in their actions. Alma and his companions work to repair the harm they have done in Mosiah 27:32–37 . Ammon, Aaron, Omner, and Himni later ask to preach among the Lamanites in Mosiah 28:1–9 . Their desire for others to receive mercy grows out of mercy they have needed themselves. Let repentance include repair Consider one relationship or responsibility where a change of heart could become a change of action. A sincere apology, a returned possession, or a promise kept may be a beginning. Keep the other person’s needs and freedom in view.

records.title: Ammon, Aaron, Lamoni’s queen, and Abish
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Ammon enters King Lamoni’s service and earns an opportunity to teach. He begins with questions and explains God’s purposes, the Creation, the Fall, and the coming of Christ in Alma 18:24–39 . Lamoni’s plea for mercy follows. When the queen seeks Ammon’s help, he recognizes her faith in Alma 19:8–13 . She is an active participant in the story, trusting a promise before she sees its fulfillment. Abish has believed for years because of a vision associated with her father. Seeing what has happened in the household, she gathers people so they too may believe. The gathering becomes confused and contentious; Abish weeps, then takes the queen by the hand. Alma 19:16–30 gives us a woman whose faithful action includes both disappointment and persistence. The queen rises and praises Jesus. Meanwhile, Aaron and his companions endure imprisonment before being freed. Later Aaron teaches Lamoni’s father, who asks what he must do to be born of God. In Alma 22:1–18 , the king moves from offering his kingdom to being willing to relinquish his sins. The two royal households have distinct stories, but both bring us to the same searching question: what are we willing to give up to know God? Notice the woman who acts This illustrated account helps you follow Abish’s part in the events surrounding Lamoni’s household. Watch for what she believes, what she does when the gathering becomes troubled, and how she helps the queen rise. Illustrated scripture story Abish Book of Mormon Stories · The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Explore and study Abish reaches for the queen Abish already believes in God before this day. When the crowd turns to confusion, she takes a practical, compassionate step toward the queen. The picture shows the moment just before their hands meet. Read Alma 19:16–30

records.title: Alma and Amulek help people begin where they are
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: While Mosiah’s sons teach among the Lamanites, Alma’s ministry follows another path. Amulek welcomes him into his home in Alma 8:19–27 . Their witness brings painful opposition, and their story does not reduce discipleship to an easy life. Later, Alma takes Amulek into his own home and cares for him in Alma 15:16–18 . The man who first offered shelter now receives it. Among the Zoramites, people excluded from worship because of their poverty ask Alma where they can turn. Alma 32:1–16 begins with that exclusion. His teaching about faith answers real people who have been told they do not belong. They can desire to believe, give the word a place in their hearts, and nourish what begins to grow in Alma 32:27–43 . Explore and study Room for those who were turned away People excluded from worship come to Alma with a painful question. He turns toward them and teaches that their circumstances need not shut them out from God. His later comparison of the word to a seed begins with room to desire and experiment. Read Alma 32:1–28 Alma then centers their belief on the Son of God in Alma 33:19–23 . Amulek teaches Christ’s infinite Atonement and invites prayer in fields, homes, and private places. His invitation immediately includes care for people who are hungry, sick, or without clothing in Alma 34:17–29 . Worship cannot be separated from how we treat the person beside us.
