records.title: Captain Moroni raises the title of liberty
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Amalickiah’s pursuit of power threatens the people’s freedom in Alma 46:1–10 . Moroni responds with a torn piece of his coat, writing a reminder of their God, their religion, their freedom, their peace, and their families. In Alma 46:12–21 , he fastens it to a pole, puts on his armor, and bows in prayer before going among the people. The title of liberty begins with remembered commitments and a plea for God’s help. Explore and study Remember what you are defending Moroni carries the title of liberty among the people after pouring out his soul in prayer. Its words call them to remember God, their faith, freedom, peace, and families. Read what he asks them to preserve, and how they answer. Read Alma 46:12–21 When Moroni calls the people to gather, he asks them to enter a covenant to maintain their rights and their religion. They come forward ready to stand together. Read the passage with the homes and ordinary lives behind those words in mind: the peace to worship, to raise children, and to care for one another. Moroni wants the people to remember what their strength is meant to protect. Mormon’s portrait of him in Alma 48:11–13 is essential to understanding the banner. Moroni is strong and courageous, but he does not delight in bloodshed. His heart is grateful to God, and he labors for the welfare and safety of his people. The account joins courage to gratitude and responsibility. It invites us to consider whether the way we use our own influence serves the people entrusted to our care. Let conviction lead to care Which commitments guide the way you use your time, influence, and strength? Name someone whose peace or well-being you can help protect through a truthful word, a promise kept, or patient service.

records.title: A buried weapon, a mother’s teaching, a young person’s choice
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: The converted people called Anti-Nephi-Lehies bury their weapons as a witness of their covenant. Alma 24:7–19 places that act within gratitude for forgiveness and a determination not to return to bloodshed. When attacked, they keep their promise at devastating cost. Read Alma 24:20–27 with reverence for those lives. Explore and study Laying the weapons down The Anti-Nephi-Lehies give visible form to a covenant they intend to keep. Their choice grows from gratitude for forgiveness and a determination to turn away from their former violence. Read their own explanation before considering what repentance asks of you. Read Alma 24:15–19 Later, when war threatens, their sons choose to defend their families. These young men have not made their parents’ covenant, and Helaman, the son of Alma the Younger, becomes their leader in Alma 53:10–22 . In Alma 56:43–48 , they remember what their mothers taught them about trusting God. Their mothers’ faith matters, and so do the sons’ own choices to act with courage. Explore and study What their mothers had taught them A mother and son turn toward one another in an imagined quiet conversation. Later, the young warriors remember their mothers’ teaching with confidence. Read the words they carry with them, and consider how faith grows through ordinary conversations at home. Read Alma 56:47–48 Helaman leads the young men who trust him These young men volunteer and ask Helaman to lead them. Alma 53:16–22 describes their courage, strength, and faithfulness, along with something less spectacular but just as important: they are true to the responsibilities entrusted to them. Their parents’ covenant remains honored while the sons accept a responsibility of their own. Before a dangerous return to battle, Helaman asks whether they will go with him. In Alma 56:44–48 , they answer with trust in God and remember their mothers’ teaching. They call Helaman their father, a tender expression within the relationship between these young soldiers and their chosen leader. He is moved by their courage. Follow their words as young people making a solemn choice, then remember that Helaman must lead and care for the people who have placed that trust in him. Explore and study We do not doubt our mothers knew it The young men answer Helaman with the faith their mothers have taught them. He calls them his sons, and they speak to him as a father. Their courage grows alongside a desire to protect their families and help others in danger. Read Alma 56:44–48 The account honors their preservation without hiding their suffering: none are killed in the battle described in Alma 57:21–27 , but all receive wounds and many faint from loss of blood. Their story invites gratitude and steadfastness. It should never become a promise that faithful families will be spared every wound or loss. Remember a faithful voice Who taught you to turn toward God? It may have been a parent, friend, teacher, or someone whose quiet example endured. Write down one teaching worth carrying forward, then choose how you will make it your own.

records.title: Captain Moroni defends; Pahoran answers with patience
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Moroni’s commitment to his people is tested by more than an opposing army. Exhaustion, shortages, and uncertain news strain the relationship between the commander in the field and Pahoran, the chief judge. Their correspondence lets us see what happens when people working toward the same purpose understand a crisis differently. Pressure does not make Moroni’s judgments infallible. When supplies and support fail to arrive, he sends Pahoran a forceful accusation. Pahoran’s reply reveals circumstances Moroni did not know: rebellion has driven him from the judgment seat. In Alma 61:2–9 , he explains the crisis and chooses not to take offense at Moroni’s anger. Pahoran does not pretend there is no problem. He invites Moroni’s help and directs their effort toward deliverance in Alma 61:14–21 . Their exchange gives us a useful moment to pause: conviction can be strong while information is incomplete. A patient, truthful answer can turn a strained relationship back toward shared service.

records.title: Nephi, Lehi, and Samuel call the people to Christ
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: In a later generation, Helaman, the son of the Helaman who led the young soldiers, teaches his sons Nephi and Lehi to build their lives on Jesus Christ. These are later prophets, not Nephi and Lehi from the opening books. Their father’s counsel in Helaman 5:5–12 becomes the center of their ministry. The Savior is the foundation that can hold when destructive winds come. Imprisoned among the Lamanites, the brothers are encircled by fire without being burned. Darkness covers the other people present. Aminadab, who once belonged to the Church, tells them to repent and cry to God. Follow the darkness giving way to peace in Helaman 5:22–48 . The account describes divine voices and ministering angels; it does not say that Jesus bodily stands in that prison. Samuel, a Lamanite prophet, later returns to a city from which he has been driven. Refused entrance, he stands on its wall to speak the words the Lord has put into his heart in Helaman 13:2–5 . He foretells the signs of Christ’s birth and death in Helaman 14:2–8 and Helaman 14:20–28 . Some believe; others attack him. Helaman 16:1–8 asks us to notice a witness who comes from outside the community’s usual expectations. Will the people hear God’s word when they dislike the messenger? Explore and study Samuel will not abandon his message After being cast out, Samuel returns to deliver the message placed in his heart. His courage serves a call to repentance. Read Helaman 13:2–5

records.title: Samuel will not abandon his message
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?

The account describes divine voices and ministering angels; it does not say that Jesus bodily stands in that prison. Samuel, a Lamanite prophet, later returns to a city from which he has been driven. Refused entrance, he stands on its wall to speak the words the Lord has put into his heart in Helaman 13:2–5 . He foretells the signs of Christ’s birth and death in Helaman 14:2–8 and Helaman 14:20–28 . Some believe; others attack him. Helaman 16:1–8 asks us to notice a witness who comes from outside the community’s usual expectations. Will the people hear God’s word when they dislike the messenger? Explore and study Samuel will not abandon his message After being cast out, Samuel returns to deliver the message placed in his heart. His courage serves a call to repentance. Read Helaman 13:2–5

records.title: Nephi prays through a day of danger
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: At the beginning of the Savior’s mortal life, believers face a deadline: if Samuel’s promised sign does not appear, they will be killed. The Nephi who prays for them is the son of Nephi and grandson of Helaman, a later generation again. 3 Nephi 1:1–14 holds the threat and the prayer together. The Lord’s voice assures him that the sign will come and that He will be born into the world. The night arrives without darkness, as Samuel promised. 3 Nephi 1:15–21 records the astonishment and the fulfillment. Yet the chapters that follow show how quickly people can forget what has moved them. A memorable experience still needs a continuing life of faith. Years later, after the destruction at the time of Christ’s death, the Savior’s voice calls the survivors to turn toward Him. Read the invitation to a broken heart and a contrite spirit in 3 Nephi 9:13–22 . Before we reach the personal ministry at Bountiful, the record has already let us hear His desire to receive, heal, and gather.

records.title: Come forward and know the Savior
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: The Father invites the people to hear His Son The people gathered at the temple in Bountiful hear a voice they do not understand at first. On the third hearing, they open their ears and understand the Father’s introduction of His Beloved Son. In 3 Nephi 11:1–8 , they look toward heaven and see Jesus descending. He comes down and stands among them. The prophets’ promise has become a person before their eyes. Explore and study The promised Savior descends The people turn toward heaven and see a Man descending in a white robe. The Father has invited them to hear His Beloved Son. Pause with the gathering at this moment of wonder, before the Savior speaks. Read 3 Nephi 11:1–8 Stay with the descent for a moment. 3 Nephi 11:8 describes a Man in a white robe coming down to stand among the people. Their eyes turn toward Him, and they fall silent, not yet understanding whom they are seeing. The Savior comes within their reach. Soon they will hear His voice and receive His invitation personally. Explore and study Coming down to His people The distant promise becomes a person before their eyes. Jesus comes down and stands among them. Stay with the quiet attention of this moment, and read the introduction that follows. Read 3 Nephi 11:8 He stands among them and declares who He is Jesus stretches out His hand and speaks. He identifies Himself as the Christ whom the prophets testified would come, then bears witness of His obedience to the Father and His suffering for the sins of the world. Read 3 Nephi 11:9–12 with His listeners in view. Remembering the prophecy that He would appear to them, the whole multitude falls to the earth. They are in the presence of the Redeemer they have been taught to await. Explore and study He stands among them Jesus identifies Himself as the Christ whom the prophets promised. He speaks of His Atonement and His obedience to the Father. As the people remember the promises they have heard, they fall to the earth before Him. Read 3 Nephi 11:9–12 Each person receives an invitation to come The Savior now asks them to rise and come forward. In 3 Nephi 11:13–17 , they feel the wounds in His side, hands, and feet. They approach one by one until every person has witnessed for themselves. A great multitude is gathered, yet the encounter reaches each individual. The Savior gives them time to see and feel for themselves. Each person’s witness becomes part of the testimony this people will preserve. Explore and study A witness, one person at a time The invitation reaches each person: arise and come forward. The multitude becomes a succession of individual witnesses who see and feel for themselves. Consider the patience and personal attention contained in the words one by one. Read 3 Nephi 11:13–17 A multitude joins in praise When everyone has come forward, their individual witnesses become a shared cry of praise. In 3 Nephi 11:15–17 , they bless the name of the Most High God and fall at Jesus’s feet in worship. Read the movement of the account: first the invitation, then each person’s encounter, and then the multitude’s united response. The living Christ stands at the center of them all. Explore and study The multitude answers with worship After each person has seen and felt for themselves, the people unite in praise and worship. Their common testimony has grown through individual encounters. Notice how the account holds personal knowledge and shared belonging together. Read 3 Nephi 11:15–17 Continue with the official film Jesus Christ Appears in the Ancient Americas | 3 Nephi 8–11 in the Watch study. Keep this chapter beside you as you follow the descent, the Savior’s introduction, and the invitation to come forward. Nephi comes when Jesus calls Jesus calls Nephi forward. The prophet bows before Him, and the Savior gives him authority to baptize in 3 Nephi 11:18–22 . This Nephi belongs to the generation living at the time of Christ’s visit; he is not the son of Lehi who began the record. The same gospel that has been taught and anticipated across the generations is now being taught by the risen Lord Himself. Explore and study Christ calls Nephi forward After Nephi bows before Him, the Savior asks him to arise and grants authority to baptize. The encounter leads from worship into a specific responsibility to serve. This is the Nephi of Third Nephi. Read 3 Nephi 11:18–22 A covenant that begins with faith in Him The Savior teaches how baptism is to be performed in 3 Nephi 11:23–28 . His directions are plain, and His warning against contention follows immediately. In 3 Nephi 11:29–40 , He teaches faith, repentance, baptism, and the Holy Ghost. The authority and the ordinance serve His invitation to become as a little child and come to Him. Explore and study One baptism and an end to contention The Savior teaches His disciples how to baptize and then speaks directly against contention. Read both parts together: shared ordinances and the spirit in which people treat one another belong to His instruction. Read 3 Nephi 11:23–30 Receive His invitation personally Return to the people coming forward one by one. What do you notice about the Savior’s willingness to be known? Record a question or a hope you would bring to Him, and let it become part of your prayer.

records.title: Mercy, prayer, and trust in the Father
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Blessed are the merciful and the peacemakers Jesus begins His sermon with blessings for people who turn toward Him: the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, and those who hunger for righteousness. Read 3 Nephi 12:1–12 slowly. The merciful, the pure in heart, and the peacemakers belong in His kingdom. These are qualities a disciple can practice in ordinary conversations long after the multitude has dispersed. Explore and study Blessed are the merciful The Savior speaks of mercy, meekness, peacemaking, and hearts that hunger for righteousness. These blessings invite a way of living with other people. Choose one invitation to carry into an ordinary conversation today. Read 3 Nephi 12:3–12 His teaching reaches beyond those who are easy to love. 3 Nephi 12:43–48 asks His followers to love their enemies and pray for those who misuse them. Begin with one real relationship rather than an imagined perfect response. What would truthfulness, restraint, and a sincere desire for another person’s good look like there? Speak to a Father who knows your need In 3 Nephi 13:5–13 , Jesus teaches prayer free from performance and empty repetition. He gives words of reverence, dependence, forgiveness, and deliverance. The Father already knows what His children need; prayer brings that need into a trusting relationship. You can pause with one line, speak honestly, and listen instead of trying to make your words impressive. Explore and study The Father hears the quiet prayer Jesus teaches people to pray to their Father without turning prayer into a performance. The image shows Him teaching that invitation. Read His words slowly and notice the trust, forgiveness, and daily dependence they express. Read 3 Nephi 13:5–13 Consider the lilies Jesus then turns specifically to the twelve He has chosen. He tells them not to let anxiety over food and clothing govern their service. In 3 Nephi 13:25–34 , birds and lilies become invitations to trust the Father’s care and seek His kingdom. Keep the original listeners in view as you reflect on the teaching. It can deepen trust while you continue the daily responsibilities of caring for yourself and others. Explore and study Trust beyond tomorrow Here the Savior turns specifically to the twelve He has chosen. He teaches them to seek the kingdom of God and trust the Father who knows their needs. Read 3 Nephi 13:25–34

records.title: The Shepherd knows His other sheep
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Jesus explains that these people are the other sheep of whom He spoke to His disciples at Jerusalem. 3 Nephi 15:21–24 connects His ministry here with His teaching in the Bible. Their place in His care was real even when another community did not understand it. His voice gathers people across the distances that separate them. Explore and study Other sheep hear His voice The people before Jesus learn that He had spoken of them as His other sheep. They belong to the same Shepherd. Consider what His knowledge of distant people reveals about His care. Read 3 Nephi 15:21–24 · Read John 10:14–16 He notices their tears and stays The Savior recognizes that the people cannot yet understand everything He has taught. He invites them to go home, ponder, pray, and prepare in 3 Nephi 17:1–3 . Then He sees their tears and stays. 3 Nephi 17:5–8 brings us close to His compassion. He asks them to bring anyone who is sick or afflicted. His invitation reaches every kind of suffering named in the passage and then embraces anyone afflicted in any manner. They bring the people who need His care The multitude responds together. 3 Nephi 17:6–10 describes people coming forward with those who are sick, blind, unable to walk, or otherwise afflicted. Notice the people who bring someone as well as those who are brought. Their shared movement toward the Savior lets us see care becoming an action: they respond to His invitation by helping others come. Explore and study They bring those who need healing Jesus invites the people to bring anyone who is afflicted. The multitude responds together, and He heals each person brought to Him. Notice the care of those who help another person approach, as well as the Savior’s compassion. Read 3 Nephi 17:6–10 He heals each person brought to Him Jesus heals every one as they are brought forward in 3 Nephi 17:9–10 . Those who have been healed and those who were already whole bow together at His feet. Their gratitude belongs to a community that has witnessed His mercy. Linger with one person’s need, and then with the Savior’s attention to that person. Explore and study Bring those who need His care Before departing, Jesus sees the people’s tears and invites them to bring those who suffer. His response is personal and compassionate. Notice both His invitation and the community’s part in bringing people forward. Read 3 Nephi 17:5–9 Children are brought into the circle The children are brought forward, and Jesus stands among them. He kneels and prays to the Father in 3 Nephi 17:11–18 . The multitude’s joy is beyond what they can put into words. Explore and study He prays with the children around Him The children are brought forward, and Jesus kneels to pray to the Father. The record emphasizes the joy His prayer brings to those who hear it. This scene precedes the later individual blessings and the ministry of angels. Read 3 Nephi 17:11–18 He blesses each child The account then tells of His tears and His blessing of each child in 3 Nephi 17:19–23 . Jesus takes the little children one by one, blesses them, and prays to the Father for them. Read it without hurrying past the individual care. Each child receives His attention, and the gathered people witness His tenderness. Explore and study Each child receives His attention The Savior takes the children one by one and blesses them. The picture dwells on the attention given to one child within a much larger gathering. Consider how individual care changes the way a community welcomes its children. Read 3 Nephi 17:21–23 The heavens open, and angels minister to the children After blessing the children, Jesus weeps again and invites the people to behold their little ones. As they look, the heavens open. 3 Nephi 17:21–25 tells of angels descending as though in the midst of fire, encircling the children, and ministering to them. The record closes this scene with the witness of those who saw and heard: men, women, and children, about twenty-five hundred people. Their children’s place in the Savior’s ministry is something the whole gathering can remember. Explore and study Angels minister to the children After blessing the children one by one, Jesus asks the multitude to behold their little ones. The heavens open, angels descend, and fire encircles the children as the angels minister to them. The people witness this together and preserve their testimony of what they have seen and heard. Read 3 Nephi 17:21–25 Stay with one act of compassion Choose a detail: His willingness to stay, His invitation to bring someone forward, His prayer, or His blessing of a child. What does it teach you about His character? Consider one person who could receive your patient attention today.

records.title: Remember Him, search His words, and keep ministering
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Jesus gives bread and wine and teaches the people to remember His body and blood. 3 Nephi 18:1–14 connects the sacrament with a willingness to follow Him and the promise of His Spirit. He also commands prayer in families and teaches the disciples to welcome those who come among them in 3 Nephi 18:15–25 . The sacred gathering is to shape the way they receive people afterward. Explore and study Remember Him in the bread Jesus blesses and breaks bread, gives it to His disciples, and asks them to give it to the multitude. He teaches them to remember His body and witness their willingness to do so. Read how this simple act joins remembrance and discipleship. Read 3 Nephi 18:1–7 He prays for those who will believe On the following day, the disciples teach and the people pray. Jesus withdraws a little distance and prays to the Father in 3 Nephi 19:19–23 . His prayer includes people who will believe the disciples’ words. Future listeners are already within the reach of His concern. He returns to the disciples, and His countenance shines upon them in 3 Nephi 19:24–25 . Explore and study A prayer for those who believe Jesus steps a little way from the disciples and prays for them and for those who will believe their words. This is His ministry among the people in Third Nephi. Read what He asks of the Father on their behalf. Read 3 Nephi 19:19–23 A missing witness is restored to the record The Savior commands the people to search the prophets, then asks Nephi to bring the record. Samuel had prophesied that many saints would rise and appear after Christ’s Resurrection, but the fulfillment had not been written. 3 Nephi 23:6–13 records the Lord’s direction to add it. Careful remembrance matters even among people who have seen Him. The witness is to remain available to readers who were not there. Explore and study The testimony is written down Jesus asks Nephi to bring the record and calls attention to a missing fulfillment of Samuel’s prophecy. The picture joins careful listening with careful keeping of testimony. Read 3 Nephi 23:6–13 A Church that bears His name and lives His gospel The disciples later pray about what to call the Church. Jesus answers in 3 Nephi 27:1–10 that it must bear His name and be built upon His gospel. He then teaches His Atonement and the invitation to repent and be sanctified in 3 Nephi 27:13–21 . The name belongs with a life shaped by Him. Explore and study Called by His name The disciples unite in prayer with a question about the name of the Church. Jesus answers and connects His name with His gospel. Read beyond the question of naming to what He says His Church must be built upon. Read 3 Nephi 27:1–10 His continuing ministry reaches children and future generations: children speak marvelous things in 3 Nephi 26:13–16 . He speaks personally with the twelve about their desires in 3 Nephi 28:1–10 . Three desire to remain and bring souls to Him. In 3 Nephi 28:4–10 , Jesus knows the desire they hesitate to voice and blesses them. His servants are prepared to keep ministering after the extraordinary gatherings end. Explore and study A desire to keep serving Three disciples hesitate to speak the desire of their hearts, but Jesus knows it. They wish to continue bringing souls to Him. Read His answer as an invitation to consider what you most want your own service to accomplish. Read 3 Nephi 28:4–10

records.title: The love of God becomes a way of living
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: After the Savior’s ministry, the record describes a people converted to the Lord. They deal justly with one another and share so that there are no rich and poor among them. 4 Nephi 1:1–5 gives a glimpse of what a community can become when belonging to Christ reaches its ordinary arrangements. The account does not say that happiness comes from everyone having an identical personality or history. It locates the end of contention in the love of God dwelling in people’s hearts. 4 Nephi 1:15–18 describes a people whose inherited divisions no longer govern their life together. Their unity has moral substance: they are just, loving, and free from the violences the passage names. That peace is not permanent. Pride in costly clothing, division into classes, and the pursuit of gain return in 4 Nephi 1:24–29 . The change invites a searching question for any generation: what everyday habits help preserve love, and what habits quietly teach us to value ourselves above a neighbor?

records.title: Mormon’s final words still offer hope in Christ
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Mormon receives responsibility for the records while young, then spends his life amid a society moving toward destruction. Mormon 1:1–5 introduces the observant child; Mormon 6:16–22 lets us hear the older man mourning his people. He has commanded armies and preserved their history, but he cannot make the people choose repentance. His sorrow comes through the record he leaves behind. At the end of that history, Mormon turns toward people who will live after him. In Mormon 7:1–10 , he asks them to remember who they are, lay down weapons of war, repent, and believe in Jesus Christ. The Savior has broken the power of death and opened the way to eternal life. These are words of hope from a man who has seen terrible loss. Explore and study Mormon’s last invitation Mormon’s sorrow for his people does not extinguish his hope for those who will read his words. His final appeal asks them to repent, lay down their weapons, and believe in Jesus Christ. Read the invitation he leaves for people he will never meet. Read Mormon 7:1–10 Mormon also joins the witness of this record with the witness that will come from the Jews. His hope reaches beyond the end of his own people’s story. Read his final counsel slowly, noticing what he chooses to place before a future reader: the Resurrection of Christ, reconciliation with God, and an invitation to follow the gospel. The life he cannot preserve through military strength can still be offered to the Redeemer. What witness would you want to leave? Think of someone who may need courage after you are no longer able to help directly. What have you learned about Christ that you would want that person to remember? Write it plainly and with kindness.

records.title: Moroni leaves us a living invitation
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Moroni survives to finish his father’s record. He also abridges the much earlier Jaredite history, returning us to the world with which this journey began. Ether’s witness comes amid another society’s collapse. In Ether 12:2–6 , faith in God opens a future that present circumstances cannot supply. Moroni adds his own concern about weakness in writing and receives the Lord’s answer about grace in Ether 12:23–27 . Moroni preserves his father’s teaching that charity is the pure love of Christ and urges prayer for that gift in Moroni 7:45–48 . His final invitation asks us to remember God’s mercy, ponder, and ask with a sincere heart and real intent in Moroni 10:3–5 . Then he calls us to come to Christ in Moroni 10:32–33 . After so many generations and stories, the book still speaks to one reader willing to turn toward Him. Return to the story directory Continue with a guided study Carry Moroni’s invitation into your reading The Church’s illustrated story introduces Moroni’s care for the record and his invitation to future readers. After reading or watching, return to his final chapter and give yourself time to remember, ponder, and pray. records.title: Moroni and Joseph Smith at the hill
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Joseph Smith’s history carries the story of the record into nineteenth-century New York. In Joseph Smith—History 1:51–54 , he describes finding the stone box in the hill near Manchester, seeing the plates, and learning from the messenger that he could not yet take them. He returns at the appointed time each year and receives instruction. The first visit and the eventual receiving of the plates are separate events, four years apart. On September 22, 1827, Joseph returns to the place where the plates have been deposited. Joseph Smith—History 1:59 records that the same heavenly messenger delivers them to him with a solemn charge to keep them safe. Joseph is twenty-one years old, based on the birth date he gives in Joseph Smith—History 1:3 . The responsibility before him is much larger than the physical act of receiving a record. Explore and study A record entrusted to Joseph Joseph receives the plates on September 22, 1827, after years of preparation. Moroni charges him to care for what has been entrusted to him. This scene imagines that moment of trust as the ancient record begins its journey toward new readers. Read Joseph Smith—History 1:59 The account helps us see the connection between a prophet preserving a witness for future readers and a young man entrusted with bringing that witness forth. The precise hand positions and arrangement of an illustrated meeting are an artist’s interpretation; the history centers on the record received and the responsibility attached to it. Continue with the Joseph Smith and Restoration study to follow that history, or return to the Book of Mormon’s invitation to come to Christ.

records.title: A First Journey Through Three Kinds of Passage
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: Explore and study Pause and ponder the promise A woman pauses beside a quiet lake with an open book in her lap. The still water and unhurried posture echo Moroni's invitation to remember, ponder and ask God with faith in Christ. Moroni 10:3-5 These focusChrist study suggestions offer a way to explore the sources at your own pace. Explore and study Let the words settle in the heart A grandmother listens as a teenage boy shares what he has found in an open book. Together they read, ponder and speak of Christ, letting understanding grow through a patient conversation. Read 3 Nephi 17 Explore and study Read a covenant through acts of care Neighbors load food and folded blankets into a car, making the covenant to bear one another's burdens visible through ordinary care. Read Mosiah 18 1. Notice Christ's care for individuals Read 3 Nephi 17:1-9, 21 . Jesus recognizes that His listeners need time to understand. He invites pondering and prayer, responds with compassion to their tears, heals those brought to Him, and blesses children individually. Write down a detail you might miss in a quick reading. As a personal application, make room for someone who needs time, attention, or help. Let the account deepen your understanding of compassion without turning its healings into a timetable for your own circumstances. 2. Follow belief into a community Read Mosiah 18:7-10, 21-29 . Alma connects baptism with caring for people who mourn or carry burdens. The community is also taught to share according to its members' resources and needs. Consider how belonging to Christ affects ordinary relationships. Who could use company, practical help, or a patient listener? Choose a specific, freely offered act of care. The passage gives a picture of covenant life you can discuss even while other questions about the book remain open. 3. Keep an honest record of your reading Return to one passage already studied. Write four short notes: what happens, what is taught about Christ, what you want to understand, and what you might do. Keep the chapter reference beside your notes so you can check your impressions against the text. On another day, revisit the question that mattered most. You may want to read a surrounding chapter, compare a Bible passage, pray, or ask someone to study with you. An ongoing conversation with the text can begin before you feel ready to make a final judgment about every claim. Where should I go when my question is historical? Use the Book of Mormon text to understand its message, then name the historical claim you want to investigate. The Joseph Smith and Restoration study offers a route into the history. Keep textual interpretation, historical evidence, and personal spiritual conviction distinct in your notes.

records.title: Make room for the Savior’s words
records.pageTitle: What Is the Book of Mormon and How Does It Relate to the Bible?
records.text: 3 Nephi 17 brings the reader close to a moment of compassion. Jesus notices His listeners’ limits and invites them to ponder and pray. Use these questions to return to the book itself. Which moment helps you know Him? Choose one action of Jesus in the chapter and describe it in your own words. What does it add to the introduction you read at the beginning of this page? Keep the verse nearby so you can distinguish the account from your response to it. What needs time to settle? Name a teaching you do not yet understand. How could pondering, prayer, or a conversation with a careful reader help you explore it? Give the question a place in your notes rather than expecting yourself to resolve the whole book at once. Who could receive your attention? Consider the people Jesus notices in this account. Who in your own life could use patient attention? Choose a small act of care that fits their needs, and ask what would help before deciding for them.

records.title: Who Was Joseph Smith?
records.text: Answers / Joseph Smith Joseph Smith (1805-1844) was the founding prophet of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Latter-day Saints believe God called him to help restore the gospel and Church of Jesus Christ in the latter days. Stand Forever · Third foundational question Was Joseph Smith a prophet? Joseph Smith reported visions, brought forth the Book of Mormon, organized the Church in 1830, and taught doctrines that continue to shape Latter-day Saint faith. His prophetic claim can be examined through his firsthand accounts, contemporary records, the texts he presented as scripture, and the lasting fruits of his ministry. Explore and study Consider the work of publishing a book Two printers set type and prepare pages by hand for the Book of Mormon's 1830 publication. The press, ink and stacked paper reveal the patience and skilled labor required to place the finished book into a reader's hands. Book of Mormon introduction Begin with the accounts. Read the First Vision sources linked below. Notice who recorded each account, when it was recorded, and which question you are asking of it. Study a scriptural claim. Follow the Book of Mormon references and the Harmony study. Distinguish what a source claims from what a later interpretation adds. Continue the inquiry. Use the reviewed videos and reflection questions to identify a useful next source. Then explore the restored Church study for the beliefs, ordinances, and community connected with this history. Read the source accounts Watch and study The face behind the history. Explore an art-led companion study of Joseph’s death masks, portraits, and the likeness developed for focusChrist. Open the portrait story → Latter-day Saints regard Joseph Smith as a prophet called by God. The historical sources below distinguish his firsthand accounts, contemporary records, later recollections, and the Church’s interpretation of his life. Watch and study Begin in the grove, then open the records The film Joseph Smith: The Prophet of the Restoration offers a dramatic introduction to his life and legacy. Begin your examination with his reported First Vision. Watch with a source question in mind: what can you identify in the written accounts, and what belongs to a filmmaker's portrayal? Church video Joseph Smith: The Prophet of the Restoration The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The Church's First Vision Accounts essay identifies four firsthand accounts. Its discussion of the 1832 account emphasizes Joseph's concern for forgiveness and personal redemption. The 1838 account places the vision within the beginnings of the Church and emphasizes his question about which church to join. These are different dates of recording, not four dates for the event. Begin with one account, noting its audience and emphasis. Then compare a second. The essay presents the Church's explanation of differences and links to documents so that you can examine more than a modern summary. The First Vision Joseph Smith grew up during intense religious revival in the northeastern United States. As a teenager, he sought divine guidance about which church to join. He later recorded that in answer to prayer he saw God the Father and Jesus Christ. Latter-day Saints call this experience the First Vision and regard it as the beginning of the Restoration. The Book of Mormon Joseph said an angel named Moroni later directed him to an ancient record written on metal plates. He translated the record by the gift and power of God, and it was published in 1830 as the Book of Mormon. The book presents itself as another testament of Jesus Christ. The Restoration of the Church Latter-day Saints believe priesthood authority, gospel ordinances, prophetic revelation, and the organization of Christ’s Church were restored through Joseph Smith. The Church was formally organized in 1830. Joseph served as its first president and received revelations that now form a substantial portion of the Doctrine and Covenants. Joseph Smith Was Not the Object of Worship Latter-day Saints honor Joseph as a prophet, but worship God the Father in the name of Jesus Christ. Joseph’s prophetic role is meaningful to believers because they understand his mission as pointing people to Jesus Christ, restoring priesthood authority, and bringing forth scripture that testifies of Christ. A Historical Figure Worth Studying Carefully Joseph Smith’s life included religious leadership, migration, conflict, legal controversy, political activity, plural marriage, and violence directed both toward and around the early Saints. A responsible study should not reduce him to either a flawless hero or a caricature. The Church’s history resources include primary-source context and essays for difficult questions as well as devotional accounts. If a Historical Question Troubles You You can examine one question at a time. Begin with the linked accounts, notice when and why each was written, and distinguish what the record says from later interpretation. If you are discussing the question with someone else, make room for what it means to them as well as the evidence. You do not need to rush past a concern to keep learning. Follow a Historical Question to the Records The Church's First Vision Accounts essay discusses differences among the accounts and explains the Church's interpretation of them. Its notes provide a path to the underlying records. Read an account before its commentary when you can, and distinguish Joseph's reported experience from a historian's explanation of the record. A devotional account and a historical essay may serve different purposes. Asking when a text was written, who preserved it, and what evidence is available is a reasonable part of study. You can hold a specific question open while examining it carefully. A Worked Example: Studying the First Vision Read the account before the summary Joseph Smith History 1:5-20 recounts religious disagreement, Joseph's reading and prayer, and his reported vision. Record the questions he describes and the response he says he received. This is the scriptural account accepted by Latter-day Saints; identifying it as an account is important when studying history. Explore and study Joseph Smith's account in his own words A reader leans over Joseph Smith's written account with another book open beside it. Beginning with his own words lets the record speak before we decide what his life and testimony mean. Read Joseph Smith–History 1 Compare accounts with attention to when they were recorded Use the First Vision Accounts essay linked above to reach the other records. Compare emphasis, wording, audience, and date of recording. The date an event is said to have occurred and the date a surviving account was written are different facts. The essay offers the Church's interpretation of differences; the underlying documents allow you to examine the evidence yourself. Keep historical and spiritual questions distinct A historical investigation can ask what records survive and how they relate. A spiritual inquiry may ask what the Restoration claim means for belief and practice. Those inquiries can inform each other, but one should not silently stand in for the other. If a concern remains, name it specifically and pursue the relevant evidence. A useful source note Write the title, author or recorder, date of the record, and exact passage you are considering. Add a separate sentence for your interpretation. This keeps a later retelling from becoming indistinguishable from the original evidence. Watch and study From a personal inquiry to shared work Explore and study Joseph Smith's accounts across time A handwritten record lies open beside an inkwell on a nineteenth-century desk. Preserved across time, Joseph Smith's accounts let readers follow how he described his search for God in his own words. Joseph Smith History 1:5-20 Explore and study Oliver Cowdery joins the work Two readers place the revelation beside their notes, tracing the shared labor, uncertainty and reassurance surrounding Oliver Cowdery's work with Joseph Smith. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6 In his October 2014 address Joseph Smith , Elder Neil L. Andersen discusses the Restoration and invites a personal witness through prayer and scripture. Compare his statement of faith with a revelation from the work surrounding the Book of Mormon. Read the heading to Doctrine and Covenants 6 as historical context. It identifies Harmony, Pennsylvania, April 1829, and Oliver Cowdery's work as a scribe beginning April 7. Church video Joseph Smith The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Verses 18-20 combine support with accountability. Oliver is asked to stand by Joseph in difficulty, and the two are to give and receive correction. Patience, faith, hope, and charity belong within that relationship. This is a useful passage to keep beside a history of religious leadership because the text itself makes room for faults and growth. In verses 21-23 the speaker identifies Himself as Jesus Christ and recalls peace given to Oliver. In verses 36-37 attention turns again to Christ and His wounds. Consider how the revelation directs a participant in the Restoration toward the Savior. Continue that connection in the full D&C 6:36 study . A study you can carry into the week These focusChrist prompts are invitations for personal reflection. Explore and study Bring the question to God A man bows his head beside a closed book on a quiet park bench, giving prayer and careful study room to work together as he seeks understanding. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6 First session: establish the question Choose a single question about Joseph's life. Write it in language that a source could help answer: what did he report, when was it recorded, or how did a particular teaching develop? Avoid making one question stand for his entire life. Second session: follow a citation Open a document linked from the First Vision essay. Read the surrounding passage. Note the recorder, recording date, and what the document actually says. If your question concerns a different period, use the Church History section to find the relevant sources. Third session: assess the interpretation Write a short account of what you learned, separating evidence from your explanation of it. Name any remaining uncertainty. A source can establish what a witness reported without resolving every question about the experience being described. Fourth session: consider the spiritual claim Read D&C 6 with the historical questions still clearly named. What does its invitation to seek wisdom, accept correction, and look to Christ mean for your own conduct? Personal reflection can accompany careful investigation without replacing it. Bring a passage and a specific question to Ask , then check the response against the linked original sources. Bring a careful question and an open heart Joseph Smith—History 1:11–13 describes Joseph reading James and considering what to do with his question. These reflections connect the source work on this page with your own honest inquiry. What question are you actually asking? Write it in one sentence. Is it about a reported event, the meaning of a teaching, or your own response to a prophetic claim? Identify the kind of source that could help you, then return to one of the records linked above. What has the record changed? Compare your first impression with what the source actually says. Which detail became clearer? What remains uncertain? Record the author and date so that the next conversation begins with evidence you can find again. What can you bring to prayer? Consider the spiritual claim after giving the historical question its proper attention. What would you like to ask God, and what are you willing to continue studying? An honest prayer can include both gratitude and unresolved questions. records.title: Why Are Families Important in Latter-day Saint Belief?
records.pageTitle: Why Are Families Important in Latter-day Saint Belief?
records.text: Answers / Families Latter-day Saints believe family is central to God’s plan because every person is a child of heavenly parents and because family relationships can become eternal through Jesus Christ and sacred covenants. Watch and study How Does Eternal Hope Shape a Home? Explore and study Practice patient companionship A father patiently helps his daughter tie her shoe. Small moments of gentleness can express the long-suffering and love that should guide family relationships. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121 In Eternal Families , President Henry B. Eyring connects the hope of family life with God to everyday service. Speaking to priesthood holders, he asks them to place their families and the families around them at the center of their concern. Near the end, he emphasizes the lasting value of small acts that help loved ones move toward eternal life. General conference video and text Eternal Families The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2016 Watch or read with two questions in mind: What does he teach about covenants? How does he describe the way family members should treat one another? He draws on Doctrine and Covenants 121:41-43 , emphasizing persuasion, patience, gentleness, and sincere love. As a personal application, consider a small act of care that fits your circumstances: listening without interruption, offering an apology for your own mistake, or keeping a promise. Eternal family teaching can give those ordinary choices meaning. It does not let us determine the worth or ultimate future of someone else's household. People come to this question from many circumstances: marriage, singleness, parenting, adoption, or life in a blended family. Some also carry grief, infertility, divorce, or painful relationships. Those experiences deserve individual care, without assumptions about anyone's faith or worth. We Belong to the Family of God Latter-day Saint teaching begins with divine identity: human beings lived with heavenly parents before birth and are sons and daughters of God. Earthly family life is therefore connected to a larger eternal family and provides a setting for learning love, sacrifice, responsibility, forgiveness, and service. Marriage and Parenting Matter Church teaching gives high importance to marriage, parenting, fidelity, nurturing children, and building homes centered on Jesus Christ. The family is viewed not merely as a social convenience but as part of God’s design for mortal growth and eternal happiness. What Does It Mean for a Family to Be Eternal? Latter-day Saints believe priesthood sealing ordinances performed in temples can unite husbands and wives, and parents and children, beyond death. These promises are connected to faithfulness to God and the covenants made in the temple. The doctrine is one reason temples and family history hold such a prominent place in Church life. What About Imperfect or Painful Family Situations? No family is perfect, and some relationships are unsafe or deeply wounded. The gospel does not require a person to pretend that abuse or serious harm is acceptable. The hope of eternal family life is centered on Jesus Christ’s power to redeem, heal, judge perfectly, and make right what cannot be fully repaired in mortality. Why This Belief Affects Everyday Life If relationships can matter eternally, daily choices toward patience, loyalty, repentance, forgiveness, teaching, and service gain added significance. Latter-day Saints are encouraged to strengthen family relationships while also extending Christlike love to people in every family circumstance. When Family Teachings Touch a Tender Place If talk of eternal families brings up longing or unanswered questions, you are welcome to take your time. You do not owe anyone a public explanation of your family life. For more focused reading, see support through divorce or hope after the death of a child . Care That Reaches Beyond One Household Family study can lead to a practical question: who needs care around me today? Mosiah 18:8-10 asks disciples to share burdens and offer comfort. That commitment can include a neighbor living alone, a parent needing a break, or someone whose relatives are far away. You might offer an invitation with room to decline, ask how someone prefers to be included, or help with an ordinary task. Belonging is easier to experience when people are known by name and treated with consideration, without having to explain why their household looks different. Study Belonging Alongside Responsibility Explore and study Let care extend beyond your household A parent and teenager clear an older neighbor's path together. Their care extends family discipleship outward through service that respects what the neighbor needs. Mosiah 18:8-9 Begin with people who need to be received Mark 10:13-16 shows adults bringing children to Jesus and disciples trying to turn them away. Jesus corrects that response and welcomes the children. Consider how a family or congregation could make room for a child who is shy, restless, disabled, or unfamiliar with worship. These are possible applications of welcome, not details supplied by the account. Explore and study Belonging means caring for one another Siblings work through a household task together, listening as they go. The ordinary moment carries the vision in Romans 12 of belonging to one body and caring for one another with affection. Read Romans 12 Love includes concrete care Romans 12:9-18 speaks of sincere love, hospitality, shared joy and sorrow, and seeking peace as far as it lies within one's power. The qualification matters: one person cannot control every relationship. Reflect on what care is yours to offer and where you need support or appropriate boundaries. Faithfulness and imperfect circumstances A teaching about the purpose of family is not a complete explanation of any particular household. Avoid turning an ideal into a ranking of people's worth. When family language brings grief or exclusion, it may help to talk with someone who can listen without requiring a defense of your circumstances. One practical way to use this study Choose one person and one form of care you can offer reliably. Ask what would help rather than assuming. If the subject raises more pain than clarity today, pause with the children's artwork study or use the focused resources on loss and divorce. Watch and study See Each Child as Someone to Know Explore and study Let someone be heard A mother listens while her teenage son speaks on the front steps. Gentleness and honest attention can keep love present in a difficult family conversation. Read Ephesians 4 Explore and study Make space for each person’s voice A multigenerational family listens as a teenager shares from their reading. Around the table, every age and question is welcomed, and kindness in Christ keeps the family learning together. Ephesians 4:31-32 3 Nephi 17:11-24 describes the Savior praying among the people and blessing their children individually. Read the account alongside the teaching about attentive parenting below. The multitude makes room for the children to come near Him, and their care receives the attention of the whole gathering. General conference video and text Fathers The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints · April 2016 In Fathers , Elder D. Todd Christofferson affirms equal partnership between parents, honors single fathers, foster fathers, and stepfathers, and recognizes circumstances requiring support and adaptation. He explicitly rejects abuse in discipline. For a parent, relative, teacher, or friend, these teachings can prompt a question about attention: what do I know about this child's interests, worries, and hopes? Listening to a child and following through on a promise are ordinary ways to practice care. You do not need to compare your household with another family's circumstances to choose a loving action today. A conversation about belonging If this would be useful, discuss one question with a willing family member or trusted friend: When have you felt heard here? What helps you feel included? Is there something we could do differently? Receive the answer without requiring agreement about every issue. Where there has been harm, a safe setting and qualified support may be needed before a joint conversation is appropriate. Practice belonging with the people before you Mark 10:13–16 shows Jesus welcoming children whom others had turned away. Let His attention guide a reflection on who feels received in your home, friendships, or congregation. Whose voice is easy to miss? Think of a child, an older person, or someone who lives alone. What makes it easier for that person to speak and be heard? Consider a quiet conversation where you can listen without turning their answer into a lesson. What would care look like in this family? Every household has particular needs. Ask someone what would lighten their week rather than assuming you already know. A shared task, a respectful boundary, or reliable company may matter more than an elaborate gesture. How could welcome reach farther? Who might feel left outside a conversation about families? Choose language and an invitation that make room for their actual circumstances. How can you express eternal hope while also honoring the joys and pain they carry today? Where would you like to go next? Study eternal marriage in depth Explore sealing, covenant faithfulness, equal partnership, tender questions, and a seven-day scripture path centered on Christ. Study Christ’s welcome of children Read two scriptural scenes and reflect on concrete ways to make room for children. When family life includes divorce Explore faith, dignity, boundaries, and support without an idealized family story.

records.title: Why Do Latter-day Saints Build Temples?
records.pageTitle: Why Do Latter-day Saints Build Temples?
records.keywords: why latter day saints build temples
records.text: Answers / Temples Latter-day Saints build temples because they believe God has commanded His people to create sacred places where worshippers make covenants, receive ordinances, learn of Jesus Christ, and seek blessings that extend beyond death. Temples are not the same as ordinary Sunday meetinghouses. This page summarizes Latter-day Saint belief; official Church temple resources are linked below. Watch and study See the purpose behind the building Explore and study Begin with the purpose of worship Two friends read scripture together on a shaded garden terrace. Their quiet study turns toward the Kirtland dedicatory prayer and its longing for learning, holiness and God's help. Read Doctrine and Covenants 109 Begin with Temples Through Time , which brings together scholars and people of different faiths to discuss ancient and modern temples. Listen for both shared interests and the distinct Latter-day Saint understanding explained on this page. The significance of a temple is best understood through what worshippers believe happens there. Church video Temples Through Time The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Doctrine and Covenants 109:1-15 records the Kirtland Temple dedication prayer in March 1836. The prayer asks the Father to accept the house in the name of Jesus Christ and seeks learning, holiness, and His presence. Study and faith appear together in verses 7 and 14 . Continue through verses 21-23 . The prayer includes repentance and restoration to blessings, then asks that servants leave the temple strengthened to share the gospel. This provides a pattern to consider: worship prepares people to go outward in service. It does not make the building an escape from the responsibilities of daily life. A House of the Lord A dedicated temple is regarded as a holy house of the Lord. Latter-day Saints connect modern temples with a scriptural pattern of sacred places where God teaches, covenants with, and blesses His people. Covenants and Ordinances A covenant is a sacred commitment between a person and God. An ordinance is a sacred religious act performed by priesthood authority. The Church explains these terms in Why Ordinances and Covenants Matter . Temple worship includes ordinances that are not performed in ordinary chapels. The endowment teaches God’s plan and includes covenants to follow Jesus Christ. Temple sealings unite husbands and wives and connect children to parents with the promise that family relationships can continue eternally when covenants are faithfully kept. Jesus Christ Is Central to Temple Worship Temple worship is intended to point disciples toward the Savior. The ordinances teach about God’s plan of salvation, the Atonement of Jesus Christ, obedience, sacrifice, consecrated discipleship, and the hope of returning to God through Christ. Why Are Some Temple Ceremonies Limited to Prepared Members? Before dedication, temples often hold public open houses. After dedication, participation in temple ordinances is reserved for Church members who have prepared spiritually and are recommended by local Church leaders. Latter-day Saints describe this as sacred preparation rather than secrecy: the covenants are treated as solemn commitments requiring readiness. What About People Who Have Died? Latter-day Saints believe God provides every person a fair opportunity to receive the gospel. In temples, living members may receive ordinances by proxy for deceased ancestors. Those ordinances are understood as an offer, not a forced conversion; the deceased retain agency to accept or reject them. When Temple Questions Are Personal For some readers, temple teachings bring hope; for others, they bring questions about a loved one, divorce, or circumstances that did not turn out as expected. A short explanation of sealing cannot resolve every individual situation. The official temple sealing overview explains the teaching, while a trusted Church leader can help with questions about your own participation. If the subject is tender, you may prefer to begin with families and belonging or support through divorce . There is no need to share private family details here in order to keep learning. Understand the Connections Behind Temple Worship Explore and study Prepare through learning Open scriptures, a notebook and a folded jacket wait in readiness for worship. The Kirtland dedicatory prayer teaches that preparation for God's house includes learning, faith and order. Doctrine and Covenants 109:7-8 Covenants grow from a relationship with God Mosiah 18:8-10 describes baptismal commitment in terms of bearing burdens, offering comfort, and serving God. These are baptismal teachings, not a description of the temple ceremony. They provide a familiar starting point for understanding why a covenant is meant to shape ordinary conduct as well as worship. Why do Latter-day Saints speak of restored keys? Doctrine and Covenants 110:1-10, 13-16 records a vision in the Kirtland Temple and the appearance of Elijah. Latter-day Saints connect this account with restored authority for temple work. Here keys means authority to direct particular priesthood work, not a physical object. The passage belongs to the Church's Restoration account and should be read in that setting. Service reaches beyond the living Read Doctrine and Covenants 138:30-35, 58-59 to connect temple service with teaching among the dead. Proxy describes one person performing an ordinance on behalf of another. It does not mean someone else's faith or willingness is decided for them. Keep the official temple resources beside this study when exploring the Church's explanation. How could this affect life outside the temple? Reflect on whether a promise to follow Christ is changing how you treat someone today. Service, honesty, and care for family and neighbors give a practical setting for considering covenant discipleship. No visitor needs to disclose their membership or temple status to use this study. Watch and study Covenant worship and joy in Christ Explore and study Connect worship with daily commitments A father and adult daughter talk while sharing the work of washing and drying dishes, connecting promises to God with patient care in daily life. Mosiah 18:8-10 Explore and study Temple building across generations Craftsmen measure and shape heavy stone with patience. Piece by piece, their devoted labor prepares a house where generations will come to worship God. Return to the Kirtland dedicatory prayer The Church's public overview of the endowment explains how temple instruction relates the Creation, Fall, and Atonement to God's plan. It also describes covenants involving obedience, sacrifice, gospel living, chastity, and consecration. Read those explanations directly so that the terms have more meaning than a list. Church video The Temple and Your Spiritual Foundation The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints The same overview encourages participants to learn over time and says they need not understand everything on their first visit. Preparation includes learning what one is committing to and choosing that commitment prayerfully. A quiet or unfamiliar experience does not need to be compared with someone else's description. In the accompanying October 2021 message, The Temple and Your Spiritual Foundation , President Russell M. Nelson connects temple covenants with a foundation in Jesus Christ. His complete address also discusses learning through continuing revelation. As a personal reflection, ask how temple learning might deepen gratitude for Him. Joy can be expressed through patient service, keeping a promise, or extending care to a family member. These are practical invitations, not a measure of another person's spiritual worth. A study you can carry into the week These focusChrist prompts are invitations for personal reflection. Explore and study Carry a covenant into daily care Two neighbors clear fallen branches from an older neighbor's path. The work is practical and personal, quietly fulfilling the baptismal promise to help carry another's burden. Read Mosiah 18:8–10 Understand a word Choose covenant, ordinance, endowment, or sealing. Read its explanation in the official resources and put it into your own words. Ask what the teaching says about the relationship between God and the person making the commitment. Connect worship and conduct Choose one ordinary responsibility that could receive greater care: your use of time, honesty at work, attention to family, or service to a neighbor. Consider what covenant discipleship would look like in that specific setting this week. Prepare an honest question If you are preparing to attend, bring questions about preparation and participation to your bishop or branch president. If you are simply learning, use the public introduction and source pages freely. This study does not require you to disclose your membership or personal circumstances. Remember an individual Consider learning one accurate detail about an ancestor or preserving a family memory with permission. Let your interest begin with a person's life and relationships. The section on service for the dead explains the belief behind proxy ordinances and the importance of agency. Bring a passage and a specific question to Ask , then check the response against the linked original sources. Let worship continue in daily life Doctrine and Covenants 109:7–9 joins learning, prayer, preparation, and going forth in the Lord’s name. Reflect on the purpose of worship as you return to ordinary responsibilities. What would you like to understand? Choose a word from the dedicatory prayer, such as faith or learning. Read its surrounding verses and the public Church sources linked above. What question would you bring to a trusted teacher before your next visit or study session? What will you carry home? Consider one commitment that could receive more care in daily life. How might prayer and learning affect your honesty, patience, or attention to another person? Choose a manageable action and a time to return to it. Whom will you remember with care? Think of someone whose life is connected with yours, living or deceased. What accurate story could you learn or preserve with permission? Let interest in family history begin with attention to an individual’s life. Read about life after death Understand the beliefs behind temple service for those who have died. Explore family relationships and belonging Consider eternal hopes alongside the varied realities of family life now. Watch an introduction to temple worship Hear an official explanation of temples, then continue with resources about listening and belonging at home.

Read its explanation in the official resources and put it into your own words. Ask what the teaching says about the relationship between God and the person making the commitment. Connect worship and conduct Choose one ordinary responsibility that could receive greater care: your use of time, honesty at work, attention to family, or service to a neighbor. Consider what covenant discipleship would look like in that specific setting this week. Prepare an honest question If you are preparing to attend, bring questions about preparation and participation to your bishop or branch president. If you are simply learning, use the public introduction and source pages freely. This study does not require you to disclose your membership or personal circumstances. Remember an individual Consider learning one accurate detail about an ancestor or preserving a family memory with permission. Let your interest begin with a person's life and relationships. The section on service for the dead explains the belief behind proxy ordinances and the importance of agency. Bring a passage and a specific question to Ask , then check the response against the linked original sources.

records.title: Be Still - Art & Study
records.text: Inspirational Art / Be Still Christ walks shoulder to shoulder with a burdened man while the city rushes around them. “Be still” becomes more than escape from noise. It becomes the courage to recognize who walks beside us. A path through this study Find Christ in the Press of the Day The man in the artwork has not stepped outside modern life. Cars, buildings, and other people remain close. Yet Christ is closer. Begin there, then read Psalm 46 in its full setting of shaking earth, roaring water, and unsettled nations. Look Notice the burdened posture of the man and the Savior's steady place beside him. Read Hear “be still” inside a psalm about refuge, upheaval, and God's presence. Respond Choose one faithful action for today and one outcome you can entrust to God. Scripture study Stillness in the Middle of Upheaval Psalm 46 opens with God as refuge and strength. The earth moves, waters roar, and kingdoms shake. The invitation to be still comes near the end, after the psalmist has described God bringing conflict to an end. Biblical stillness is not denial. It is a reorientation toward the God who remains present when the world feels unstable. The Lord repeats the invitation in Doctrine and Covenants 101:13-17 . Here too, comfort comes to people living through distress. The command and promise belong together: be still, and know that He is God. Peace with the storm still close In Mark 4:35-41 , frightened disciples wake Jesus in a storm. He calms the sea and then asks about their fear and faith. John 14:27 adds a promise of peace that differs from what the world gives. Together, the passages invite us to seek Christ's presence without pretending every storm ends on our preferred schedule. Look again Peace That Walks with Us These artworks do not all show quiet surroundings. They show companionship, trust, and release within real movement and strain. The Savior in the Storm Wind and water fill the boat, but the disciples are not alone. Read the fear, their cry for help, and the great calm in Mark 4:35-41 . Closer Than the Noise Traffic and crowds continue around them, yet Christ matches the man's pace and listens. His promise of peace meets life as it is in John 14:27 . A Breath Before the Next Step No answer is being forced in this moment. The still water and closed journal allow time to remember the refuge named in Psalm 46 . Peace with Work Still to Do The burden is not imagined away; it is lifted together. Faithful stillness can lead into willing action, as taught in Doctrine and Covenants 58:26-28 . Give the Moment Your Attention The phone lies face down, and the open Bible has his attention. A quiet moment can help us return to God amid a busy day. Read the invitation in Psalm 46:10 . Quiet reflection Be Still, Then Walk Forward Stillness can prepare the heart for faithful action. Open one prompt and stay with it for a few minutes. What remains steady when life feels unsettled? Read Psalm 46 and list what changes in the chapter. Then list what the psalm says about God. Let the contrast shape a short, honest prayer. What can I do, and what can I entrust to God? Name one responsibility you can act on today. Then name one outcome you cannot control. Doctrine and Covenants 58:26-28 can help you hold agency and trust together. Who could use a quiet companion? The Savior in the artwork does not speak from across the street. Think of someone whose burden may need your presence more than your advice. Anchor Stillness in Jesus Christ In “Be Still, and Know That I Am God” , Elder David A. Bednar connects spiritual stillness with covenant confidence in Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ. Read it beside Psalm 46 rather than treating stillness as a technique by itself. records.title: Suffer the Little Children - Art & Study
records.pageTitle: Suffer the Little Children - Art & Study
records.text: Inspirational Art / Suffer the Little Children Children press close to Jesus without fear. One rests against Him, another reaches toward Him, and the Savior receives their trust with complete attention. A path through this study Come Close Without Fear The painting is full of touch, movement, and trust. Jesus is not speaking to a distant crowd; He is giving the children His time. The Gospel accounts make that welcome even more striking because the disciples had tried to turn them away. Look Notice each child's posture and the calm attention Jesus gives them. Read Follow the movement from being rebuked at the edge to being held and blessed. Respond Ask what helps a child or vulnerable person feel safe, heard, and cherished. Scripture study He Took Them in His Arms Read Mark 10:13-16 slowly. People bring children to Jesus so He can touch them. The disciples object, but Jesus is displeased with the barrier they create. He calls the children to Him, takes them in His arms, places His hands upon them, and blesses them. His welcome is spoken and embodied. Jesus also teaches the adults: the kingdom of God must be received as a little child. The passage honors qualities such as trust and openness without pretending children never feel fear or pain. The adults around them carry a sacred responsibility to protect, listen, and lead with love. A day of prayer, tears, and joy at Bountiful In 3 Nephi 17 , Jesus perceives that the people desire Him to remain. He heals their sick, prays with them, and asks that their little children be brought to Him. The chapter lingers over compassion. Read verses 21-24 and notice what the children receive and what the gathered adults are allowed to witness. Look again Every Child Drawn Near These artworks carry the same welcome into different places and relationships. Open each one at full size before reading the scripture beside it. Unhurried Welcome One child rests against Him while another shares a small treasure. Jesus gives them His full attention, just as He takes the children into His arms in Mark 10:13-16 . Gentleness at Her Pace Christ lowers Himself to the child's eye level and waits with an open hand. The small distance between them makes His invitation, “forbid them not” in Mark 10:14 , feel especially tender. Joy in Every Place The children are not a background around Jesus; their voices and faces fill the circle. His invitation is extended “unto all” in 2 Nephi 26:33 . Time Enough to Listen The child holds a stone and a story; the Savior turns toward both. Matthew 18:1-5 asks adults to learn from a child rather than look past one. Time to Listen A backpack rests beside the bench while a mother gives her son her attention. Receiving a child can begin with time to listen. Consider the Savior’s invitation in Mark 9:36–37 . Quiet reflection Receive and Protect Use these questions for prayer, a journal, or a family conversation. What do I see in the children's faces and hands? Look again before answering. Notice who is reaching, resting, watching, or smiling. What does Jesus do that allows closeness and trust? How can I listen to a child more fully? Choose one ordinary moment this week to put distractions down, listen without interrupting, and take a child's words seriously. What does Christlike protection require? The Savior removed a barrier and welcomed the children. Consider whether a family, congregation, school, or community practice needs more patience, safety, or attentive care from you. Keep the Children at the Center For a child-friendly retelling, read Jesus Blesses the Little Children . For further teaching about our responsibility toward children, continue with Little Children by President Boyd K. Packer.
