records.title: The Good Shepherd - Art & Study
records.text: Inspirational Art / The Good Shepherd The Savior moves through a crowded street with a warm, attentive expression. The image carries the tenderness of a Shepherd who knows His sheep, seeks the wandering, and never treats a wounded life as an inconvenience. A path through this study Listen for the Shepherd's Voice Look first at the Savior's face and the life moving around Him. He is not distant from the street or the people in it. John 10 gives language to that closeness: He knows, calls, leads, protects, and lays down His life for the sheep. Look Notice the Savior's expression and the people nearest Him in the crowded street. Read Listen for every action Jesus uses to describe the Good Shepherd in John 10 . Respond Consider one person you can notice, call, or walk beside with greater care. Scripture study Known, Led, and Loved In John 10:1-18 , Jesus describes a relationship built on recognition and trust. The shepherd knows the sheep and calls them; the sheep recognize his voice and follow. The image grows deeper when Jesus says the Good Shepherd gives His life for the sheep. His care is not sentimental. It is costly, faithful, and personal. Psalm 23 adds the language of provision, rest, guidance, and companionship through the valley of the shadow of death. The shepherd does not promise a path with no valley. He promises His presence through it. The sheep beyond the present fold Jesus speaks of “other sheep” in John 10:16 . In 3 Nephi 15:11-24 , the risen Christ identifies the people at Bountiful with that promise. Read the two passages together and notice how His voice reaches people in more than one place. Look again The Shepherd Draws Near These scenes place the Savior beside people in need of healing, strength, and companionship. Open each artwork, then let the linked passage shape what you see. Gathered into His Arms The lamb rests against the Shepherd while the flock follows through rough country. Isaiah's promise is both strong and tender in Isaiah 40:11 . The One Is Not Overlooked The street keeps moving, but Jesus stops and comes close. His parable in Luke 15:3-7 counts one wandering sheep as worth seeking. Strength Shared Under Strain Mud and effort cover everyone in the scene. The Savior's focused care gives weight to His invitation for the weary in Matthew 11:28-30 . Known in a Crowd Many faces fill the street, yet Jesus looks toward one man and calls him down by name. Follow the welcome and change in Luke 19:1-10 . Until He Finds It One sheep stands apart among the rocks, and the shepherd turns toward it. This scene invites us into the persistent care of the lost-sheep parable in Luke 15:4–7 . Quiet reflection Hear and Follow Choose the prompt that feels most honest today. Where have I noticed the Shepherd's care? Read Psalm 23 slowly. Name one place where you have received rest, direction, nourishment, or companionship. Offer thanks for the person or moment through which that care came. Which voice am I learning to trust? John 10 describes sheep recognizing the shepherd's voice. Compare a thought that leads toward Christlike love with one that produces contempt or despair. What fruit does each voice bear? Who might need someone to walk beside them? Think of one person who may feel unseen or burdened. Choose a small act of steady care: listen, send a message, share a meal, or help with something practical. Study the Shepherd's Compassion In Our Good Shepherd , Elder Dale G. Renlund teaches about the Savior's compassion for imperfect people and His joy as they heal. You can also follow the theme through the Good Shepherd entry in the Guide to the Scriptures . records.title: The Living Christ - Art & Study
records.text: Inspirational Art / The Living Christ The portrait meets us with light, warmth, and an open expression. Christian hope rests on the witness that Jesus Christ rose from the tomb and still calls people by name. A path through this study Come Near to the Living Christ Begin with the face in the portrait. The light is bright, yet the Savior's expression is gentle. Nothing in the image asks us to hurry past Him. Let that first impression accompany you into the Resurrection accounts, where grief, fear, recognition, and joy all unfold in the presence of the risen Lord. Look Notice the light, the Savior's expression, and where your attention settles first. Read Walk through John 20 with Mary Magdalene, the gathered disciples, and Thomas. Respond Name one way belief in a living Savior changes the way you meet this day. Scripture study Follow the Witnesses in John 20 John 20:1-18 begins before the morning is clear. Mary comes to the tomb carrying grief and discovers that the stone has been moved. She does not recognize Jesus until He speaks her name. The change in the account is deeply personal: sorrow becomes recognition, and recognition becomes a message she is trusted to carry. Continue with John 20:19-31 . The disciples are behind closed doors when Jesus comes among them and speaks peace. Thomas receives time, an invitation to see, and a reason to believe. John closes by telling readers why these signs were written: that they might believe Jesus is the Christ and find life in His name. Why the Resurrection reaches beyond one morning Paul connects Christ's Resurrection with the promised resurrection of humankind in 1 Corinthians 15:12-22 . The hope is not that death is insignificant. The hope is that death will not have the final word. That promise can be precious even when grief is still present. Look again Images of His Continuing Care Each image turns toward a different human need. Open any artwork to explore its scripture and study options, view the full-size picture, or continue the lesson. Called by Name Morning light reaches the garden as Mary turns toward the voice she knows. Stay with the tenderness of recognition in John 20:11-18 . Peace Behind Closed Doors Fear has gathered the disciples into one room. Christ comes among them with open hands and the first gift He names is peace in John 20:19-23 . Faith Met with Patience Jesus does not reduce Thomas to a label. He meets him face to face and answers his longing to know. Read the encounter in John 20:24-29 . Hope That Does Not Rush Grief The open Bible and quiet companionship hold sorrow and hope in the same morning. The risen Christ's promise reaches toward mourning in John 11:25-26 . Breakfast on the Shore Bread passes from hand to hand beside the morning fire. The risen Savior welcomes His disciples to a meal before inviting Peter to care for His sheep. Read the encounter in John 21:9–17 . Quiet reflection Let the Witness Become Personal These prompts are invitations, not a test. Open the one that meets you today. When have I felt known by name? Return to Mary in John 20:11-18 . Sit for a moment with the change that comes when Jesus speaks her name. Write the name of someone who may need to feel remembered today. What closed door am I standing behind? The disciples received the words “Peace be unto you” while the doors were shut. records.title: Follow the Witnesses in John 20
records.text: Scripture study Follow the Witnesses in John 20 John 20:1-18 begins before the morning is clear. Mary comes to the tomb carrying grief and discovers that the stone has been moved. She does not recognize Jesus until He speaks her name. The change in the account is deeply personal: sorrow becomes recognition, and recognition becomes a message she is trusted to carry. Continue with John 20:19-31 . The disciples are behind closed doors when Jesus comes among them and speaks peace. Thomas receives time, an invitation to see, and a reason to believe. John closes by telling readers why these signs were written: that they might believe Jesus is the Christ and find life in His name. Why the Resurrection reaches beyond one morning Paul connects Christ's Resurrection with the promised resurrection of humankind in 1 Corinthians 15:12-22 . The hope is not that death is insignificant. The hope is that death will not have the final word. That promise can be precious even when grief is still present.

For example, read John 20:24-31 and notice Thomas's absence, his later encounter with Jesus, and the author's explanation for writing. You might ask, “How does this account speak to readers who were not there?” That question is more specific than asking for a general statement about doubt. Read the response alongside the source. Check whether it explains the passage's setting, distinguishes the text from an application, and leaves room for what the passage does not settle. A fluent answer still needs checking. You can ask a follow-up about a verse or an unfamiliar term, and you are free to disagree with an interpretation. Continue the John 20 study Walk through Mary, the disciples, and Thomas; then consider why resurrection matters. When your question is personal Explore scripture and discernment without treating an automated response as personal revelation. When two passages seem different Use a comparison that preserves context and separates the text from your own conclusions. You do not have to share private experiences to study here. records.title: The Atonement of Jesus Christ
records.text: An invitation to linger Because He lives, we can begin again Jesus Christ is at the heart of this study. His suffering in Gethsemane and on the cross, His death, and His Resurrection open the way home to our Heavenly Father. We come to Him with sins to forsake, sorrows to share, questions to ask, and hope that may still be small. He invites us to come. Begin with John 3:16–17 and the official Atonement of Jesus Christ study guide . Follow the story from the beginning, or choose the part you need today. Open any picture for its scripture and study options. The artwork offers reverent, imaginative scenes; the linked scriptures provide the accounts we study. 01 · Before the world Before the world: chosen from the beginning The Beloved Son and the Father's will The Pearl of Great Price takes the story of redemption back before mortal life. Moses records the Beloved Son's willingness to do the Father's will and give Him the glory. Abraham describes the council before the world and the choice of one who would be sent. Jesus Christ's mission belongs within the Father's loving purpose for His children. Moses 4:1–4 · Abraham 3:22–28 · Moses 1:39 Explore the picture and scripture The heavens above us Stars fill the sky above still water. Let the quiet of this imagined landscape lead you to the scriptures about Jesus Christ, the Creator. Moses 2:1 John 1:1–5 Pause and reflect Read the Son's response in Moses 4:2 beside His prayer in Luke 22:42. What continuity do you see in His willingness to serve the Father? Creation belongs to the story Moses records God creating through His Only Begotten. John's Gospel identifies the Word who was with God and through whom all things were made. The Savior who came into mortality is also the Creator. His love for the world is personal. Continue from the Creator’s premortal mission into the birth of Jesus Christ , following the scriptural promises and the witnesses who welcomed Him into mortality. Moses 2:1 · John 1:1–5, 14 · Doctrine and Covenants 76:22–24 Official Church study guide Atonement of Jesus Christ Begin with the Church’s guide, then follow its questions and scriptures into a deeper personal study. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Continue · Why a Savior? ↓ All chapters ↑ 02 · Why a Savior? Why we need a Savior Mortal life, agency, and the Fall Our lives include real choices and real consequences. Lehi places agency within God's plan and teaches that redemption comes through the Holy Messiah. The Fall brought mortality and separation from God's presence; Jesus Christ makes redemption possible. We are also responsible for our own sins. Our need for Him includes both the death we cannot prevent and the sins from which we cannot cleanse ourselves. Explore the picture and scripture The road through mortality A path leads from green shelter into open, rugged country. Read Lehi’s teaching about agency and redemption. 2 Nephi 2 Read 2 Nephi 2:6–9, 22–27 and Mosiah 3:17 . Justice and mercy Alma does not treat wrongdoing as unimportant. He teaches that mercy reaches the repentant through the Redeemer while justice remains real. Repentance is possible because of Christ. His invitation gives us a reason to face the truth about our choices and a way to move forward. Read Alma 42:13–25 . Reflect: What changes when I see repentance as an invitation from someone who loves me? Deeper reading: 2 Nephi 9 , Alma 34:8–17 , Moses 5:9–12 . Explore the picture and scripture The Shepherd seeks the one The sheep rests in His arms. Jesus tells of a shepherd who goes after the one that is lost. Luke 15:3–7 Continue · The promise ↓ All chapters ↑ 03 · The promise The promise reaches Adam, Eve, and the prophets Redemption taught from the beginning An angel taught Adam that sacrifice pointed to the Only Begotten. Adam and Eve heard the promise of redemption and rejoiced. Enoch's teaching connects the Fall, repentance, baptism, the Spirit, and the blood of the Only Begotten. The invitation to come to Christ runs through these earliest accounts. Moses 5:5–12 · Moses 6:48–62 Explore the picture and scripture Hope beyond Eden Two figures face the morning beside cultivated ground and a simple altar. This imagined scene of Adam and Eve invites us to read the promise of redemption they received. Moses 5:5–12 Enoch sees the Redeemer Enoch mourned as he saw human wickedness and suffering. He also saw the coming of the Son of Man, the cross, and the promise of resurrection. The vision joins sorrow with hope. Read the account carefully and notice where Enoch's attention turns toward the Savior. Moses 7:44–47, 53–57 · Moses 7:62 The Lamb and the suffering servant The Passover account tells of deliverance. Isaiah speaks of the servant who bears grief and sorrow. John the Baptist identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God. Read these passages together and consider how scripture prepares us to understand His sacrifice. Exodus 12:1–14 · Isaiah 53:3–7 · John 1:29 · 1 Corinthians 5:7 Pause and reflect Which image helps you understand Him today: Creator, Redeemer, Lamb, Shepherd, or the One who carries our sorrows? Follow one title through its linked passages. Explore the picture and scripture Remembering deliverance Bread, herbs, a cup, and a lamp invite a pause to remember Passover. This symbolic still life leads to the account of deliverance and to Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God. Exodus 12:1–14 John 1:29 Continue · His sacrifice ↓ All chapters ↑ 04 · His sacrifice His willing sacrifice At the table Before Gethsemane, Jesus shared bread and the cup with His Apostles. Remembering Him would become part of their worship. Read slowly and notice how personally He speaks about His body and blood. Luke 22:14–20 · Matthew 26:26–29 Explore the picture and scripture In remembrance of Him Bread and a cup rest on a quiet table. Return to the Savior’s words at the Last Supper. Luke 22:14–20 In Gethsemane Jesus prayed to the Father in anguish and submitted to His will. The account calls for reverence. We can attend to His words without pretending to measure everything He endured. In latter-day revelation, the Savior speaks of His suffering and invites us to repent. Luke 22:39–46 · Doctrine and Covenants 19:16–19 Explore the picture and scripture Not my will, but thine Under the olive trees, Jesus bows in prayer. Read His words to the Father. Luke 22:39–46 At the cross John records the title placed on the cross, the two others crucified beside Jesus, and His mother standing nearby. Even there, He spoke to His mother and the beloved disciple about their care for one another. He later declared His work finished and died. His burial followed; His Resurrection would transform the disciples' grief. John 19:17–30 · Matthew 27:45–54 · John 19:38–42 Sensitive scene: The Crucifixion This artwork depicts the Savior’s suffering. You may continue reading without viewing it. Show image — At the cross Hide image — At the cross Explore the picture and scripture At the cross From above and behind the cross, we look toward the people gathered below and Jerusalem beyond. John records the Savior’s love and His finished work. John 19:17–30 Matthew 27:45–54 Pause and reflect What do His words reveal about His love? Read John 10:17–18 and 3 Nephi 27:13–16 . Sensitive scene: The Crucifixion This artwork depicts the Savior’s suffering. You may continue reading without viewing it. Show image — Those who stayed nearby Hide image — Those who stayed nearby Explore the picture and scripture Those who stayed nearby From beside and behind the cross, we see those who have stayed nearby. John records the Savior’s tender care for His mother and the beloved disciple. John 19:25–27 Conference message · Watch or read The Purifying Power of Gethsemane Bruce R. McConkie bears witness of the Savior’s sacrifice. Read or listen, then return to the Gospel accounts. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Conference message · Watch or read None Were with Him Jeffrey R. Holland follows the Savior’s lonely journey and bears witness of His love for us. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Conference message · Watch or read Lifted Up upon the Cross Jeffrey R. Holland reflects on the cross and the meaning of following Jesus Christ. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Continue · He is risen ↓ All chapters ↑ 05 · He is risen Resurrection and living hope The tomb was empty. Mary Magdalene encountered the risen Lord. The disciples' witness concerns a living Savior, not only the memory of a teacher they loved. John 20:1–18 · Luke 24:36–43 Explore the picture and scripture The tomb was empty Morning light enters a rock-cut tomb. Read the witnesses’ accounts of the risen Savior. John 20:1–9 Through Jesus Christ, everyone will be resurrected: spirit and body will be reunited. Eternal life with God is a distinct gift. Christ invites us to receive it through faith in Him, repentance, His ordinances and covenants, and faithful discipleship. 1 Corinthians 15:20–22 · Alma 11:42–45 · 3 Nephi 27:19–21 Explore the picture and scripture Mary A woman turns toward the risen Jesus in a garden. John records that He called Mary by name. John 20:11–18 Pause and reflect How does the promise of Resurrection change the way I remember someone I love? Explore the picture and scripture Along the road Jesus walks beside two listeners on a country road. Read how He opened the scriptures to the disciples traveling to Emmaus. Luke 24:13–32 Official Church study guide Resurrection Follow the scripture witnesses and explore the promise of life beyond death. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Continue · One by one ↓ All chapters ↑ 06 · One by one The Book of Mormon witnesses of His love A Redeemer promised Nephi's vision joins the birth and ministry of the Son of God with an explanation of God's love. King Benjamin teaches of the Savior's suffering and the salvation that comes through Him. Abinadi draws on Isaiah, and Alma speaks of the Redeemer's intimate knowledge of pain. These witnesses prepare readers to recognize Jesus Christ. 1 Nephi 11:13–33 · Mosiah 3:5–11 · Mosiah 14 · Alma 7:10–13 Explore the picture and scripture He had compassion on them Jesus leans toward an older woman as others wait nearby. Read of His compassion and healing among the people in the Book of Mormon. 3 Nephi 17:5–9 One by one The risen Jesus invited the people to come forward and know that He was the God of Israel who had been slain for the sins of the world. They came one by one. Later He healed their sick, prayed for them, and blessed their children. His ministry gives the doctrine a personal setting: people heard Him, approached Him, and received His compassion. 3 Nephi 11:10–17 · 3 Nephi 17:5–9, 11–24 · 3 Nephi 18:1–11 Pause and reflect What do you notice when you read the account slowly, one person at a time? Which invitation would you like to respond to today? An invitation that remains open Moroni ends with an invitation to come to Christ and be perfected in Him. The book's testimony leads to a relationship with the Savior and a life changed through His grace. Moroni 10:32–33 · 2 Nephi 26:23–28, 33 Continue · His living voice ↓ All chapters ↑ 07 · His living voice His living voice in the Doctrine and Covenants Hear the Savior speak In modern revelation Jesus Christ speaks of His suffering, calls us to repent, and describes Himself as our Advocate with the Father. These passages invite careful, personal reading. Notice who is speaking and what He asks us to trust. Doctrine and Covenants 19:15–20 · Doctrine and Covenants 45:3–5 · Doctrine and Covenants 18:10–13 Explore the picture and scripture A place in the day An open book and notebook sit before a thoughtful reader. Choose a passage and linger with it. 2 Nephi 32:3 Mercy reaches beyond the grave Joseph F. Smith's vision describes the Savior's work among the righteous dead and the organization of messengers to carry the gospel to those who had not received it. The vision expands our view of His redeeming work while honoring the need for repentance and the ordinances of His gospel. Doctrine and Covenants 138:11–19, 29–35, 57–59 · 1 Peter 3:18–20 · 1 Peter 4:6 Look unto Him Christ's invitation to look to Him belongs in ordinary days as well as moments of crisis. Read His words about His wounds, fear, and faith together. Return to the same passage when your circumstances change; there may be more to hear. Doctrine and Covenants 6:32–37 · Doctrine and Covenants 50:40–42 Pause and reflect Which of His invitations would you like to carry with you this week? Write it in your own notebook and return to the complete passage. Continue · Repentance ↓ All chapters ↑ 08 · Repentance Sin, repentance, and forgiveness Come honestly Repentance begins with turning toward God. We recognize wrong, feel sorrow for it, confess, seek forgiveness, and forsake the sin. Where possible, we repair the harm. Serious sins require help from the appropriate priesthood leader. The process is personal and sincere; a checklist cannot measure a changed heart. Explore the picture and scripture An honest prayer A man bows his head in the quiet of his home. There is room to speak honestly with God. Enos 1:2–8 Official guide: Repentance . Scripture: Doctrine and Covenants 58:42–43 . A heart can turn Alma remembered Jesus Christ and cried for mercy. His account moves from anguish to joy. We need not expect everyone's experience to follow the same emotional timetable to trust the same Redeemer. Alma 36:17–21 · Luke 15:11–24 · Enos 1:2–8 Explore the picture and scripture Coming home An elderly father holds his returning son. Read the parable Jesus told about repentance and welcome. Luke 15:11–24 Pause and reflect What is one honest step I can take today? Choose a private prayer, a needed conversation, or a safe act of repair. Do not use an apology to demand reconciliation or place someone in danger. Making amends calls for sensitivity and respect for the other person's wishes. Seek trusted guidance when direct contact could cause further harm. Read the Church's recovery guide on making amends . Explore the picture and scripture Taking a step to make things right Two neighbors exchange a tool at a workshop door. Consider the practical work of making amends. Mosiah 27:35 Official Church study guide Repentance Explore how faith in Jesus Christ leads to sincere change, confession, forgiveness, and a new direction. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Official Church study guide Step 9: Wherever possible, make direct restitution to all persons we have harmed. Read practical guidance for making amends with humility, care, and respect for those affected. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the complete resource ↗ Continue · Grace ↓ All chapters ↑ 09 · Grace Grace and becoming new Grace is God's gift through Jesus Christ. We do not purchase it by accumulating good deeds. His grace also helps us grow as we exercise faith and follow Him. Obedience can become a grateful response to His love, and weakness can become a place where we learn to rely on Him. records.excerpt: An illustrated study of Jesus Christ and His Atonement, from the Pearl of Great Price through all the scriptures. Explore His love, sacrifice, Resurrection, repentance, grace, and healing.

records.title: Because He lives, we can begin again
records.text: Jesus Christ is at the heart of this study. His suffering in Gethsemane and on the cross, His death, and His Resurrection open the way home to our Heavenly Father. We come to Him with sins to forsake, sorrows to share, questions to ask, and hope that may still be small. He invites us to come. Begin with John 3:16–17 and the official Atonement of Jesus Christ study guide . Follow the story from the beginning, or choose the part you need today. Open any picture for its scripture and study options. The artwork offers reverent, imaginative scenes; the linked scriptures provide the accounts we study.

records.title: Before the world: chosen from the beginning
records.text: 01 · Before the world Before the world: chosen from the beginning The Beloved Son and the Father's will The Pearl of Great Price takes the story of redemption back before mortal life. Moses records the Beloved Son's willingness to do the Father's will and give Him the glory. Abraham describes the council before the world and the choice of one who would be sent. Jesus Christ's mission belongs within the Father's loving purpose for His children. Moses 4:1–4 · Abraham 3:22–28 · Moses 1:39 Explore the picture and scripture The heavens above us Stars fill the sky above still water. Let the quiet of this imagined landscape lead you to the scriptures about Jesus Christ, the Creator. Moses 2:1 John 1:1–5 Pause and reflect Read the Son's response in Moses 4:2 beside His prayer in Luke 22:42. What continuity do you see in His willingness to serve the Father? Creation belongs to the story Moses records God creating through His Only Begotten. John's Gospel identifies the Word who was with God and through whom all things were made. The Savior who came into mortality is also the Creator. His love for the world is personal. Continue from the Creator’s premortal mission into the birth of Jesus Christ , following the scriptural promises and the witnesses who welcomed Him into mortality. Moses 2:1 · John 1:1–5, 14 · Doctrine and Covenants 76:22–24 Official Church study guide Atonement of Jesus Christ Begin with the Church’s guide, then follow its questions and scriptures into a deeper personal study. records.title: Why we need a Savior
records.text: 02 · Why a Savior? Why we need a Savior Mortal life, agency, and the Fall Our lives include real choices and real consequences. Lehi places agency within God's plan and teaches that redemption comes through the Holy Messiah. The Fall brought mortality and separation from God's presence; Jesus Christ makes redemption possible. We are also responsible for our own sins. Our need for Him includes both the death we cannot prevent and the sins from which we cannot cleanse ourselves. Explore the picture and scripture The road through mortality A path leads from green shelter into open, rugged country. Read Lehi’s teaching about agency and redemption. 2 Nephi 2 Read 2 Nephi 2:6–9, 22–27 and Mosiah 3:17 . Justice and mercy Alma does not treat wrongdoing as unimportant. He teaches that mercy reaches the repentant through the Redeemer while justice remains real. Repentance is possible because of Christ. His invitation gives us a reason to face the truth about our choices and a way to move forward. Read Alma 42:13–25 . Reflect: What changes when I see repentance as an invitation from someone who loves me? Deeper reading: 2 Nephi 9 , Alma 34:8–17 , Moses 5:9–12 . Isaiah speaks of the servant who bears grief and sorrow. John the Baptist identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God. records.title: Sin, repentance, and forgiveness
records.text: 08 · Repentance Sin, repentance, and forgiveness Come honestly Repentance begins with turning toward God. We recognize wrong, feel sorrow for it, confess, seek forgiveness, and forsake the sin. Where possible, we repair the harm. Serious sins require help from the appropriate priesthood leader. The process is personal and sincere; a checklist cannot measure a changed heart. Explore the picture and scripture An honest prayer A man bows his head in the quiet of his home. There is room to speak honestly with God. Enos 1:2–8 Official guide: Repentance . Scripture: Doctrine and Covenants 58:42–43 . A heart can turn Alma remembered Jesus Christ and cried for mercy. His account moves from anguish to joy. We need not expect everyone's experience to follow the same emotional timetable to trust the same Redeemer. Do not use an apology to demand reconciliation or place someone in danger. Making amends calls for sensitivity and respect for the other person's wishes. Seek trusted guidance when direct contact could cause further harm. Read the Church's recovery guide on making amends . records.title: The Birth of Jesus Christ
records.text: Answers / The birth of Christ The birth of Jesus Christ is the coming of the Savior into mortal life. Scripture invites us to see the child in the manger in light of His whole mission: to reveal the Father, redeem us from sin and death, and know how to help us in our weakness. Follow the reading journey or choose a question to begin. The linked passages open with their surrounding chapter. The pictures invite attention to particular moments; the scriptures remain the source for the account. These witnesses speak from different settings. We can connect their testimony without turning every passage into one continuous scene. Ancient faces, clothing, buildings, visions, and dreams are depicted through respectful artistic interpretation. Their exact appearance is not established by these texts. Look for what a passage records, what the picture helps you notice, and what remains a question. Promises before Bethlehem The Promised Son Isaiah speaks into the fears of a real king and people. In Isaiah 7:3-14 , he meets Ahaz and announces the sign of Immanuel. Read the encounter before isolating the familiar promise. The passage has an immediate historical setting even as later scripture draws our attention to its fulfillment in Jesus Christ. Explore and study Isaiah brings the promise to Ahaz Amid fear for Jerusalem, Isaiah brings a word from the Lord. Read the encounter and the promise of Immanuel in its setting. Isaiah 7:3–14 Matthew 1:22-23 explicitly connects Isaiah's words with Jesus' birth and explains Emmanuel as God with us. This is the Gospel's stated connection. We need not erase Isaiah's earlier audience to receive Matthew's witness of the Savior. The light in Isaiah 9:2 and the child and royal names in Isaiah 9:6-7 widen the promise beyond one birth scene. Isaiah 11:1-5 speaks through Jesse and branch imagery, the Spirit of the Lord, and righteous judgment. These prophecies invite us to know the Messiah through His character and to hope for the peace of His kingdom. Explore and study Bethlehem in the promise The quiet hills invite us to consider Micah’s promise about Bethlehem and the ruler who would come from it. Micah 5:2 Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem Ephratah in a prophecy of a coming ruler. In Matthew 2:4-6 , the chief priests and scribes cite the connection when Herod asks where Christ should be born. A small place becomes part of a much larger promise. The coming ruler will be known through the purposes of God, even as His mortal life begins in humble circumstances. Read the promise in its setting Choose one prophetic passage. What concern or hope appears around it? Then read its linked Gospel connection. Write what each text contributes, keeping the original setting and the later witness in view. Distinct prophets, one Redeemer Witnesses across the Book of Mormon In 1 Nephi 11:13-21 , Nephi sees the mother of the Son of God and the child in her arms. In this vision, his question about God's love leads toward the Son entering human life. The picture draws our attention to the mother and child Nephi sees. A child held in His mother's arms becomes part of the answer to a prophet seeking to understand divine love. Explore and study The mother and child Nephi saw Nephi sees a mother with the Son of God in her arms. Through this vision, he comes to understand the love of God. 1 Nephi 11:18–23 Nephi later connects the Messiah's coming with His death and Resurrection in 2 Nephi 25:12-19 . In 2 Nephi 26:1-3 , he anticipates Christ's later ministry and signs of His birth, death, and Resurrection. These are different occasions. Together they keep the Christmas story connected to the redemption the Savior will accomplish. King Benjamin reports that an angel awakened him with a message. Mosiah 3:2-8 announces the Lord's coming among human beings, names Mary, and describes healing and deliverance. Benjamin shares this message with his people as a witness of the Redeemer. His account moves from the wonder of the announcement toward the mercy that Christ will extend to those who come to Him. Explore and study Alma teaches of the coming Savior Alma teaches that the Son will be born of Mary and take upon Himself the pains and infirmities of His people. His coming brings help for the whole human journey. Alma 7:7–13 Alma 7:7-13 gives another reason to care about the birth: the Son will know pains, sicknesses, and infirmities and know how to help His people. Alma names Mary and the land of his people's forefathers while looking ahead to her Son's ministry. Luke gives Bethlehem as the town of His birth. Alma's emphasis here is the Savior's willingness to enter our mortal experience and His knowledge of how to help us. Samuel speaks from a city wall in Helaman 13:2-4 . His message in Helaman 14:2-6 looks five years ahead to the Savior's birth, a night without darkness, and a new star. At this point the signs are promised. His preaching and their later fulfillment belong to different scenes. Explore and study Samuel promises the signs Samuel announces the signs that will accompany the Savior’s birth. His message asks his hearers to trust the Lord through the years of waiting. Helaman 14:2–6 What does each witness add? Nephi sees, Benjamin reports an angelic message, Alma teaches the Savior's coming ministry, and Samuel announces signs. Choose one witness and name his particular contribution. Resist filling his account with details from another. Watch Samuel announce the signs Listen for the difference between his promises about Christ's birth and His later death. The excerpt helps you revisit the prophet's message before reading the fulfillment. Book of Mormon video excerpt Samuel Prophesies the Signs of Christ's Birth and Death The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Samuel speaks from the city wall about the promised signs of Christ’s coming. Read his prediction in Helaman 14:2-6 before turning to its later fulfillment in 3 Nephi 1:15-21 . John points to Christ A People Prepared for the Lord Luke begins with Zacharias and Elisabeth, their long waiting, and an announcement about a son. In Luke 1:8-19 , Gabriel speaks to Zacharias at the temple. The child is John, whose calling is to prepare people for the Lord. The joy of this long-awaited birth reaches beyond one family: John will help others recognize and receive Jesus Christ. A name, a birth, and a voice of praise Luke 1:57-64 follows the promise into the life of the family. records.excerpt: Study the birth of Jesus Christ through Old Testament promises, New Testament witnesses, and Book of Mormon prophecies and signs, with art and official Church resources.

records.title: The Promised Son
records.text: Promises before Bethlehem The Promised Son Isaiah speaks into the fears of a real king and people. In Isaiah 7:3-14 , he meets Ahaz and announces the sign of Immanuel. Read the encounter before isolating the familiar promise. The passage has an immediate historical setting even as later scripture draws our attention to its fulfillment in Jesus Christ. Explore and study Isaiah brings the promise to Ahaz Amid fear for Jerusalem, Isaiah brings a word from the Lord. Read the encounter and the promise of Immanuel in its setting. Isaiah 7:3–14 Matthew 1:22-23 explicitly connects Isaiah's words with Jesus' birth and explains Emmanuel as God with us. This is the Gospel's stated connection. We need not erase Isaiah's earlier audience to receive Matthew's witness of the Savior. The light in Isaiah 9:2 and the child and royal names in Isaiah 9:6-7 widen the promise beyond one birth scene. Isaiah 11:1-5 speaks through Jesse and branch imagery, the Spirit of the Lord, and righteous judgment. These prophecies invite us to know the Messiah through His character and to hope for the peace of His kingdom. Explore and study Bethlehem in the promise The quiet hills invite us to consider Micah’s promise about Bethlehem and the ruler who would come from it. Micah 5:2 Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem Ephratah in a prophecy of a coming ruler. In Matthew 2:4-6 , the chief priests and scribes cite the connection when Herod asks where Christ should be born. A small place becomes part of a much larger promise. The coming ruler will be known through the purposes of God, even as His mortal life begins in humble circumstances. Read the promise in its setting Choose one prophetic passage. What concern or hope appears around it? Then read its linked Gospel connection. Write what each text contributes, keeping the original setting and the later witness in view.

records.title: Witnesses across the Book of Mormon
records.text: Distinct prophets, one Redeemer Witnesses across the Book of Mormon In 1 Nephi 11:13-21 , Nephi sees the mother of the Son of God and the child in her arms. In this vision, his question about God's love leads toward the Son entering human life. The picture draws our attention to the mother and child Nephi sees. A child held in His mother's arms becomes part of the answer to a prophet seeking to understand divine love. Explore and study The mother and child Nephi saw Nephi sees a mother with the Son of God in her arms. Through this vision, he comes to understand the love of God. 1 Nephi 11:18–23 Nephi later connects the Messiah's coming with His death and Resurrection in 2 Nephi 25:12-19 . In 2 Nephi 26:1-3 , he anticipates Christ's later ministry and signs of His birth, death, and Resurrection. These are different occasions. Together they keep the Christmas story connected to the redemption the Savior will accomplish. King Benjamin reports that an angel awakened him with a message. Mosiah 3:2-8 announces the Lord's coming among human beings, names Mary, and describes healing and deliverance. Benjamin shares this message with his people as a witness of the Redeemer. His account moves from the wonder of the announcement toward the mercy that Christ will extend to those who come to Him. Explore and study Alma teaches of the coming Savior Alma teaches that the Son will be born of Mary and take upon Himself the pains and infirmities of His people. His coming brings help for the whole human journey. Alma 7:7–13 Alma 7:7-13 gives another reason to care about the birth: the Son will know pains, sicknesses, and infirmities and know how to help His people. Alma names Mary and the land of his people's forefathers while looking ahead to her Son's ministry. Luke gives Bethlehem as the town of His birth. Alma's emphasis here is the Savior's willingness to enter our mortal experience and His knowledge of how to help us. Samuel speaks from a city wall in Helaman 13:2-4 . His message in Helaman 14:2-6 looks five years ahead to the Savior's birth, a night without darkness, and a new star. At this point the signs are promised. His preaching and their later fulfillment belong to different scenes. Explore and study Samuel promises the signs Samuel announces the signs that will accompany the Savior’s birth. His message asks his hearers to trust the Lord through the years of waiting. Helaman 14:2–6 What does each witness add? Nephi sees, Benjamin reports an angelic message, Alma teaches the Savior's coming ministry, and Samuel announces signs. Choose one witness and name his particular contribution. Resist filling his account with details from another. Watch Samuel announce the signs Listen for the difference between his promises about Christ's birth and His later death. The excerpt helps you revisit the prophet's message before reading the fulfillment. Book of Mormon video excerpt Samuel Prophesies the Signs of Christ's Birth and Death The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Samuel speaks from the city wall about the promised signs of Christ’s coming. Read his prediction in Helaman 14:2-6 before turning to its later fulfillment in 3 Nephi 1:15-21 .
