records.title: What can the English language tell us?
records.text: Explore and study Make time for the written word Joseph studies an open Bible with a writing tool close at hand. His attention invites a slower reading: notice a phrase, record a question, and return to the passage in context. What might patient study help you see that a hurried reading would miss? Read James 1 Stanford Carmack: look at sentence patterns Stanford Carmack's command-syntax study examines how forms of “command” connect to another verb. Compare the ordinary possibilities “ordered them to leave” and “ordered that they should leave.” The important question is not whether either construction can occur, but how the alternatives are distributed through a substantial text. Carmack reports that Book of Mormon command patterns differ markedly from those in the King James Bible and find closer parallels in earlier English material, including a work printed by William Caxton in 1483. He interprets this as support for Joseph receiving specific wording rather than producing it himself. That last step should be identified as his inference. Readers can investigate the counted constructions and comparison texts without treating the resulting translation model as an experimentally demonstrated fact. The study concerns the language of the English text; it does not date the events narrated in that text. Read Carmack's command-syntax study . Why unusual grammar deserves more than a joke In a later grammatical study, Carmack considers combinations of features rather than isolated archaic words. Examples include relatives referring to people, older verbal constructions, and forms judged nonstandard by later usage. He compares the earliest Book of Mormon wording with historical English, biblical language, imitation-biblical writings, and Joseph's early personal writing. The method invites a better question than whether a sentence sounds polished to a modern reader: what grammatical pattern is present, and where else is that pattern found? A useful comparison should preserve the actual wording under examination. Modernized editions may remove the feature being discussed. Examine Carmack's grammatical comparisons . What the Early Modern English proposal does not claim Carmack's 2025 question-and-answer essay acknowledges that the Book of Mormon is not entirely Early Modern English. It also says that the precise process by which the proposed English translation was produced is unknown. He argues strongly for revealed wording, but the historical language patterns and an account of the unseen translation process remain different kinds of claims. Early Modern English is a period in the history of English; it is not a language spoken by Nephi. Identifying an older English construction would therefore concern the translation's English expression, not directly establish the antiquity of its narrative. Nor does the proposal identify a particular earlier English translator through documentary evidence. Readers can find the linguistic argument suggestive while withholding judgment about mechanisms that cannot be observed. Keeping those limits clear allows interest in the research without turning an interpretive model into a required article of faith. Read Carmack's questions and answers . Explore and study Compare the words with care A pencil follows connections across three working copies. Careful comparison begins by looking closely at the wording, then asking whether the proposed explanation accounts for it. Read the researchers' own arguments, including where they disagree, before deciding what a pattern can establish. Follow Carmack's command-syntax comparison , then consider Davis's alternative analysis . Bring a question from this picture into the reading. Ask about this part of the study . A serious alternative interpretation William L. Davis's 2025 study accepts that the discussion cannot be reduced to copying King James vocabulary. He challenges the inference that archaic features necessarily lay outside Joseph's linguistic resources. Davis emphasizes older religious books still read in the nineteenth century and the difference between a person's everyday speech and a deliberately sacred register. He proposes that Joseph actively formulated the English wording. This disagreement helps identify the real question. It is not simply whether an older parallel exists, but whether that parallel excludes the linguistic resources and habits available to the person dictating. Davis's explanation is itself an argument to assess, not a complete recording of Joseph's mental activity. Reading both positions lets a visitor distinguish shared observations from disputed explanations. Careful study makes that comparison possible without implying that all researchers have reached the same conclusion. Read Davis's alternative analysis .

records.title: A household that made room for the work
records.text: The story of the translation also leads into a family's fields, a journey, and the daily work of opening a home. In June 1829, Peter and Mary Whitmer welcomed Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery to their home in Fayette, where the translation was completed. Explore the Peter and Mary Whitmer home . Three remembered experiences help us understand how the Whitmers connected their practical service with faith. These accounts reach us through later histories, interviews, and family recollections. Read them with appreciation for what their tellers wanted to preserve, while noticing who recorded each story and when. A later memory can be meaningful without becoming a contemporary transcript. You might study these accounts together as a family: let one person follow the sources, another notice the acts of service, and another choose a question for prayer. Leave room for each person to speak honestly. David's fields and the journey he wanted to make Explore and study Help for the journey David pauses beside the worked field, a plow resting nearby. This scene draws on the later account of overnight plowing; Lucy Mack Smith recorded separate help with harrowing and spreading plaster. As you compare the accounts, consider how practical help can free another person to serve. Read the plowing recollection Compare Lucy’s account Lucy Mack Smith's 1845 history describes David facing urgent farm work before he could collect Joseph and Oliver. In that account, he harnessed his horses to a harrow and finished two days' work in one. The next morning, he found that the plaster intended for his fields had already been spread. His sister reported seeing three men doing that work; she had assumed David had hired them. The family understood the unexpected help as divine assistance. Read Lucy's account of the harrowing and the three men spreading plaster . A different recollection, quoted in the Church's Revelations in Context , describes David finding several acres plowed overnight. Plowing, harrowing, and spreading plaster are distinct tasks. The accounts should be read in their own wording rather than blended into one detailed reconstruction. Compare David's reported recollection . These stories invite a practical question: what makes it possible for someone to answer a call to serve? Sometimes another person's willingness to finish a task, provide a ride, or take responsibility for a household opens the way. Think of someone whose quiet help has given you time to do something that mattered. How could you offer that kind of help this week? A traveler beside the wagon Explore and study An offer of hospitality An ordinary offer of a ride becomes a remembered moment of sacred purpose in David’s later account. This artistic interpretation invites us to notice the person beside us. The faces, setting, and precise arrangement of the encounter are imagined, not a contemporary visual record. Read the traveler account David later told Orson Pratt and Joseph F. Smith of an encounter during the return journey with Joseph and Oliver. An older man greeted them beside their wagon. When offered a ride, he replied, “No, I am going to Cumorah.” David said the man then disappeared and identified him as the messenger carrying the plates. The Church's history manual reproduces this report and cites its publication in the Millennial Star on December 9, 1878. It is David's recollection many decades after the journey. Read the traveler account and its source notes . The memorable exchange belongs to the history of David's testimony. It does not supply a measured route or settle a modern geographical model. As you consider it, notice how the story moves from an ordinary offer of hospitality to David's sense of sacred purpose. What habits of attention help you make room for the person beside you, even before you understand their story? Mary's work and her own witness Explore and study Encouragement amid the work Mary’s later family account remembers encouragement in the midst of demanding household work. This interpretive scene honors that experience without claiming an authenticated likeness or an exact view of the plates. Whose quiet service could you notice, thank, or help carry today? Read Mary’s story Read Mosiah 2:17 The work of hosting also fell heavily on Mary. The Church's account draws on a grandson's report that she was burdened by caring for additional people. While going to milk the cows, she encountered a stranger who showed her the plates, turning their leaves, and encouraged her to continue faithfully. The cited report appeared in Andrew Jenson's Historical Record in October 1888. This preserves a family recollection of Mary's experience, rather than a statement written by Mary in 1829. Read Mary's story and the household's contribution . Her place in this history invites us to notice the person carrying work that others may overlook. Hospitality takes time, strength, food, and patience. Acknowledging that cost need not diminish its generosity. Mary's story offers a moment to consider both receiving encouragement and giving it: who around you needs their effort to be seen, thanked, or shared? Read Mosiah 2:17 alongside Doctrine and Covenants 14:8 , the invitation given to David. Consider how service and witness meet in a life of discipleship. Continue into the formal witness statements , explore the people of Church history , or return to the artwork gallery to revisit these stories through their pictures.

records.title: The witnesses: read the claims in their own words
records.text: Explore and study Three witnesses, distinct voices Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris pause in an imagined conversation. Their different faces invite us to hear each witness as a person with his own history. Continue into their statements and the separate sequence of Martin’s reported experience, rather than treating this grouping as the angelic encounter. Read about the witnesses The Three Witnesses: read the statement and its history The Three Witnesses' published statement reports an angelic showing of the plates and a divine affirmation of the translation. The Joseph Smith Papers provides the 1830 printed text alongside an editorial account of its transmission. Its editors note that the earliest surviving manuscript copy is in Oliver Cowdery's handwriting, including the other witnesses' names; that copy is not an original sheet of separate autographs. This does not establish that the witnesses disowned the statement. It tells us what kind of document survives. Read the testimony's claim, then distinguish that claim from the provenance of the surviving copy. Read the Three Witnesses' statement and source history . The Eight Witnesses: a different kind of testimony The Eight Witnesses' statement emphasizes seeing and handling plates shown by Joseph Smith. Its wording describes their appearance and workmanship. It should not be expanded into an assay establishing purity, an independent translation of the engravings, or an archaeological excavation. Those are different procedures, and they are not what the statement reports. The distinction gives this testimony its particular place beside that of the Three. Readers are considering a reported tangible encounter as well as a reported angelic encounter. The evidentiary question is how to evaluate those reports, not how to transform them into experiences the speakers never described. Read the Eight Witnesses' statement . Continuing testimony and differing recollections The Church's historical overview describes repeated affirmations by witnesses, including after estrangement from Joseph or the Church. It also acknowledges that surviving reports are not equally reliable: some were recorded long afterward, and some passed through interviewers with their own interests. The men named in the statements were connected through early Church involvement and family relationships. Persistence can matter when assessing sincerity. It does not turn every later interview into a verbatim record or make connected witnesses statistically independent observations. A useful comparison identifies the speaker, recorder, date, and distance from the event. Study the witnesses' later accounts and their limitations .

records.title: Literary patterns: read, compare, and test
records.text: A book that rewards a second reading A reader can encounter the Book of Mormon first as a sequence of journeys, sermons, conflicts, and encounters with Jesus Christ. A second reading brings other questions into view. Why does a passage return to its opening language? Who is speaking, and who has chosen to preserve that speech? What changes when a father retells his conversion to his son? Literary study begins with these questions and asks us to look closely enough to explain what we notice. Grant Hardy’s Understanding the Book of Mormon , published by Oxford University Press in 2010, organizes its reading around Nephi, Mormon, and Moroni. His approach examines how narrators arrange documents, dialogue, and parallel stories while setting aside the question of ultimate authorship. That distinction makes careful discussion possible among readers with different beliefs. A person can recognize a meaningful literary structure before deciding what that structure implies about the book’s origin. Hardy, Understanding the Book of Mormon . For this study, keep three questions beside one another: What is actually present in the text? Which explanation best accounts for it? How much can that explanation establish? The first encourages observation, the second invites investigation, and the third keeps an interesting discovery from becoming an exaggerated claim. Explore and study Hope in a prayer for mercy A man pauses in prayer, his expression opening toward hope. Inspired by Alma’s account, this reflection invites us to consider the turning of a heart toward the Savior. Consider the hope that grows when a person turns toward Christ for mercy. Read Alma 36 Alma 36 : turning toward Christ at the center Chiasmus arranges related elements in reverse order, such as A–B–C–B′–A′. A simple illustration is an original sentence: “We carried the record into the wilderness; through the wilderness we carried the record home.” Reversal can connect an ending to a beginning and emphasize what happens between them. John W. Welch’s analysis of Alma 36 proposes an extended pattern around Alma’s remembrance of, and appeal to, Jesus Christ. His interpretation treats the chapter as a deliberately shaped account of conversion. Read the entire chapter before following an outline; the outline is an interpretation of the writing, not a substitute for it. Welch, “Chiasmus in Alma 36” . Several correspondences are easy to investigate directly: Earlier in the chapter Later in the chapter Keeping the commandments and prospering, verse 1 The same counsel returns, verse 30 Remembering ancestral captivity and deliverance, verse 2 Remembering ancestral deliverance, verses 28–29 Loss of bodily strength, verse 10 Strength returns, verse 23 Distressing remembrance of sins, verse 17 That distress is relieved, verse 19 Between suffering and relief, Alma remembers his father’s teaching and appeals to Jesus in verses 17–18 . Whatever judgment a reader reaches about the complete pattern, this movement from anguish to mercy belongs to the passage itself. Notice how the return to earlier subjects gives the account a changed emotional direction. Alma 36 . Explore and study A father shares the mercy he remembers Alma speaks while Helaman listens, their faces turned toward one another. Before tracing the patterns in Alma 36, hear the father telling his son how remembering Jesus Christ changed his despair into joy. What would you want someone you love to remember from your own experience of mercy? Read Alma 36 Bring a question from this picture into the reading. Ask about this part of the study . How strong is the proposed pattern? Welch published fifteen criteria for evaluating proposed chiasms. They invite attention to matters such as meaningful boundaries, convincing correspondences, balance, density, and repetitions that fall outside the proposed arrangement. His framework recognizes that confidence about intentional composition can vary. A long diagram deserves especially careful testing because an analyst has many opportunities to select convenient words or ideas. Welch, “Criteria for Identifying and Evaluating the Presence of Chiasmus” . Earl M. Wunderli challenged the extended Alma 36 analysis in Dialogue . He argued that some proposed pairs depend on paraphrase and that additional occurrences of important words do not follow the suggested reversal. His criticism gives readers a concrete test: mark every occurrence of a proposed key term, including inconvenient ones, and compare the diagram with the full passage. The scholarly disagreement concerns the strength and explanatory value of the proposed structure. Wunderli, “Critique of Alma 36 as an Extended Chiasm” . Boyd F. Edwards and W. Farrell Edwards developed statistical methods for examining whether specified arrangements could occur by chance. Their work considers repeated elements and opportunities for patterns within larger texts. Such calculations depend on the defined elements and the model of chance. A small probability under a random-order model does not supply a probability that a book is ancient or divinely revealed; those are different questions. Edwards and Edwards, “Does Chiasmus Appear in the Book of Mormon by Chance?” . Try a smaller passage next. In Alma 41:13–14 , the sequence good, righteous, just, merciful is followed by counsel moving through mercy, justice, righteousness, and goodness. The return of the vocabulary supports the passage’s discussion of restoration. Read the surrounding argument and ask how the arrangement helps explain what a person gives and receives. This example allows a reader to examine verbal order without first accepting a large reconstruction. Alma 41:12–15 .

records.title: Voices and records within the book
records.text: Explore and study Let a careful question guide the comparison A reader compares a book, notes, and an illustrative scatterplot. The chart suggests the work of asking how patterns differ; its dots do not reproduce the findings of a named authorship study. Consider how checking the samples and assumptions can make a conclusion more responsible. Read Doctrine and Covenants 88 Explore and study Receive the voices of the record A reader attends closely to a record held in his hands. His quiet concentration invites us to slow down, notice who is speaking, and consider why a testimony was preserved. What would you want a future reader to understand about the faith you hope to pass on? Read 1 Nephi 6 Can a computer recognize different voices? Stylometry measures features of writing and compares their distributions. Depending on the study, those features may include frequent words, recurring word combinations, or vocabulary diversity. The important questions concern the samples and the comparison: which passages were assigned to which speaker, which writers were included, and which features the method could reliably distinguish. Wayne A. Larsen, Alvin C. Rencher, and Tim Layton’s 1980 study reported differences among Book of Mormon speaker samples and between those samples and selected nineteenth-century writers. It helped establish the modern statistical debate over the book’s authorship. Its conclusion supports distinguishable styles under its particular preparation and analysis; the stronger inference to separate ancient authors requires additional assumptions about quotation, editing, and translation. Larsen, Rencher, and Layton, “Who Wrote the Book of Mormon? An Analysis of Wordprints” ; the authors’ later presentation . David I. Holmes reached a different result in a 1992 paper in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society . His vocabulary-richness measures did not separate Book of Mormon samples into consistent prophet-by-prophet groups. Joseph Smith’s personal writing did form a separate cluster, while much of the scriptural material grouped together. Holmes interpreted the wider findings as supporting Smith’s prophetic voice, drawing on historical arguments as well as statistics. His study therefore cannot accurately be summarized as a straightforward match between the Book of Mormon and Smith’s ordinary prose. Holmes, “A Stylometric Analysis of Mormon Scripture and Related Texts,” especially conclusions, pp. 116–118 . Matthew L. Jockers, Daniela M. Witten, and Craig S. Criddle used Delta and nearest shrunken centroid classification in 2008. Their seven-candidate comparison produced results they interpreted as supporting a nineteenth-century composition involving Sidney Rigdon, Solomon Spalding, and Oliver Cowdery. This is a real competing result in the research literature, and a balanced account should acknowledge it. A classification result still depends on which possible authors the analysis permits. Jockers, Witten, and Criddle, “Reassessing Authorship of the Book of Mormon” . In 2011, G. Bruce Schaalje, Paul J. Fields, Matthew Roper, and Gregory L. Snow extended the method to address an open set of possible authors and differing text sizes. Their reanalysis produced markedly different results. The central issue is understandable without advanced mathematics: an unknown text may belong to somebody outside the list supplied to the computer. A method needs a meaningful way to handle that possibility. An “unknown” result does not identify an ancient author, but it prevents the nearest listed candidate from automatically becoming the answer. Schaalje and colleagues, “Extended Nearest Shrunken Centroid Classification,” DOI 10.1093/llc/fqq029 . Imagine comparing an unsigned letter only with samples from three neighbors. One neighbor will probably be the closest match even if a cousin wrote it. This hypothetical illustrates why “best match among these candidates” and “identified author” need separate wording. It also shows why findings should be evaluated with historical information about access, chronology, and the production of the text. Modern authorship research treats changes in subject and genre as substantial challenges. Experiments on controlled corpora show why a method must distinguish a writer’s habits from the characteristics of an essay, conversation, or topic. Applied here, that calls for particular care when comparing scriptural narration with personal correspondence. “Cross-Domain Authorship Attribution Using Pre-trained Language Models” . Research comparing different feature sets likewise shows that their usefulness depends on the dataset. Sari, Stevenson, and Vlachos, “Topic or Style?” . Translation adds another layer. Mormon 9:32–34 describes the record’s language and writing system as changed over time and anticipates interpretation. Those are claims within the text. English-language measurements alone cannot recover an unavailable source-language manuscript or decide how much of an observed style belongs to a source, editor, or translator. That is a limit of the inference, even when the numerical comparison is competently performed. Mormon 9:32–34 . Names that invite a closer reading Some linguistic proposals concern possible wordplay concealed by translation. Matthew L. Bowen argues that Nephi’s name may be connected with Egyptian nfr , associated with goodness or beauty, and reads the repeated goodness language at the beginning and end of Nephi’s writings as an intentional frame. This is an attributed etymological and literary proposal. The exact source-language spelling of the name is unavailable for independent comparison. Bowen, “Nephi’s Good Inclusio” . The observable English pattern can be studied first. Nephi begins with his parents, learning, afflictions, and knowledge of God’s goodness. Near his conclusion, he again invites participation in God’s goodness. Reading those passages together directs attention to what he wants his audience to receive. The framing remains available for reflection even while the proposed etymology is evaluated separately. 1 Nephi 1:1–3 ; 2 Nephi 33:10–15 . Bowen offers a related reading of Benjamin’s sermon: the traditional meaning “son of the right hand” is set beside the people’s becoming Christ’s children and their promised place at God’s right hand. His argument proposes deliberate name-related rhetoric. These expressions also belong to a broader biblical religious vocabulary, so their occurrence alone cannot establish the language or date of composition. Bowen, “Becoming Sons and Daughters at God’s Right Hand” . Read Mosiah 5:7–10 slowly and notice whose name the people are asked to receive. The sermon turns their attention to Christ and to living faithfully within that relationship. A discussion of wordplay is most useful when it helps readers attend to this invitation rather than making the proposed pun carry the entire weight of an origin argument. Mosiah 5:7–10 . Explore and study A record entrusted to his son Mormon and Moroni hold the wrapped record between them. An aging father is placing more than an object in his son's care: the words will continue beyond his own voice. Read Mormon 6:6 and notice the small record he preserves for Moroni amid the danger facing their people. Read Mormon 6:6 Bring a question from this picture into the reading. Ask about this part of the study . Records within a record Narrative complexity becomes clearer when we follow how accounts are introduced and brought together. Mosiah 9 changes into Zeniff’s first-person account. His opening includes both sympathy toward the people he had been sent to spy on and an admission of excessive eagerness to recover ancestral land. This is an invitation to read a narrator’s retrospective judgment alongside his description of events. Mosiah 9:1–4 . In Mosiah 25 , records of Zeniff’s people and Alma’s people are read to an assembled audience. Their response includes joy for deliverance, sorrow for losses, and thanksgiving. Reading itself becomes an event within the story: remembered experiences shape a community that did not experience them all together. This is a concrete literary connection a visitor can follow directly. Mosiah 25:5–11 . Such features give a historical-origin proposal material to explain. They also give literary readers material to analyze. Complexity alone is not a test that distinguishes history from fiction, and several devices in one text should not automatically be counted as independent proofs. A stronger conversation specifies the feature, examines plausible alternatives, and explains what additional evidence would help discriminate among them. As you continue, choose one passage and write three short notes: a feature you can point to, an interpretation you find persuasive, and a question that remains open. Then return to the passage’s invitation. Literary discovery can deepen attention, gratitude, and thoughtful faith while leaving room for careful scholarship and honest disagreement.

records.title: Ancient context: journeys, names, and material records
records.text: Explore and study Faith along an uncertain road Travelers move together through a rugged landscape, carrying what they need for the next part of the journey. The scene evokes shared effort and the uncertainty of leaving familiar ground. Consider the patience and care a family needs while the road ahead remains uncertain. Read 1 Nephi 17:1–6 Follow the text before drawing a map Nephi's account gives readers more than a generic desert journey. It describes travel generally south-southeast, stops for provisions, hunting, family grief, and a burial at a place already called Nahom. Read those details together in 1 Nephi 16:13–34 . The difference between a place the travelers name and a place with an existing name matters when evaluating proposed geographical connections. The next chapter describes an eastward course followed by arrival at a coastal place the travelers call Bountiful because it provides food. Nephi then receives a command to build a ship. These details supply questions for fieldwork: could a proposed route reach a coast with the resources the narrative requires? 1 Nephi 17:1–16 . An instructive study activity is to list the textual requirements before looking at any modern candidate. This helps keep the proposed map accountable to the record rather than quietly changing the requirements to fit a favorite location. Nahom: a real inscription and a proposed connection Three ancient South Arabian limestone altars from the Bar'an temple near Marib, Yemen, name a donor associated with the Nihm tribe. Their consonantal designation includes NHM. Warren Aston argues that this ancient attestation is an important connection with the Book of Mormon's Nahom. His later study discusses revised dating earlier than initial reports and describes the inscription's tribal context. Warren P. Aston, “A History of NaHoM,” BYU Studies 51:2 . The distinction is essential: the altars are actual archaeological objects; identifying their NHM with Nephi's Nahom is an interpretation. They do not name Lehi or Ishmael, locate Ishmael's grave, or record a journey to America. The consonants alone do not supply the Book of Mormon's English vowels. The proposed connection brings together name, place, and chronology; the inscription itself does not say that Ishmael was buried there. Older publications date the altars differently. Aston’s later study places the attestation before the period of Lehi’s proposed journey. The dates remain scholarly estimates; they do not establish an altar from exactly 600 BC. The eastward turn and Bountiful Explore and study Hope beside the sea A green coastal inlet opens between rugged hills and quiet water. This imagined landscape invites us to pause with the relief of reaching a place of abundance after a difficult journey. Consider the gratitude that can grow when a long road opens toward a new beginning. Read 1 Nephi 17 Kent Brown links the Nahom proposal with the regional setting of the incense routes and the narrative's later eastward movement. This is a geographical argument joining several observations, rather than a second inscription independently naming Nephi's route. Readers can examine how much of the argument rests on ancient routes, tribal geography, and modern reconstruction. Kent S. Brown, “Nahom and the Eastward Turn” . Field researchers have examined the green coastal pockets of southern Oman as possible settings for Bountiful. Aston favors Khor Kharfot at Wadi Sayq and discusses competing proposals, including Khor Rori. The interest lies in a combination of terrain, water, vegetation, access, and possible shipbuilding resources. Warren P. Aston, “Into Arabia” . A plausible landscape is not a recovered campsite. Compare which requirements a researcher considers satisfied, which depend on ancient environmental conditions, and which alternatives remain possible. None of these proposals conclusively identifies Nephi's shipyard. Explore and study Words worth preserving Hands guide an engraving tool across a metal sheet. The close view draws attention to the deliberate work of leaving a record for others. What makes a testimony worth the effort of preserving it for someone you may never meet? Read 1 Nephi 19:1–6 Writing sacred words on metal Ancient people did sometimes preserve religious writing on precious metal. The National Etruscan Museum documents three gold sheets from Pyrgi, dated to the end of the sixth century BC. Two bear Etruscan texts and one a related Phoenician dedication. They concern a sanctuary and its dedication, not the Book of Mormon. National Etruscan Museum, “Lamine d'oro da Pyrgi” . The British Museum also preserves the Petelia gold tablet, a small Greek religious text dated to the third–second centuries BC. Its catalog distinguishes the earlier tablet from its later Roman pendant case. British Museum, object 1843,0724.3 . Such objects answer a limited but meaningful question: writing religious material on metal was a real ancient practice. They do not establish the existence, size, contents, or provenance of Joseph Smith's plates. A short dedication on a sheet of gold and a long historical record are different kinds of object. The museum records let us examine the actual objects and the specific ancient practices they document. Names: a promising field that needs careful controls Names are useful because inscriptions can preserve forms that ordinary historical narratives overlook. Paul Hoskisson examines Alma as a Semitic personal name, drawing attention to evidence that complicates the assumption that it must be a modern feminine name. Paul Y. Hoskisson, “What's in a Name? Alma as a Hebrew Name” . Later work revisits additional attestations rather than treating the first proposal as the last word. Neal Rappleye and Allen Hansen, “More Evidence for Alma as a Semitic Name” . A name's ancient attestation demonstrates that such a form existed; it does not demonstrate that the person in the inscription is the Book of Mormon character. A careful entry should show the underlying spelling, language, approximate date, and proposed pronunciation. Similar sounds can arise by coincidence, and a familiar English spelling can conceal different ancient consonants. The relevant question is how specific the comparison is, and whether it survives examination alongside names that do not fit the proposed pattern. This is evidence to weigh, not a shortcut around linguistic analysis. Hebrew and Egyptian proposals Eve Koller investigates an Egyptian component in several Book of Mormon names, including proposed grammatical relationships. Her study provides a concrete example of comparative language research: a proposal should explain how the ancient language works, not merely find a word that resembles an English name. Eve Koller, “An Egyptian Linguistic Component in Book of Mormon Names,” BYU Studies 57:4 . These proposals should retain their scholarly status. An English transliteration does not preserve all the information available in an original inscription. Multiple possible derivations may compete, and an attractive meaning is not necessarily the historical source of a name. Ancient-language correspondence is most informative when its spelling, grammar, context, and chronology reinforce one another. Compare one worked example with its full argument. A list of English names does not give scholars direct access to the original Book of Mormon language. The original plate text is unavailable for that kind of direct comparison, so the proposed linguistic ancestry remains an inference.

records.title: Archaeology, populations, and questions still open
records.text: Archaeology in the Americas Latter-day Saint archaeologist John E. Clark argues that archaeological discoveries have improved the plausibility of numerous features in the Book of Mormon. His work is valuable as a substantial scholar's positive case, with arguments that readers can examine rather than a collection of anonymous assertions. John E. Clark, “Archaeological Trends and the Book of Mormon Origins” . Clark’s assessment presents an argument to examine. A resemblance between an ancient American practice and a narrative detail does not by itself identify the people who practiced it as Nephites. Questions of location, chronology, scale, and competing explanations still matter. Several correspondences may also depend on the same proposed geographical model; they should not automatically be counted as independent proofs. The Church takes no position identifying the specific locations of Book of Mormon events in the ancient Americas. Its official guidance asks members not to imply prophetic endorsement for personal maps. “Book of Mormon Geography,” Topics and Questions . This leaves room for study while keeping institutional teaching distinct from a researcher's reconstruction. Explore and study Notice what lies around a find An archaeologist records the layers beside her before moving on. The patient work around an object helps others ask when, where and how it came to rest there. As you examine a proposed connection, look for that surrounding evidence as carefully as the object itself. The National Park Service explains how field observations are recorded . Read that practice beside the Church's guidance on Book of Mormon geography . Bring a question from this picture into the reading. Ask about this part of the study . Horses: distinguish new discoveries from the wrong time period A 2023 study in Science combines archaeology, genetics, and Indigenous knowledge to investigate how domestic horses spread through the Great Plains and northern Rockies. It places horses within Indigenous communities earlier than some older accounts assumed, but the relevant dates are in the period following European introduction, including the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. William T. T. Taylor and colleagues, “Early dispersal of domestic horses into the Great Plains and northern Rockies” . This is important research on Indigenous history. It is not evidence for horses in the Americas during the Book of Mormon narrative. A headline saying horses arrived “earlier than thought” must be read with its actual dates. Horses remain an open historical question for this comparison; this study does not settle it. A proposed answer needs securely dated remains in the relevant place and period, or a carefully argued explanation of the translated term. These are different proposals, and neither becomes established merely because the archaeological record is incomplete. Metals: the material, technique, and date all matter Ancient Americans developed sophisticated metalworking traditions. A study of metalworking at Mayapan describes copper-based materials, alloys, and technical practices, situating Mesoamerican metallurgy's introduction around AD 650. “Metalworking at Mayapan, Yucatan, Mexico: Discoveries from the R-183 Group,” Ancient Mesoamerica . Those achievements deserve accurate description. They are not interchangeable with evidence for an earlier iron-and-steel industry. Finding a copper object, working native metal, smelting ore, and manufacturing steel are materially different claims. A comparison with the Book of Mormon must specify which claim is being tested and the dates of the evidence. BYU's Religious Studies Center acknowledges that apparent anachronisms, including horses and steel, raise real interpretive difficulties. It outlines approaches involving translation and ancient context without presenting every difficulty as settled. Becerra, Easton-Flake, Frederick, and Spencer, “Common Questions” . Honest discussion can describe proposed answers while allowing a reader to recognize the work still needed. DNA: evidence about populations and limits on identification Ancient DNA research strongly supports deep connections between the founding populations of the Americas and northeast Asia/Beringia. An analysis of an ancient Alaskan genome models early population relationships long before the Book of Mormon's historical setting. Moreno-Mayar and colleagues, “Terminal Pleistocene Alaskan genome reveals first founding population of Native Americans,” Nature . The Church's DNA essay acknowledges the predominantly Asian ancestry found in Indigenous American populations. It also explains why a small migration could be difficult to identify after population mixing and lineage loss, especially when no known reference sample establishes the migrants' genetic signature. The essay cautions against speculative pro-Book-of-Mormon DNA claims as well as overly sweeping rejection arguments. “Book of Mormon and DNA Studies” . These distinctions prevent two mistakes: claiming that DNA has identified Lehi's descendants, and treating lack of an identifiable lineage as identical to proof that no small migration occurred. They also mean that a model claiming virtually all Indigenous ancestry comes from a recent Near Eastern migration cannot simply ignore the actual genetic evidence. Indigenous peoples have their own histories; respect for those histories is part of careful study.

records.title: Let the study lead you toward Jesus Christ
records.text: Explore and study Bring the question to God An adult Joseph bows in a quiet place of prayer. The stillness gives room to reflect on seeking God with an honest heart. Consider what you can bring to prayer today, including the questions you cannot yet resolve and the gratitude you can already express. Read Doctrine and Covenants 6 Explore and study A welcome for the one Jesus Christ meets an older man with attentive warmth. Their joined hands and shared gaze invite a moment of reflection on being known and welcomed by the Savior. Let this imagined encounter lead into the scriptural account of His personal invitation to those gathered around Him. Read 3 Nephi 11:14–17 The witness the book invites each reader to seek The Book of Mormon's invitation ultimately concerns Jesus Christ. Moroni asks readers to remember God's mercy, ponder the record, and ask God sincerely with faith in Christ; his concluding invitation is to come unto Christ. Moroni 10:3–5, 32 . That is a spiritual invitation, not an archaeological experiment that yields a universally reproducible measurement. Alma describes beginning with a desire to believe and then nourishing the word, discerning its growth over time. Alma 32:27–43 . A visitor can study scholarship, pray, and observe whether living the book's teachings deepens repentance, love, and trust in the Savior. Intellectual inquiry and spiritual experience need not be forced into competition, but they should not be mislabeled as the same kind of evidence. As you read, consider: What does this record help me understand about Jesus Christ, and what will I do with that understanding today? Explore and study At a child’s level Jesus Christ bends to meet a young girl at her level while an attentive woman stands nearby. His warmth gives the encounter a sense of safety and belonging. Consider how attentive listening and gentle words can help a child feel seen and welcomed. Read 3 Nephi 17:21–24 A welcome that becomes personal Read the Savior’s invitation to approach Him in 3 Nephi 11:14–17 . Then spend time with His attention to the sick and the children in 3 Nephi 17:5–24 . Notice the people He sees and the time He gives them. What would it mean to make room for someone that way today? You do not need to settle every historical question before reading with sincerity. Bring both gratitude and uncertainty into your prayer. Let the study be patient enough for a difficult question and practical enough to change how you treat another person. Explore and study Be present with the person before you Jesus Christ bends toward an older woman and meets her gaze with quiet compassion. Their joined hands bring the encounter close. Consider what it means to offer another person your attention, without rushing their words or deciding what they need before you have listened. Read 3 Nephi 17

records.title: A careful way to continue
records.text: Explore and study Make room to learn together Three people share a quiet moment around an open book, with a notebook close at hand. Their attention suggests the value of reading, listening, and leaving room for questions. Consider one person with whom you could study a passage or discuss something you hope to understand. Read Moroni 10:3–5 Choose a claim small enough to investigate. Write down the observation, the proposed explanation, and one question that remains. Read the linked source in context before sharing a conclusion. When two authors disagree, look for the point where their reasoning separates. Kind of material Question to ask Keep the conclusion within reach A document or artifact What survives, and how is it dated? Distinguish the visible object from a proposed identification. A linguistic or literary pattern What was counted, and what comparisons were allowed? A pattern needs an explanation; it does not choose its own explanation. A witness account Who reported what, and how was the report preserved? Evaluate the actual testimony without enlarging its scope. A spiritual experience How am I responding to God and to Christ’s teachings? Describe personal conviction honestly without presenting it as a laboratory result. Questions for personal study or a conversation Which detail can I point to directly in the source? What assumptions connect that detail to the conclusion I find persuasive? Have I read a thoughtful alternative explanation? What would cause me to qualify or revise my understanding? How can this study help me listen more carefully and follow Jesus Christ more fully? This guide distinguishes official Church teaching from the arguments of individual scholars. An institutional publisher does not make every author’s interpretation Church doctrine. Linked sources include documentary editions, original research, museum records, scripture, and official teaching; they serve different purposes.

records.title: Church History Study
records.text: Faith, Restoration, and Remembrance Church History Explore the Restoration through trusted Church history sources. Ask a History Question Open Official Church History An illustrated Joseph Smith study The Face Behind the History Explore the death masks, portraits from life, and the creative likeness developed for focusChrist through an art-led journey. Explore Joseph’s Portrait Story The coming forth of scripture Explore Book of Mormon Evidences Follow the translation and its surviving manuscripts, compare witness accounts, and explore the record’s language and ancient context. The enriched study connects historical sources with the invitation to come unto Jesus Christ. Explore the Evidences Study Read the Witness Accounts Source standard: focusChrist may summarize and explain, but the linked official Church History resources are the source of truth on this page. When a detail is uncertain or the source path does not establish it clearly, the history assistant is instructed to say so rather than fill the gap from model memory. Sacred beginnings The First Vision Begin with Joseph Smith's accounts of the experience that opened the Restoration, then follow the official historical sources as the story unfolds. Study the First Vision accounts Source-grounded study assistant Ask Church History Ask naturally. The assistant predicts the likely historical source family, adds verified official study routes, remembers the current conversation for follow-up questions, and keeps official Church History and Saints above model memory. Official Source Hub Ask about a person, event, place, practice, date, or historical question. Official Church History sources will be shown with the response. Follow-up questions stay in the same conversation until you choose New Question. AI-assisted answers are study aids and may contain errors. Unreviewed questions and limited recent context may be sent to external AI providers for research and verification. Please do not submit sensitive personal information. Faith in daily work Joseph and Emma at Harmony The history of the Restoration includes quiet days of writing, supporting, questioning, and continuing with faith. Study Emma Hale Smith A focused priesthood study Aaronic Priesthood Follow Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery from their question about baptism to John the Baptist’s message and the baptisms that followed. Read the scriptural account alongside its historical sources, then consider how preparation, repentance, and service point toward Jesus Christ. Open the Aaronic Priesthood study A focused priesthood study Melchizedek Priesthood Study the testimony of Peter, James, and John’s ministry to Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery. Follow the surviving scriptural and historical witnesses, keep the unanswered questions visible, and consider the Lord’s teaching about how priesthood authority should be exercised. Open the Melchizedek Priesthood study The current narrative history Read Saints Across Four Eras The Church's Saints series currently presents the history from the early Restoration through 2020 in four volumes. Use the era cards as the primary narrative path, then move into topic-specific Church History sources when a question needs closer examination. Witnesses of the record The Three Witnesses Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris gave their names and testimony to the Book of Mormon record. Study the witnesses Volume 1 1815–1846 The Standard of Truth Early Restoration, Joseph Smith, the rise of the Church, Kirtland, Missouri, Nauvoo, and the opening of the westward exodus. Read on ChurchofJesusChrist.org → Volume 2 1846–1893 No Unhallowed Hand The pioneer era, settlement and global gathering, conflict and change, temples, plural marriage, and the closing decades of the nineteenth century. Read on ChurchofJesusChrist.org → Volume 3 1893–1955 Boldly, Nobly, and Independent A changing worldwide Church through modernization, two world wars, new institutions, growing missions, and expanding international membership. Read on ChurchofJesusChrist.org → Volume 4 1955–2020 Sounded in Every Ear The increasingly global Church, worldwide growth, temples, missionary expansion, institutional change, and the modern era through 2020. Read on ChurchofJesusChrist.org → From manuscript to book The Restoration Print Shop The translated record moved into print, where ordinary labor helped carry its witness to readers and generations beyond. Study the Book of Mormon's publication Kirtland · March 27, 1836 Kirtland: A House Built for Learning and Prayer Explore and study A house built through sacrifice People approach the temple along a worn path. Its walls recall years of shared labor and sacrifice before the dedication in 1836. Read the dedicatory prayer and consider what it means to enter the Lord’s house seeking learning, faith, and a heart prepared to serve. Read Doctrine and Covenants 109:7–9 Read Doctrine and Covenants 110 The Kirtland Temple brought worship and learning into a house built through shared sacrifice. Stone came from a nearby quarry; carpenters and other workers contributed their skills. Its assembly rooms included tiers of pulpits at opposite ends. On March 27, 1836, the Saints gathered for the dedication, and Joseph Smith offered the prayer now preserved in Doctrine and Covenants 109. Study the temple’s construction and purpose. Begin with Doctrine and Covenants 109:7–9 . The prayer brings learning, faith, order, and worship together. Let each part become a question about your own preparation. What helps you listen? What are you willing to learn? Where could greater order make room for prayer without turning your home into a place of pressure or perfectionism? Then read Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10 , the account of Joseph and Oliver’s vision a week after the dedication. Attend to the Savior’s words and to the relationship between a sacred place and a people who seek Him. The building’s meaning reaches beyond its architecture into the lives of those who worshipped there. Consider an ordinary skill you could contribute to someone else’s spiritual growth: teaching a child, preparing a lesson, repairing something, or making a gathering welcoming. Write down one action. Remembering the temple’s builders can help us notice the quiet labor through which a community makes room for worship. Explore the Historic Kirtland Temple Practice Faithful Study Kirtland's financial hopes and a painful failure Explore and study Faith amid financial loss The open ledger and Joseph’s troubled expression invite a careful look at Kirtland’s financial crisis. The losses affected real families and strained trust. Study the record honestly, then consider how humility, accountability, and compassion can guide us when hopes and decisions go wrong. Read the Kirtland Safety Society history In 1836, Joseph Smith and associates organized the Kirtland Safety Society, hoping to provide credit and support a growing community. The Ohio legislature did not grant it a bank charter. Its leaders nevertheless began operating an unchartered financial institution in January 1837. It failed that year, bringing substantial losses to Joseph and other participants. The Church's history acknowledges that disappointed expectations contributed to a crisis of confidence and faith. Read the Church's historical account . The failure had several causes. Insufficient funding, opposition, and the lack of a charter created vulnerabilities; the broader Panic of 1837 deepened the difficulties. National conditions provide context without removing responsibility for local decisions. Examine the Joseph Smith Papers' economic analysis . There were legal consequences as well: Joseph and Sidney Rigdon were tried and fined for circulating notes contrary to an Ohio banking statute. Leaders had expressed optimism about the institution, and some members felt betrayed when financial pain followed. A careful reading makes room for those losses and reactions; it does not dismiss everyone who struggled as faithless. Study the legal context and the Saints' responses . The surviving notes and financial records invite study beyond a simple success-or-failure slogan. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–42 as a later standard for compassionate leadership. How can we acknowledge harm, listen to disappointment, and act with integrity? Studying difficult decisions can deepen our concern for the people affected, even when their experiences and responses differ from our own. Continue with a careful approach to historical evidence . Courage before Liberty Jail Richmond: A Voice against Cruelty The scenes below invite us to imagine these moments in Church history. Read their linked accounts alongside the artwork; the records preserve the events, while the pictures give them an interpretive setting. Explore and study Courage in the room at Richmond Joseph stands before the guards while his companions remain close beside him. This scene draws on Parley Pratt’s later account of the rebuke at Richmond. Consider the courage it takes to speak with dignity when another person’s words cause harm. Read the Richmond account Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–44 In November 1838, before Joseph Smith was confined in Liberty Jail, he and other prisoners were held in a log house in Richmond, Missouri. Shackles and a heavy chain bound them together as they tried to rest on the cold floor. Parley P. Pratt later recalled the guards speaking boastfully about violence against the Saints. In Pratt’s account, Joseph stood and commanded them to stop in the name of Jesus Christ. The guards quieted and asked his pardon. Read the episode in Saints , chapter 31 , which cites Pratt’s later recollection and autobiography. Consider the courage it takes to defend the dignity of people who cannot answer for themselves. Then carry that question into Liberty Jail: how do conviction, compassion, and restraint belong together? The teachings that emerged there invite us to examine how we use our own words and influence. Continue into Liberty Jail Prayer, patience, and the use of power Liberty Jail: Words of Peace from a Place of Suffering In March 1839, Joseph Smith was separated from his family while the Saints struggled to find safety beyond Missouri. He and his fellow prisoners had spent months in Liberty Jail. Cold, poor food, and uncertainty wore on them. Letters could bring comfort, but they also carried news of other people’s suffering. Read the experience within the walls before turning to the words that came from them. Explore and study A prayer from within the walls Joseph’s upward gaze holds the strain of waiting and the courage to keep asking. Read his plea alongside the Lord’s answer, then bring a question of your own into prayer. Peace can begin as we turn toward Christ, even while a difficult circumstance continues. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 Read Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 Bring the question into prayer “O God, where art thou?” begins the plea preserved in Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 . Joseph asks how long suffering will continue. The answer addresses him as a son and offers peace, endurance, and the assurance of friendship. Read the question and the answer together. Faith here includes the courage to tell God how hard the waiting has become. In Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 , the response turns Joseph toward the Son of Man, who descended below all things. Christ’s suffering gives the passage its depth. Consider what it means to trust His understanding while an answer, release, or healing is still beyond your sight. This is an invitation to seek His companionship in pain, never a reason to dismiss someone else’s distress. Explore and study Words for a scattered people Joseph studies pages in the quiet of the jail. His letters reached beyond those walls to people facing fear and displacement. Read the counsel about gentle influence and willing action, and consider one word of encouragement or practical kindness you could offer someone today. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–46 Read Doctrine and Covenants 123:17 Let suffering change how you treat others Passages from Joseph’s March letters became Doctrine and Covenants 121 , 122 , and 123 . Explore the Church History Library’s letter exhibit. The surviving letter carries the handwriting of Alexander McRae and Caleb Baldwin, with insertions by Joseph. These were words dictated, written, and shared with a scattered Church. Examine the manuscript and its source note. The document lets us follow the counsel beyond familiar quotations into the circumstances of the people receiving it. Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–46 describes influence through persuasion, patience, gentleness, and genuine love. Read it with a relationship in mind: where could listening replace pressure? Doctrine and Covenants 123:17 joins willing action with trust in God. Choose one helpful thing within your power today, then bring what you cannot control back to Him. As you finish, write down the phrase you most need to remember. Beside it, name someone whose burden you could help carry. Let your reading become a patient conversation, a practical kindness, or a prayer offered with greater honesty. Explore Liberty Jail’s History Continue Studying Prayer Turn to Christ in Trials The Nauvoo Legion: protection, public service, and tension Explore and study Responsibility in a growing city Joseph listens as a volunteer speaks. The Legion’s history brings together the Saints’ desire for protection and the fears their growing power stirred among neighbors. Read the record with care, and consider how responsibility, restraint, and respect for others can shape a community’s peace. Read the Nauvoo Legion history The Nauvoo Legion was a contingent of the Illinois militia authorized by the city's charter, not merely an informal gathering of armed Church members. Joseph Smith became its lieutenant general on February 4, 1841. Its organization included infantry and cavalry, with regular training and public reviews. Explore the Joseph Smith Papers' records of the Legion . For people who had fled violence in Missouri, civic protection held deep meaning. Joseph described the Legion's purpose as protecting Nauvoo against mobs and enforcing the law. The Church History Museum preserves his military effects, including a cloak, epaulets, and sword, and explains the militia's place in the community. Its parades also became prominent public occasions. View the objects and their history . The same growing force that reassured many Saints alarmed some neighbors and political leaders. Questions about military power became entangled with Nauvoo's wider conflicts. In June 1844, Governor Thomas Ford ordered the Legion to surrender its state arms; the museum account records its compliance. Repeal of the city charter in January 1845 ended the Legion's legal standing under that charter. These tensions belong in the story alongside the community's desire for safety. Read about opposition and disarmament . Maudsley's historical uniform portrait helps distinguish ceremonial appearance from an imagined battle scene. Consider Doctrine and Covenants 134:1–5 : how can a community protect religious liberty while respecting the rights and security of others? Continue to faith during imprisonment or the earlier witnesses of the Book of Mormon . Nauvoo · March 17, 1842 Relief Society: Faith Organized to Care Explore and study A society ready to serve Emma meets a listener’s eyes as the women gather to organize their work. Their shared attention invites us to consider how belonging becomes service. Read the founding minutes and ask whom your own circle could strengthen through practical care. Read Mosiah 18:8–9 In the upstairs room of the Red Brick Store, women gathered to organize their service. The surviving minutes of March 17, 1842 record a meeting with prayer, discussion, decisions, and donations. Emma Smith was unanimously elected president and chose Sarah Cleveland and Elizabeth Ann Whitney as counselors. Caring for people in need was part of their stated responsibility. These pages let us hear women considering how to act together. Notice how much faithful service involves listening and deciding. The minutes preserve discussion about the society’s name and the work it would undertake. After the men withdrew, the women appointed a secretary and treasurer. Read slowly enough to notice their initiative, voices, and practical responsibilities. A record of names and motions can open into a story of people learning to share the work. Read Doctrine and Covenants 25:7–10 alongside the meeting record. Consider the relationship between learning, teaching, and encouragement. Then turn to Mosiah 18:8–10 : whose burden could you help carry without taking away their dignity or voice? Choose one need you can understand more fully this week. Ask, listen, and offer something specific. A meal, a visit, patient teaching, or shared responsibility can make care tangible. The historical record invites us to see organized service as people making room for one another, with Christ at the center of their effort. As you read, notice whose contribution you might otherwise overlook. Who keeps the record, provides the resources, notices a need, or encourages someone to speak? Give thanks for a person whose steady service has helped you belong. Explore and study Care Takes Shape in Ordinary Hands A small shirt is held up beside folded cloth as two women share the work. The early Relief Society donation record includes clothing and household textiles, reminding us how practical gifts can meet ordinary needs. Read the March 1842 donation record Explore Relief Society’s Beginnings Let Study Lead to Christ Friendship through hardship Porter Rockwell: A Friend Recognized at the Door Explore and study Recognized and welcomed Joseph’s hands rest on Porter’s arms as the two friends recognize one another. Their welcome draws us into the Christmas reunion recorded in Joseph’s journal. Think of someone returning from a hard experience: how could your attention and friendship help that person feel known? Read John 15:12–13 Explore Porter’s history and sources On Christmas Day in 1843, a road-worn stranger walked into the Smith family’s celebration in Nauvoo. His hair fell over his shoulders, and his behavior caused such a disturbance that Joseph called for him to be put outside. Then Joseph saw his face. The stranger was his old friend Porter Rockwell. Joseph’s journal records the recognition with the words “Joy untold.” After months of imprisonment and a difficult journey home, Porter had reached people who knew him. Read the contemporary journal entry. Their friendship reached back to the neighborhood where the Book of Mormon came forth. The Rockwells and Smiths were neighbors in western New York, and Porter joined the Church in 1830. He was part of the circle of friends and families whose lives became bound to the Restoration. His story opens another way to study that community alongside the scribes, witnesses, and printers who helped bring the record to readers. Explore Porter’s documented life. Porter’s loyalty is memorable, and his life also requires careful reading. It involved violence, accusations, and a reputation later enlarged by frontier stories. In the case behind his 1843 imprisonment, a grand jury did not indict him for the attempted murder of former governor Lilburn Boggs; that does not settle every historical question. The Church History Library explains why many familiar stories about him are difficult to verify. Examine the records behind the legends. The Christmas reunion offers something quieter to consider: what does it mean to recognize and welcome a friend after hardship? We can begin with this documented human encounter, ask what it teaches us about friendship, and keep reading the rest of Porter’s complicated life with honesty and care. Explore the Translation Record Follow the Manuscripts into Print Read History with Care Nauvoo · 1841–1846 Nauvoo: Strength for the Journey Ahead Explore and study Hope above the river The temple rises above a city preparing for an uncertain future. Many Saints labored to finish it while also preparing to leave their homes. Study their sacrifices and the promises they carried west, then consider how worship can strengthen hope when the next step is difficult. Read Doctrine and Covenants 124:26–28 The original Nauvoo Temple rose through years of donated labor and resources. As departure from Illinois approached, Saints continued seeking its blessings. The temple was dedicated on May 1, 1846, although some portions remained unfinished. records.title: Kirtland: A House Built for Learning and Prayer
records.text: Explore and study A house built through sacrifice People approach the temple along a worn path. Its walls recall years of shared labor and sacrifice before the dedication in 1836. Read the dedicatory prayer and consider what it means to enter the Lord’s house seeking learning, faith, and a heart prepared to serve. Read Doctrine and Covenants 109:7–9 Read Doctrine and Covenants 110 The Kirtland Temple brought worship and learning into a house built through shared sacrifice. Stone came from a nearby quarry; carpenters and other workers contributed their skills. Its assembly rooms included tiers of pulpits at opposite ends. On March 27, 1836, the Saints gathered for the dedication, and Joseph Smith offered the prayer now preserved in Doctrine and Covenants 109. Study the temple’s construction and purpose. Begin with Doctrine and Covenants 109:7–9 . The prayer brings learning, faith, order, and worship together. Let each part become a question about your own preparation. What helps you listen? What are you willing to learn? Where could greater order make room for prayer without turning your home into a place of pressure or perfectionism? Then read Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10 , the account of Joseph and Oliver’s vision a week after the dedication. Attend to the Savior’s words and to the relationship between a sacred place and a people who seek Him. The building’s meaning reaches beyond its architecture into the lives of those who worshipped there. Consider an ordinary skill you could contribute to someone else’s spiritual growth: teaching a child, preparing a lesson, repairing something, or making a gathering welcoming. Write down one action. Remembering the temple’s builders can help us notice the quiet labor through which a community makes room for worship. Explore the Historic Kirtland Temple Practice Faithful Study

records.title: Kirtland's financial hopes and a painful failure
records.text: Explore and study Faith amid financial loss The open ledger and Joseph’s troubled expression invite a careful look at Kirtland’s financial crisis. The losses affected real families and strained trust. Study the record honestly, then consider how humility, accountability, and compassion can guide us when hopes and decisions go wrong. Read the Kirtland Safety Society history In 1836, Joseph Smith and associates organized the Kirtland Safety Society, hoping to provide credit and support a growing community. The Ohio legislature did not grant it a bank charter. Its leaders nevertheless began operating an unchartered financial institution in January 1837. It failed that year, bringing substantial losses to Joseph and other participants. The Church's history acknowledges that disappointed expectations contributed to a crisis of confidence and faith. Read the Church's historical account . The failure had several causes. Insufficient funding, opposition, and the lack of a charter created vulnerabilities; the broader Panic of 1837 deepened the difficulties. National conditions provide context without removing responsibility for local decisions. Examine the Joseph Smith Papers' economic analysis . There were legal consequences as well: Joseph and Sidney Rigdon were tried and fined for circulating notes contrary to an Ohio banking statute. Leaders had expressed optimism about the institution, and some members felt betrayed when financial pain followed. A careful reading makes room for those losses and reactions; it does not dismiss everyone who struggled as faithless. Study the legal context and the Saints' responses . The surviving notes and financial records invite study beyond a simple success-or-failure slogan. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–42 as a later standard for compassionate leadership. How can we acknowledge harm, listen to disappointment, and act with integrity? Studying difficult decisions can deepen our concern for the people affected, even when their experiences and responses differ from our own. Continue with a careful approach to historical evidence .

records.title: Richmond: A Voice against Cruelty
records.text: The scenes below invite us to imagine these moments in Church history. Read their linked accounts alongside the artwork; the records preserve the events, while the pictures give them an interpretive setting. Explore and study Courage in the room at Richmond Joseph stands before the guards while his companions remain close beside him. This scene draws on Parley Pratt’s later account of the rebuke at Richmond. Consider the courage it takes to speak with dignity when another person’s words cause harm. Read the Richmond account Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–44 In November 1838, before Joseph Smith was confined in Liberty Jail, he and other prisoners were held in a log house in Richmond, Missouri. Shackles and a heavy chain bound them together as they tried to rest on the cold floor. Parley P. Pratt later recalled the guards speaking boastfully about violence against the Saints. In Pratt’s account, Joseph stood and commanded them to stop in the name of Jesus Christ. The guards quieted and asked his pardon. Read the episode in Saints , chapter 31 , which cites Pratt’s later recollection and autobiography. Consider the courage it takes to defend the dignity of people who cannot answer for themselves. Then carry that question into Liberty Jail: how do conviction, compassion, and restraint belong together? The teachings that emerged there invite us to examine how we use our own words and influence. Continue into Liberty Jail

records.title: Liberty Jail: Words of Peace from a Place of Suffering
records.text: In March 1839, Joseph Smith was separated from his family while the Saints struggled to find safety beyond Missouri. He and his fellow prisoners had spent months in Liberty Jail. Cold, poor food, and uncertainty wore on them. Letters could bring comfort, but they also carried news of other people’s suffering. Read the experience within the walls before turning to the words that came from them. Explore and study A prayer from within the walls Joseph’s upward gaze holds the strain of waiting and the courage to keep asking. Read his plea alongside the Lord’s answer, then bring a question of your own into prayer. Peace can begin as we turn toward Christ, even while a difficult circumstance continues. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 Read Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 Bring the question into prayer “O God, where art thou?” begins the plea preserved in Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 . Joseph asks how long suffering will continue. The answer addresses him as a son and offers peace, endurance, and the assurance of friendship. Read the question and the answer together. Faith here includes the courage to tell God how hard the waiting has become. In Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 , the response turns Joseph toward the Son of Man, who descended below all things. Christ’s suffering gives the passage its depth. Consider what it means to trust His understanding while an answer, release, or healing is still beyond your sight. This is an invitation to seek His companionship in pain, never a reason to dismiss someone else’s distress. Explore and study Words for a scattered people Joseph studies pages in the quiet of the jail. His letters reached beyond those walls to people facing fear and displacement. Read the counsel about gentle influence and willing action, and consider one word of encouragement or practical kindness you could offer someone today. Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–46 Read Doctrine and Covenants 123:17 Let suffering change how you treat others Passages from Joseph’s March letters became Doctrine and Covenants 121 , 122 , and 123 . Explore the Church History Library’s letter exhibit. The surviving letter carries the handwriting of Alexander McRae and Caleb Baldwin, with insertions by Joseph. These were words dictated, written, and shared with a scattered Church. Examine the manuscript and its source note. The document lets us follow the counsel beyond familiar quotations into the circumstances of the people receiving it. Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–46 describes influence through persuasion, patience, gentleness, and genuine love. Read it with a relationship in mind: where could listening replace pressure? Doctrine and Covenants 123:17 joins willing action with trust in God. Choose one helpful thing within your power today, then bring what you cannot control back to Him. As you finish, write down the phrase you most need to remember. Beside it, name someone whose burden you could help carry. Let your reading become a patient conversation, a practical kindness, or a prayer offered with greater honesty. Explore Liberty Jail’s History Continue Studying Prayer Turn to Christ in Trials
