records.title: The Nauvoo Legion: protection, public service, and tension
records.text: Explore and study Responsibility in a growing city Joseph listens as a volunteer speaks. The Legion’s history brings together the Saints’ desire for protection and the fears their growing power stirred among neighbors. Read the record with care, and consider how responsibility, restraint, and respect for others can shape a community’s peace. Read the Nauvoo Legion history The Nauvoo Legion was a contingent of the Illinois militia authorized by the city's charter, not merely an informal gathering of armed Church members. Joseph Smith became its lieutenant general on February 4, 1841. Its organization included infantry and cavalry, with regular training and public reviews. Explore the Joseph Smith Papers' records of the Legion . For people who had fled violence in Missouri, civic protection held deep meaning. Joseph described the Legion's purpose as protecting Nauvoo against mobs and enforcing the law. The Church History Museum preserves his military effects, including a cloak, epaulets, and sword, and explains the militia's place in the community. Its parades also became prominent public occasions. View the objects and their history . The same growing force that reassured many Saints alarmed some neighbors and political leaders. Questions about military power became entangled with Nauvoo's wider conflicts. In June 1844, Governor Thomas Ford ordered the Legion to surrender its state arms; the museum account records its compliance. Repeal of the city charter in January 1845 ended the Legion's legal standing under that charter. These tensions belong in the story alongside the community's desire for safety. Read about opposition and disarmament . Maudsley's historical uniform portrait helps distinguish ceremonial appearance from an imagined battle scene. Consider Doctrine and Covenants 134:1–5 : how can a community protect religious liberty while respecting the rights and security of others? Continue to faith during imprisonment or the earlier witnesses of the Book of Mormon .

records.title: Relief Society: Faith Organized to Care
records.text: Explore and study A society ready to serve Emma meets a listener’s eyes as the women gather to organize their work. Their shared attention invites us to consider how belonging becomes service. Read the founding minutes and ask whom your own circle could strengthen through practical care. Read Mosiah 18:8–9 In the upstairs room of the Red Brick Store, women gathered to organize their service. The surviving minutes of March 17, 1842 record a meeting with prayer, discussion, decisions, and donations. Emma Smith was unanimously elected president and chose Sarah Cleveland and Elizabeth Ann Whitney as counselors. Caring for people in need was part of their stated responsibility. These pages let us hear women considering how to act together. Notice how much faithful service involves listening and deciding. The minutes preserve discussion about the society’s name and the work it would undertake. After the men withdrew, the women appointed a secretary and treasurer. Read slowly enough to notice their initiative, voices, and practical responsibilities. A record of names and motions can open into a story of people learning to share the work. Read Doctrine and Covenants 25:7–10 alongside the meeting record. Consider the relationship between learning, teaching, and encouragement. Then turn to Mosiah 18:8–10 : whose burden could you help carry without taking away their dignity or voice? Choose one need you can understand more fully this week. Ask, listen, and offer something specific. A meal, a visit, patient teaching, or shared responsibility can make care tangible. The historical record invites us to see organized service as people making room for one another, with Christ at the center of their effort. As you read, notice whose contribution you might otherwise overlook. Who keeps the record, provides the resources, notices a need, or encourages someone to speak? Give thanks for a person whose steady service has helped you belong. Explore and study Care Takes Shape in Ordinary Hands A small shirt is held up beside folded cloth as two women share the work. The early Relief Society donation record includes clothing and household textiles, reminding us how practical gifts can meet ordinary needs. records.title: Porter Rockwell: A Friend Recognized at the Door
records.text: Explore and study Recognized and welcomed Joseph’s hands rest on Porter’s arms as the two friends recognize one another. Their welcome draws us into the Christmas reunion recorded in Joseph’s journal. Think of someone returning from a hard experience: how could your attention and friendship help that person feel known? Read John 15:12–13 Explore Porter’s history and sources On Christmas Day in 1843, a road-worn stranger walked into the Smith family’s celebration in Nauvoo. His hair fell over his shoulders, and his behavior caused such a disturbance that Joseph called for him to be put outside. Then Joseph saw his face. The stranger was his old friend Porter Rockwell. Joseph’s journal records the recognition with the words “Joy untold.” After months of imprisonment and a difficult journey home, Porter had reached people who knew him. Read the contemporary journal entry. Their friendship reached back to the neighborhood where the Book of Mormon came forth. The Rockwells and Smiths were neighbors in western New York, and Porter joined the Church in 1830. He was part of the circle of friends and families whose lives became bound to the Restoration. His story opens another way to study that community alongside the scribes, witnesses, and printers who helped bring the record to readers. Explore Porter’s documented life. Porter’s loyalty is memorable, and his life also requires careful reading. It involved violence, accusations, and a reputation later enlarged by frontier stories. In the case behind his 1843 imprisonment, a grand jury did not indict him for the attempted murder of former governor Lilburn Boggs; that does not settle every historical question. The Church History Library explains why many familiar stories about him are difficult to verify. Examine the records behind the legends. The Christmas reunion offers something quieter to consider: what does it mean to recognize and welcome a friend after hardship? We can begin with this documented human encounter, ask what it teaches us about friendship, and keep reading the rest of Porter’s complicated life with honesty and care. Read Doctrine and Covenants 124:26–28 The original Nauvoo Temple rose through years of donated labor and resources. As departure from Illinois approached, Saints continued seeking its blessings. The temple was dedicated on May 1, 1846, although some portions remained unfinished. Its story holds together devotion, urgency, and loss: the building they had worked to complete could not remain their home. Read the history of the original temple. The question is personal as well as historical: what can a sacred commitment give you when your circumstances become uncertain? In her later recollection, Sarah Pea Rich described temple blessings as a source of faith for the difficult journey west. The Church’s history preserves her perspective alongside the events of construction and departure. Her memory invites us to consider strength that can be carried beyond the place where it was first received. Read Doctrine and Covenants 128:18–19 with family relationships in mind. What changes when you see your life as connected to generations before and after you? Continue with verse 22 and consider how gratitude can accompany difficult work. Choose a family story, name, or memory to preserve. Ask someone a thoughtful question and record their answer with care. You do not need a complete family history to begin honoring those who came before you. Let this study lead to a small act of remembrance, reconciliation, or service that strengthens a living relationship today. Study Doctrine and Covenants 128 Consider How Records Are Preserved

records.title: Work through one historical question carefully
records.text: Try the question, “What do the First Vision accounts tell us, and why do they differ?” Begin with the Church’s First Vision Accounts essay , which introduces the accounts and discusses their settings. Follow its links to the records rather than relying only on a summary. For each account, note who produced it, when it was recorded, its audience, and whether you are reading an original document, a transcript, or a later explanation. The date of an event and the date of a surviving account are different facts. Compare what each source includes before deciding what a difference means. Historical study asks what the surviving evidence supports and where it leaves uncertainty. A spiritual inquiry asks a related but different question about religious meaning and belief. Neither a strong feeling nor a single missing detail settles every historical question. You can examine evidence carefully while treating the people and beliefs involved with respect. Place Joseph Smith in the inquiry Continue with his role, the claims associated with him, and a practical way to take source notes. Explore the book and its claims Move from the historical question to what the text teaches, keeping the two inquiries clear. Carry these source habits into pioneer history Distinguish individual records, wider historical context, and devotional application. A useful closing note is modest: “This source supports…” followed by “I would need another source to know…” That practice makes room for learning without forcing a conclusion before the evidence warrants it. The Stand Forever study offers a companion framework for keeping foundational questions about Christ and the Restoration in view while examining secondary questions carefully.

records.title: Jesus Christ Before Bethlehem
records.text: Read and discover The Word was with God John opens his Gospel before the manger, before the ministry and before the world. In John 1:1–5 , the Word already exists with God, and creation comes through Him. John then identifies this divine life with the One who enters human experience in John 1:14 . The child born into the world did not begin to exist when He was born. Explore and study Life above the waters Fish move through clear water as birds fly above the shore. Genesis names the life of sea and sky among the wonders of creation. Genesis 1:20–23 Latter-day Saints understand this witness as an introduction to the premortal Jesus Christ, distinct from the Father and united with Him in divine purpose. John holds His majesty and His nearness together: the source of life comes to dwell among people. As you continue into His earthly encounters, remember that His attention to an individual is the attention of the Lord through whom the world was made. Genesis 1:20–23 gives the creation witness tangible subjects: the waters teem with life and birds move above the earth. These creatures invite us to notice the abundance within the world John says was made through the Word. Pause and consider How does John’s opening change the way you read a simple encounter between Jesus and one person? John 1:1–5 John 1:14 Genesis 1:20–23 Read and discover A willing Son before the world Abraham’s vision in Abraham 3:24–28 places earthly life within a larger divine purpose. An earth will be prepared, people will have the opportunity to obey God, and a messenger will be sent. Read it beside Moses 4:1–4 , where the Beloved Son accepts the Father’s will while Satan seeks to destroy human agency and claim the Father’s honor. Explore and study Abram looks toward the stars Abram looks into the night sky. The Lord directs his attention to the stars as He promises descendants beyond his counting. Genesis 15:1–6 The contrast helps explain the kind of Savior Jesus is. His mission grows from willing obedience and love, rather than a plan to force every person into righteousness. His later invitations to follow, repent and believe belong to that same respect for agency. The choice of the Beloved Son prepares us to recognize the willingness we will hear again in His prayers and see in His service during mortality. The purposes formed before mortality reach a particular household in Genesis 15:1–6 . Abram is brought outside to consider the stars and receives a promise concerning his descendants. His trust becomes part of the covenant history through which later generations learn to await the Redeemer. Pause and consider What difference does it make that the Savior’s mission honors both the Father’s will and our agency? Abraham 3:24–28 Moses 4:1–4 Genesis 15:1–6 Read and discover Created through the Only Begotten Explore and study A world filled with life Light reaches the valley as water runs between the stones and flowers grow along the bank. The life and beauty of the earth invite us to remember the Son through whom it was created. Moses 1:31–39 Moses asks about the earth and its inhabitants. In Moses 1:31–39 , God answers by connecting creation to the Only Begotten Son and then placing human immortality and eternal life at the heart of His work. The passage lets Moses see his own world within a much larger creation, while keeping God’s concern for His children in view. This gives the natural world a place in a study of Christ. Mountains, water and living things invite gratitude for the Creator, and human life deserves reverence because people belong within the Father’s purpose. The vastness of the vision does not make Moses’s life insignificant. God speaks to him personally about a work that reaches far beyond him. We can receive that same invitation to wonder while caring faithfully for the lives and places close to us. Pause and consider What ordinary part of creation could become a reminder to treat another person with greater care? Moses 1:31–39 Read and discover Moses hears the Lord at the bush Explore and study Moses turns aside Moses pauses beside the burning bush and removes his sandal. An ordinary place of shepherding becomes holy ground as the Lord calls him. Exodus 3:1–6 Moses is tending a flock when a bush that burns without being consumed draws his attention. In Exodus 3:1–15 , the Lord calls him by name, identifies the place as holy and speaks of Israel’s suffering. The encounter leads toward a task: Moses is to go to Pharaoh and bring the people out of Egypt. Divine holiness and concern for an oppressed people meet in the same account. Latter-day Saint teaching identifies Jehovah, the covenant Lord of Israel, with the premortal Jesus Christ. John’s record of Jesus speaking about Abraham in John 8:56–58 belongs to the New Testament witness of His identity. Read the bush account on its own terms as well: Moses hears a commission, raises questions and receives the promise of divine presence. His uncertainty does not prevent the Lord from calling him to serve. Pause and consider Where do you see both reverence and honest questioning in Moses’s response? Exodus 3:1–15 John 8:56–58 Read and discover A way through the sea Explore and study A path through the sea The travelers move forward on dry ground with water on either side. Exodus tells of the way the Lord opened for His people when the sea lay before them. Exodus 14:21–22 Israel’s escape reaches a moment when the sea lies ahead and the Egyptian army approaches behind. In Exodus 14:13–31 , Moses is told to stretch his hand over the water, and the people cross on dry ground. The pillar that has accompanied them stands between the camps. The account remembers deliverance as the Lord’s work, received by a people who still have to move forward. For a study of Jesus Christ, the Exodus helps give depth to the word Redeemer: the Lord frees people from bondage and leads them toward covenant life. That connection does not make every hard experience an equivalent of Israel at the sea, nor promise that every danger will end in the same way. It invites us to see the Savior’s power to deliver as part of a long scriptural witness, reaching toward His victory over sin and death. Pause and consider What does the command to move forward add to the invitation to trust the Lord? Exodus 14:13–31 Read and discover Bread in the wilderness Explore and study Enough for the household People bend to gather the food the Lord has provided. Day by day, the wilderness teaches them to trust Him for their bread. Exodus 16:13–18 After deliverance comes the need to live day by day. Exodus 16:11–18 describes food given to Israel in the wilderness and gathered according to the needs of each household. The passage turns our attention from a great crossing to an ordinary morning, when people must gather what will sustain them. In John 6:31–35 , Jesus recalls the manna while teaching about bread from heaven. He points His listeners toward the Father's gift and names Himself the bread of life. The daily gathering in the wilderness helps us hear that invitation: mortal hunger brings people to seek food, and the Savior calls them to receive the lasting life He offers. Pause and consider What would it mean to seek nourishment from Christ regularly, rather than only in a crisis? Exodus 16:11–18 John 6:31–35 Read and discover The Lord speaks with Moses Explore and study The people watch from their tent doors The people watch from their tent doors as Moses goes to the tent of meeting. The cloud at its entrance accompanies the account of the Lord speaking with him. Exodus 33:7–11 In Exodus 33:7–11 , Moses goes to the tent of meeting outside the camp. The people watch from their own tent doors as the cloudy pillar descends, and the Lord speaks with Moses with the directness of a person speaking to a friend. Joshua remains at the tent. The details locate the encounter within a community learning to recognize and respond to God’s presence. The passage adds relationship to the themes of creation and deliverance. Moses is more than a messenger carrying distant instructions; he speaks with the Lord. The people’s response at their tent doors makes this more than an isolated private moment. The covenant Lord communicates, and His community learns to worship and listen. A patient reading can help us recognize both the personal nearness and the shared responsibility within covenant life. Pause and consider What does this account suggest about the relationship between personal revelation and a worshiping community? Exodus 33:7–11 Read and discover Known before Bethlehem Explore and study Stones carried to the mountain The brother of Jared prepares sixteen stones on the mountain before asking the Lord to give them light. His careful preparation leads into an earnest prayer. Ether 3:1–5 The brother of Jared has prepared stones and asked the Lord to provide light for his people’s journey. In Ether 3:6–16 , he sees the Lord’s finger touch the stones and falls in fear. The conversation moves beyond his immediate need as the Lord reveals His identity and explains that He will take upon Himself flesh and blood. This Book of Mormon account gives a direct witness of Christ before His mortal birth. The Lord identifies Himself as Jesus Christ and describes the body the brother of Jared sees as the body of His spirit. The encounter is therefore not a visit from the already resurrected Savior. It joins a practical request for help with a much greater revelation of the One who answers, while preserving the particularity of this man’s experience rather than making it a required pattern for everyone’s faith. Explore and study He sees the finger of the Lord The brother of Jared draws back as he sees the Lord's finger touch a stone. Ether records his fear before the Lord reveals Himself more fully. Ether 3:6–10 Pause and consider How does the question of who the Lord is become larger than the original question about light? Ether 3:6–16 Read and discover The suffering servant and the coming Redeemer Isaiah’s servant passage in Isaiah 53:1–12 speaks of rejection, suffering, transgression and the bearing of others’ sorrows. Christians read these words in relation to Jesus Christ. Acts 8:26–35 provides a scriptural example of that reading: Philip meets a traveler studying Isaiah and begins with the passage to teach him about Jesus. Explore and study A traveler asks about Isaiah A traveler turns from his reading to seek understanding. Philip joins him in the account where Isaiah becomes a starting point for teaching about Jesus. Acts 8:27–35 This is a fitting place to turn from expectation toward the Savior’s mortal life. The story ahead will contain healing and welcome, but also rejection and a freely given sacrifice. Isaiah’s language should be read carefully in its prophetic setting, with the New Testament connection made openly. The separate Birth of Christ and Atonement studies follow those parts of His mission in greater detail. In Acts 8:27–35, the Ethiopian official asks for help with the passage he is reading. Philip meets him at that question and begins to teach him about Jesus. A shared reading becomes a personal invitation to know the Savior. Pause and consider Which part of Isaiah’s description would you like to understand more deeply through the life of Jesus? Isaiah 53:1–12 Acts 8:26–35 Continue with Jesus Christ Next study in the journey Walk through His mortal ministry Follow His baptism, invitations, journeys, disciples, and the growing witness of who He is. Genesis 15:1–6 The contrast helps explain the kind of Savior Jesus is. His mission grows from willing obedience and love, rather than a plan to force every person into righteousness. His later invitations to follow, repent and believe belong to that same respect for agency. The choice of the Beloved Son prepares us to recognize the willingness we will hear again in His prayers and see in His service during mortality. The purposes formed before mortality reach a particular household in Genesis 15:1–6 . Abram is brought outside to consider the stars and receives a promise concerning his descendants. His trust becomes part of the covenant history through which later generations learn to await the Redeemer. Pause and consider What difference does it make that the Savior’s mission honors both the Father’s will and our agency? Abraham 3:24–28 Moses 4:1–4 Genesis 15:1–6

records.title: Created through the Only Begotten
records.text: Read and discover Created through the Only Begotten Explore and study A world filled with life Light reaches the valley as water runs between the stones and flowers grow along the bank. The life and beauty of the earth invite us to remember the Son through whom it was created. Moses 1:31–39 Moses asks about the earth and its inhabitants. In Moses 1:31–39 , God answers by connecting creation to the Only Begotten Son and then placing human immortality and eternal life at the heart of His work. The passage lets Moses see his own world within a much larger creation, while keeping God’s concern for His children in view. This gives the natural world a place in a study of Christ. Mountains, water and living things invite gratitude for the Creator, and human life deserves reverence because people belong within the Father’s purpose. The vastness of the vision does not make Moses’s life insignificant. God speaks to him personally about a work that reaches far beyond him. We can receive that same invitation to wonder while caring faithfully for the lives and places close to us. Pause and consider What ordinary part of creation could become a reminder to treat another person with greater care? Moses 1:31–39

records.title: Moses hears the Lord at the bush
records.text: Read and discover Moses hears the Lord at the bush Explore and study Moses turns aside Moses pauses beside the burning bush and removes his sandal. An ordinary place of shepherding becomes holy ground as the Lord calls him. Exodus 3:1–6 Moses is tending a flock when a bush that burns without being consumed draws his attention. In Exodus 3:1–15 , the Lord calls him by name, identifies the place as holy and speaks of Israel’s suffering. The encounter leads toward a task: Moses is to go to Pharaoh and bring the people out of Egypt. Divine holiness and concern for an oppressed people meet in the same account. Latter-day Saint teaching identifies Jehovah, the covenant Lord of Israel, with the premortal Jesus Christ. John’s record of Jesus speaking about Abraham in John 8:56–58 belongs to the New Testament witness of His identity. Read the bush account on its own terms as well: Moses hears a commission, raises questions and receives the promise of divine presence. His uncertainty does not prevent the Lord from calling him to serve. Pause and consider Where do you see both reverence and honest questioning in Moses’s response? Exodus 3:1–15 John 8:56–58

records.title: A way through the sea
records.text: Read and discover A way through the sea Explore and study A path through the sea The travelers move forward on dry ground with water on either side. Exodus tells of the way the Lord opened for His people when the sea lay before them. Exodus 14:21–22 Israel’s escape reaches a moment when the sea lies ahead and the Egyptian army approaches behind. In Exodus 14:13–31 , Moses is told to stretch his hand over the water, and the people cross on dry ground. The pillar that has accompanied them stands between the camps. The account remembers deliverance as the Lord’s work, received by a people who still have to move forward. For a study of Jesus Christ, the Exodus helps give depth to the word Redeemer: the Lord frees people from bondage and leads them toward covenant life. That connection does not make every hard experience an equivalent of Israel at the sea, nor promise that every danger will end in the same way. It invites us to see the Savior’s power to deliver as part of a long scriptural witness, reaching toward His victory over sin and death. Pause and consider What does the command to move forward add to the invitation to trust the Lord? Exodus 14:13–31

records.title: Bread in the wilderness
records.text: Read and discover Bread in the wilderness Explore and study Enough for the household People bend to gather the food the Lord has provided. Day by day, the wilderness teaches them to trust Him for their bread. Exodus 16:13–18 After deliverance comes the need to live day by day. Exodus 16:11–18 describes food given to Israel in the wilderness and gathered according to the needs of each household. The passage turns our attention from a great crossing to an ordinary morning, when people must gather what will sustain them. In John 6:31–35 , Jesus recalls the manna while teaching about bread from heaven. He points His listeners toward the Father's gift and names Himself the bread of life. The daily gathering in the wilderness helps us hear that invitation: mortal hunger brings people to seek food, and the Savior calls them to receive the lasting life He offers. Pause and consider What would it mean to seek nourishment from Christ regularly, rather than only in a crisis? Exodus 16:11–18 John 6:31–35

records.title: The Lord speaks with Moses
records.text: Read and discover The Lord speaks with Moses Explore and study The people watch from their tent doors The people watch from their tent doors as Moses goes to the tent of meeting. The cloud at its entrance accompanies the account of the Lord speaking with him. Exodus 33:7–11 In Exodus 33:7–11 , Moses goes to the tent of meeting outside the camp. The people watch from their own tent doors as the cloudy pillar descends, and the Lord speaks with Moses with the directness of a person speaking to a friend. Joshua remains at the tent. The details locate the encounter within a community learning to recognize and respond to God’s presence. The passage adds relationship to the themes of creation and deliverance. Moses is more than a messenger carrying distant instructions; he speaks with the Lord. The people’s response at their tent doors makes this more than an isolated private moment. The covenant Lord communicates, and His community learns to worship and listen. A patient reading can help us recognize both the personal nearness and the shared responsibility within covenant life. Pause and consider What does this account suggest about the relationship between personal revelation and a worshiping community? Exodus 33:7–11

records.title: Known before Bethlehem
records.text: Read and discover Known before Bethlehem Explore and study Stones carried to the mountain The brother of Jared prepares sixteen stones on the mountain before asking the Lord to give them light. His careful preparation leads into an earnest prayer. Ether 3:1–5 The brother of Jared has prepared stones and asked the Lord to provide light for his people’s journey. In Ether 3:6–16 , he sees the Lord’s finger touch the stones and falls in fear. The conversation moves beyond his immediate need as the Lord reveals His identity and explains that He will take upon Himself flesh and blood. This Book of Mormon account gives a direct witness of Christ before His mortal birth. The Lord identifies Himself as Jesus Christ and describes the body the brother of Jared sees as the body of His spirit. The encounter is therefore not a visit from the already resurrected Savior. It joins a practical request for help with a much greater revelation of the One who answers, while preserving the particularity of this man’s experience rather than making it a required pattern for everyone’s faith. Explore and study He sees the finger of the Lord The brother of Jared draws back as he sees the Lord's finger touch a stone. Ether records his fear before the Lord reveals Himself more fully. Ether 3:6–10 Pause and consider How does the question of who the Lord is become larger than the original question about light? Ether 3:6–16

records.title: The suffering servant and the coming Redeemer
records.text: Read and discover The suffering servant and the coming Redeemer Isaiah’s servant passage in Isaiah 53:1–12 speaks of rejection, suffering, transgression and the bearing of others’ sorrows. Christians read these words in relation to Jesus Christ. Acts 8:26–35 provides a scriptural example of that reading: Philip meets a traveler studying Isaiah and begins with the passage to teach him about Jesus. Explore and study A traveler asks about Isaiah A traveler turns from his reading to seek understanding. Philip joins him in the account where Isaiah becomes a starting point for teaching about Jesus. Acts 8:27–35 This is a fitting place to turn from expectation toward the Savior’s mortal life. The story ahead will contain healing and welcome, but also rejection and a freely given sacrifice. Isaiah’s language should be read carefully in its prophetic setting, with the New Testament connection made openly. The separate Birth of Christ and Atonement studies follow those parts of His mission in greater detail. In Acts 8:27–35, the Ethiopian official asks for help with the passage he is reading. Philip meets him at that question and begins to teach him about Jesus. A shared reading becomes a personal invitation to know the Savior. Pause and consider Which part of Isaiah’s description would you like to understand more deeply through the life of Jesus? Isaiah 53:1–12 Acts 8:26–35

records.title: The Miracles and Compassion of Jesus Christ
records.pageTitle: The Miracles and Compassion of Jesus Christ
records.text: Read and discover He reaches toward an excluded man A man with leprosy kneels before Jesus and asks to be made clean. In Mark 1:40–45 , Jesus responds with compassion, reaches out and touches him. He then tells the healed man to show himself to the priest and fulfill the requirements connected with cleansing. The encounter concerns both a bodily affliction and a person’s place within his community. Explore and study Moved with compassion The man kneels before Jesus and asks to be made clean. Moved with compassion, the Savior reaches out and touches him. Mark 1:40–45 The touch makes the scene deeply personal. Jesus does not treat the man as a problem to be kept at a distance. The story invites us to examine how we respond to someone whose illness or circumstances make others withdraw. Following Christ may involve listening, practical help and appropriate care; it does not require pretending we can promise another person the same immediate healing. Another encounter, Mark 3:1–5 , brings compassion into a synagogue dispute. Jesus asks the man to stand and stretch out his hand. The restored hand gives concrete weight to His question about doing good on the Sabbath. Explore and study Stretch out your hand The man meets Jesus after the restoration of his hand. This imagined moment of gratitude stays close to the personal care at the heart of Luke's Sabbath healing account. Luke 6:6–10 Pause and consider What might a respectful act of nearness look like for someone who is often avoided? Mark 1:40–45 Mark 3:1–5 Read and discover Healing within a home Explore and study He lifts her by the hand Jesus takes Simon's mother-in-law by the hand and lifts her up. Mark records that her fever leaves and she begins to serve those in the home. Mark 1:29–31 After leaving the synagogue, Jesus enters the home of Simon and Andrew with James and John. Simon’s mother-in-law is ill with a fever. Mark 1:29–31 describes Jesus taking her hand and lifting her, after which the fever leaves her and she serves those present. The account is brief, but its household setting gives it an intimate scale. The scene reveals His attention in ordinary rooms as well as public places. The woman is neither named nor given a long speech, yet her need matters within the Gospel story. Her service follows her recovery; it should not be turned into an expectation that people who are ill must prove their faith by working. We can honor the account by noticing both the help she receives and the life she resumes. Pause and consider What needs close to home might deserve the same attention you give to more visible concerns? Mark 1:29–31 Read and discover Trust carried by messengers Explore and study A message of trust Friends bring the centurion's message to Jesus. Luke places the conversation with these messengers, while the centurion expresses trust in the authority of Jesus' word. Luke 7:6–10 A centurion’s valued servant is gravely ill. In Luke’s account, Luke 7:1–10 , Jewish elders first approach Jesus on the officer’s behalf. Friends later carry the centurion’s message that Jesus need not enter his house: he trusts the authority of His word. Jesus responds to this faith, and those returning find the servant well. Luke’s messengers matter. They show relationships crossing social boundaries and keep us from casually replacing this account with a different Gospel’s presentation. The centurion understands authority through his own experience, but directs that understanding toward a power beyond military command. His trust is accompanied by concern for someone dependent on him, giving this encounter a practical question for anyone entrusted with responsibility over others. Pause and consider How can the influence you hold be used to seek another person’s good? Luke 7:1–10 Read and discover A child’s hand in His Explore and study A child rises at His word The twelve-year-old girl sits upright and meets Jesus's eyes as He holds her hand. Her parents and the three disciples witness the life He restores. Mark 5:37–43 News reaches Jairus that his daughter has died while Jesus is still on the way. In Mark 5:35–43 , Jesus continues to the house, takes the girl’s parents and three disciples into the room, and takes the child by the hand. She rises and walks. Mark tells us she is twelve years old and records Jesus’s instruction that she be given food. The final request brings care back to the child’s immediate needs. A remarkable act is followed by the ordinary kindness of feeding her. This return to mortal life is not yet the permanent Resurrection Jesus will inaugurate. The account witnesses His power over death while letting us remain gentle with those who mourn a child: their sorrow is not evidence that they or their child were less loved. Pause and consider Why might Mark preserve the instruction to give the girl something to eat? Mark 5:35–43 Read and discover He turns toward a woman in the crowd Explore and study An unseen reach in the crowd The woman reaches through the crowd and touches Jesus's clothing. Mark then records Him turning to ask who touched Him, drawing a hidden act of faith toward a personal encounter. Mark 5:25–30 On the way to Jairus’s home, a woman who has suffered bleeding for twelve years reaches for Jesus’s clothing. Mark 5:25–34 describes the cost and difficulty of her search for relief before she comes to Him. After she is healed, Jesus stops and asks who touched Him. She comes forward and tells Him what has happened. The account gives her more than an anonymous place at the edge of a miracle. Jesus addresses her directly and sends her in peace. Her long suffering helps us hear the weight of that attention. The passage does not authorize judging someone else’s faith by a medical outcome. It offers a particular witness of His power and of a woman whom He allows the crowd to see as a person. Explore and study Daughter, go in peace Jesus gives the woman His attention after she tells what has happened. He calls her daughter, recognizes her faith and sends her in peace. Scripture describes her falling before Him; this companion picture imagines Him kneeling beside her, bringing His recorded reassurance to eye level. Luke 8:47–48 · Mark 5:33–34 Pause and consider What changes when the story moves from an unseen touch to a face-to-face conversation? Mark 5:25–34 Read and discover Away from the crowd He took him aside Away from the crowd, Jesus gives the man His attention and looks toward heaven. Mark records the opening of his ears and the release of his speech. Open study → People bring Jesus a man who is deaf and has difficulty speaking. In Mark 7:31–37 , Jesus takes him aside from the multitude before acting. Mark records a physical, personal encounter, Jesus looking toward heaven and sighing, and the man’s hearing and speech being restored. The people’s amazement follows what the man himself has received. The movement away from the crowd is worth noticing. Another person’s need is not treated simply as a public spectacle. People who live with deafness or a speech disability have dignity and full human worth before any change in their condition. As an invitation to discipleship, this account can lead us to make communication more accessible and to ask how a person wishes to receive support. Pause and consider How could you make a conversation more attentive to the person receiving your help? Mark 7:31–37 Read and discover He leads the man by the hand Explore and study He leads the man outside Jesus takes the blind man's hand and leads him out of Bethsaida. Before the healing, Mark lets us see the Savior walking beside him. Mark 8:22–23 At Bethsaida, people bring a blind man to Jesus. Mark 8:22–26 says that Jesus takes his hand and leads him out of the town. The healing unfolds in two stages: after the first touch the man describes indistinct sight, and Jesus touches him again until he sees clearly. Mark includes that intermediate answer rather than compressing the encounter into a single instant. This account differs from the man born blind in John 9 and should be allowed its own details. The two stages do not supply a universal explanation for gradual recovery or incomplete answers in our own lives. They do show the Savior attending to this man’s actual response. His question and continued care invite us to listen carefully rather than assuming we already know how another person is doing. Pause and consider What can you learn from Jesus asking the man what he can see? Mark 8:22–26 Read and discover A question about blame becomes a work of mercy Explore and study Water at Siloam The man washes after following Jesus' instruction to go to Siloam. Water runs through his hands in this quiet moment of response. John 9:6–7 When the disciples see a man blind from birth, they ask whose sin caused his condition. In John 9:1–7 , Jesus rejects the proposed choice between the man’s guilt and his parents’ guilt. He makes clay, places it on the man’s eyes and sends him to wash at Siloam. The man goes, washes and returns able to see. John’s chapter continues through questioning, conflict and the man’s growing witness. Later, in John 9:35–38 , Jesus finds him again and speaks with him about belief in the Son of God. The story is larger than a cure: it follows a person learning who Jesus is. Its opening also asks us to resist explanations that make disability a verdict on someone’s moral worth or turn another person’s life into an easy lesson. Pause and consider Which assumptions about suffering does Jesus’s first answer ask you to set aside? John 9:1–7 John 9:35–38 Read and discover One returns Ten men with leprosy call to Jesus from a distance. In Luke 17:11–19 , He tells them to show themselves to the priests, and they are cleansed as they go. One turns back, praises God and falls at Jesus’s feet in thanks. Luke identifies him as a Samaritan, and Jesus draws attention to his return. Explore and study Good news on the road home Servants meet the official on his way home with news that his son is alive. He listens and asks when the recovery began. John 4:50–53 All ten receive cleansing; the account does not say that only the thankful man was healed. The returning man lets the story move from receiving a gift to recognizing its giver. Gratitude here is personal and expressed. We can practice it without comparing whose blessings are greater: remembering a kindness, speaking thanks and allowing received mercy to change the care we give others. John 4:46–53 tells of another household receiving help: an official believes Jesus’s word about his son and starts home. Servants meet him with news of recovery. The story is distinct from the centurion’s servant and gives trust a place on the road before the father sees the child. The one who returned One of the ten men who were cleansed returns to give thanks. Luke identifies him as a Samaritan. Open study → Pause and consider What kindness could you acknowledge directly rather than leaving your gratitude unspoken? records.title: The Mortal Ministry of Jesus Christ
records.pageTitle: The Mortal Ministry of Jesus Christ
records.text: Read and discover The Son enters the water Jesus comes from Galilee to John at the Jordan. In Matthew 3:13–17 , John hesitates, recognizing that Jesus is greater than he is. Jesus asks him to proceed so that righteousness may be fulfilled. After the baptism, the Spirit descends like a dove and a heavenly voice identifies Jesus as the beloved Son. Explore and study What should we do? People bring John a practical question about how to live. His answers turn repentance toward sharing, honesty and the fair treatment of others. Luke 3:10–14 The scene joins obedience with divine witness. Father, Son and Holy Ghost are distinguishable in the account: the Son receives baptism, the Spirit descends and the Father speaks. 2 Nephi 31:5–10 reflects on why the Holy One is baptized and connects His obedience to the path He invites others to follow. His example gives baptism meaning beyond a ceremony performed in isolation from a life turned toward God. Before Luke records Jesus’s baptism, people ask John what they should do. His answers in Luke 3:10–14 concern sharing necessities, honest collection and refusing extortion. Repentance has a practical shape in the lives of those preparing to receive the Lord. Pause and consider What does Jesus’s willingness to receive baptism reveal about the way He leads? Matthew 3:13–17 2 Nephi 31:5–10 Luke 3:10–14 Read and discover An invitation becomes a friendship Come and see Andrew and another disciple follow Jesus. His invitation gives them an opportunity to spend time with Him and begin to know Him. Open study → Two of John the Baptist’s disciples follow Jesus after hearing John identify Him as the Lamb of God. In John 1:35–42 , Jesus asks what they seek and invites them to come and see where He stays. Andrew then finds his brother Simon and brings him to Jesus. The account begins with testimony but moves into personal encounter. Andrew’s part is modest and meaningful. He shares what he has found and helps another person come to the Savior. This meeting should be kept distinct from the later fishing scenes in the Gospels; John gives this encounter its own sequence and purpose. It invites us to consider how a sincere introduction, a shared passage or time spent listening may help someone explore faith without pressure. Pause and consider What do you notice about the space Jesus gives these first followers to come and see? John 1:35–42 Read and discover A question is met with an invitation Known before the meeting Philip brings Nathanael to Jesus. The conversation moves from Nathanael’s question to recognition of the Son of God. Open study → Philip tells Nathanael that they have found the One anticipated in the law and prophets. Nathanael questions whether anything good can come from Nazareth. In John 1:43–51 , Philip answers by inviting him to come and see. Jesus then addresses Nathanael personally, and the conversation opens into a testimony of His identity. The passage does not explain what happened beneath the fig tree or why Jesus’s knowledge of it mattered so much to Nathanael. We can let that detail remain open while attending to what is recorded: a question did not end the encounter. Nathanael came, listened and responded. The invitation to know Christ can include honest questions, even when the answers unfold differently from what a person first expected. Pause and consider How could Philip’s brief response help you welcome another person’s sincere question? John 1:43–51 Read and discover A need at a wedding Explore and study Fill the jars The servants attend to the stone waterpots at Jesus's direction. At Cana, their ordinary work becomes part of the first sign John records. John 2:6–9 At a wedding in Cana, Mary brings the lack of wine to Jesus’s attention. In John 2:1–11 , servants fill six stone waterpots, draw from them and take what has become wine to the person overseeing the feast. John presents this as the beginning of Jesus’s signs and connects it with His disciples’ belief. The account places His power within a shared human occasion. Mary’s instruction directs the servants toward what Jesus says, and the servants participate through concrete actions. John does not identify the bride and bridegroom or tell us their relationship to Jesus; those details need not be supplied to appreciate the scene. The sign points beyond the provision itself toward the glory of the One who gives it. Explore and study His Father’s house Jesus acts with resolve among the temple tables. John records His challenge to those who had made His Father's house a place of merchandise. John 2:13–17 John next records Jesus going to Jerusalem and clearing the temple precinct in John 2:13–17 . The sign at Cana reveals His power, while this action reveals His concern for the reverence owed to His Father’s house. Explore and study Compassion in His Father’s house Amid the temple's upheaval, Jesus turns His attention to a person before Him. This imagined companion moment reflects on His compassion beside John's account of the cleansing; John does not record this particular conversation. John 2:13–17 Pause and consider Which small actions in this account help the larger sign unfold? John 2:1–11 John 2:13–17 Read and discover A place at the table Explore and study Jesus calls Levi Jesus meets Levi at his work and calls him to follow. Levi looks toward Him, his attention turning from the counter to the invitation. Mark 2:13–15 Jesus sees Levi at the place where taxes are collected and calls him to follow. Mark 2:13–17 moves from that invitation to a meal with tax collectors, people described as sinners and Jesus’s disciples. When religious teachers question the company He keeps, Jesus answers by speaking of a physician’s work among those who need healing. Jesus's welcome and His call to repentance belong together. He draws near enough to share a meal and invites Levi into a changed life. The account asks us to look beyond the labels that can make a person easy to dismiss. Jesus sees Levi at his work and calls him toward what he can become as a disciple. Pause and consider Who might be easier to understand if you first saw a person rather than a category? Mark 2:13–17 Read and discover Women along the road Explore and study Service along the road Hands prepare provisions for the road ahead. These unnamed women picture the practical support Luke remembers from women who gave of their resources to sustain Jesus's ministry. Luke 8:1–3 Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna among the women associated with Jesus’s traveling ministry. In Luke 8:1–3 , the Twelve are with Him, and women who have received healing help support the work from their own resources. The brief passage brings people into view whose service can be missed when attention stays only on the most familiar disciples. Each named woman has her own identity. Mary Magdalene is not identified here as Mary of Bethany or as the unnamed woman in another anointing account. Joanna is identified through her connection to Chuza, and Susanna is named without an extended biography. Their presence gives us enough to recognize that the ministry drew on real commitment and practical support, while leaving room for what the record does not tell us. Pause and consider Whose quiet, practical service has helped you receive something spiritually important? Luke 8:1–3 Read and discover The Twelve are sent Explore and study Sent to preach and heal The disciples begin the journey Jesus has entrusted to them. This partial gathering recalls His charge to the Twelve to proclaim the kingdom and heal. Luke 9:1–6 In Luke 9:1–6 , Jesus gives the Twelve authority and sends them to proclaim God's kingdom and heal. He asks them to travel simply and receive the hospitality offered along the way. Their service begins with His trust and with the message and authority He gives them. The disciples move from watching His ministry to participating in it. The simplicity of their preparation places attention on the commission and the households that will receive them. They leave as people entrusted with a message, not as spectators collecting another memorable experience. We can ask what we have received from the Savior that could now become useful service, and what unnecessary concerns make us slower to respond. Pause and consider Where could something you have learned from Christ become a useful act of service? Luke 9:1–6 Read and discover Hear the beloved Son Explore and study Arise, and be not afraid Jesus comes to the frightened disciples and touches them. As Peter looks up, the Savior's quiet attention accompanies His invitation to rise without fear. Matthew 17:6–8 Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain. In Matthew 17:1–9 , His appearance changes, Moses and Elias appear, and a voice from the bright cloud directs the disciples to hear the beloved Son. The disciples fall in fear; Jesus approaches, touches them and tells them to rise without fear. When they look up, they see Jesus alone. The scene brings glory and gentleness close together. The One whose face shines also reaches toward frightened followers. This happens during His mortal ministry, before His death and Resurrection, as the disciples are still learning what His mission will require. The Father’s direction to hear the Son gives them a way forward when they cannot yet understand everything they have witnessed. Listening will matter as much on the road ahead as it does on the mountain. Pause and consider What do you learn by holding the glorious revelation and Jesus’s reassuring touch together? Matthew 17:1–9 Read and discover He sees the city and weeps Explore and study He weeps over the city Jesus looks toward Jerusalem and weeps. Luke records His sorrow for a city that has not recognized the things that belong to its peace. Luke 19:41–44 As Jesus comes near Jerusalem, Luke 19:41–44 records Him looking at the city and weeping. He speaks of the peace it has not recognized and the destruction that will come upon it. The scene is distinct from His tears at Lazarus’s tomb: here His sorrow reaches toward a city and its people. His words have gravity, and His tears keep us from reading them as cold satisfaction at another’s suffering. The account invites a deeper understanding of His love, one that includes both grief and a call to recognize what leads to peace. It must never become a reason for contempt toward Jewish people. Jesus’s own life and this encounter belong within the Jewish world in which He ministered. Pause and consider What changes when you hear this warning as words spoken through tears? records.title: The Barren Fig Tree
records.text: Read and discover Tragedy is not proof of greater guilt Explore and study Looking for fruit The owner looks among the leaves and finds no fruit. In Jesus' parable, his repeated search brings a serious question about the tree's place in the vineyard. Luke 13:6-7 Jesus has been asked about people killed under Pilate, and He also mentions those who died when a tower fell. He rejects the assumption that their deaths establish them as worse sinners than others. In that setting, He calls His hearers to repentance and tells of a fig tree. Luke 13:1-9 Luke 13:1-9 Read and discover One more season of care Explore and study The gardener asks for time The gardener asks the owner to leave the tree for another year. His appeal includes a promise of work: digging around it and nourishing the soil. Luke 13:8 The owner has looked for fruit for three years and found none. He proposes cutting the tree down. The gardener asks for another year in which to dig around it and nourish it, holding together the need for fruit and a willingness to provide further care. The story ends with that proposed opportunity. It does not tell us whether the tree later bears fruit. The open ending leaves the invitation before the hearer rather than allowing the conclusion to be assigned to an imaginary person safely outside the reader's own life. Luke 13:1-9 Read and discover Cultivate a response Explore and study The care the gardener proposes The gardener's proposed care is pictured here: digging around the tree and adding nourishment. Jesus leaves its later fruitfulness unstated; the image visualizes the work promised in the appeal, not a reported outcome. Luke 13:8 Patient cultivation is a different response from either indifference or instant removal. You might consider what needs tending in your own response to God. Keep the beginning of the passage in view: this reflection should never become an explanation that other people's tragedies prove a lack of righteousness. Pause and consider Where is patient cultivation needed? How can you respond to repentance without judging victims of tragedy? records.title: Birds and Lilies
records.text: Read and discover Creation within a teaching about trust Explore and study Birds finding food Small birds find food among stones and tree roots. Jesus directs His listeners to the birds as He teaches them about their Heavenly Father's care. Matthew 6:26 Jesus turns His hearers' attention toward birds and flowers while teaching about life's needs. Birds do not organize their lives around barns, yet the heavenly Father feeds them. Lilies do not spin clothing, yet their beauty exceeds royal splendor. Ordinary creation becomes a setting for trust. Matthew 6:19-34 Explore and study Flowers of the field White flowers open among the rough grasses of a hillside. Their quiet beauty accompanies Jesus' invitation to consider the lilies as He teaches about clothing and trust. Matthew 6:28-29 Matthew 6:19-34 Luke 12:22-31 Read and discover Needs known by the Father The comparisons follow teaching about treasure and the impossibility of serving both God and mammon. They do not float free from the question of what governs a life. Jesus directs His hearers to seek God's kingdom and righteousness as they face needs the Father already knows. Luke preserves the same movement through birds, clothing, grass, and the call to seek the kingdom. The teaching invites freedom from being consumed by concern; it does not state that faithful people never experience hunger, poverty, or anxiety. Luke 12:22-31 Explore and study Grass in the evening light Evening light catches the green blades and dry stalks of ordinary grass. Jesus draws attention to the Father's care for such brief beauty as He invites His hearers to trust Him. Matthew 6:30 Matthew 6:19-34 Luke 12:22-31 Read and discover Bring your needs without pretending A gentle response might be to name a present need in prayer and consider one practical step consistent with your priorities. Seeking help is not a failure of trust. The passage invites attention to the Father's care without demanding that a burdened reader pretend to feel untroubled. Pause and consider What need can you bring to God? How might seeking His kingdom shape a priority? Matthew 6:19-34 Luke 12:22-31 Related studies The Rich Fool A rich harvest promises the owner many comfortable years. The story asks what possessions can and cannot secure. Open study → Sources for further study Matthew 6:19-34 Luke 12:22-31 Bible Dictionary: Parables

records.title: The Bridegroom and His Guests
records.text: Read and discover A question about fasting A question about fasting leads Jesus to speak of wedding guests and a bridegroom. While the bridegroom is with them, the guests have a reason for joy. His presence changes what is fitting for that moment. Jesus also says a time will come when the bridegroom is taken away. Matthew 9:14-17 Matthew 9:14-17 Mark 2:18-20 Luke 5:33-35 Read and discover Joy, presence, and coming absence The comparison answers the question through the significance of Jesus Himself, rather than through a simple rejection of fasting. The future absence belongs in the answer as much as the present joy. A practice is being understood in relation to His presence and mission. Mark 2:18-20 Explore and study Joy while the bridegroom is present Jesus compares His presence with the joy of wedding companions while the bridegroom is with them. This imagined gathering illustrates that comparison, rather than the wedding at Cana or a portrait of Jesus. Matthew 9:15 Luke preserves this exchange before the new garment and wineskin comparisons. Read together, the images resist forcing Jesus' disciples into an expectation that ignores what His coming means. This is not the same story as the ten virgins waiting for a bridegroom. records.title: The Budding Fig Tree
records.text: Read and discover A familiar change of season Explore and study Tender fig branch leafing Tender leaves unfold at the tip of the fig branch. Jesus draws on this familiar sign of approaching summer to teach His hearers to pay attention. Matthew 24:32 Jesus speaks of a fig tree within His discourse about coming events. When its branch becomes tender and leaves appear, observers recognize that summer is near. Luke broadens the view to the fig tree and all the trees. A familiar seasonal change supplies the comparison. Matthew 24:32-44 Matthew 24:32-44 Mark 13:28-31 Luke 21:29-33 Read and discover Recognition without a timetable The hearers are invited to recognize rather than ignore what is before them. Yet the surrounding discourse also warns that the precise day and hour are unknown. Attentiveness to His words and refusal to calculate an unauthorized timetable belong together. Mark 13:28-31 Explore and study A leafy fig tree In this imagined scene, travelers pause beside a leafy fig tree and notice the green hillside. Jesus asks His hearers to observe the fig tree and other trees, recognizing summer's approach from their growth. Luke 21:29-30 This is neither the story of a fruitless tree given more time nor the account of Jesus cursing a fig tree. Shared imagery does not make those passages one event. Here the ordinary appearance of leaves illustrates discernment and the reliability of His words. Luke 21:29-33 Matthew 24:32-44 Mark 13:28-31 Luke 21:29-33 Read and discover Readiness in ordinary life Readiness can become part of ordinary discipleship rather than a cycle of alarm. You might ask what Christ's teaching calls you to do today even without knowing what tomorrow will bring. Caring for others, repenting, and keeping commitments do not depend on discovering a date. Pause and consider What does recognition require beyond curiosity? How can readiness become daily faithfulness? Matthew 24:32-44 Mark 13:28-31 Luke 21:29-33 Related studies The Doorkeeper The master leaves work for each servant and watchfulness for the porter. The unknown hour does not erase their present responsibility. Open study → The Barren Fig Tree The gardener asks for time to dig and nourish. Jesus places urgent repentance beside a patient opportunity to bear fruit. records.title: Children in the Marketplace
records.text: Read and discover Two ministries, two complaints Explore and study Children who will not join Some children respond to the music while others remain apart. Jesus compares His generation to children dissatisfied with either a joyful tune or a lament. In context, the criticism exposes a refusal to receive either John's austere ministry or the Son of man's fellowship with others. Matthew 11:16–19 Jesus speaks about John the Baptist and the reactions both of them have received. John comes with an austere way of life and is accused of having a devil. Jesus eats and drinks with others and is called a glutton and a friend of sinners. The criticism changes, but the refusal remains. Matthew 11:7-19 Matthew 11:7-19 Luke 7:31-35 Read and discover The invitation always refused Children in a marketplace give Him a picture for that response. They call to one another about music and mourning, but their companions will join neither. The image exposes a demand that others participate only on the critic's terms, followed by dissatisfaction whichever invitation is offered. Luke 7:31-35 Explore and study A second invitation refused A solemn song receives little response from the seated children. Jesus pairs the unanswered lament with the earlier invitation to dance, exposing a refusal that finds fault with either approach. The comparison leads into the rejection of both John the Baptist and the Son of man, calling listeners to examine their willingness to receive God's messengers. Luke 7:31–35 Jesus does not ask His hearers to judge truth by a teacher's personality or by whether a messenger matches their preferred style. John and Jesus have different roles. Their difference does not excuse refusing both. The concluding reference to wisdom invites attention to what their ministries actually bring forth. Matthew 11:7-19 Luke 7:31-35 Read and discover Listening beyond preference This passage can turn us from quick dismissal toward honest listening. You might notice the standards you apply to a message you do not want to hear. Are those standards consistent, or do they shift so that no messenger could satisfy them? Pause and consider What remains constant in the two criticisms? How can you recognize a message without demanding your preferred messenger? records.title: The Closed Door
records.text: Read and discover A question about how many Explore and study The householder shuts the door Jesus describes the master of the house rising and shutting the door. This picture illustrates that closing moment before the appeals from those left outside. Luke 13:25 Someone asks Jesus whether few will be saved. His response turns from speculation about a number toward the hearers' own response. The image of a householder who has risen and shut the door gives that call urgency. People outside begin to knock and ask admission. Luke 13:23-30 Luke 13:23-30 Read and discover Familiarity is not the whole response They appeal to familiarity: they have eaten and drunk in his presence, and he has taught in their streets. The reply does not accept proximity as a substitute for belonging. The account makes a distinction between having been near the teaching and having responded to it. Explore and study Appealing from outside Those outside knock and ask the master to open, appealing to their former familiarity with him. In Jesus' warning, that claim does not bring admission, and the pictured door remains closed. Luke 13:25-27 The surrounding verses picture people coming from different directions to sit in God's kingdom and speak of the last and the first. This widening horizon resists a comfortable assumption that one's current place or association settles the question. Luke 13:23-30 Read and discover Answer the invitation before you You might ask where knowledge about Christ has yet to become a response to Him. The passage calls for seriousness without authorizing you to pronounce a neighbor's final standing. Its question can be received personally: what invitation is open before you now, and what would answering it mean? Pause and consider Where might familiarity substitute for response? What invitation can you answer now? Luke 13:23-30 Related studies The Great Supper The supper is ready, but the first invitees excuse themselves. The widening invitation brings overlooked people toward a place at the table. Open study → The Ten Virgins All ten wait and all ten sleep, but their preparation differs. The midnight announcement reveals what they have brought to the waiting. records.title: A Divided Kingdom and House
records.text: Read and discover The claim against Jesus Opponents claim that Jesus casts out devils through the ruler of devils. He replies by considering what happens when a kingdom or household is divided against itself. Internal opposition undermines the very power the accusation claims He is serving. Matthew 12:25-26 Matthew 12:25-26 Mark 3:23-26 Luke 11:17-18 Read and discover An explanation that contradicts the work Mark records Jesus asking how Satan can cast out Satan, then applies the divided-kingdom and divided-house comparisons. His reasoning calls attention to the work actually being done. A person is being delivered from evil, and the proposed explanation does not fit that deliverance. Mark 3:23-26 Explore and study A household divided Jesus teaches that a house divided against itself cannot stand. The two people turned apart picture that division symbolically, without claiming a particular family dispute or its outcome. Mark 3:25 Luke preserves the same answer before developing the strong-man comparison. The two images belong to the argument but contribute different parts: division exposes the contradiction, and the stronger challenger explains the breaking of an existing hold. Luke 11:17-18 Matthew 12:25-26 Mark 3:23-26 Luke 11:17-18 Read and discover Judge a claim with attention The passage can encourage careful judgment about claims and their evidence. A memorable accusation should not replace attention to what has happened. Its household image is not a command to remain in an unsafe relationship for the sake of appearances; the immediate subject is the charge against Jesus' deliverance. Pause and consider What contradiction does He expose? How does His actual work answer the accusation? The comparison directs attention to His authority to deliver. Open study → The Returning Unclean Spirit An emptied house is not the same as a renewed life. This unsettling comparison asks for a response deeper than a temporary change. records.title: The Doorkeeper
records.text: Read and discover Each servant has work Explore and study Each receives work to do Jesus compares watchfulness to a man leaving his house and giving each servant work to do. He also commands the doorkeeper to keep watch. Mark 13:34 Jesus tells His hearers that they do not know when the time will come. A man leaving his house provides the picture: he gives authority to his servants, assigns each work, and commands the porter to watch. Responsibility continues during the master's absence. Mark 13:28-37 Mark 13:28-37 Read and discover The unknown hour of return Explore and study Keeping watch at the door The doorkeeper remains attentive at the open entrance. He does not know when his master will return, but he is ready to receive him. Mark 13:34-35 The possible return is described through different times of night. No single watch is announced as the one that will settle the question. The repeated instruction is to remain ready, not to solve a hidden schedule. The porter is memorable, but the story also includes every servant's work. Watchfulness is therefore not merely standing still and looking for signs. It belongs with faithfully doing what has been entrusted while the return remains unknown. Explore and study Faithful work while watching The household's work continues while the doorkeeper remains attentive. Folding linen and tending stored vessels illustrate the work entrusted to each servant as Jesus calls all His listeners to watch. Mark 13:34–37 Mark 13:28-37 Read and discover Watching while serving You might ask what attentive readiness looks like within today's ordinary responsibilities. Prayer, care for others, and keeping a commitment can all belong to the waiting. Jesus' final extension of the call to watch makes the invitation broader than the one figure at the doorway. Pause and consider What work has been entrusted while you wait? How can readiness stay peaceful rather than fearful? records.text: Read and discover Watching while serving You might ask what attentive readiness looks like within today's ordinary responsibilities. Prayer, care for others, and keeping a commitment can all belong to the waiting. Jesus' final extension of the call to watch makes the invitation broader than the one figure at the doorway. Pause and consider What work has been entrusted while you wait? How can readiness stay peaceful rather than fearful? Mark 13:28-37

records.title: The Faithful and Unfaithful Servant
records.text: Read and discover Responsibility for the household Explore and study Food for the household The steward places food into another person's hands. Jesus describes a faithful servant entrusted with feeding the household at the proper time; responsibility becomes care for the people before him. Matthew 24:45 The master places a servant over the household with responsibility to provide food at the proper time. The question is what that servant will do while the master is absent. Jesus makes readiness concrete through care that other people need to receive. Matthew 24:45-51 Matthew 24:45-51 Luke 12:41-48 Read and discover What the delay reveals Explore and study Responsibility turned toward self A contrasting steward keeps his attention on his own table while others wait. This restrained scene pictures neglected care alongside Jesus' warning about a servant who uses his master's delay as permission to mistreat the household. Luke 12:45 The faithful servant continues the work. The unfaithful servant takes the delay as permission to mistreat others and indulge himself. The master's return reveals which attitude has governed the entrusted authority. Waiting has not been empty time; it has shown the servant's character. Luke records Peter asking whether the teaching is for the disciples or for everyone. Jesus' answer develops accountability in relation to knowledge and what has been entrusted. Greater responsibility is not merely greater status; it carries an obligation to use the trust faithfully. Luke 12:41-48 Matthew 24:45-51 Luke 12:41-48 Read and discover Care that remains dependable Explore and study Found serving when the master returns The returning master finds the steward still serving the household. Jesus calls that servant blessed: the master's arrival reveals the faithful work already underway. Matthew 24:46 Consider a place where another person depends on your attention. The parable invites service that remains dependable when no one appears to be checking. Its warning against abuse also matters: authority in the household is given for care, not as a license to dominate. Pause and consider Who depends on your faithful attention? How does responsibility change when you remember it is entrusted? records.title: The Friend at Midnight
records.text: Read and discover A guest arrives and bread is needed Explore and study A traveler arrives at night A friend arrives after a journey, and his host has nothing to set before him. The nighttime welcome introduces a need that will send the host to another friend's door. Luke 11:5–6 After teaching His disciples to pray, Jesus describes a host whose friend arrives from a journey at midnight. The host has nothing to set before the guest, so he goes to another friend's house and asks for three loaves. The need arises through the desire to welcome someone else. Luke 11:1-13 Luke 11:1-13 Read and discover The request beyond the closed door Explore and study A request at the closed door At midnight, the host asks a friend to lend him three loaves for his guest. An answer comes from within: the door is shut, and the household has gone to bed. Luke 11:5–7 The friend inside says the door is shut and his children are with him in bed. The request is inconvenient. Yet the story moves toward the bread being provided, emphasizing persistence in bringing the need rather than retreating at the first obstacle. Jesus follows the account with invitations to ask, seek, and knock, then speaks of the Father's good gifts. Those surrounding verses guard against treating God as an irritated neighbor who must be worn down. The movement is toward confidence in the Father, not distrust of His willingness to care. Luke 11:1-13 Read and discover Keep turning toward the Father Explore and study Bread for the waiting guest The friend rises and provides the bread the host needs for his guest. Jesus connects this response with the requester's persistence, inviting His listeners to keep turning to God. Luke 11:5–8 You can bring a need honestly, including a need you carry for someone else. Persistent prayer need not be polished or accompanied by certainty about an outcome. The passage invites continued turning toward God while leaving the timing and form of the answer in His hands. Pause and consider What need can you bring honestly to God? How does the Father's generosity change the way you ask? Luke 11:1-13 Related studies The Persistent Widow and the Judge A widow keeps bringing a claim that a judge dismisses. Jesus directs weary hearers toward continued prayer and the goodness of God. Open study → A Parent's Good Gifts A child's request for food becomes a way to think about prayer. Jesus directs trust toward the Father's goodness. records.title: The Good Samaritan
records.text: Read and discover The question about a neighbor Explore and study Wounded traveler on the road The wounded traveler lies alone beside the road. Jesus begins His parable with a person's urgent need, before asking who will draw near to help. Luke 10:30 A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus directs him to the law, and the reply joins love of God with love of neighbor. When the man then asks who his neighbor is, Jesus answers with a traveler on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. Luke 10:25-37 Luke 10:25-37 Read and discover Three travelers encounter a need Explore and study Priest passing at a distance The priest continues along the other side while the traveler remains on the ground. Jesus tells us that he saw the man and passed by, without explaining his private reasons. Luke 10:31 Robbers strip and beat the traveler, leaving him half dead. A priest sees him and passes on the other side. A Levite also sees him and passes by. Jesus records their actions without explaining their private reasons; a careful retelling should not invent motives for either. Explore and study Levite passing The Levite looks toward the injured traveler but continues past him. In Jesus' account, coming near and seeing the need do not yet become an act of care. Luke 10:32 A Samaritan comes near, sees the wounded man, and is moved with compassion. That compassion becomes practical work. He binds the wounds, uses oil and wine, places the man on his own beast, and takes him to an inn. Explore and study The Samaritan stops beside him The Samaritan kneels beside the injured traveler and meets his eyes with a hand resting gently on his shoulder. Jesus describes compassion that brings the stranger close enough to help. Luke 10:33 Explore and study Binding the traveler's wounds The Samaritan bends over the traveler's arm, supporting it while he wraps a strip of cloth around the wound. In Jesus's story, compassion becomes practical care as he binds the wounds and tends them with oil and wine. Luke 10:34 Explore and study Carrying him toward care The traveler sits on the animal's woven covering while the Samaritan steadies his arm and holds the lead. Jesus tells how the Samaritan brought him to an inn, continuing the care he had begun beside the road. Luke 10:34 Luke 10:25-37 Read and discover Mercy that continues beyond the road Explore and study Care continues at the inn At the inn, the Samaritan remains beside the injured man and cares for him. The cup and reassuring touch picture that continuing attention, carrying mercy beyond the roadside. Luke 10:34 The care continues after the first emergency. The Samaritan tends the traveler, gives money to the host, and undertakes further expense if needed. Mercy in the story includes interruption, transport, provision, and follow-through. Jesus' final question changes the direction of the lawyer's original question. Rather than drawing a boundary around who qualifies for help, He asks which person became a neighbor to the wounded man. The lawyer identifies the one who showed mercy, and Jesus calls him to act likewise. Explore and study Provision for continued care The Samaritan gives the innkeeper two pence and asks him to care for the traveler. He promises to repay any further expense when he returns, providing for care that will continue after he leaves. Luke 10:35 Luke 10:25-37 Read and discover Becoming a neighbor The contrast with a Samaritan would matter to the story's original hearers, but we should not turn that contrast into caricatures of whole communities. Nor should we identify the unnamed traveler or the innkeeper as historical people whose biographies are known. As you reflect, notice both the first moment of stopping and the later work of sustaining care. A person may need more than an expression of sympathy. What responsible, practical help can you offer, and when should you involve others who can provide the care you cannot? Pause and consider What makes stopping costly for you? What practical follow-through could turn concern into care? Luke 10:25-37 Related studies The Sheep and the Goats The King remembers meals, visits, clothing, and welcome. This judgment scene places ordinary acts of care within our response to Christ. Open study → The Great Supper The supper is ready, but the first invitees excuse themselves. The widening invitation brings overlooked people toward a place at the table. Open study → Loving Our Neighbor Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Luke 10:25-37 Bible Dictionary: Parables
