records.title: The Good Shepherd and the Door
records.pageTitle: The Good Shepherd and the Door
records.text: Read and discover Jesus develops the image Explore and study Calling the flock A shepherd turns toward the sheep at the open fold. His attentive call pictures the familiar voice and personal care Jesus describes in His teaching. John 10:3 Jesus speaks of sheep, a doorway, a shepherd, strangers, and a hired worker after the account of a man born blind and the controversy surrounding his healing. His hearers do not at first understand the figure, so He develops it by naming Himself as the door and the good shepherd. John 10:1-21 John 10:1-21 Read and discover A voice known and a life freely given The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. They follow because they know his voice. The picture includes recognition and relationship, not merely movement within a crowd. The shepherd's knowledge of the flock gives direction a personal character. The hired worker abandons the sheep when danger comes because they are not his own. Jesus contrasts that flight with the good shepherd's willingness to lay down his life. He then speaks of laying down His life and taking it again, giving the image a direct connection with His saving mission. Explore and study The hired worker flees The hired worker runs as danger approaches, leaving the sheep behind. Jesus contrasts this flight with the care of the good shepherd. John 10:12 Explore and study Remaining with the sheep The shepherd stays beside the flock as danger approaches. His protective presence accompanies Jesus' contrast between the hired worker and the good shepherd who gives his life for the sheep. John 10:11-15 John 10:1-21 Read and discover The gathering beyond this fold He also speaks of other sheep who will hear His voice and of one flock under one shepherd. A full study should retain this outward movement rather than use the image only for private reassurance. His care is personal and His gathering reaches beyond the immediate fold. Explore and study The flock follows The shepherd goes ahead, and the flock follows his familiar presence. Jesus describes sheep who recognize the voice of the one who leads them. John 10:4 The Bible Dictionary classifies this teaching as an allegory, while the Harmony uses the broader label of parable. That difference in study terminology does not diminish the passage. Unlike a character in an ordinary parable, Jesus explicitly identifies Himself within this extended teaching image. John 10:1-21 Read and discover Learning the Shepherd's voice You might consider how you come to recognize a trustworthy voice. In this passage trust is connected with knowledge, care, and willing sacrifice. Following the Savior invites learning His words and character, rather than treating every strong impression or confident speaker as His voice. Pause and consider What marks a trustworthy voice? How does willing sacrifice reveal His care? John 10:1-21 Related studies The Lost Sheep The missing one is worth a search and the finding is worth a celebration. Read how Jesus answers criticism of His welcome. Open study → The True Vine and the Branches A branch lives through its connection to the vine. Jesus joins abiding, love, obedience, and fruitfulness in His farewell teaching. records.title: The Grain of Wheat
records.text: Read and discover The hour approaches Explore and study A grain alone One grain rests alone. Jesus begins His comparison with the solitary grain before speaking of the fruitfulness connected with His approaching death. John 12:24 Some Greeks have asked to see Jesus when He announces that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. He speaks of a grain of wheat falling into the earth and dying. The agricultural image belongs to the approach of His death, not to an unrelated lesson about farming. John 12:20-33 John 12:20-33 Read and discover A grain and its fruit Explore and study A grain falls toward the soil A grain falls from an open pinch toward the earth. This simple planting moment accompanies Jesus' words about the grain that falls into the ground. John 12:24 A grain that remains alone is contrasted with one that, through the process described, bears much fruit. Jesus places this image beside words about losing and keeping one's life and about the servant following where He is. Explore and study A grain beginning to grow Small roots and a shoot emerge from a grain in the soil. This beginning of growth accompanies Jesus' comparison of a solitary grain with the fruitfulness He connects to His approaching death. John 12:24 The comparison prepares readers to understand that His approaching death is not simply the termination of His work. The passage joins sacrifice with fruitfulness while the surrounding chapter makes clear that He faces a real and troubling hour. John 12:20-33 Read and discover Following without denying the cost A reflection on relinquishment should remain connected to following Christ in love and faithfulness. This is not an invitation to self-harm or a claim that every personal loss will produce a visible compensating benefit. You might instead ask what self-protective habit makes it harder to serve or follow honestly. Pause and consider How does this prepare readers for the Passion? What might following Him require you to release? John 12:20-33 Related studies The True Vine and the Branches A branch lives through its connection to the vine. records.title: The Great Supper
records.text: Read and discover Words about the kingdom at a meal Explore and study Servant announcing supper The servant announces that the supper is ready. Jesus begins the story with a prepared meal and an invitation to come. Luke 14:16-17 At a meal, a guest speaks of the blessedness of eating bread in God's kingdom. Jesus replies with a story about a man who prepares a great supper. When it is ready, his servant goes to summon the invited guests. Luke 14:12-24 Luke 14:12-24 Read and discover Excuses and an expanding invitation Explore and study The field excuse An invited man gestures toward his field as he asks to be excused. records.title: The Seed Growing Secretly
records.text: Read and discover Growth beyond the farmer's command Explore and study Seed entrusted to the ground The farmer releases the seed into the soil. Jesus begins this kingdom comparison with an ordinary act of sowing, then turns to growth the farmer cannot fully explain. Faithful action matters, even when the life that follows exceeds the worker's understanding. Mark 4:26–29 Mark records a kingdom comparison found only in his Gospel. A person casts seed into the ground, then continues through nights and days while the seed grows. The farmer participates in the process, yet does not command or fully explain its unfolding. Jesus lets that limit remain in the picture. Mark 4:26-29 Mark 4:26-29 Read and discover From sowing to harvest Explore and study Growth beyond the farmer's sight The field has changed since the seed was scattered. Jesus describes growth unfolding while the farmer sleeps and rises, though he does not know how it happens. The comparison invites patience with God's work without making the farmer's sowing or eventual harvest unnecessary. Mark 4:27–29 The growth has a sequence: blade, ear, and full grain. Harvest follows when the crop is ready. Waiting is therefore neither emptiness nor an abandonment of the field. Much is happening between sowing and reaping, even when the sower cannot make it happen faster. This story differs from the wheat and tares. There is no enemy planting weeds and no proposal to pull them out. Its attention rests on growth and its appointed ripeness. Combining the two stories would hide the particular contribution of Mark's account. Mark 4:26-29 Read and discover Faithful effort and patient trust Explore and study The harvest has come The farmer returns to the field with a sickle when the grain is ready. Jesus' story moves from sowing through growth the farmer cannot explain to timely action at harvest. Trust in God's hidden work is joined here with readiness to do the work that the season requires. Mark 4:26–29 Faithful effort can coexist with limited control. You might consider a good responsibility you are tending whose results are not yet visible. The parable invites patience, while the sowing and harvest remind us that patience still has work to do. Pause and consider What can you faithfully tend without controlling the result? What small growth might you overlook? Mark 4:26-29 Related studies The Mustard Seed Jesus places a small seed beside the branches it becomes. The kingdom's beginning does not reveal the full reach of its growth. Open study → The Leaven A woman's work with meal becomes a picture of the kingdom. The change reaches throughout the batch before the story ends. Open study → The Kingdom of God Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. records.title: Hearing and Living His Word
records.text: Read and discover Listen for the response the passage asks for The sower includes Jesus' own explanation, so begin with the meanings He supplies. The builders explicitly join hearing with doing. The two sons distinguish agreeable words from obedience. Read those direct connections before assigning additional symbolism to soil, tools, or household objects. Matthew 13:18–23 Explore and study Returning to practice The musician watches the score as her fingers and bow work together. The good ground in Jesus' parable bears fruit with patience, reminding us of the value of steady, continuing effort. Luke 8:15 Compare parallel accounts without flattening them. The lamp appears in teaching about visible good works and in teaching about how people hear. The new patch and wineskins answer a question about fasting. The setting helps determine what a familiar image is doing in a particular passage. Mark 4:21–25 The modern pictures imagine people learning, listening and returning to practical work. They offer ways to consider your own response to Christ's words, while the meaning of each teaching remains grounded in its scripture passage. A faithful beginning may still call for patience through difficulty. Matthew 13:18–23 Mark 4:21–25 Read and discover Receive with attention and questions Explore and study Making room for a question A learner raises his hand, and the teacher turns toward him. The sower's teaching about hearing and understanding encourages us to ask honestly when we need help to understand. Matthew 13:18-23 The disciples ask Jesus about the parable, and He explains. The question is part of learning rather than evidence that the hearers should already understand everything. His later question about their understanding also connects receiving teaching with what they will be able to bring forward. Luke 8:9–18 We can practice attention in an ordinary conversation: ask sincerely, set aside a distraction and hear the answer. Such habits may help us become more willing listeners. As we return to scripture, Christ's words remain the teaching we are seeking to receive. Matthew 13:51–52 Explore and study Giving attention The young person explains a bridge model while the woman looks toward her and the phone rests on the counter. Jesus' counsel to take care how we hear gives purpose to the attention we offer another person. Luke 8:18 Luke 8:9–18 Matthew 13:51–52 Read and discover Give the word room to take root Explore and study Making space to act Papers move to a shelf while a stool and tools wait on the bench. The sower's warning about competing concerns asks us to notice what crowds out the response we intend to give. Mark 4:18–20 Jesus distinguishes quick reception from lasting root and describes cares and riches crowding growth. Luke names patience in the fruitful response. Enthusiasm may be a beginning, but the passage asks what remains when difficulty or competing concerns arrive. Mark 4:14–20 Practice and protected attention provide present-day ways to consider endurance. A musician returns to a hard passage; an unfinished task receives a cleared space. Spiritual growth is not identical to acquiring a skill, yet these scenes can help us ask whether a good beginning has been given time and room to deepen. Luke 8:11–15 Mark 4:14–20 Luke 8:11–15 Read and discover Let agreement become action Explore and study Putting a changed mind into action The young person gathers bottles as the hall is cleared. The two-sons parable encourages us to let a changed mind become willing action. Matthew 21:28-32 The son who first refuses later works in the vineyard. The son who agrees does not go. Jesus' question makes actual response central. In the builders, the foundation likewise concerns hearing His words and doing them, not merely admiring the sermon. Matthew 21:28–32 A return to finish neglected work can give a changed mind a visible form. Accepting correction and trying it can make learning more than polite agreement. These ordinary scenes invite a spiritual question: which word of Christ has remained an intention, and what would one faithful action look like? Matthew 7:24–27 Explore and study Practicing what is learned The learner holds a square against the wood while another person points toward the work. Jesus' comparison of the builders joins hearing with doing, giving instruction a place in daily practice. Matthew 7:24-27 Matthew 21:28–32 Matthew 7:24–27 Read and discover Look at fruit and examine yourself Explore and study Pausing before sharing The two young people turn toward each other beside their devices. Jesus' teaching about speech and its fruit encourages us to consider the words we share and their effect on others. Luke 6:43-45 Jesus warns about unreliable guidance, speaks of a tree's fruit, and exposes the person who sees a speck while ignoring a beam. Discernment is necessary, but the comparisons do not excuse contempt. They bring the hearer's own conduct and capacity to see into the examination. Luke 6:39–45 Pausing a rumor or reviewing your own work before criticizing another can be useful applications. They do not require pretending wrongdoing is harmless. Instead, they ask whether your response is truthful, proportionate, and open to the correction you may also need. Matthew 7:1–5 Explore and study Beginning with self-examination The man studies a page with a pencil in hand while a woman sits nearby. Jesus' teaching about the beam and mote asks us to examine ourselves before correcting someone else. records.title: The Hen Gathering Her Chicks
records.text: Read and discover A lament and a protective image Jesus laments over Jerusalem, speaking of prophets killed and messengers rejected. He describes His desire to gather its children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings. The small, protective image appears within a grief-filled address. Matthew 23:37-39 Matthew 23:37-39 Luke 13:34-35 Read and discover The gathering desired and refused The gathering is desired but refused. That tension belongs to the passage: His care does not remove the hearers' agency. The image expresses both the shelter He would offer and the sorrow of an invitation that is not received. Explore and study Sheltered beneath her wings Chicks nestle beneath a hen's outstretched wings. Jesus uses this tender picture of shelter as He expresses His desire to gather Jerusalem's children. Matthew 23:37 Luke preserves the lament in another surrounding sequence of His journey. Reading both accounts can deepen attention to His words without requiring us to resolve every chronological question. Neither account authorizes contempt toward Jewish people today. Luke 13:34-35 Matthew 23:37-39 Luke 13:34-35 Read and discover Offer care while preserving agency As an application, consider what makes an invitation caring rather than controlling. Protection, belonging, and patient love can be offered while another person's response remains their own. The passage may also invite you to ask what it means to receive the Savior's gathering call personally. Pause and consider What does gathering show about care? records.title: The Hidden Treasure
records.text: Read and discover A discovery worth responding to Explore and study Discovery in the field A buried jar has come to light beneath the soil. Jesus tells of a man finding treasure in a field and responding with joy, willing to sell all he has to obtain it. The picture introduces that discovery; the contents of the jar remain out of view. Matthew 13:44 The hidden treasure is one of Jesus' shortest kingdom comparisons. A man finds treasure in a field, hides it, sells what he owns with joy, and buys the field. Matthew records the whole movement in one verse, leaving the hearer to feel the force of the discovery. Matthew 13:44 Matthew 13:44 Read and discover Joy and a changed priority Explore and study Letting possessions go The finder now offers possessions for sale. Jesus describes his willingness to sell all he has because of the joy of the discovery. The visible exchange illustrates that response without claiming to display everything he owned. Matthew 13:44 Joy is an important part of the account. The man's costly action follows recognition of something he considers worth more than his previous possessions. The narrative gives no name, family history, or long search; it moves directly from discovery to decisive response. The kingdom is not presented as one attractive possession among many equally valuable choices. The comparison brings its worth into focus. Incidental questions about the field's legal history should not displace that central movement or become unsupported rules for modern property dealings. Matthew 13:44 Read and discover What your choices call precious Explore and study The field is purchased The finder pays for the field. Jesus brings the story from unexpected discovery to a deliberate commitment, showing the kingdom's surpassing worth through the man's joyful willingness to act. Matthew 13:44 What we treasure becomes visible in what we are willing to arrange our lives around. You might reflect on a truth about Christ that has changed your priorities. Wholehearted response can be considered with gratitude, without turning the verse into pressure to make an impulsive financial decision. Pause and consider Why does joy matter in this story? records.title: A discovery worth responding to
records.text: Read and discover A discovery worth responding to Explore and study Discovery in the field A buried jar has come to light beneath the soil. Jesus tells of a man finding treasure in a field and responding with joy, willing to sell all he has to obtain it. The picture introduces that discovery; the contents of the jar remain out of view. Matthew 13:44 The hidden treasure is one of Jesus' shortest kingdom comparisons. A man finds treasure in a field, hides it, sells what he owns with joy, and buys the field. Matthew records the whole movement in one verse, leaving the hearer to feel the force of the discovery. Matthew 13:44 Matthew 13:44

records.title: Joy and a changed priority
records.text: Read and discover Joy and a changed priority Explore and study Letting possessions go The finder now offers possessions for sale. Jesus describes his willingness to sell all he has because of the joy of the discovery. The visible exchange illustrates that response without claiming to display everything he owned. Matthew 13:44 Joy is an important part of the account. The man's costly action follows recognition of something he considers worth more than his previous possessions. The narrative gives no name, family history, or long search; it moves directly from discovery to decisive response. The kingdom is not presented as one attractive possession among many equally valuable choices. The comparison brings its worth into focus. Incidental questions about the field's legal history should not displace that central movement or become unsupported rules for modern property dealings. Matthew 13:44

records.title: The Householder's Treasure
records.text: Read and discover After the disciples understand At the close of the kingdom parables, Jesus asks His disciples whether they have understood. Their reply leads to one final household comparison: a scribe instructed in the kingdom brings out treasure that is both new and old. The image is connected to learning and understanding. Matthew 13:51-53 Matthew 13:51-53 Read and discover Treasures brought forward The householder has resources to bring out, rather than merely objects to admire in storage. Jesus does not list the individual treasures or assign a separate meaning to each. The teaching can remain rich without turning the contents of the house into an invented symbolic inventory. Explore and study Treasures brought out The householder brings an item out of his store of valuables. After asking whether His listeners understand, Jesus compares a scribe instructed in the kingdom to a householder bringing forth things new and old. The image can invite reflection on receiving His teaching deeply enough to share its riches with others. Matthew 13:51–52 The pairing of new and old resists a careless assumption that understanding requires either discarding everything previously learned or refusing everything unfamiliar. The emphasis rests on a person instructed in the kingdom who can draw upon what has been received. records.title: The King Considering War
records.text: Read and discover Another picture of counting the cost Explore and study Considering the opposing forces Jesus asks whether a king with ten thousand soldiers would first consider his ability to meet an army of twenty thousand. The unequal groups of stones picture that comparison as the king weighs what lies ahead. Luke 14:31 Jesus places a king's decision beside a builder's calculation. Both appear while He is teaching a large accompanying crowd about discipleship. The images ask people to think seriously about the commitment before them rather than move forward only through the momentum of the crowd. Luke 14:25-35 Luke 14:25-35 Read and discover Assessment before confrontation The king considers whether ten thousand can meet an opposing force of twenty thousand. If not, he sends a delegation to seek terms of peace while the other king is still far away. The decisive action is thoughtful assessment, not an exciting battle. Explore and study Envoys seek terms of peace If the king cannot meet the greater force, Jesus says he sends an embassy while the other king is still far away. The envoys seek conditions of peace, illustrating a request rather than an agreement already reached. Luke 14:32 The comparison does not report a particular historical campaign or praise aggression. Nor should each army be assigned an unsupplied symbolic identity. Its immediate connection is the seriousness of counting the cost, followed by Jesus' words about forsaking what competes with discipleship. Luke 14:25-35 Read and discover The humility to consider As a reflection, consider where honest assessment might change your response to a commitment. Humility can acknowledge what is beyond your strength. Following Christ may require asking for help and reordering priorities instead of defending the appearance that you already have everything in hand. Pause and consider What honest assessment are you avoiding? Where would humility change your decision? Luke 14:25-35 Related studies The Tower Builder A foundation does not finish a tower. The returning master asks what each has done with the responsibility received. records.title: The Kingdom of God
records.text: Read and discover Keep the kingdom comparisons distinct Matthew gathers several kingdom parables in one chapter, while Mark preserves the seed that grows through nights and days. Read each image on its own terms. The growing seed concerns growth and harvest; the wheat and tares adds an enemy, mixed growth, and restraint before separation. Mark 4:26–32 Explore and study A small beginning in shared ground The gardener lowers a seed into a tray of soil. Jesus' mustard-seed comparison teaches us to value a small beginning in light of the kingdom's growth. Mark 4:30-32 Jesus supplies explanations for some comparisons and leaves others brief. The treasure and pearl invite attention to surpassing worth. The net receives an explicit connection with judgment. Begin with these stated movements instead of inventing a separate doctrine for every object in the scene. Matthew 13:44–50 In the modern pictures, people plant, make bread, welcome others and choose how to spend their time. These imagined applications help us ask about patience, priorities and humble judgment. The kingdom parables remain our starting point; their promises belong to God's work, beyond what any one project may achieve. Mark 4:26–32 Matthew 13:44–50 Read and discover Allow small beginnings to matter Explore and study Leaven worked through the dough The baker presses and folds dough on the worktop. This familiar work recalls Jesus' comparison of leaven spreading its effect through the whole batch. Matthew 13:33 The mustard seed directs attention from an unimpressive beginning to substantial growth. The leaven directs attention to a change that reaches throughout the meal. These are related pictures, but their different actions matter: a seed grows, while leaven works through what surrounds it. Mark 4:26–32 A small planting and a baker's patient work let the original images remain visible in a present-day setting. Neither illustration claims that growth can be demanded on our timetable. The invitation is to consider the worth of faithful participation when the result is not yet fully seen. Matthew 13:33 Mark 4:26–32 Matthew 13:33 Read and discover Let recognized worth shape a choice Explore and study A commitment kept amid distractions A phone is set on the shelf as the two adults give each other their attention. The pearl of great price asks us to consider how the use of our time expresses what we treasure. Matthew 13:45-46 The treasure is found in a field; the pearl is found by a merchant already seeking fine pearls. In each, recognition leads to a wholehearted response. The joy of discovery and the willingness to rearrange priorities belong together in these compact accounts. Matthew 13:44–46 An application can ask what your schedule and attention reveal you consider precious. Keeping a meaningful commitment or choosing substance over display may require giving something else less room. These are invitations to examine priorities, not instructions to make an impulsive financial decision or treat every sacrifice as a purchase of divine favor. Explore and study Choosing substance over display One young person sets a handmade display on a shelf while the others arrange fabric at the table. The hidden-treasure parable asks what we are willing to set aside when we recognize something of greater worth. Matthew 13:44 Matthew 13:44–46 Read and discover Restrain haste and remember judgment's limits Explore and study Protecting the roots while tending The gardener lifts dry stems from beside the young plants. The owner's concern for the wheat reminds us to consider what our actions might harm, even when we intend to put something right. Matthew 13:28-30 The owner restrains servants who might uproot wheat while removing tares. In the net, Jesus places final separation at the end and identifies angels with that work. The accounts take judgment seriously while refusing to make the hearer the final judge of every person nearby. Matthew 13:24–30 A gardener protecting roots or a mediator listening carefully offers an application of restraint. Ordinary decisions still have to be made, and harmful conduct still matters. Humility asks us to consider what we might damage through haste and what we do not know about another person's whole story. Matthew 13:47–50 Explore and study Listening before passing judgment One person speaks while the others listen across the table. Jesus places the final separation in the net parable under God's authority, encouraging humility in our own judgments. Matthew 13:47-50 Matthew 13:24–30 Matthew 13:47–50 Read and discover Receive the invitation and follow in service Explore and study A place in the shared work People prepare the table together, carrying cutlery and pointing out places. The wide invitation in Jesus' banquet teaching encourages a welcome in which others can participate. Matthew 22:9-10 The king's wedding invitation is widened after the first invitees refuse, yet the account continues to ask about a fitting response. Welcome and responsibility appear together. John's grain-of-wheat image, in a different setting, points toward Jesus' approaching death and the call to follow Him. Matthew 22:1–14 The modern scenes invite participation and generous service: a newcomer receives a real place in shared work, and a teacher gives another person room to grow. They are applications, not extra meanings supplied by the parables. Service may ask what we can release without turning another person's growth into a claim about ourselves. John 12:23–26 Explore and study Giving time without taking the spotlight The potter shapes the clay while those around the table watch. Jesus' call to serve Him asks us to consider how the time and attention we give can benefit another person. John 12:24-26 Matthew 22:1–14 John 12:23–26 Read and discover Bring the teaching into your own reflection Pause and consider Which comparison needs to be read in its own setting rather than blended with another? What do your ordinary choices reveal about what you treasure? Where would patience protect something valuable that haste might harm? records.title: The Laborers in the Vineyard
records.text: Read and discover A question about reward Explore and study The first agreement The landowner speaks with the first workers as the day's hiring begins. In Jesus' story they agree on a day's wage before entering the vineyard, establishing the promise the owner will later keep. Matthew 20:1-2 The vineyard story follows Peter's question about what the disciples will receive after leaving everything to follow Jesus. Its opening and conclusion are framed by sayings about the first and the last. That context makes the account more than a lesson about an employer's unusual payment decision. Matthew 20:1-16 Matthew 20:1-16 Read and discover Hiring, payment, and comparison Explore and study Workers still waiting Two waiting workers meet the landowner's gaze as he addresses them beside their baskets. Jesus says they had remained because no one had hired them, and the owner's invitation gives them a place in the vineyard even at the late hour. Matthew 20:6-7 The householder hires workers early for an agreed wage, then returns at later hours to hire others. Some are still waiting near the end of the day because no one has hired them. The owner sends them into the vineyard as well. The text does not call the late workers lazy. At payment, the last workers receive a full day's wage. Those hired first expect more, then resent receiving the amount they agreed to. The owner answers both their claim of unfairness and their reaction to his generosity. Nothing has been taken from them, yet another person's good has become hard to welcome. Explore and study Equal payment The steward pays the workers at evening, beginning with those hired last. When the early workers receive the same wage, their expectation of more brings the owner's generosity into question. Matthew 20:8-10 Matthew 20:1-16 Read and discover Can another person's good become your joy? Explore and study Owner answering complaint Holding his wage, an early worker brings his complaint to the owner. The owner answers that he has kept their agreement and asks why his generosity to another should provoke resentment. Matthew 20:11-15 The story invites us to examine comparison in our response to grace. Do we measure another person's welcome against the time and effort of our own service? Gratitude can be undermined when blessing becomes a competition for position. This is a kingdom parable, not a comprehensive rule for present-day employment. Its spiritual challenge remains searching: faithfulness does not require resentment toward someone whose opportunity or return came later. The invitation is to recognize generosity without treating it as a personal loss. Pause and consider When does another person's blessing feel like your loss? What would gratitude notice about the owner's first agreement? Matthew 20:1-16 Related studies The Prodigal Son and His Brother One son comes home from far away; the other stands outside the celebration. The father goes toward both, and the story leaves an invitation before us. Open study → The Talents Different amounts are entrusted to different servants. The returning master asks what each has done with the responsibility received. records.title: Can another person's good become your joy?
records.text: Read and discover Can another person's good become your joy? Explore and study Owner answering complaint Holding his wage, an early worker brings his complaint to the owner. The owner answers that he has kept their agreement and asks why his generosity to another should provoke resentment. Matthew 20:11-15 The story invites us to examine comparison in our response to grace. Do we measure another person's welcome against the time and effort of our own service? Gratitude can be undermined when blessing becomes a competition for position. This is a kingdom parable, not a comprehensive rule for present-day employment. Its spiritual challenge remains searching: faithfulness does not require resentment toward someone whose opportunity or return came later. The invitation is to recognize generosity without treating it as a personal loss. Pause and consider When does another person's blessing feel like your loss? What would gratitude notice about the owner's first agreement? Matthew 20:1-16

records.title: The Lamp on a Stand
records.text: Read and discover A light meant to be seen Explore and study Would a lamp be hidden? An overturned basket is held around a lamp whose flame is still visible. Jesus asks whether a lamp is brought in to be hidden beneath a basket or bed. The familiar household question draws attention to light received so that it can be seen, and to the care with which we hear His teaching. Mark 4:21–25 A lamp is useful because its light reaches beyond itself. Jesus returns to this ordinary household image in several settings. In Matthew, He speaks of the light His disciples should show through good works. In Mark and Luke, the lamp also appears beside teaching about what people hear and how they receive it. Matthew 5:14-16 Matthew 5:14-16 Mark 4:21-25 Luke 8:16-18 Luke 11:33-36 Read and discover Listening and shining Mark asks whether a lamp is brought in to be hidden beneath a basket or bed. Luke describes placing it where those entering can see. The absurdity of concealing a useful light makes the teaching memorable: what has been received is not meant to remain ineffective. Mark 4:21-25 Explore and study Light where it can be seen The lamp stands above the floor, casting light across the people nearby. Luke records Jesus' saying that a lit lamp belongs where those entering can see its light. The passage goes on to ask how we hear, joining the image of visible light with an attentive response to His word. Luke 8:16–18 The accounts should be read together without erasing their different emphases. Matthew directs attention from good works to the Father. Luke's later saying moves toward the condition of the eye and the light within a person. The same familiar object can illuminate more than one aspect of discipleship. Luke 11:33-36 Matthew 5:14-16 Mark 4:21-25 Luke 8:16-18 Luke 11:33-36 Read and discover Let goodness reach another person Sharing light need not mean drawing attention to yourself. A patient explanation, an honest act, or a needed kindness may help another person see goodness more clearly. You can also ask how attentively you are receiving the light you hope to share. Pause and consider What changes when the lamp is covered? How could your conduct help someone see goodness? records.title: The Leaven
records.text: Read and discover A woman's ordinary work Explore and study Leaven worked into the dough The woman's hands work the dough, while the leaven's effect is not yet something the eye can measure. Jesus likens the kingdom to leaven placed in flour until the whole is leavened. The quiet household image encourages attention to transforming work that can begin without public display. Matthew 13:33 A woman placing leaven into meal becomes Jesus' picture of the kingdom. Matthew gives the comparison in a single verse; Luke places it beside the mustard seed. Its brevity is part of its strength. An ordinary household action opens a way to think about a change that reaches beyond what is first visible. Matthew 13:33 Matthew 13:33 Luke 13:20-21 Read and discover Change throughout the meal The woman hides the leaven in three measures of meal, and the whole is leavened. The story does not describe separate stages or give her a name. Its attention rests on the relation between the introduced leaven and the resulting change throughout the batch. Luke 13:20-21 Explore and study Dough transformed The risen dough fills the bowl after the woman's earlier work. Jesus likens the kingdom to leaven whose quiet beginning affects the whole batch. Matthew 13:33 Leaven does not carry one fixed moral meaning wherever it appears in scripture. Jesus also uses it in warnings elsewhere. In this passage He explicitly compares it with the kingdom, so the surrounding teaching determines how the image should be read. Matthew 13:33 Luke 13:20-21 Read and discover The influence we cannot yet measure You might consider the quiet influence of a sincere word, repeated kindness, or faithful example. That is a present-day application, not an additional explanation supplied in the verse. The picture invites attention to effects that may be real before they become easy to measure. Pause and consider What is unseen while the dough changes? What quiet influence can you offer? records.title: The Lost Coin
records.text: Read and discover One piece still matters Explore and study Searching diligently Jesus tells of a woman who lights a lamp, sweeps her house, and searches carefully for a lost coin. This is an illustration of His parable. Luke 15:8 A woman has ten silver coins and loses one. Jesus tells her story between the lost sheep and the returning son, answering complaints that He receives sinners. The domestic search belongs to the same movement toward recovery and shared joy. Luke 15:1-10 Luke 15:1-10 Read and discover Light, effort, and shared rejoicing She lights a lamp, sweeps the house, and searches diligently until she finds the coin. These actions give attention a visible form. What is missing is not dismissed because nine remain; the search continues because the lost piece still matters. On finding it, she calls friends and neighbors to rejoice. Jesus connects that celebration with joy in the presence of God's angels over one sinner who repents. The explanation supplied in the passage should remain central rather than an invented account of the woman's marriage or possessions. Explore and study Rejoice with me Finding the coin leads to shared joy. Jesus connects that rejoicing with the joy before God’s angels over one person who repents. Luke 15:9–10 Luke 15:1-10 Read and discover Celebrate another person's return The coin's recovery invites us to consider whether our response to another person's return includes genuine gladness. We may also notice the care of the search itself. Attention, effort, and welcome can communicate value more clearly than a statement that someone ought to come back. Pause and consider What does careful searching show about value? How can you share joy over another person's return? records.title: The Lost Sheep
records.text: Read and discover Why Jesus tells of the missing one Explore and study Turning toward the one who is missing The flock remains behind as the shepherd turns his attention toward the rocky hillside. Jesus asks whether a man with one wandering sheep would leave the others and seek it. This image shows the beginning of that search, pointing toward the Father's care that none of His little ones should perish. Matthew 18:12–14 Luke places the lost sheep at the beginning of Jesus' answer to people who complain that He receives sinners and eats with them. Before we enter the story, that criticism helps us understand why the search and the celebration matter. Jesus is answering an objection to His welcome. Luke 15:1-7 Matthew 18:12-14 Luke 15:1-7 Read and discover The search and the shared joy Explore and study The sheep is found The search has given way to relief. Luke describes the shepherd laying the found sheep on his shoulders with joy. Jesus uses the recovery to speak of heaven's joy over a sinner who repents. Luke 15:5–7 A shepherd notices that one of a hundred sheep is missing. He goes after it, finds it, carries it on his shoulders, and calls friends and neighbors to share his joy. The sheep's recovery is not treated as a minor correction to the flock's total. It is an occasion worth celebrating. Matthew preserves the comparison in teaching about care for the little ones. There Jesus concludes that the Father does not will that one of them should perish. The two contexts illuminate the value of the one without requiring us to pretend they have identical surrounding conversations. Matthew 18:12-14 Matthew 18:12-14 Luke 15:1-7 Read and discover Notice who is absent Explore and study Rejoicing with neighbors The shepherd calls others to share his joy over the sheep he has found. Luke's account carries the recovery beyond a private moment into rejoicing with friends and neighbors, then connects that joy with repentance. The welcome invites us to receive another person's return with gladness. Luke 15:6–7 You might begin reflection with someone who is easy to overlook. The story does not supply a formula for approaching another person or permission to disregard their agency. It invites care that notices absence, makes a sincere effort, and rejoices in another person's good without making the searcher the center. Pause and consider Who might be overlooked in a crowd? How can welcome preserve someone's dignity? Matthew 18:12-14 Luke 15:1-7 Related studies The Lost Coin A lamp, a broom, and a careful search show that one missing coin still matters. records.title: Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning
records.pageTitle: Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning
records.text: Read and discover Read the welcome in its setting Begin Luke 15 with the complaint that Jesus receives sinners. The searches and celebration answer that complaint. They are not isolated stories about sentimental kindness; they invite the hearers to reconsider what it means for a person to be found and welcomed. Luke 15:1–32 Explore and study Sharing another person's joy A woman applauds a graduate holding flowers and a folder. Beside the elder son's story, their celebration asks whether we can share another person's joy. Luke 15:25-32 Read the whole movement of each account before deciding which character seems most like you. The returning son and the brother outside both matter. The forgiven servant's later conduct matters. A selected happy moment can be true to the story while still leaving out the question Jesus intends to ask. Matthew 18:21–35 Begin with the passage, then listen for the explanation Jesus gives before considering your own response. The modern pictures in this collection imagine mercy in ordinary life: searching carefully, listening honestly and giving someone time to take a next step. Luke 15:1–32 Matthew 18:21–35 Read and discover Notice the one who is missing Explore and study A search worth the effort Two people search the ground together beside a path. Their patient attention recalls the woman searching for her lost coin and asks how carefully we notice what matters to someone else. Luke 15:8-10 The shepherd searches for one sheep, and the woman searches for one coin. Their effort makes the value of the missing one visible. Jesus joins both searches with joy over repentance, asking His hearers to recognize the good in the welcome they have criticized. Luke 15:4–10 Attention can be a beginning in ordinary life. Someone may need practical help finding what was lost, or a clear way back into participation after an absence. Those actions are applications of attentive care; they do not make us responsible for controlling another person's response or completing their journey for them. Explore and study A route back into participation At the music-room doorway, a woman helps a man with an open rehearsal folder. A practical welcome can help someone take a next step toward joining in. Luke 15:4-7 Luke 15:4–10 Read and discover Let mercy meet an honest response Explore and study Truth about a damaged bicycle A teenager speaks beside a bicycle with a damaged basket while an adult listens. The returning son's confession invites us to begin making things right with honest words and willing action. Luke 15:17-21 The younger son decides to return and speak truthfully about what he has done. The father's welcome does not require him to hide that truth. In the unmerciful servant, a released debt becomes the measure of a response the servant refuses to give. Mercy and accountability are not treated as unrelated matters. Luke 15:17–24 An application may begin with acknowledging an error and taking a responsible step to correct it. Receiving mercy also asks how we treat the next person who needs patience. Forgiveness does not require pretending harm was harmless, abandoning appropriate boundaries, or restoring unsafe access. Matthew 18:27–35 Explore and study Correcting a mistake openly Two people examine a record together, one pointing while the other writes. Jesus' story of the two sons asks whether a change of mind becomes a change in what we do. Matthew 21:28-32 Luke 15:17–24 Matthew 18:27–35 Read and discover Make room for patient cultivation Explore and study Patient cultivation Two gardeners tend the soil around a small tree. The gardener's patient care in Jesus' fig-tree parable encourages us to consider the time and attention growth may need. Luke 13:6-9 Before the barren fig tree, Jesus rejects the assumption that victims of tragedy were worse sinners. The gardener then asks for time to dig and nourish rather than cut the tree down at once. The story holds urgency and patient care together, and it does not report the tree's later outcome. Luke 13:1–9 Learning a different response can take practice. A person may need guidance, support, and a chance to put a better choice into action. Patient care is not indifference to fruit, but neither is it a demand that growth arrive on the observer's schedule. An illustration of cultivation invites reflection; it cannot explain why a particular person suffers. Explore and study Learning a merciful response Two people talk across an open notebook, giving one another time to speak. The call to forgive can lead us to practice listening, honesty, and restraint while keeping appropriate boundaries. Matthew 18:21-35 Luke 13:1–9 Matthew 18:21–35 Read and discover Learn to share the joy Explore and study Making room for shared joy A group applauds as one woman receives a small card. The father's welcome in Jesus' story invites us to join in joy rather than measure who deserves the most attention. Luke 15:22-24 The elder son remains outside the celebration, and the father goes out to him. His brother's welcome feels like a judgment on his own service. The father answers that resentment without denying the elder son's place with him. The story leaves the son's final response open. Luke 15:25–32 Another person's welcome, recognition, or progress can stir feelings we would rather conceal. We can acknowledge those feelings without making them the final word. The debtors' story also asks how awareness of mercy can deepen love. A small act of shared gladness may be a meaningful place to begin. Luke 7:41–47 Luke 15:25–32 Luke 7:41–47 Read and discover Bring the teaching into your own reflection Pause and consider Which part of receiving mercy is difficult for you to trust? Who could receive patient attention without being pressured to respond on your timetable? What might help you rejoice in another person's good? Read and discover Explore every study in this collection The Lost Sheep Luke places the search amid criticism of Jesus receiving sinners; Matthew emphasizes care for the little ones. Let visitors read both contexts. Open study → The Unmerciful Servant Peter asks about forgiveness. The enormous forgiven debt throws the servant's refusal of mercy into sharp relief; forgiveness does not require returning to danger. Open study → The Two Debtors Jesus tells the brief debt story during a meal with Simon, then relates it to the woman's love and forgiveness. Do not identify the unnamed woman as Mary Magdalene. Open study → The Barren Fig Tree Read the gardener's request for time and care after Jesus rejects assumptions that victims were worse sinners. Repentance and patient cultivation belong together. Open study → The Lost Coin A woman searches carefully and calls others to share her joy. Jesus connects the recovery with joy over repentance. Open study → The Prodigal Son and His Brother Follow both sons and the father's invitations. The elder brother's response remains open; do not invent a final reconciliation absent from the account. Open study → Parables and story pictures Related comparisons and allegories The Good Shepherd and the Door Jesus identifies Himself as the door and good shepherd who lays down His life. The Bible Dictionary calls this an allegory; Harmony uses the broader parable label. Open study → The Hen Gathering Her Chicks Jesus laments over Jerusalem with a picture of protective gathering. Preserve both His invitation and the sorrow of refusal. Open study → Related studies Loving Our Neighbor Follow mercy into practical help, hospitality, and continued attention to a person's needs. Open study → Hearing and Living His Word Explore how a changed mind becomes a changed response in the two sons and the builders. Open study → Prayer, Readiness, and His Return Consider humble prayer and persistent trust when change or justice takes time. Open study → Sources for further study Bible Dictionary: Parables Harmony of the Gospels Luke 15 Matthew 18 Luke 13 Luke 7

Luke 15:17-21 The younger son decides to return and speak truthfully about what he has done. The father's welcome does not require him to hide that truth. In the unmerciful servant, a released debt becomes the measure of a response the servant refuses to give. Mercy and accountability are not treated as unrelated matters. Luke 15:17–24 An application may begin with acknowledging an error and taking a responsible step to correct it. Receiving mercy also asks how we treat the next person who needs patience. Forgiveness does not require pretending harm was harmless, abandoning appropriate boundaries, or restoring unsafe access. Matthew 18:27–35 Explore and study Correcting a mistake openly Two people examine a record together, one pointing while the other writes. Jesus' story of the two sons asks whether a change of mind becomes a change in what we do. Matthew 21:28-32 Luke 15:17–24 Matthew 18:27–35

records.title: Make room for patient cultivation
records.pageTitle: Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning
records.text: Read and discover Make room for patient cultivation Explore and study Patient cultivation Two gardeners tend the soil around a small tree. The gardener's patient care in Jesus' fig-tree parable encourages us to consider the time and attention growth may need. Luke 13:6-9 Before the barren fig tree, Jesus rejects the assumption that victims of tragedy were worse sinners. The gardener then asks for time to dig and nourish rather than cut the tree down at once. The story holds urgency and patient care together, and it does not report the tree's later outcome. Luke 13:1–9 Learning a different response can take practice. A person may need guidance, support, and a chance to put a better choice into action. Patient care is not indifference to fruit, but neither is it a demand that growth arrive on the observer's schedule. An illustration of cultivation invites reflection; it cannot explain why a particular person suffers. Explore and study Learning a merciful response Two people talk across an open notebook, giving one another time to speak. The call to forgive can lead us to practice listening, honesty, and restraint while keeping appropriate boundaries. Matthew 18:21-35 Luke 13:1–9 Matthew 18:21–35

records.title: Learn to share the joy
records.pageTitle: Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning
records.text: Read and discover Learn to share the joy Explore and study Making room for shared joy A group applauds as one woman receives a small card. The father's welcome in Jesus' story invites us to join in joy rather than measure who deserves the most attention. Luke 15:22-24 The elder son remains outside the celebration, and the father goes out to him. His brother's welcome feels like a judgment on his own service. The father answers that resentment without denying the elder son's place with him. The story leaves the son's final response open. Luke 15:25–32 Another person's welcome, recognition, or progress can stir feelings we would rather conceal. We can acknowledge those feelings without making them the final word. The debtors' story also asks how awareness of mercy can deepen love. A small act of shared gladness may be a meaningful place to begin. Luke 7:41–47 Luke 15:25–32 Luke 7:41–47

records.title: Bring the teaching into your own reflection
records.pageTitle: Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning
records.text: Read and discover Bring the teaching into your own reflection Pause and consider Which part of receiving mercy is difficult for you to trust? Who could receive patient attention without being pressured to respond on your timetable? What might help you rejoice in another person's good?

records.title: The Ten Pounds or Minas
records.text: Read and discover Why the kingdom does not appear immediately Explore and study Entrusted with money Before leaving to receive a kingdom, a nobleman entrusts money to ten servants and tells them to trade until he returns. Each begins with one mina, and this partial group pictures their shared responsibility. Luke 19:12–13 Luke explains why Jesus tells this parable: He is near Jerusalem, and people suppose the kingdom of God will appear immediately. A nobleman who travels to receive a kingdom and then return provides a story about an interval, entrusted work, and later accountability. Luke 19:11-27 Luke 19:11-27 Read and discover Work during the nobleman's absence Explore and study Putting the money to work The servants are charged to trade with what they have received, and later report what their money has gained. This cloth-market exchange is an illustration of that activity, not merchandise specified in the parable. Luke 19:13, 15–19 The nobleman gives ten servants money and directs them to put it to use. Citizens who oppose him send a message rejecting his rule. When he returns, he calls the servants to learn what they have gained. The servants' work has taken place during the contested and uncertain interval. One reports ten pounds gained and another five. A further servant has kept the pound wrapped in a cloth, explaining his inaction through fear. The account examines what the servants do with the trust, not merely whether they retain possession of the original coin. Luke 19:11-27 Read and discover The account at his return Explore and study Money kept unused in cloth Another servant returns the mina he has kept laid away in a cloth. His explanation reveals that the entrusted money was preserved unused rather than put to work. Luke 19:20 The nobleman orders the unused pound taken from the servant and given to the one who has ten. The closing words also command that the opponents who rejected his rule be brought before him and slain. Luke records that command without narrating its execution; these severe features belong to the story Jesus tells, not to instructions for His hearers to harm others. The nobleman's harsh features should not be treated as a complete portrait of God. A parable compares particular aspects of a story with a teaching; it does not require every action of every character to be imitated or assigned directly to the Savior. Explore and study An account on the nobleman's return After receiving the kingdom and returning, the nobleman calls the servants to learn what each has gained by trading. The meeting pictures that reckoning, with the results to be heard from those he entrusted. Luke 19:15 Keep this account distinct from Matthew's talents. Luke includes ten servants, equal initial pounds, opposition to the nobleman, and authority over cities. Its opening specifically challenges the expectation of an immediate manifestation of the kingdom. Luke 19:11-27 Read and discover Faithfulness during the interval As an application, consider what faithful work belongs to a season of waiting. Uncertainty about a larger outcome does not erase the responsibility that is already in your hands. The story invites attention to that responsibility while resisting both passivity and speculative timetables. Pause and consider What would faithful work during waiting look like? What fear might lead you to hide a responsibility? Luke 19:11-27 Related studies The Talents Different amounts are entrusted to different servants. The returning master asks what each has done with the responsibility received. Open study → The Doorkeeper The master leaves work for each servant and watchfulness for the porter. The unknown hour does not erase their present responsibility. Open study → Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Luke 19:11-27 Bible Dictionary: Parables

records.title: The Mote and the Beam
records.text: Read and discover An impossible obstruction Jesus places a tiny speck beside a wooden beam to expose the absurdity of hypocritical judgment. A person notices a small obstruction in someone else's eye while failing to consider a much larger one in his own. The exaggerated picture makes self-deception difficult to miss. Matthew 7:1-5 Matthew 7:1-5 Luke 6:41-42 Read and discover Clear sight before correction The instruction does not end by saying that no one should ever help another person. Jesus tells the hearer to remove the beam first, so that he can see clearly to help with the speck. Honest self-examination changes the manner and credibility of that help. Explore and study The mote and the beam Jesus contrasts noticing a mote in another person's eye with overlooking a beam in one's own. The large timber and tiny splinter picture His call to examine ourselves before correcting someone else. Matthew 7:3-5 Luke preserves the same contrast amid teaching about mercy, judgment, and the influence of teachers. Read in that setting, the image asks for more than a temporary pause before criticism. It calls for a truthful view of oneself and a less condemning posture toward others. Luke 6:41-42 Matthew 7:1-5 Luke 6:41-42 Read and discover Begin with honest self-examination You might notice a fault that quickly provokes you, then ask what your own response reveals. The goal is not self-hatred or pretending that harm does not matter. It is clearer sight, through which a needed conversation can become more humble, accurate, and compassionate. Pause and consider What fault do you readily notice in others? What self-examination could make your help gentler? Matthew 7:1-5 Luke 6:41-42 Related studies The Pharisee and the Publican Two people pray, but their posture toward God and others differs. Jesus invites a searching look at comparison, confidence, and mercy. Open study → The Blind Leading the Blind A guide cannot supply sight that the guide does not possess. Jesus' brief question asks disciples to consider whom they follow. Open study → Hearing and Living His Word Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Matthew 7:1-5 Luke 6:41-42 Bible Dictionary: Parables

records.title: The Mustard Seed
records.text: Read and discover A small beginning Explore and study A small beginning Small seeds rest in an open hand. Jesus draws attention to the mustard seed's small beginning before describing the remarkable growth that follows. The comparison turns our attention toward the kingdom of heaven rather than toward judging God's work by its initial appearance. Matthew 13:31–32 Jesus compares the kingdom with a mustard seed planted in the ground. He directs attention to a striking difference in scale: the small beginning and the substantial growth that follows. The Synoptic accounts preserve this movement even as their wording and immediate settings differ. Matthew 13:31-32 Matthew 13:31-32 Mark 4:30-32 Luke 13:18-19 Read and discover Growth that gives shelter The grown plant has branches in which birds can lodge. The picture therefore ends with more than an increase in size; the grown plant has become a place that can receive other living things. Mark describes branches large enough to provide shade. Mark 4:30-32 Explore and study Branches that offer shelter The grown plant offers branches where birds can rest. Jesus carries the mustard-seed comparison from a small beginning to a plant large enough to provide shelter. Its surprising growth directs hope toward God's kingdom, without promising that every personal plan will become large or successful. Mark 4:30–32 This kingdom comparison should be distinguished from Jesus' separate sayings about faith like a mustard seed. Here the emphasis is the kingdom's beginning and growth. The language speaks within an everyday agricultural picture rather than offering a modern ranking of all botanical seeds. Matthew 13:31-32 Mark 4:30-32 Luke 13:18-19 Read and discover Do not overlook what begins quietly Something small need not be insignificant. A quiet beginning in study, service, or repentance may deserve care even when it attracts little notice. That is an invitation to patient participation, not a promise that every personal project will become large or publicly successful. Pause and consider What makes the beginning seem unimpressive? Where might patient participation matter more than scale? Matthew 13:31-32 Mark 4:30-32 Luke 13:18-19 Related studies The Leaven A woman's work with meal becomes a picture of the kingdom. The change reaches throughout the batch before the story ends. Open study → The Seed Growing Secretly Between sowing and harvest, growth unfolds beyond the farmer's control. Mark's brief parable invites patient attention to God's kingdom. Open study → The Kingdom of God Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Matthew 13:31-32 Mark 4:30-32 Luke 13:18-19 Bible Dictionary: Parables

records.title: Loving Our Neighbor
records.text: Read and discover Let Jesus reshape the question The lawyer asks who his neighbor is. At the end of the Good Samaritan, Jesus asks which traveler acted as a neighbor. Attend to that change in the question. It directs the study away from finding the narrowest boundary of responsibility and toward the shape of merciful action. Luke 10:25–37 Explore and study Making room for communication Three people face one another and communicate with hand gestures. Jesus' teaching about welcome asks whether we will learn what helps others participate. Luke 14:12-14 Read the particular needs in each passage. The injured traveler needs immediate care and an inn; the guest needs welcome; the person at the gate needs attention that never comes. Combining them into a general instruction to be kind can hide what each story asks us to see. Luke 16:19–31 The imagined modern encounters below bring the question of neighborly care close to home. Consider what useful help might look like for the person before you: ask, listen and think about what continuing care may require. Luke 10:25–37 Luke 16:19–31 Read and discover See the need before passing by Explore and study Listening before helping A wheelchair user gestures toward the bus entrance while another rider listens. The Samaritan's attentive care asks us to notice a need and listen to how help is wanted. Luke 10:33-35 The wounded traveler is seen by three passersby, but seeing produces different actions. Jesus does not explain the priest's and Levite's private motives. The Samaritan's compassion becomes treatment, transport, and care. The account gives us enough to consider the response without inventing excuses or secret thoughts. Luke 10:30–35 Practical help often begins by asking what is needed. A person using a wheelchair may know exactly which action would be useful; a stranded motorist may need a safe call rather than an improvised repair. Mercy can respect competence, seek consent, and involve the right help. Explore and study Safe help beside a stalled car Two people wait together in a broad pullout while one makes a call. Arranging useful help can be a practical way to respond to the person before us. Luke 10:34-35 Luke 10:30–35 Read and discover Make the invitation usable Explore and study Access that supports participation A visitor explores a model through touch while a woman attends beside him. A thoughtful welcome includes access and respects each person's pace. Luke 14:12-14 At a meal, Jesus moves from the places guests seek for themselves to the people a host chooses to invite. He names those who cannot repay the invitation, then tells of a supper whose welcome reaches people first left outside it. Hospitality is connected with humility and generosity. Luke 14:7–24 A welcome becomes tangible when people can communicate, move through a space and take part. The pictured encounters ask us to listen to the person being welcomed and make useful changes together, respecting their choices and experience. Luke 14:7–24 Read and discover Let concern become continued care Explore and study Preparing clean bedding A woman folds a blanket among stacks of bedding. Jesus' teaching about clothing and welcoming others can guide quiet preparation for someone else's need. Matthew 25:35-36 The Samaritan does not leave the traveler at the edge of the road after an expression of sympathy. He makes provision for continued care. The King's words in Matthew also name ordinary needs with concrete actions: food, drink, clothing, welcome, and visits. Luke 10:34–35 Some care is visible; some happens before anyone arrives. Preparing clean bedding, adjusting a shared space after listening, or keeping a promised visit can matter without applause. The spiritual connection is an invitation to attend to people, not a claim that completing a checklist allows us to announce the final judgment of ourselves or others. Matthew 25:35–40 Explore and study Making a room easier to use One coworker adjusts a lamp and fan while another raises a hand near her eyes. Care can begin with noticing discomfort and working together on a useful change. Luke 10:34-35 Luke 10:34–35 Matthew 25:35–40 Read and discover Offer mercy with responsible care Explore and study Keeping a prison visit Two people give one another their attention across a visiting-room table. Jesus includes visiting prisoners among the acts of care remembered by the King. Matthew 25:36 Jesus includes visiting a prisoner among the acts remembered by the King. He also challenges resistance to Sabbath healing through a rescue everyone recognizes. These teachings keep attention on people who might be overlooked or treated as an inconvenience. Matthew 25:36 Care does not require ignoring safety, skill, or healthy limits. We may need to coordinate a visit, clear a hazard carefully, or involve a professional. Responsible boundaries can help mercy become dependable instead of impulsive. The question remains what good can be done for the person before us. Matthew 12:9–13 Explore and study Reopening the shared path Neighbors work on a fallen branch while a woman with a walker waits nearby. Jesus' teaching about doing good can become a careful shared task that helps others use the path. Matthew 12:11-12 Matthew 25:36 Matthew 12:9–13 Read and discover Bring the teaching into your own reflection Pause and consider Whose practical knowledge should you listen to before trying to help? What would make an invitation in your community easier to use? Which act of care needs follow-through rather than another promise? Read and discover Explore every study in this collection The Sheep and the Goats The Son of Man identifies care for people in need with service to Him. This is an extended judgment scene with a shepherd comparison, commonly included among parables. Open study → The Good Samaritan A question about the neighbor leads to concrete mercy across hostility. The conclusion asks who acted as a neighbor; avoid assigning unsupplied motives to passersby. Open study → Choosing the Lower Place Jesus observes guests choosing places of honor. His instruction moves from humility to hospitality that does not seek repayment. Open study → The Great Supper Invited guests excuse themselves while the host welcomes people often excluded. Keep the specific invitations and excuses intact; do not merge with Matthew's royal wedding. Open study → The Rich Man and Lazarus The reversal of the rich man's comfort and Lazarus's suffering culminates in the call to hear Moses and the prophets. This Lazarus is not identified as Lazarus of Bethany. Open study → Parables and story pictures Related comparisons and allegories Settling with an Adversary The legal journey illustrates urgency. Offer spiritual reflection without turning it into individualized legal advice. Open study → The Sheep in the Pit A rescue question supports doing good on the Sabbath. Luke uses an ass or ox in a related scene; do not label the two identical stories. Open study → Related studies Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning Explore the searches and welcomes that teach the worth of the one. Open study → Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship Consider how time, resources, and responsibility can be used for another person's good. Open study → Hearing and Living His Word Move from recognizing a good teaching to practicing it with attention and humility. Open study → Sources for further study Bible Dictionary: Parables Harmony of the Gospels Luke 10 Luke 16 Luke 14 Matthew 25 Matthew 12

The King's words in Matthew also name ordinary needs with concrete actions: food, drink, clothing, welcome, and visits. Luke 10:34–35 Some care is visible; some happens before anyone arrives. Preparing clean bedding, adjusting a shared space after listening, or keeping a promised visit can matter without applause. The spiritual connection is an invitation to attend to people, not a claim that completing a checklist allows us to announce the final judgment of ourselves or others. Matthew 25:35–40 Explore and study Making a room easier to use One coworker adjusts a lamp and fan while another raises a hand near her eyes. Care can begin with noticing discomfort and working together on a useful change. Luke 10:34-35 Luke 10:34–35 Matthew 25:35–40

records.title: Offer mercy with responsible care
records.text: Read and discover Offer mercy with responsible care Explore and study Keeping a prison visit Two people give one another their attention across a visiting-room table. Jesus includes visiting prisoners among the acts of care remembered by the King. Matthew 25:36 Jesus includes visiting a prisoner among the acts remembered by the King. He also challenges resistance to Sabbath healing through a rescue everyone recognizes. These teachings keep attention on people who might be overlooked or treated as an inconvenience. Matthew 25:36 Care does not require ignoring safety, skill, or healthy limits. We may need to coordinate a visit, clear a hazard carefully, or involve a professional. Responsible boundaries can help mercy become dependable instead of impulsive. The question remains what good can be done for the person before us. Matthew 12:9–13 Explore and study Reopening the shared path Neighbors work on a fallen branch while a woman with a walker waits nearby. Jesus' teaching about doing good can become a careful shared task that helps others use the path. Matthew 12:11-12 Matthew 25:36 Matthew 12:9–13

records.title: The Fishing Net
records.text: Read and discover The whole catch comes ashore Explore and study A net cast into the sea A net opens above the water before any catch is seen. Jesus compares the kingdom to a net gathering fish of every kind, then continues to the drawing ashore and sorting. This beginning prepares for His teaching about final judgment, which the passage places in the hands of angels. Matthew 13:47–50 A net cast into the sea gathers fish of every kind. When it is full, the fishers bring it to shore, keep the good in vessels, and discard the bad. Jesus begins with a familiar sequence of work, then explicitly connects the separation with judgment. Matthew 13:47-50 Matthew 13:47-50 Read and discover Gathering and final separation Explore and study Drawing the catch ashore The full net is being drawn ashore. Jesus' comparison moves from gathering to examination of the catch, preparing His listeners for the teaching about final judgment that follows. Matthew 13:48 The catch is gathered before it is sorted. Those moments belong to one story, but they are not interchangeable. Jesus' explanation identifies angels with the final separation at the end. The hearer is not appointed to determine the final standing of particular people. The passage has a serious conclusion that should neither be erased nor expanded into imagined scenes of punishment. Its purpose is not satisfied by attractive fishing imagery alone. The account asks readers to consider that the kingdom's gathering and the reality of judgment both matter. Matthew 13:47-50 Read and discover Responsibility with humility Explore and study The catch is sorted The gathered catch is examined on the shore, with some fish placed in baskets and others set apart. Jesus uses this separation to teach about judgment at the end of the world. He identifies angels as the agents of that final division; the comparison does not appoint readers to determine their neighbors' ultimate worth. Matthew 13:48–50 A personal response can hold responsibility and humility together. You can examine your own conduct, seek repentance, and treat people with care while acknowledging the limits of your judgment. The Lord's final assessment is not a task that disciples should casually claim for themselves. Pause and consider How does the shore differ from the gathering stage? What responsibility remains yours without judging another's final outcome? Matthew 13:47-50 Related studies The Wheat and the Tares The servants want to pull out what does not belong. This judgment scene places ordinary acts of care within our response to Christ. records.title: The New Patch
records.text: Read and discover The question about fasting Explore and study A new patch beside a worn garment A fresh piece of cloth is held above a worn garment. Jesus uses the familiar problem of an unsuitable repair while answering a question about fasting: the new patch can pull at the old cloth and make the tear worse. The comparison invites His hearers to consider what His ministry means before forcing it into their expectations. Matthew 9:14–17 A question about fasting gives this small picture its setting. John's disciples ask why they and the Pharisees fast while Jesus' disciples do not. Jesus first speaks of the joy of wedding guests while the bridegroom is with them, then turns to the familiar work of repairing clothing. Matthew 9:14-17 Matthew 9:14-17 Mark 2:21 Luke 5:36 Read and discover A repair that deepens the tear A piece of new cloth does not make a sound repair simply because it covers the hole. When it pulls against an old garment, the damage becomes worse. Luke sharpens the picture by describing a piece taken from a new garment: the attempted repair harms what is new and does not match what is old. Luke 5:36 Explore and study When the repair deepens the tear Stitches still hold part of the pale patch, but the older cloth has opened around it. Jesus' comparison turns on that worsening tear: placing new cloth on an old garment does not make a sound repair simply because it covers the first hole. Read the image within His answer about fasting and the significance of His presence. Matthew 9:14–17 The comparison belongs to Jesus' answer about His ministry. He is asking His hearers to understand what is happening in His presence, rather than force His disciples into an expectation without considering its setting. The picture's practical logic matters more than an invented symbolic meaning for every thread. Matthew 9:14-17 Mark 2:21 Luke 5:36 Read and discover Receiving what Jesus is teaching There can be a place for examining how we receive unfamiliar teaching. Do we listen long enough to understand it, or immediately trim it to fit an existing habit? That reflection should remain humble: Jesus' image does not mean that everything old is worthless or every novelty is true. Pause and consider What question prompted this picture? Where might habit keep you from listening carefully? Matthew 9:14-17 Mark 2:21 Luke 5:36 Related studies New Wine and Wineskins Wine needs a vessel able to receive it. Jesus uses this ordinary image to help His hearers consider the significance of His presence and teaching.
