records.title: New Wine and Wineskins
records.text: Read and discover The moment shapes the practice Explore and study When an old skin gives way Wine escapes through the old skin's split seam. Jesus uses the loss of both wine and container to explain why new wine needs suitable skins. In the surrounding discussion about fasting, His images call listeners to recognize the significance of His presence and teaching, rather than simply fit Him into familiar expectations. Matthew 9:14–17 Jesus places the wineskin comparison beside the image of a new patch on an old garment. Both answer a question about fasting. The surrounding conversation matters: His presence is likened to the bridegroom's presence with wedding guests, and He also speaks of a future time when the bridegroom will be taken away. Matthew 9:14-17 Matthew 9:14-17 Mark 2:22 Luke 5:37-39 Read and discover Wine and a fitting vessel New wine placed in old skins bursts them, losing both wine and container. New skins provide the fitting vessel. Jesus describes preservation, not merely destruction: the point of receiving the wine properly is that what is given can be kept. Mark and Luke retain the same central contrast. Mark 2:22 Explore and study New wine in a suitable skin The wine enters through the skin's open upper mouth while its lower opening is securely closed. Jesus says new wine belongs in new bottles, or skins. In the conversation about fasting, the image asks listeners to recognize what His presence requires rather than assume every familiar arrangement can remain unchanged. Luke 5:33–39 Luke adds that someone accustomed to old wine does not immediately desire new. That observation makes the passage more searching. Familiarity can shape what a person is willing to receive. It should not be used to overturn the comparison or announce that Jesus simply preferred the old order. Luke 5:37-39 Matthew 9:14-17 Mark 2:22 Luke 5:37-39 Read and discover Becoming willing to receive The picture invites careful receptiveness. You might ask whether an established expectation helps you recognize Christ's teaching or prevents you from hearing it. Receiving Him need not mean treating your past with contempt; it can mean allowing understanding and practice to change as you learn. Pause and consider How does this companion image strengthen the garment comparison? What might readiness to learn require? records.title: A Parent's Good Gifts
records.text: Read and discover A hungry child's request Explore and study A child asks for bread Jesus asks which parent would give a child a stone when asked for bread. This imagined exchange pictures the ordinary care behind His comparison. Matthew 7:9 Jesus invites His hearers to ask, seek, and knock, then turns to a parent's response to a hungry child. If a child asks for bread, a stone is not a fitting answer; if the request is for fish, a serpent is not a good substitute. The contrast is deliberately plain. Matthew 7:7-12 Matthew 7:7-12 Luke 11:11-13 Read and discover From human care to the Father's goodness The argument moves from imperfect human care toward the Father's greater goodness. Luke's account names the Holy Ghost as the gift the Father gives to those who ask. The passage therefore directs trust toward God's character, not merely toward the act of repeating a request. Luke 11:11-13 Explore and study A good gift for the child Jesus contrasts giving a child fish with offering a serpent, and speaks of parents giving good gifts. He then directs His listeners to the Heavenly Father's willingness to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Luke 11:11-13 Some readers have experienced parents who did not protect or nourish them. This comparison need not require denying that experience. Jesus points toward the goodness of the Father by naming what a caring response should be, rather than declaring that every earthly parent has acted that way. Matthew 7:7-12 Luke 11:11-13 Read and discover Ask with honest trust Prayer can be honest about both need and uncertainty. You might consider what it means to seek a good gift while leaving room for an answer you cannot yet describe. The passage encourages confidence in the Father without promising every desired outcome in the form or timing requested. Pause and consider What does the contrast reveal about God? What gift can you seek without dictating its timing? Matthew 7:7-12 Luke 11:11-13 Related studies The Friend at Midnight An unexpected guest leaves a host asking for bread in the night. records.title: The Pearl of Great Price
records.text: Read and discover A merchant who recognizes worth Explore and study Seeking a pearl of great value The merchant examines a pearl carefully among many others. Jesus describes someone already seeking fine pearls who recognizes one of exceptional worth. The next movement of the story will be a wholehearted response to that discovery; this image stays with the moment of attentive appraisal. Matthew 13:45–46 Jesus places a merchant's search beside the story of treasure found in a field. The merchant is already seeking fine pearls. When he finds one of exceptional worth, he sells all that he has and buys it. The brief account connects discernment with commitment. Matthew 13:45-46 Matthew 13:45-46 Read and discover Seeking, finding, and choosing Explore and study One pearl of great worth One pearl holds the merchant's attention. Jesus describes a discovery of such worth that the merchant is willing to sell all he has to obtain it. Matthew 13:45–46 The two stories share a costly response, but their beginnings differ. One person encounters hidden treasure; the other finds what he has been seeking. Reading them together allows room for differing paths toward recognition while preserving the decisive action in each. The pearl's beauty is not described in detail. Jesus does not give a travel history for the merchant or name the ports he visits. The focus remains on recognizing worth and responding. A visual retelling should keep that concentration rather than invent an adventure around two verses. Matthew 13:45-46 Read and discover Giving recognition a response Explore and study Obtaining the pearl The merchant gives what he has to obtain the pearl. Jesus describes a discovery whose worth calls forth his wholehearted response. Matthew 13:46 This picture invites a searching question about priorities: what do you recognize as precious, and how does that recognition affect your choices? Coming to know Christ can deepen both understanding and commitment. The parable offers a way to examine that relationship without comparing the speed of one person's journey with another's. Pause and consider What distinguishes seeking from recognizing? What commitment follows recognition for you? records.title: The Persistent Widow and the Judge
records.pageTitle: The Persistent Widow and the Judge
records.text: Read and discover A prayer that continues Explore and study The widow asks for justice A widow comes to the judge asking for justice against her adversary. Her appeal is direct and persistent, though the parable leaves the details of her dispute unnamed. Luke 18:3 Luke introduces the story by stating its purpose: people should keep praying and not lose heart. A widow repeatedly comes to a judge seeking justice against an adversary. The judge is described as neither fearing God nor regarding people, so he is not introduced as a model of divine character. Luke 18:1-8 Luke 18:1-8 Read and discover The widow and an unjust judge Explore and study The judge refuses for a time For a time, the judge refuses to act. The widow's continued appeal meets a closed response, illustrated here by his turned face and raised hand. Luke 18:4 For a time he refuses. Eventually he acts because her continued coming troubles him. The story gives persistence a concrete setting in a person whose claim has been dismissed, but it does not praise the judge's indifference. Jesus draws attention to what even this unjust judge says, then turns toward God's response to His chosen people who cry to Him. The movement is a contrast, not an assertion that God must be irritated into concern. The closing question turns toward the presence of faith when the Son of Man comes. Explore and study The judge decides to act The judge at last resolves to grant the widow justice because she keeps coming. Jesus lets her persistence stand against his long refusal to act. Luke 18:5 Luke 18:1-8 Read and discover Trust the God Jesus points toward Readers who have waited long for justice may hear the opening invitation with particular weight. Continued prayer can include weariness, grief, and plain speech. The account does not supply a timetable for a specific legal case or promise that every requested outcome will occur immediately. You might consider how to remain in prayer while also supporting practical efforts toward justice and care. Another person's long wait is not evidence of weak faith. records.title: A prayer that continues
records.pageTitle: The Persistent Widow and the Judge
records.text: Read and discover A prayer that continues Explore and study The widow asks for justice A widow comes to the judge asking for justice against her adversary. Her appeal is direct and persistent, though the parable leaves the details of her dispute unnamed. Luke 18:3 Luke introduces the story by stating its purpose: people should keep praying and not lose heart. A widow repeatedly comes to a judge seeking justice against an adversary. The judge is described as neither fearing God nor regarding people, so he is not introduced as a model of divine character. Luke 18:1-8 Luke 18:1-8

records.title: The widow and an unjust judge
records.pageTitle: The Persistent Widow and the Judge
records.text: Read and discover The widow and an unjust judge Explore and study The judge refuses for a time For a time, the judge refuses to act. The widow's continued appeal meets a closed response, illustrated here by his turned face and raised hand. Luke 18:4 For a time he refuses. Eventually he acts because her continued coming troubles him. The story gives persistence a concrete setting in a person whose claim has been dismissed, but it does not praise the judge's indifference. Jesus draws attention to what even this unjust judge says, then turns toward God's response to His chosen people who cry to Him. The movement is a contrast, not an assertion that God must be irritated into concern. The closing question turns toward the presence of faith when the Son of Man comes. Explore and study The judge decides to act The judge at last resolves to grant the widow justice because she keeps coming. Jesus lets her persistence stand against his long refusal to act. Luke 18:5 Luke 18:1-8

records.title: The Pharisee and the Publican
records.text: Read and discover Who trusts in being righteous? Explore and study Two men go up to pray In Jesus' parable, two men go up to the temple to pray: a Pharisee and a publican. The shared destination introduces two very different prayers. Luke 18:10 Luke names the audience before telling the story: people who trust in their own righteousness and despise others. Two men go to the temple to pray, a Pharisee and a publican, or tax collector. The opening already directs attention toward confidence, comparison, and contempt. Luke 18:9-14 Luke 18:9-14 Read and discover Two men pray Explore and study A prayer centered on comparison The Pharisee thanks God that he is unlike other people, including the publican. He speaks of his fasting and tithing, placing his own record at the center of his prayer. Luke 18:11-12 The Pharisee recounts his practices and distinguishes himself from people he considers worse, including the man nearby. The tax collector stands at a distance, will not lift his eyes to heaven, and asks God for mercy as a sinner. Explore and study A plea for mercy Standing afar off, the publican will not lift his eyes to heaven and beats upon his breast. His prayer is a plea for God to be merciful to him, a sinner. Luke 18:13 Jesus says that the latter goes home justified rather than the former. His concluding statement about humility and self-exaltation explains the reversal. The issue is not that prayer, fasting, or giving are bad; it is the use of religious practice as grounds for superiority before God. Luke 18:9-14 Read and discover Let the comparison turn inward The story can be misread if we congratulate ourselves for being unlike the Pharisee. That would reproduce the comparison it exposes. A more searching response is to examine our own prayer: are we presenting a case for our rank, or coming honestly before God with need and gratitude? Pause and consider When does comparison enter your prayer? What would an honest request for mercy sound like? records.title: The Prodigal Son and His Brother
records.pageTitle: The Prodigal Son and His Brother
records.text: Read and discover A father and two sons Explore and study The inheritance divided The younger son asks his father for the portion of goods that belongs to him. The father divides his living between his sons, pictured here through the bags placed before them. Luke 15:12 Jesus tells of a father with two sons after people criticize His welcome of sinners. That opening context matters throughout the account. The story includes the son who leaves, but it also includes a son who remains near home and struggles to share the father's joy. Luke 15:1-32 Luke 15:1-32 Read and discover The road away and the road home Explore and study Leaving for the far country Not many days later, the younger son gathers his belongings and journeys to a far country. The father watching at the gate is an artistic detail that gives the departure a personal setting. Luke 15:13 The younger son asks for his portion of the property, leaves for a distant country, and wastes what he has. When a famine comes, he is in need. He takes work feeding swine and longs for food, yet no one gives him what he needs. Explore and study Resources gone, need begins In the far country, the younger son wastes his substance in reckless living. After he has spent everything, a severe famine arises and he begins to be in want. Luke 15:13-14 Explore and study Feeding swine in the far country The younger son feeds swine while hunger deepens his need. Jesus says he longs for the food the animals eat, bringing the story to the painful distance between his earlier abundance and his present want. Luke 15:15-16 In that low place he remembers that his father's hired servants have bread. He resolves to return, acknowledge his sin, and ask for the place of a servant. The movement toward home includes a changed recognition of his condition and a willingness to speak truthfully. Explore and study Remembering his father's house The son remembers that his father's hired servants have bread enough while he is hungry. He resolves to return and acknowledge his sin, a decision pictured here before the journey home begins. Luke 15:17-19 Luke 15:1-32 Read and discover Welcome and the brother outside Explore and study The father welcomes his son The father meets his returning son with compassion and draws him close. Their embrace pictures the welcome Jesus describes as the son comes home in need. Luke 15:20 While the son is still far away, the father sees him and runs to meet him. He embraces and kisses him. The son begins his confession, and the father calls for a robe, a ring, shoes, and a feast. The welcome is not delayed until the son has repaid the lost inheritance. Explore and study Welcomed as a son The father calls for the best robe, a ring, and shoes for his son, and orders a feast. His welcome celebrates the son who was lost and is found. Luke 15:22-24 The elder son hears music and learns why there is a celebration. Angry, he refuses to enter. The father goes out to him as well. Their conversation reveals the elder son's sense that long service has gone unrecognized and that his brother's welcome diminishes his own place. Luke 15:1-32 Read and discover The invitation remains open The father affirms the elder son's place with him while insisting that the brother's return is reason for joy. The story ends without telling us whether the elder son enters. We should not invent a final embrace or use the open ending to announce that he is permanently beyond mercy. Explore and study The father comes out to the elder son When the elder son refuses to enter, his father comes out and pleads with him. He affirms their enduring bond and explains why the return of this brother calls for rejoicing. Luke 15:28-32 Both conversations can invite honest reflection. Some readers may recognize the difficulty of coming home with failure to acknowledge; others may recognize resentment when mercy seems more generous than their accounting allows. Neither recognition requires pretending that real family wounds resolve as quickly as a story is read. You might pause with the father's movement toward each son: running to the returning one and going out to the one who will not enter. The invitation to reconciliation does not erase agency. The account leaves room to ask what receiving mercy and rejoicing in another person's return might require of you. Pause and consider Which son's struggle is harder for you to understand? How might you receive mercy and also rejoice when another receives it? Luke 15:1-32 Related studies The Lost Sheep The missing one is worth a search and the finding is worth a celebration. Read how Jesus answers criticism of His welcome. Open study → The Laborers in the Vineyard Equal generosity becomes difficult for workers who expected more. The vineyard story examines gratitude, comparison, and resentment. Open study → Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Luke 15:1-32 Bible Dictionary: Parables

records.title: The Returning Unclean Spirit
records.text: Read and discover The house becomes empty Explore and study The house swept and ordered Jesus describes the returning spirit finding its former house empty, swept, and put in order. The quiet room illustrates that image without claiming an ordinary empty home is spiritually dangerous. Matthew 12:44 Jesus describes an unclean spirit leaving a person, passing through dry places, and returning to the former house. It finds the house empty, swept, and arranged, then returns with seven others more wicked than itself. The final condition is worse than the first. Matthew 12:38-45 Matthew 12:38-45 Luke 11:24-26 Read and discover A warning about the later condition The unsettling picture makes an empty interval different from lasting renewal. Matthew connects the warning to the generation He is addressing. Luke places it after the dispute about Jesus' deliverance and before a saying about hearing and keeping God's word. Luke 11:24-26 Explore and study The warning of a return Jesus warns that the returning spirit brings seven others and the person's last state becomes worse than the first. The open threshold is a symbolic illustration of that warning, not evidence of evil in ordinary shadow or darkness. Matthew 12:45 The passage should not be turned into a diagnosis of mental illness or a set of medical instructions. Nor does it provide a method for identifying unseen spirits in another person's life. Its spiritual warning deserves to be read in the context of response to Jesus. Matthew 12:38-45 Luke 11:24-26 Read and discover Cultivate good in the cleared space As a personal application, removing something harmful can be followed by the work of cultivating what is good. You might ask what prayer, truthful companionship, learning, or service could help fill space left by a changed habit. That application is a reflection prompted by the image, not an additional explanation stated in the story. Pause and consider What good needs to replace a harmful habit? What would fill cleared space constructively? Matthew 12:38-45 Luke 11:24-26 Related studies The Strong Man Jesus answers an accusation by asking how an existing hold can be broken. The comparison directs attention to His authority to deliver. Open study → The Wise and Foolish Builders Jesus pictures a life that can stand by taking us beneath the walls to the foundation. His invitation is to let heard words become practiced truth. Open study → Hearing and Living His Word Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. records.title: The Rich Fool
records.text: Read and discover An inheritance question Explore and study An abundant harvest The ground of a rich man brings forth an abundant crop. Full baskets and gathered sheaves picture the plenty with which Jesus begins the parable. Luke 12:16 Someone in the crowd asks Jesus to tell a brother to divide an inheritance. Jesus does not take up the requested role of divider. He warns about covetousness and tells a story in which abundant possessions cannot provide the security their owner expects. Luke 12:13-21 Luke 12:13-21 Read and discover The future the barns cannot secure Explore and study Considering greater storage With more produce than he knows where to store, the owner considers what to do. He resolves to pull down his barns and build greater ones for his crops and goods. Luke 12:17-18 The land of a rich man produces plentifully. Faced with more than he can store, he plans to tear down his barns and build larger ones. His imagined future centers on goods laid up for many years and the ease those goods will allow. Explore and study Imagining years of ease The owner imagines years of ease, telling himself to rest, eat, drink, and be merry. This scene pictures the comfort he plans for himself, not a future the parable says he lived. Luke 12:19 The interruption is abrupt: his life will be required that night. The stored possessions cannot keep the future he has planned within his control. Jesus concludes by contrasting treasure laid up for oneself with being rich toward God. Luke 12:13-21 Read and discover What does being rich toward God change? The story does not say the crop was dishonestly gained, nor does it condemn every act of saving or practical preparation. Its challenge concerns the place possessions occupy in the man's understanding of life. Reflection might ask what you expect money to secure and whose needs disappear when everything is arranged only around your own ease. Pause and consider What does enough mean to you? What would being rich toward God change about a current choice? Luke 12:13-21 Related studies The Rich Man and Lazarus A suffering man lies at a rich man's gate. The invitation is to seek the kingdom with trust in the Father's care. records.title: The Rich Man and Lazarus
records.text: Read and discover The need beside the gate Explore and study The rich man's abundance Jesus describes a rich man clothed in purple and fine linen who feasts splendidly every day. The abundant table pictures his comfort before the account turns to the suffering at his gate. Luke 16:19 Jesus describes a rich man who dresses splendidly and feasts daily, while Lazarus lies in need at his gate. The contrast is close at hand rather than far away. The suffering person is visible within the rich man's ordinary surroundings. Luke 16:19-31 Explore and study Lazarus at the gate Lazarus lies at the rich man's gate, covered with sores and longing for what falls from the table. Even the dogs come and lick his sores, underscoring the need beside the rich man's abundance. Luke 16:20-21 Luke 16:19-31 Read and discover A reversal and a plea Death changes the scene. Lazarus is carried to Abraham's bosom, while the rich man experiences torment. His request for relief receives an answer that recalls their former conditions and the gulf now between them. The rich man then asks that Lazarus be sent to warn his brothers. Abraham directs attention to Moses and the prophets. The final exchange challenges the assumption that an extraordinary sign would produce the response that the hearers have refused to give to scripture. Explore and study Lazarus comforted with Abraham After Lazarus dies, Jesus describes him being carried by angels to Abraham's bosom, where he is comforted. This embrace pictures that comfort symbolically; its surroundings and bodily appearance are artistic choices, not a literal map of the afterlife. Luke 16:22-25 Luke 16:19-31 Read and discover Hear the word already given The account should not be treated as a complete diagram of every aspect of life after death. Nor is this Lazarus identified as the man of Bethany whom Jesus raises. The story's moral force does not depend on merging those figures. You might reflect first on the gate: who is near enough to notice, yet remains outside your attention? The ending also asks what you already know from God's word that calls for a response. Waiting for a more dramatic message can become a way of postponing an ordinary act of mercy. Pause and consider Who is close enough to see yet easy to ignore? Even the dogs come and lick his sores, underscoring the need beside the rich man's abundance. Luke 16:20-21 Luke 16:19-31

records.title: A reversal and a plea
records.text: Read and discover A reversal and a plea Death changes the scene. Lazarus is carried to Abraham's bosom, while the rich man experiences torment. His request for relief receives an answer that recalls their former conditions and the gulf now between them. The rich man then asks that Lazarus be sent to warn his brothers. Abraham directs attention to Moses and the prophets. The final exchange challenges the assumption that an extraordinary sign would produce the response that the hearers have refused to give to scripture. Explore and study Lazarus comforted with Abraham After Lazarus dies, Jesus describes him being carried by angels to Abraham's bosom, where he is comforted. This embrace pictures that comfort symbolically; its surroundings and bodily appearance are artistic choices, not a literal map of the afterlife. Luke 16:22-25 Luke 16:19-31

records.title: Hear the word already given
records.text: Read and discover Hear the word already given The account should not be treated as a complete diagram of every aspect of life after death. Nor is this Lazarus identified as the man of Bethany whom Jesus raises. The story's moral force does not depend on merging those figures. You might reflect first on the gate: who is near enough to notice, yet remains outside your attention? The ending also asks what you already know from God's word that calls for a response. Waiting for a more dramatic message can become a way of postponing an ordinary act of mercy. Pause and consider Who is close enough to see yet easy to ignore? What existing teaching already calls for your response? Luke 16:19-31

records.title: The Wedding of the King's Son
records.pageTitle: The Wedding of the King's Son
records.text: Read and discover The invitation is ready Explore and study The invitation is spoken The servants bring the king's invitation, but those first invited will not come. The doorway scene pictures an oral summons rather than a written invitation. Matthew 22:3 A king prepares a wedding for his son and sends servants to summon invited guests. Their refusal is followed by another invitation announcing that everything is ready. Some go to their own affairs; others mistreat and kill the servants. The story gives the rejection serious weight. Matthew 22:1-14 Matthew 22:1-14 Read and discover Refusal, welcome, and the garment Explore and study The invitation reaches the roads The servants go out to the roads and gather everyone they find. The king's invitation reaches beyond the original guests, and the wedding hall begins to fill. Matthew 22:9-10 The king then sends servants to the roads to gather people they find. The wedding fills with guests described as both bad and good. The widening invitation is a central movement, but the account does not end at the doorway. The king enters and addresses a guest without wedding clothing. That final exchange prevents a reading in which receiving an invitation makes every response irrelevant. At the same time, the text does not itself supply a detailed history of how wedding garments were distributed. An explanation should not turn an unverified custom into the key on which the whole passage depends. Explore and study The wedding hall is filled The wedding hall is filled with guests gathered by the servants. Faces turn toward one another around the tables, picturing the breadth of the invitation in Jesus' story. Matthew 22:10 Matthew 22:1-14 Read and discover An invitation that calls for response Explore and study The king questions a guest The king notices a guest without a wedding garment and asks how he entered. The man has no answer. Jesus' story holds the wide invitation together with the seriousness of responding to it. Matthew 22:11-12 Matthew's story is distinct from Luke's great supper. The king's son, the violence, and the garment episode belong here and should not be silently inserted into Luke. Keeping the accounts separate allows each to ask its own questions about invitation, refusal, and response. You might consider what draws your attention away from an invitation that matters. Reflection can also ask how preparation expresses respect for what has been offered. The passage is a summons to a serious response, not permission to decide which present-day people belong outside the feast. Pause and consider What competes with a meaningful invitation? How might receiving a gift also call for preparation? Matthew 22:1-14 Related studies The Great Supper The supper is ready, but the first invitees excuse themselves. The widening invitation brings overlooked people toward a place at the table. Open study → The Ten Virgins All ten wait and all ten sleep, but their preparation differs. The midnight announcement reveals what they have brought to the waiting. Open study → The Kingdom of God Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. records.title: Salt of the Earth
records.text: Read and discover What gives salt its use? Explore and study Salt in the hand Jesus calls His disciples the salt of the earth and asks what use salt has if it loses its savor. The crystals in the hand illustrate the familiar substance at the heart of His comparison. Matthew 5:13 Jesus tells His disciples that they are the salt of the earth. The comparison asks what use salt has if it loses its savor. Its point rests on the difference between a quality that makes something useful and an outward form from which that quality is missing. Matthew 5:13-16 Matthew 5:13-16 Mark 9:49-50 Luke 14:34-35 Read and discover The image in different settings Mark places salt near teaching about conduct within the disciples' community and concludes with being at peace with one another. Luke uses the loss of savor after teaching about the cost of discipleship. Those settings give the image distinct emphases while preserving its concern with meaningful character. Mark 9:49-50 Explore and study Salt and peace Jesus speaks of salt retaining its savor and calls His listeners to have salt in themselves and peace with one another. This ordinary table setting offers a visual reflection on His words, not a recorded meal. Mark 9:50 The saying should not become a debate that forgets why Jesus uses the comparison. Nor should it become a declaration that some people have no worth. It challenges disciples to consider whether their life carries the qualities to which He calls them. Luke 14:34-35 Matthew 5:13-16 Mark 9:49-50 Luke 14:34-35 Read and discover Preserve what gives service meaning As an application, ask what gives a particular act of service its value. Attention, honesty, and care may matter more than making the act visible. Mark's connection with peace also invites reflection on whether your way of defending a good thing preserves the spirit of the teaching you defend. Pause and consider What gives your service its value? Why does Mark connect salt with peace? records.title: The Servant's Duty
records.text: Read and discover Faith, forgiveness, and service Explore and study Returning from work in the field Jesus asks His listeners to imagine a servant coming in from plowing or tending sheep. The return from fieldwork begins His comparison about a servant's duty. Luke 17:7 After teaching about forgiveness and responding to the Apostles' request for increased faith, Jesus describes a servant returning from work. The picture belongs to a world in which a servant might labor in the field and then attend the household meal. Luke 17:1-10 Luke 17:1-10 Read and discover Duty without leverage The servant does not return expecting the master immediately to serve him. He prepares the meal and completes the assigned work. Jesus uses that familiar expectation to challenge the idea that fulfilling a duty puts the master under an obligation to the servant. Explore and study Serving the meal In Jesus' comparison, the servant is told to prepare supper and serve before eating and drinking himself. The pictured meal illustrates the sequence in His example, which leads into teaching about humble service. Luke 17:8–10 The conclusion concerns the disciples' posture after doing what they have been commanded. Their obedience is not leverage by which they force God to repay them. The language should not be detached from that point and used to deny their worth as people. Luke 17:1-10 Read and discover Serve without making God a debtor A present-day application might examine resentment when service goes unnoticed. Can gratitude and love sustain an act that receives no applause? That question does not excuse exploitation or remove the need for rest and fair treatment; it asks what attitude we bring to faithful service before God. Pause and consider When does service become a demand for recognition? What would grateful faithfulness look like? Luke 17:1-10 Related studies The Faithful and Unfaithful Servant Someone else's daily bread is placed in a servant's care. The master's absence reveals how that trust will be used. Open study → The Laborers in the Vineyard Equal generosity becomes difficult for workers who expected more. The vineyard story examines gratitude, comparison, and resentment. Open study → Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Luke 17:1-10 Bible Dictionary: Parables
records.excerpt: Completed service is not leverage over God. Jesus' household picture challenges entitlement while calling disciples toward faithfulness.

records.title: Settling with an Adversary
records.text: Read and discover The road toward judgment Explore and study Seek agreement along the way Jesus urges His listener to come to agreement with an adversary quickly while still on the way. The conversation pictures that opportunity, without showing whether the two reach a settlement. Matthew 5:25 In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus connects anger and reconciliation with a brief picture of two adversaries on their way to judgment. There is an opportunity to address the conflict before they arrive. Delay can carry consequences that are harder to undo. Matthew 5:21-26 Matthew 5:21-26 Luke 12:58-59 Read and discover The opportunity before arrival Luke records a related saying in teaching about discerning the present time. The path toward the magistrate becomes a setting in which the need for timely action is visible. The picture does not dwell on the full legal dispute or tell us which modern procedure should be followed. Luke 12:58-59 Explore and study Before reaching the magistrate Jesus counsels making an effort to settle with an adversary before reaching the magistrate. Their approach illustrates the urgency of that warning, not a completed hearing or conviction. Luke 12:58 The spiritual invitation concerns taking unresolved wrong seriously while there is an opportunity to respond. It should not be expanded into individualized legal advice or a demand that an injured person negotiate alone with someone unsafe. Matthew 5:21-26 Luke 12:58-59 Read and discover Take a responsible step toward peace Reflection might identify a conflict where an honest, responsible step is possible: acknowledging a wrong, correcting an account, or seeking appropriate help. Reconciliation cannot always be secured by one person, but delay need not become an excuse for avoiding the part that is yours. Pause and consider What conflict needs honest attention? What safe step toward peace is available? Matthew 5:21-26 Luke 12:58-59 Related studies The Unmerciful Servant A servant receives compassion and then refuses it to another. Jesus asks how mercy received should change the way we respond. Open study → The Mote and the Beam A speck and a beam expose the distortion of hypocritical judgment. Clearer help begins with truthful self-examination. Open study → Loving Our Neighbor Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. records.title: The Sheep and the Goats
records.text: Read and discover Before the Son of Man Explore and study Providing food and drink A cup passes between two people while bread rests within reach. This illustration recalls the food and drink Jesus names among acts of care for another person's need. Matthew 25:35 Matthew closes this teaching sequence with the Son of Man seated in glory and the nations gathered before Him. A shepherd separating sheep from goats supplies the opening comparison. The passage then becomes an extended judgment scene in which the King addresses those before Him. Matthew 25:31-46 Matthew 25:31-46 Read and discover The needs the King remembers Explore and study Welcoming and clothing someone At an open doorway, a folded covering is offered with a warm welcome. The scene illustrates the hospitality and clothing Jesus remembers in His teaching about caring for others. Matthew 25:35-36 The acts He names are concrete: feeding the hungry, giving drink, welcoming a stranger, clothing someone, caring for the sick, and visiting a prisoner. Those addressed are surprised. They ask when they saw Him in those conditions. The King's answer joins their treatment of people in need to their treatment of Him. The corresponding failure to care is also taken seriously. The passage refuses to let devotion remain detached from the person who needs food, company, clothing, or welcome. Explore and study Visiting the sick A visitor sits close and holds the hand of a woman resting in bed. This imagined moment of companionship reflects Jesus' invitation to visit those who are sick. Matthew 25:36 Matthew 25:31-46 Read and discover Care offered to Him Explore and study Visiting a prisoner A visitor gives his attention to a man seated in confinement. This illustration recalls Jesus' words about visiting a prisoner and seeing a person others may overlook. Matthew 25:36 This is not an invitation to turn another person's hardship into a chance to advertise our goodness. Nor does a checklist authorize us to announce anyone's final judgment. The needs in the account belong to real people whose dignity matters. You might begin with one need that is within your ability to meet responsibly. A visit, a meal, or attentive companionship can be a meaningful act without being a complete solution to suffering. The study invites us to recognize service to Christ in care for those before us. Pause and consider Whose ordinary need can you notice? How does seeing service as offered to Christ alter your attention? records.title: The Sheep in the Pit
records.text: Read and discover The rescue everyone understands Explore and study A sheep in a pit Jesus asks His hearers to consider a sheep that has fallen into a pit on the Sabbath. The vulnerable animal makes His question about practical care immediate and recognizable. Matthew 12:11 During a dispute about healing on the Sabbath, Jesus asks what a person would do if a sheep fell into a pit. The expected rescue exposes a practical care His hearers already recognize. He then turns attention to the greater value of a person. Matthew 12:9-13 Matthew 12:9-13 Luke 14:1-6 Read and discover The person before the rule The argument reaches a clear conclusion: it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. Jesus' comparison is not separated from the person before Him whose hand needs healing. Mercy is not an abstract exception considered at a safe distance from need. Explore and study Lifting the sheep from the pit In Jesus' comparison, a person takes hold of the sheep and lifts it out. This imagined rescue pictures the ordinary care He uses to challenge resistance to doing good on the Sabbath. Matthew 12:11 Luke records a related question about an ass or ox fallen into a pit while Jesus heals a man. These are related comparisons in distinct accounts; a retelling should not blend the animals and encounters into one event. Each connects recognized care with a challenge to resistance toward healing. Luke 14:1-6 Matthew 12:9-13 Luke 14:1-6 Read and discover Let compassion clarify the good You might reflect on whether a concern for correct observance sometimes prevents you from seeing the person the observance should help you love. Careful practice and compassion need not be enemies. In this passage Jesus brings the good of the person clearly into view. Pause and consider What need might compassion help you see? records.title: The Sower
records.text: Read and discover The crowd beside the water Explore and study Seed on the path In the parable, birds consume the seed that falls beside the way. Jesus later explains the image as part of His teaching about receiving the word. Matthew 13:4, 19 A crowd gathers while Jesus teaches from a boat. He begins with a sower scattering seed, an action His hearers can readily picture. Later the disciples ask about the teaching. The Gospel accounts preserve both the story and Jesus' explanation, so the study should keep those two parts together. Matthew 13:1-23 Matthew 13:1-23 Mark 4:3-9,14-20 Luke 8:4-8,11-15 Read and discover What happens to the seed Explore and study No depth of earth The seed springs up quickly in shallow soil but withers under the sun. This picture illustrates the parable’s contrast between early growth and enduring roots. Matthew 13:5–6, 20–21 Some seed falls along a path and is taken by birds. Some reaches shallow ground, sprouts quickly, and withers under heat. Other growth is crowded by thorns. Finally, seed in good soil bears a harvest. The movement is not simply from bad people to good people; it examines what happens to the received word. Mark 4:3-9,14-20 Jesus names obstacles to lasting fruit: failure to understand, tribulation that exposes a lack of root, and cares or riches that choke growth. Luke describes fruitful hearers as keeping the word and bringing forth fruit with patience. Initial enthusiasm and patient endurance are therefore different moments in receiving His teaching. Luke 8:4-8,11-15 Explore and study Choked by thorns Thorns choke this growth. Jesus connects the image to worldly care and the deceitfulness of riches that make the word unfruitful. Matthew 13:7, 22 Matthew 13:1-23 Mark 4:3-9,14-20 Luke 8:4-8,11-15 Read and discover Tending the ground of a life Explore and study Fruit in good ground The good ground bears fruit. Jesus invites His hearers to receive and understand His word, allowing it to shape their lives. Matthew 13:8, 23 The soils make space for honest self-examination without becoming permanent labels for ourselves or others. You may recognize more than one condition in your own life. A useful response is to identify one competing concern, one shallow habit, or one way to give the word more sustained attention. Pause and consider What currently competes for your attention? What would help the word take deeper root? His invitation is to let heard words become practiced truth. Open study → Hearing and Living His Word Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. records.title: Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship
records.pageTitle: Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship
records.text: Read and discover Begin with the particular trust The talents and the ten pounds are related accounts, not interchangeable versions to blend. Matthew describes differing sums given to three featured servants. Luke describes ten servants, equal starting pounds, and a nobleman's journey while people expect the kingdom to appear immediately. Matthew 25:14–30 Explore and study Checking entrusted records Two people check receipts against an open ledger. Faithfulness in small things includes care and openness with what has been entrusted to us. Luke 16:10-12 Read difficult stories through their conclusions. The unjust steward's shrewd preparation is not approval of dishonesty; Jesus continues by teaching faithfulness and the impossibility of serving God and mammon. The character in a comparison is not a complete portrait of God or a model to imitate in every detail. Luke 16:1–13 The imagined present-day scenes bring stewardship into plans, shared resources and ordinary responsibilities. In the talents parable, the entrusted gift is money; applying it to our skills is a further reflection. Faithfulness asks how we use what we receive, without promising wealth, ease or status. Matthew 25:14–30 Luke 16:1–13 Read and discover Consider what the commitment requires Explore and study Planning the work Three people compare a plan with lumber and a tape measure. Jesus' example of counting before building asks us to consider what a commitment will require. Luke 14:28-30 The tower builder considers whether the work can be finished before laying a foundation. The king considers his forces before confrontation. Jesus places both comparisons within teaching about discipleship's cost. Careful consideration supports a real commitment rather than an impressive beginning alone. Luke 14:28–33 Preparation and accurate records are ordinary ways to honor trust. Measuring materials before building or correcting an account openly can protect the people who depend on the work. These applications do not reduce discipleship to efficient administration; they ask whether faithfulness reaches the details of what is entrusted. Luke 16:10–12 Luke 14:28–33 Luke 16:10–12 Read and discover Use the portion actually received Explore and study Sharing a useful skill Two people study a bicycle brake, one pointing while the other holds a tool nearby. The talents parable asks how we will use what we receive, including skills we can share. Matthew 25:14-23 The servants begin with differing amounts. The first two put their portions to use and receive the same welcoming commendation. Their shared faithfulness matters more than a competition to have received the largest starting sum. The third servant's fear leads instead to a buried trust. Matthew 25:14–30 Skills, tools, time, or an opportunity to teach can provide present-day applications. A person may be able to help with a simple repair or preserve a shared resource without having impressive equipment. The question is what a faithful use of the actual portion might be, not whether it resembles someone else's. Explore and study Caring for a shared resource A woman smooths repair cloth along a worn book's spine. Caring for an ordinary responsibility can be one quiet expression of faithful stewardship. Matthew 25:14-23 Matthew 25:14–30 Read and discover Let responsibility become care Explore and study Planning together Three people discuss a board of notes, each taking part in the planning. Responsible care includes listening to those who will carry out the work. Luke 12:42-44 The faithful steward provides food at the proper time. When entrusted authority becomes an excuse to mistreat the household, the responsibility has been betrayed. Jesus makes the needs of those served central to the assessment of the servant's conduct. Luke 12:42–48 Listening to a team's capacity and completing a final unnoticed task are applications of that attention. The servant's-duty comparison also challenges the idea that completed service gives us leverage over God. This does not deny human worth or excuse exploitation; it asks what attitude accompanies our work. Luke 17:7–10 Explore and study Care when the room is quiet A man rolls a floor mat in a quiet hall beside stacked chairs. Jesus' teaching about duty asks whether we will serve faithfully when there is little recognition. Luke 17:7-10 Luke 12:42–48 Luke 17:7–10 Read and discover Serve without making blessing a contest Explore and study Appreciating another contribution An older man speaks warmly to another participant across a planning drawing. The vineyard laborers' story asks how we respond when generosity is shown to someone else. Matthew 20:1-16 The early vineyard workers receive their agreed wage, yet resent the owner's generosity to the latecomers. The rich fool imagines that larger barns can secure the future he desires. In different ways, the stories reveal how possessions and comparison can govern a person's response. Matthew 20:1–16 An application might involve appreciating a newcomer or reconsidering possessions kept only for oneself. Such choices are not a formula for earning greater material blessings. They invite us to ask what gratitude, generosity, and trust could change in the resources and relationships already before us. Luke 12:13–21 Explore and study Considering what can be shared A man gathers hand tools into a wooden box. Beside the rich fool's story, this moment asks what our possessions might do beyond remaining in our keeping. Luke 12:16-21 Matthew 20:1–16 Luke 12:13–21 Read and discover Bring the teaching into your own reflection Pause and consider What responsibility is yours even when no one appears to be checking? How could fear be keeping a useful gift or opportunity buried? When does another person's blessing become difficult for you to welcome? Read with Matthew 19:27-30; avoid making the story a formula for modern wages. Open study → The Wicked Tenants Tenants reject servants and the owner's son. Keep the confrontation with particular leaders in context; do not turn the account into hostility toward Jewish people. Open study → The Talents Servants receive differing sums and later account for their stewardship. Explain the original monetary meaning of talent before offering applications to abilities. Open study → The Rich Fool An inheritance dispute prompts a warning about covetousness. More storage does not secure life; the account contrasts possessions with being rich toward God. records.title: The Strong Man
records.text: Read and discover An accusation against deliverance Explore and study A strong man guards his house The guard stands alert beside the goods he protects. Jesus introduces this strong man's security before describing the arrival of someone stronger. Spoken amid accusations about His deliverance of a suffering person, the comparison points toward His power to overcome evil. Luke 11:17–22 The strong-man image answers a serious accusation. After Jesus delivers a person from an evil spirit, opponents attribute His power to the ruler of devils. Jesus first points out the contradiction of a kingdom fighting against itself. He then asks what must happen before a strong man's goods can be taken. Matthew 12:25-29 Matthew 12:25-29 Mark 3:23-27 Luke 11:17-22 Read and discover Power that breaks a hold Explore and study The stronger one has overcome The guard who once stood watch now sits without his weapons in hand. Jesus describes a stronger one overcoming the armed man and taking the armor in which he trusted. In context, the comparison answers opposition to Jesus' work of deliverance and directs attention to His authority over evil. Luke 11:20–22 In Matthew and Mark, the strong man must be bound before his house is plundered. Luke tells the comparison with a strong, armed guard and a stronger challenger who overcomes him. Each version directs attention to power sufficient to break the existing hold. Luke 11:17-22 The image helps explain Jesus' work of deliverance. He is not an ally of the evil He confronts. The comparison does not praise burglary or ask disciples to imitate an aggressor; it uses a recognizable contest of strength to answer the accusation about His authority. Matthew 12:25-29 Mark 3:23-27 Luke 11:17-22 Read and discover Look at the good He does Explore and study The goods are divided Goods once under the guard's protection are now being distributed. The final movement of Jesus' comparison shows how completely the stronger one has overcome the guard's power. Its setting concerns Jesus' authority over evil; the image does not offer an example of theft for His disciples to imitate. Luke 11:20–23 When studying this passage, begin with what Jesus has actually done for the person in need. His opponents' explanation obscures that act of deliverance. Reflection might ask whether a fixed opinion sometimes prevents us from recognizing goodness, help, or truth when it appears. Pause and consider How does the image answer the accusation? What does deliverance reveal about His authority? Matthew 12:25-29 Mark 3:23-27 Luke 11:17-22 Related studies A Divided Kingdom and House An accusation fails to explain the deliverance before the hearers. Jesus exposes the contradiction through a kingdom and household divided. Open study → The Returning Unclean Spirit An emptied house is not the same as a renewed life. This unsettling comparison asks for a response deeper than a temporary change. Open study → The Kingdom of God Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. records.title: The Talents
records.text: Read and discover What the master entrusts Explore and study Resources entrusted to three servants Before leaving, the master entrusts his property to three servants, giving different amounts according to their ability. Each receives a substantial sum and a responsibility to care for it. Matthew 25:14-15 A man going away entrusts property to his servants. One receives five talents, another two, and another one, each according to ability. In the story a talent is a large monetary amount. The familiar modern use of the word for personal gifts can be an application, but it is not the original object being distributed. Matthew 25:14-30 Matthew 25:14-30 Read and discover Different amounts, faithful work Explore and study Putting the entrusted money to work The servants put what they have received to work. The cloth market pictures their trading; Jesus does not specify the merchandise or the particular transactions. Matthew 25:16-17 The first two servants work with what they receive and increase it. The third digs in the ground and hides his master's money. Their different starting amounts do not prevent the first two from being described through the same pattern of faithful action. After a long time, the master returns and settles accounts. The first and second servants each report what they have done and receive the same welcoming commendation. The story does not make equal starting resources the condition for faithful service. Explore and study The first servant gives his account The servant reports what he has gained with the five talents entrusted to him. His master welcomes the faithful response and invites him to enter into his joy. Matthew 25:19-21 Matthew 25:14-30 Read and discover Fear and the buried trust The third servant explains his inaction through fear and his view of the master. He returns what he hid but has done nothing productive with the trust. The exchange exposes the consequence of allowing fear to govern the whole stewardship. Explore and study The money hidden in the ground The servant who received one talent hides his master's money in the ground. The open chest pictures the act of concealment, before the earth covers it. Matthew 25:18 This account should remain distinct from Luke's ten pounds. The number of servants, initial distributions, surrounding events, and details of the accounting differ. Keeping those differences allows readers to hear Matthew's story rather than a blended version. Matthew 25:14-30 Read and discover Use what is actually in your hands A present-day reflection may consider resources, ability, time, or opportunities that have actually been entrusted to you. The invitation is faithful use, not comparison with someone else's amount. It is also not a promise of investment returns: the spiritual question concerns your response to trust and responsibility. Pause and consider What has actually been entrusted to you? How might fear be keeping one responsibility buried? Matthew 25:14-30 Related studies The Ten Pounds or Minas People expect the kingdom immediately; Jesus tells of work during an absence. Luke's account joins waiting with stewardship. Open study → The Faithful and Unfaithful Servant Someone else's daily bread is placed in a servant's care. The master's absence reveals how that trust will be used. Open study → Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. After a long time, the master returns and settles accounts. The first and second servants each report what they have done and receive the same welcoming commendation. The story does not make equal starting resources the condition for faithful service. Explore and study The first servant gives his account The servant reports what he has gained with the five talents entrusted to him. His master welcomes the faithful response and invites him to enter into his joy. Matthew 25:19-21 Matthew 25:14-30

records.title: Fear and the buried trust
records.text: Read and discover Fear and the buried trust The third servant explains his inaction through fear and his view of the master. He returns what he hid but has done nothing productive with the trust. The exchange exposes the consequence of allowing fear to govern the whole stewardship. Explore and study The money hidden in the ground The servant who received one talent hides his master's money in the ground. The open chest pictures the act of concealment, before the earth covers it. Matthew 25:18 This account should remain distinct from Luke's ten pounds. The number of servants, initial distributions, surrounding events, and details of the accounting differ. Keeping those differences allows readers to hear Matthew's story rather than a blended version. Matthew 25:14-30

records.title: Use what is actually in your hands
records.text: Read and discover Use what is actually in your hands A present-day reflection may consider resources, ability, time, or opportunities that have actually been entrusted to you. The invitation is faithful use, not comparison with someone else's amount. It is also not a promise of investment returns: the spiritual question concerns your response to trust and responsibility. Pause and consider What has actually been entrusted to you? How might fear be keeping one responsibility buried? Matthew 25:14-30

records.title: The Ten Virgins
records.text: Read and discover A wait longer than expected Explore and study Ten women with their lamps Ten women gather with their lamps to meet the bridegroom. The opening of Jesus' parable brings them together before the delay reveals the difference in their preparation. Matthew 25:1 Ten virgins take their lamps and go to meet a bridegroom. Five bring additional oil and five do not. The story belongs to Jesus' teaching about watchfulness, but the waiting itself becomes longer than expected. All ten grow drowsy and sleep. Matthew 25:1-13 Matthew 25:1-13 Read and discover The midnight call and the lamps Explore and study Oil kept ready The women have brought oil in separate vessels with their lamps. Their quiet preparation pictures the provision that distinguishes the wise attendants in Jesus' story. Matthew 25:4 The midnight announcement wakes them all. They rise to prepare their lamps, and the lack of oil becomes urgent. The distinction is not that the wise never slept. Their earlier preparation enables them to respond when the moment arrives. While the others go to buy oil, the bridegroom comes and the prepared attendants enter the marriage feast. The closed door gives the ending its seriousness. Jesus concludes with the call to watch because the day and hour are not known. Explore and study The midnight cry At midnight, the call announces the bridegroom. Jesus says all ten had grown drowsy and slept; this close view pictures several attendants waking and getting ready to meet him. Matthew 25:5-7 Explore and study Preparing the lamps One woman tends her lamp with the oil she brought, while another asks for help. The scene brings preparation and need together at the moment the attendants are called to meet the bridegroom. Matthew 25:7-8 Matthew 25:1-13 Read and discover Preparation cannot be borrowed Explore and study Entering with the bridegroom The five who are ready enter with the bridegroom to the wedding feast. The open doorway pictures their welcome before the door is shut, keeping the story's call to readiness in view. Matthew 25:10 The account should not be stretched into a rule against sharing material help. Its central concern is a readiness that cannot simply be transferred at the last moment. Nor does it justify calculating the return's date from imagined meanings in the lamps or hours. As an application, some forms of preparation grow through repeated personal response: turning to God, learning His words, and acting on them. Another person's faithfulness can encourage you, but it cannot make every response on your behalf. You might choose one small practice that helps you prepare steadily rather than fearfully. Pause and consider What preparation grows through repeated choices? What can you begin without fear or comparison? records.title: The Householder and the Thief
records.text: Read and discover The hour the householder does not know Explore and study A house in the night Warm light shines around the door of a quiet house beneath the night sky. Jesus asks His listeners to consider how a homeowner would keep watch if he knew when a thief would come. Matthew 24:43 Jesus uses the unexpected arrival of a thief to teach readiness. A householder who knew the watch in which a thief would come would stay awake to prevent the break-in. The difficulty is precisely that the hour is not known. Matthew 24:42-44 Matthew 24:42-44 Luke 12:39-40 Read and discover Surprise and preparation The comparison moves from that uncertainty to the coming of the Son of Man. Its point concerns surprise and preparedness. It does not compare the Lord's character with a thief's dishonesty, and it does not invite readers to imagine that fear is the highest form of faith. Explore and study Keeping watch at the door The householder rests a hand on the wooden bolt while an oil lamp burns beside him. Jesus uses the watchful homeowner to teach the value of being ready before an unexpected arrival. Luke 12:39 Luke places the saying beside servants awaiting their master's return and follows it with a discussion of entrusted responsibility. That setting helps keep readiness connected with how a person lives and serves, rather than with fascination about the time of arrival. Luke 12:39-40 Matthew 24:42-44 Luke 12:39-40 Read and discover What can be made ready today? A useful reflection is to ask what would remain worth doing if the timetable stayed unknown. Faithful attention, reconciliation where possible, and care for an entrusted task can be practiced now. The passage calls for preparation without giving a warrant for speculation. Pause and consider What would faithful readiness look like today? What changes when preparation is steady rather than alarmed? records.title: The Tower Builder
records.text: Read and discover A crowd and the cost of following Explore and study Counting the cost Jesus asks who would begin a tower without first sitting down to count its cost. The careful consideration pictured here illustrates the question of having enough to finish. Luke 14:28 Large crowds accompany Jesus when He speaks about the cost of discipleship. The tower appears within that demanding teaching, not as a detached proverb about project planning. Jesus asks His hearers to consider what they are undertaking when they choose to follow Him. Luke 14:25-35 Luke 14:25-35 Read and discover A foundation is only the beginning Explore and study A foundation without completion Jesus describes a builder who lays a foundation but is unable to finish. The low stonework pictures the unfinished beginning at the heart of His warning. Luke 14:29 A person intending to build first sits down and counts whether there is enough to finish. If a foundation is laid and the work stops, observers can see the gap between intention and completion. Jesus lets an unfinished structure embody an unfinished commitment. Explore and study The unfinished work draws comment In Jesus' comparison, those who see the unfinished work begin to mock the builder. They point out that he began to build but could not finish, making the cost of an unconsidered beginning plain. Luke 14:29-30 The companion comparison about a king considering war develops the same call to sober consideration. The passage then returns directly to discipleship. Reading the surrounding verses helps keep the tower from becoming merely advice about avoiding embarrassment. Luke 14:25-35 Read and discover Choose with honest commitment You might ask what support, changed priorities, or sustained effort a faithful commitment will require. Honest consideration is not the same as waiting until nothing will be difficult. It can be part of choosing deliberately, with a clearer understanding that following Christ reaches into the whole life. Pause and consider What commitment are you considering lightly? What support would help you follow through? Luke 14:25-35 Related studies The King Considering War Before advancing, a king weighs what he can meet. Jesus uses the decision to deepen His call to deliberate discipleship. Open study → The Pearl of Great Price A merchant recognizes something worth a wholehearted response. The pearl invites a careful look at seeking, discerning, and choosing. Open study → Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. records.title: A Tree and Its Fruit
records.text: Read and discover Look beyond the outward appearance Explore and study A tree and its fruit Jesus teaches that a good tree does not bring forth corrupt fruit, nor a corrupt tree good fruit. The fig-bearing branch pictures the connection between a tree and what it produces. Luke 6:43 Jesus uses a tree's fruit to teach discernment. In Matthew's sermon, the warning concerns false prophets who appear harmless. Fruit provides a way to look beyond the outward covering. The familiar difference between productive trees and thorny growth brings conduct into the question of trust. Matthew 7:15-20 Matthew 7:15-20 Matthew 12:33-37 Luke 6:43-45 Read and discover What a heart brings forth Luke connects fruit with what comes out of the heart. Good and evil treasures issue in corresponding speech and action. Matthew also records the tree comparison in a discussion that includes words and accountability. These related settings should be kept visible rather than collapsed into a single occasion. Luke 6:43-45 Explore and study Figs are not gathered from thorns Jesus says that each tree is known by its fruit: figs are not gathered from thorns, nor grapes from a bramble. The thorny branches illustrate the contrast with the fruit-bearing tree. Luke 6:44 The picture asks us to pay attention to what a teaching or way of life produces. It does not make one difficult moment a complete account of a person, nor does it authorize instant certainty about another's heart. Careful discernment can remain patient and open to repentance. Matthew 7:15-20 Matthew 12:33-37 Luke 6:43-45 Read and discover Attend to the fruit you cultivate For reflection, consider the guidance you receive and the speech you offer. Does it grow honesty, mercy, and faithful action, or deepen contempt and evasion? That question can be brought first to your own habits, where a change in what you cultivate may change what others receive. Pause and consider What fruit follows the guidance you trust? What does your speech reveal? Matthew 7:15-20 Matthew 12:33-37 Luke 6:43-45 Related studies The Sower The same seed meets different ground. Jesus explains what can prevent His word from taking root and what makes room for enduring fruit. Open study → The True Vine and the Branches A branch lives through its connection to the vine. Jesus joins abiding, love, obedience, and fruitfulness in His farewell teaching. records.title: The Two Debtors
records.text: Read and discover At Simon's table Explore and study Neither could repay Two debtors stand before the creditor with nothing to pay. Jesus describes debts of different sizes, bringing both men to the same need for mercy. Luke 7:41-42 Jesus is eating in Simon's house when an unnamed woman comes with ointment and weeps at His feet. Simon's inward judgment prompts Jesus to tell a short story about a creditor and two debtors. The surrounding encounter matters because Jesus returns to it after Simon answers His question. Luke 7:36-50 Luke 7:36-50 Read and discover Forgiveness and the response of love One debtor owes five hundred pence and the other fifty. Neither can pay, and the creditor forgives them both. Jesus asks which will love him more. Simon identifies the one forgiven the larger amount, and Jesus accepts his answer. Explore and study Both debts forgiven The creditor freely forgives both debts when neither man can repay. The welcoming gesture pictures that mercy, inviting us to consider the grateful love at the heart of Jesus' teaching. Luke 7:42 Jesus then contrasts the woman's acts of care with the welcome He received from Simon. The debt comparison helps Simon look again at the woman he had judged. Forgiveness and love are at the center; she is not reduced to the reputation through which he first viewed her. Luke 7:36-50 Read and discover Look again at the person before you The passage does not name this woman as Mary Magdalene, and a retelling should not supply that identity. Reflection can instead stay with the question Jesus puts before Simon: how might receiving mercy change the way a person loves, and how might judgment prevent us from seeing that love? Pause and consider What makes mercy easy to underestimate? How might gratitude become an act of love? records.title: The Two Sons
records.text: Read and discover Authority, John, and response Explore and study The father's request The father addresses his son beside the open vineyard gate. Jesus begins with a request to work, then shows how the son's first refusal will give way to a different response. Matthew 21:28–29 Jesus tells this story in Jerusalem after religious leaders challenge His authority. The discussion has turned to John the Baptist and their response to him. A father asking two sons to work in his vineyard provides a direct way to examine the difference between words and obedience. Matthew 21:23-32 Matthew 21:23-32 Read and discover What the sons actually do Explore and study A changed mind becomes action The son is now at work among the vines, gathering grapes into a basket. Jesus says he changed his mind and went, giving substance to repentance through what he did. Matthew 21:29 The first son refuses, then changes his mind and goes. The second speaks agreeably but does not go. Jesus asks which did the father's will. The question is simple enough to answer, but its simplicity exposes the distance between a respectable response and an actual response. Jesus applies the account to people who believed John and to hearers who, even after seeing that response, did not repent and believe. The story is therefore not merely praise for independent action. Its setting concerns receiving a call from God and allowing that call to change conduct. Matthew 21:23-32 Read and discover There is still room to change Explore and study Words that still need action The second son looks toward his father with a hand against his chest as he answers. Jesus says that this son agreed to go but did not, asking us to weigh obedience by action as well as words. Matthew 21:30–31 There is hope in the first son's changed mind. An earlier refusal need not be the last word. You might consider one promise that remains only words, or one neglected good you can still begin. The passage invites a concrete response without requiring a polished account of your intentions. Pause and consider Where might a changed mind become a faithful action? What promise still needs to become practice? Matthew 21:23-32 Related studies The Wise and Foolish Builders Jesus pictures a life that can stand by taking us beneath the walls to the foundation. His invitation is to let heard words become practiced truth. Open study → The Barren Fig Tree The gardener asks for time to dig and nourish. Jesus places urgent repentance beside a patient opportunity to bear fruit. Open study → Hearing and Living His Word Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Matthew 21:23-32 Bible Dictionary: Parables

records.title: The Unjust Steward
records.text: Read and discover The steward faces an account Explore and study Called to give an account A rich man hears that his steward has been wasting his goods and calls him to account. He tells the steward that he can no longer remain in charge of the household's management. Luke 16:1-2 A rich man hears that his steward has wasted his goods and calls him to account. Facing removal, the steward considers how he will live afterward. The story begins with failing stewardship and an urgent attempt to prepare for a changed future. Luke 16:1-13 Luke 16:1-13 Read and discover Preparation without approval of dishonesty Explore and study The oil debt reduced The steward directs a debtor to change a hundred measures of oil to fifty. The writing follows the steward's scheme to secure welcome after he loses his position. Luke 16:5-6 He calls his master's debtors and reduces their bills. One who owes oil is told to write a smaller amount, and another who owes wheat does the same. His purpose is to secure welcome in their houses when he loses his position. The commendation concerns his shrewd action in view of what is coming. It does not turn the story into approval of dishonesty. Jesus' following words stress faithfulness in little and much, responsibility with what belongs to another, and the impossibility of serving both God and mammon. The altered account continues his dishonest scheme as he prepares for the loss of his position. records.title: The Unmerciful Servant
records.text: Read and discover Peter asks about forgiveness Explore and study A plea for patience The servant kneels before the king with a debt he cannot pay. In Jesus' story he asks for patience and promises repayment, setting the scene for an extraordinary act of mercy. The question will soon become whether the mercy he receives changes the way he treats someone who owes him far less. Matthew 18:23–28 Peter asks Jesus how often he must forgive a brother who sins against him. Jesus answers with a story about a king settling accounts. One servant owes an immense sum and cannot pay. Faced with consequences that reach his whole household, he begs for patience. Matthew 18:21-35 Matthew 18:21-35 Read and discover A debt released and mercy refused Explore and study Mercy beyond the plea The king's response exceeds the servant's request for more time. Moved with compassion, he releases him and forgives the debt. Jesus gives this mercy a central place before testing whether the servant will extend mercy to another. Matthew 18:27 The king does more than extend the deadline: moved with compassion, he forgives the debt. The servant then encounters a fellow servant who owes him far less. Despite hearing a plea resembling his own, he seizes the man and has him imprisoned. The contrast makes his refusal of mercy unmistakable. Other servants are distressed and report what happened. The king's question brings the central issue into the open: should the man who received compassion not also have shown it? Jesus concludes by directing attention to forgiveness from the heart. The forgiven debt is meant to change the way the servant treats others. Explore and study A plea the servant refuses The plea for patience now comes from someone else. The servant who received mercy confronts a fellow servant owing far less and refuses the appeal. Jesus makes the echo of the earlier plea difficult to miss, exposing the gap between receiving forgiveness and extending it. Matthew 18:28–30 Explore and study The wrong is reported Other servants are deeply troubled by what has happened and tell their lord. Their response brings the unmerciful treatment before the one who had granted forgiveness. The story does not treat cruelty toward another person as a private matter without consequence. Matthew 18:31 Matthew 18:21-35 Read and discover Receiving mercy changes the question Explore and study The king confronts the servant The servant stands before the king again. His master recalls the mercy he received and asks why he did not show compassion to his fellow servant. The confrontation brings the story's central failure into view: mercy received had not become mercy given. Matthew 18:32-33 The parable does not make cruelty harmless or demand that a wounded person restore unsafe access. Its call is to relinquish a merciless posture while taking wrongdoing seriously. Reflection can begin with the difference between necessary boundaries and the desire to keep another person permanently under your judgment. Forgiveness may involve difficult and repeated work. A reader carrying deep injury need not pretend that the feeling has already changed. The account invites an honest turning toward the mercy of God and a willingness to consider what receiving that mercy might make possible in one's own heart. Pause and consider Where are you keeping a harsh ledger? How might compassion change one response while preserving needed boundaries? Matthew 18:21-35 Related studies The Two Debtors A brief story changes the conversation at Simon's table. Forgiveness invites him to look again at a woman whose love he has overlooked. Open study → The Prodigal Son and His Brother One son comes home from far away; the other stands outside the celebration. The father goes toward both, and the story leaves an invitation before us. Open study → Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Matthew 18:21-35 Bible Dictionary: Parables
