records.title: The True Vine and the Branches
records.pageTitle: The True Vine and the Branches
records.text: Read and discover The vine, the Father, and the disciples Explore and study Joined to the vine A living branch remains joined to the vine. Jesus uses this simple relationship to teach His disciples about abiding in Him. John 15:1-5 During His farewell teaching, Jesus names Himself as the true vine and His Father as the husbandman. The disciples are the branches. The picture begins with dependence: a branch does not supply its own life independently of the vine to which it belongs. John 15:1-17 John 15:1-17 Read and discover The life that bears fruit Explore and study Tending the vine A keeper works carefully among the vine's leaves and branches. Jesus uses the tending of a fruitful vine in His teaching about abiding in Him. John 15:2 The Father tends the growth, and Jesus invites the disciples to abide in Him. The repeated concern is fruitfulness. Remaining connected is not described as a decorative attachment; it is the relation through which the branch can bear fruit. As the passage develops, abiding is joined with Jesus' words, His love, and keeping His commandments. He speaks of His joy and commands love for one another. Those surrounding teachings keep the vine from becoming a vague picture of feeling close without response. Explore and study Fruit on the living branch Fruit hangs from the living branch. Jesus joins this image of fruitfulness with His invitation to abide in Him. John 15:5 John 15:1-17 Read and discover Abiding in His love Pruning is part of the image, but it should not be used to announce why a particular person has suffered. The passage does not authorize us to identify a bereavement, illness, or injury as a specific act of divine pruning. Its stated invitation is to abide in Christ. For reflection, consider what helps His words remain present in your choices and relationships. Prayer, study, repentance, and acts of love can be considered as responses to that invitation. Fruit is received through dependence on Him, not offered as proof that a person needs no help. Pause and consider What helps you remain close to Him? How do love and obedience belong together? John 15:1-17 Related studies The Sower The same seed meets different ground. Jesus explains what can prevent His word from taking root and what makes room for enduring fruit. Open study → The Good Shepherd and the Door The shepherd knows, calls, leads, and gives His life. Jesus identifies Himself through a sustained picture of care and willing sacrifice. Open study → Hearing and Living His Word Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study John 15:1-17 Bible Dictionary: Parables

records.title: Servants Waiting for Their Lord
records.text: Read and discover Lamps burning for a welcome Explore and study Servants with lit lamps The servants keep their lamps burning and their clothing gathered for work. Jesus uses this picture of readiness to invite watchful attention. Luke 12:35 Jesus describes servants with lamps burning, waiting for a lord who is returning from a wedding. Their task is to be ready to open when he knocks. The scene gives watchfulness an attentive and welcoming character, rather than presenting it only as alarm about an approaching event. Luke 12:22-40 Luke 12:22-40 Read and discover A master who serves Explore and study Opening at the master's knock The door opens to the returning master while the servants are ready to receive him. In Jesus' comparison, they wait so they can respond when he knocks. Luke 12:36 The waiting may extend into later watches of the night. The servants do not control the hour, but they can remain prepared for the master's arrival. The passage keeps uncertainty about timing beside clarity about their present responsibility. The surprising promise is that the master will gird himself, have the servants sit down, and serve them. Jesus includes this reversal in the picture of the welcomed return. The servants' readiness is met with generosity that exceeds a routine account of duty. Explore and study Master serving the attendants The master gathers his clothing for service and brings food to the seated servants. Jesus describes this unexpected welcome for those he finds watching. Luke 12:37 Luke 12:22-40 Read and discover Make the waiting attentive You might reflect on the difference between waiting with attention and merely postponing life. Faithful care, prayer, and readiness to respond can belong to the interval itself. The image also invites us to receive the Lord's kindness rather than imagine discipleship solely as an endless demand to perform. Pause and consider What does a ready lamp suggest about your attention? How does the master's service surprise you? Luke 12:22-40 Related studies The Ten Virgins All ten wait and all ten sleep, but their preparation differs. The midnight announcement reveals what they have brought to the waiting. Open study → The Faithful and Unfaithful Servant Someone else's daily bread is placed in a servant's care. The master's absence reveals how that trust will be used. Open study → Prayer, Readiness, and His Return Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Luke 12:22-40 Bible Dictionary: Parables
records.excerpt: The lamps are ready and the door can be opened. Jesus pictures waiting that is attentive, then surprises His hearers with the master's welcome.

records.title: Prayer, Readiness, and His Return
records.text: Read and discover Read both the invitation and its limits Luke states that the persistent widow teaches continued prayer. The judge's indifference is part of a contrast, not a description of the Father's character. Read the friend at midnight with Jesus' following words about the Father's gifts, so persistence does not become a method for wearing God down. Luke 18:1–14 Explore and study Keeping the promised watch An attendant watches the entrance as people move through the lobby. Watchful service can mean remaining attentive and available in an ordinary place. Luke 12:35-38 Keep readiness beside ordinary responsibility. The servant feeds the household, the porter watches, and the attendants prepare their lamps. Jesus repeatedly leaves the hour unknown. His teaching gives work for the present, not a code for calculating a date. Mark 13:32–37 The imagined modern scenes picture honest prayer, quiet preparation and attention to work that still needs doing. They invite us to remain faithful while we wait, even when a decision, recovery or other hoped-for outcome remains beyond our control. Luke 18:1–14 Mark 13:32–37 Read and discover Bring need without a performance Explore and study A concern named plainly A woman writes quietly in a notebook beside a window. Jesus' teaching about humble prayer invites us to bring our needs honestly before God. Luke 18:9-14 The publican asks for mercy while the Pharisee compares his conduct with other people's. Jesus directs attention to humility rather than a performance of standing before God. The widow's continued request, in a different story, gives persistence a voice in the face of dismissal. Luke 18:9–14 Naming a concern plainly or returning respectfully to an unanswered request can help make those questions concrete. Prayer may include fatigue and uncertainty. Continued asking is not a guarantee that we will receive a particular decision on our timetable, and a long wait is not evidence of another person's weak faith. Luke 18:1–8 Explore and study Returning to the unanswered request A wheelchair user points to a document and discusses it with a listener across the desk. The widow's persistence invites us to consider faithful, respectful perseverance. Luke 18:1-8 Luke 18:9–14 Luke 18:1–8 Read and discover Prepare steadily rather than fearfully Explore and study Supplies checked before the need Two people check a flashlight and spare batteries beside a bag of supplies. The ten virgins' story asks us to consider the preparation that is ours to undertake. Matthew 25:1-13 All ten attendants sleep while the bridegroom is delayed. The difference is the preparation they have brought, not a contrast between those who sleep and those who never do. The porter likewise watches without being told which hour will bring the master. Matthew 25:1–13 An emergency kit or a practiced route is a modest analogy for preparation that takes place before a need. Spiritual readiness is not identical to preparedness equipment, but the example can ask whether we are acting steadily rather than waiting for alarm to move us. Attention to others belongs in that preparation too. Mark 13:33–37 Explore and study Learning the safe route together Three people pause at an open doorway to discuss the route. Attentive preparation can include listening to those who will use the space. Mark 13:33-37 Matthew 25:1–13 Mark 13:33–37 Read and discover Give the waiting its work Explore and study A careful handoff at night Two staff members speak at a quiet desk, one holding a folder while the other takes notes. The faithful-servant teaching asks how we care for responsibilities entrusted to us. Matthew 24:45-47 The faithful servant continues to provide what the household needs. The waiting servants keep their lamps ready to open at the master's knock. In these pictures, the interval is not meaningless; it is where dependable service and attentive welcome take shape. Matthew 24:45–47 At the end of a shift or through a quiet hour, someone may still depend on a careful handoff or a promise kept. These imagined scenes ask us to notice the work entrusted to us now, even as we wait for something larger. Luke 12:35–38 Matthew 24:45–47 Luke 12:35–38 Read and discover Trust without denying the burden Explore and study Taking the next practical step A man reviews papers while a woman listens beside him. Jesus' teaching about worry invites us to seek the Father's care as we take the next practical step. Matthew 6:25-34 Jesus points to birds and lilies while speaking about needs the Father knows. In His farewell teaching, He also names sorrow before promising His disciples reunion. Neither passage requires readers to pretend that pain or uncertainty is imaginary. Matthew 6:25–34 You may be able to take one practical step, seek appropriate support, or pause to notice ordinary life while an outcome remains unresolved. These applications do not explain why a burden has come or promise that it will soon disappear. The invitation is to bring a real life before God, including what cannot yet be settled. John 16:20–22 Explore and study A pause to notice living things A walker pauses to watch small birds beside flowers along the path. Jesus asks His hearers to consider birds and flowers as He teaches about the Father's care. Matthew 6:26-30 Matthew 6:25–34 John 16:20–22 Read and discover Bring the teaching into your own reflection Pause and consider What need could you bring to God more honestly? Which form of preparation can become a calm repeated practice? What faithful task is yours during this season of waiting? Read and discover Explore every study in this collection The Budding Fig Tree Seasonal growth illustrates recognizing signs. Read with the warnings about the unknown time; it is not permission to calculate a date. Open study → The Householder and the Thief The unexpected arrival calls for readiness. The comparison concerns timing, not a claim that the Lord shares a thief's character. Open study → The Faithful and Unfaithful Servant Entrusted care is tested while the master is away. Luke connects responsibility with what a servant knows and has received. Open study → The Ten Virgins All ten wait and sleep, but only five have the needed oil when the bridegroom arrives. Focus on readiness rather than blaming sleep itself. Open study → The Friend at Midnight A late visitor creates a need for bread. Read the story with Jesus' invitation to ask and His teaching about the Father's gifts. Open study → Servants Waiting for Their Lord Servants remain ready to welcome a master returning from a wedding. The master's surprising service is part of the story; keep it beside, but distinct from, the thief comparison. Open study → The Persistent Widow and the Judge Luke states the invitation to keep praying. God's justice is contrasted with the unjust judge; do not promise a particular answer on a chosen timetable. Open study → The Pharisee and the Publican The introduction identifies trust in one's own righteousness and contempt for others. The tax collector's plea invites humility, not contempt toward Pharisees as a people. Open study → The Doorkeeper A departing master assigns work and commands watchfulness. The repeated call to watch rests on not knowing the time. Open study → Parables and story pictures Related comparisons and allegories The Closed Door A shut door answers a question about salvation. Familiarity is not the same as responding to the Lord. Open study → A Parent's Good Gifts The comparison argues from human care to the Father's goodness. Luke specifically names the Holy Ghost. Open study → Sorrow Turning to Joy Childbirth illustrates sorrow giving way to joy in the farewell discourse. It is an analogy, not a prediction about an individual pregnancy. Open study → Birds and Lilies Creation illustrates the Father's care amid teaching about anxious concern. Do not suggest faithful people never experience deprivation or anxiety. Open study → Related studies Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship Explore responsibility during an absence in the talents, minas, and servant teachings. Open study → Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning Read humble prayer beside the welcome and forgiveness Jesus teaches. Open study → The Kingdom of God Keep hope in the kingdom connected with patient growth and careful attention to His words. Open study → Sources for further study Bible Dictionary: Parables Harmony of the Gospels Luke 18 Mark 13 Matthew 25 Matthew 24 Luke 12 Matthew 6 John 16
records.excerpt: Jesus joins prayer with humility, readiness with service, and hope with honest attention to uncertainty. These studies invite steady faithfulness without pretending to know the time or outcome.

They invite us to remain faithful while we wait, even when a decision, recovery or other hoped-for outcome remains beyond our control. Luke 18:1–14 Mark 13:32–37

records.title: Bring need without a performance
records.text: Read and discover Bring need without a performance Explore and study A concern named plainly A woman writes quietly in a notebook beside a window. Jesus' teaching about humble prayer invites us to bring our needs honestly before God. Luke 18:9-14 The publican asks for mercy while the Pharisee compares his conduct with other people's. Jesus directs attention to humility rather than a performance of standing before God. The widow's continued request, in a different story, gives persistence a voice in the face of dismissal. Luke 18:9–14 Naming a concern plainly or returning respectfully to an unanswered request can help make those questions concrete. Prayer may include fatigue and uncertainty. Continued asking is not a guarantee that we will receive a particular decision on our timetable, and a long wait is not evidence of another person's weak faith. Luke 18:1–8 Explore and study Returning to the unanswered request A wheelchair user points to a document and discusses it with a listener across the desk. The widow's persistence invites us to consider faithful, respectful perseverance. Luke 18:1-8 Luke 18:9–14 Luke 18:1–8

records.title: Prepare steadily rather than fearfully
records.text: Read and discover Prepare steadily rather than fearfully Explore and study Supplies checked before the need Two people check a flashlight and spare batteries beside a bag of supplies. The ten virgins' story asks us to consider the preparation that is ours to undertake. Matthew 25:1-13 All ten attendants sleep while the bridegroom is delayed. The difference is the preparation they have brought, not a contrast between those who sleep and those who never do. The porter likewise watches without being told which hour will bring the master. Matthew 25:1–13 An emergency kit or a practiced route is a modest analogy for preparation that takes place before a need. Spiritual readiness is not identical to preparedness equipment, but the example can ask whether we are acting steadily rather than waiting for alarm to move us. Attention to others belongs in that preparation too. Mark 13:33–37 Explore and study Learning the safe route together Three people pause at an open doorway to discuss the route. Attentive preparation can include listening to those who will use the space. Mark 13:33-37 Matthew 25:1–13 Mark 13:33–37

records.title: Give the waiting its work
records.text: Read and discover Give the waiting its work Explore and study A careful handoff at night Two staff members speak at a quiet desk, one holding a folder while the other takes notes. The faithful-servant teaching asks how we care for responsibilities entrusted to us. Matthew 24:45-47 The faithful servant continues to provide what the household needs. The waiting servants keep their lamps ready to open at the master's knock. In these pictures, the interval is not meaningless; it is where dependable service and attentive welcome take shape. Matthew 24:45–47 At the end of a shift or through a quiet hour, someone may still depend on a careful handoff or a promise kept. These imagined scenes ask us to notice the work entrusted to us now, even as we wait for something larger. Luke 12:35–38 Matthew 24:45–47 Luke 12:35–38

records.title: Trust without denying the burden
records.text: Read and discover Trust without denying the burden Explore and study Taking the next practical step A man reviews papers while a woman listens beside him. Jesus' teaching about worry invites us to seek the Father's care as we take the next practical step. Matthew 6:25-34 Jesus points to birds and lilies while speaking about needs the Father knows. In His farewell teaching, He also names sorrow before promising His disciples reunion. Neither passage requires readers to pretend that pain or uncertainty is imaginary. Matthew 6:25–34 You may be able to take one practical step, seek appropriate support, or pause to notice ordinary life while an outcome remains unresolved. These applications do not explain why a burden has come or promise that it will soon disappear. The invitation is to bring a real life before God, including what cannot yet be settled. John 16:20–22 Explore and study A pause to notice living things A walker pauses to watch small birds beside flowers along the path. Jesus asks His hearers to consider birds and flowers as He teaches about the Father's care. Matthew 6:26-30 Matthew 6:25–34 John 16:20–22

records.title: Bring the teaching into your own reflection
records.text: Read and discover Bring the teaching into your own reflection Pause and consider What need could you bring to God more honestly? Which form of preparation can become a calm repeated practice? What faithful task is yours during this season of waiting?

records.title: Explore every study in this collection
records.text: Read and discover Explore every study in this collection The Budding Fig Tree Seasonal growth illustrates recognizing signs. Read with the warnings about the unknown time; it is not permission to calculate a date. Open study → The Householder and the Thief The unexpected arrival calls for readiness. The comparison concerns timing, not a claim that the Lord shares a thief's character. Open study → The Faithful and Unfaithful Servant Entrusted care is tested while the master is away. Luke connects responsibility with what a servant knows and has received. Open study → The Ten Virgins All ten wait and sleep, but only five have the needed oil when the bridegroom arrives. Focus on readiness rather than blaming sleep itself. Open study → The Friend at Midnight A late visitor creates a need for bread. Read the story with Jesus' invitation to ask and His teaching about the Father's gifts. Open study → Servants Waiting for Their Lord Servants remain ready to welcome a master returning from a wedding. The master's surprising service is part of the story; keep it beside, but distinct from, the thief comparison. Open study → The Persistent Widow and the Judge Luke states the invitation to keep praying. God's justice is contrasted with the unjust judge; do not promise a particular answer on a chosen timetable. Open study → The Pharisee and the Publican The introduction identifies trust in one's own righteousness and contempt for others. The tax collector's plea invites humility, not contempt toward Pharisees as a people. Open study → The Doorkeeper A departing master assigns work and commands watchfulness. The repeated call to watch rests on not knowing the time. Open study → Parables and story pictures Related comparisons and allegories The Closed Door A shut door answers a question about salvation. Familiarity is not the same as responding to the Lord. Open study → A Parent's Good Gifts The comparison argues from human care to the Father's goodness. Luke specifically names the Holy Ghost. Open study → Sorrow Turning to Joy Childbirth illustrates sorrow giving way to joy in the farewell discourse. It is an analogy, not a prediction about an individual pregnancy. Open study → Birds and Lilies Creation illustrates the Father's care amid teaching about anxious concern. Do not suggest faithful people never experience deprivation or anxiety. Open study →

records.title: Choosing the Lower Place
records.text: Read and discover The seats people choose Explore and study Choosing a place of honor Jesus notices how guests choose places of honor and teaches them about humility. This imagined wedding gathering introduces the contrast between seeking prominence and taking a lower place. Luke 14:7-8 Jesus notices how guests choose places of honor at a meal. His teaching grows from something happening in front of Him. He describes the embarrassment of taking a high place that must later be given to a more distinguished guest. Luke 14:1-14 Explore and study Asked to give up the higher place In Jesus' example, someone who takes the highest place may be asked to yield it to a more honored guest. The host's request exposes the shame of claiming an honor that was never offered. Luke 14:8-9 Luke 14:1-14 Read and discover Humility and hospitality The alternative is to take the lower place and allow the host to invite one forward. The story culminates in a saying about self-exaltation and humility. Its purpose is deeper than providing an efficient technique for gaining public recognition. Explore and study Invited to a higher place Jesus counsels His listeners to take the lowest place when invited. In His example, the host then invites the humble guest to move higher, allowing honor to come as a gift rather than a claim. Luke 14:10 Jesus then turns to the person who invited Him. He speaks of welcoming those who cannot repay the invitation, including people often excluded from honored tables. The movement from seating oneself to choosing one's guests joins humility with generosity. Luke 14:1-14 Read and discover A welcome without repayment You might ask whose approval determines your sense of place, and who could receive welcome without increasing your status. A meal, gathering, or act of hospitality can become less concerned with repayment. The invitation is to honor people rather than arrange them according to what they can return. Pause and consider When are you tempted to secure visible honor? Who could receive hospitality without being able to repay? Luke 14:1-14 Related studies The Pharisee and the Publican Two people pray, but their posture toward God and others differs. Jesus invites a searching look at comparison, confidence, and mercy. Open study → The Great Supper The supper is ready, but the first invitees excuse themselves. The widening invitation brings overlooked people toward a place at the table. Open study → Loving Our Neighbor Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Luke 14:1-14 Bible Dictionary: Parables

records.title: The Wheat and the Tares
records.text: Read and discover A field with mixed growth Explore and study An enemy sows in the field Someone moves through the planted field under cover of night. Jesus says an enemy sowed tares among the wheat while others slept. In His later explanation, the enemy is the devil; this scene illustrates the story's action without claiming to show the devil's physical appearance. Matthew 13:24–25, 37–39 Jesus tells of a field deliberately planted with good seed. An enemy introduces tares while people sleep, and the mixed growth becomes apparent later. The servants' first question is understandable: how did the unwanted plants appear in a field that began with good seed? Matthew 13:24-43 Matthew 13:24-43 Read and discover Why the owner tells them to wait Explore and study The mixed field is discovered The mixed growth has become noticeable, and the workers stop to examine it. In Jesus' story, the servants ask how tares appeared in a field planted with good seed. Their question begins a conversation about the enemy's work and the owner's care for the wheat. Matthew 13:26–29 Their proposed solution is immediate removal. The owner refuses because pulling up the tares could uproot the wheat as well. He directs them to let both grow until harvest, when separation can take place. His restraint protects what the servants are trying to save. After the crowd leaves, the disciples ask Jesus to explain. He identifies the sower of good seed as the Son of Man, the field as the world, and the harvest with the end. Because the passage supplies these meanings, they should guide the study rather than an imagined code attached to every detail. Explore and study Let both grow until harvest The owner stops the workers from pulling up the unwanted plants at once. Jesus explains the owner's concern: uprooting the tares could also uproot the wheat. The delayed separation expresses care for the crop; in His interpretation, the final harvest belongs to the end of the world and to God's appointed judgment. Matthew 13:28–30, 39–43 Matthew 13:24-43 Read and discover Care without claiming final judgment Explore and study The harvest is separated The harvested plants now stand in separate bundles. Jesus' story ends with the tares gathered apart and the wheat brought into the barn. His explanation places the final separation under God's authority, encouraging trust in His judgment rather than a rush to decide another person's final worth. Matthew 13:30, 39–43 The account cautions against acting as though we possess the final discernment of the Lord. It does not ask us to call our neighbors weeds or excuse harmful conduct. A personal reflection can focus on the patience, care, and humility needed to protect people while leaving final judgment to Him. Pause and consider Why does the owner delay separation? How can patience protect someone vulnerable? Matthew 13:24-43 Related studies The Fishing Net The net gathers a mixed catch, and the shore becomes a place of separation. Jesus connects an ordinary fishing scene with the seriousness of judgment. Open study → The Seed Growing Secretly Between sowing and harvest, growth unfolds beyond the farmer's control. Mark's brief parable invites patient attention to God's kingdom. Open study → The Kingdom of God Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Matthew 13:24-43 Bible Dictionary: Parables

records.title: The Wicked Tenants
records.text: Read and discover A vineyard entrusted to others Explore and study Prepared vineyard leased out The owner has prepared the vineyard before entrusting it to tenants. Its hedge, winepress and tower frame Jesus' story about the responsibility that follows receiving another's trust. Matthew 21:33 A vineyard owner prepares his property and entrusts it to tenants while he goes away. When the time comes to receive its fruit, he sends servants. Jesus tells the story amid a confrontation about His authority, and the Gospel accounts report that the leaders recognize its challenge to them. Matthew 21:23-46 Matthew 21:23-46 Mark 12:1-12 Luke 20:9-19 Read and discover Messengers rejected and the son sent Explore and study Servants turned away The first servant leaves empty-handed after the tenants mistreat him. Their refusal to return the vineyard's fruit turns entrusted responsibility into rejection. Mark 12:2-3 The tenants respond to successive servants with violence. The owner finally sends his son, but they treat even that arrival as an opportunity to seize the inheritance. The vineyard is not theirs, yet they act as though removing the owner's representatives will make it so. Mark 12:1-12 Jesus brings the hearers to the question of what the owner will do, then speaks of the rejected stone becoming the head of the corner. The account connects rejection with accountability. Luke likewise preserves both the tenants' actions and the leaders' recognition that Jesus has spoken against them. Luke 20:9-19 Explore and study The son approaching the vineyard The owner's son approaches the vineyard after the servants have been rejected. His arrival brings the tenants' response to the owner's trust to its gravest test. Mark 12:6-8 Matthew 21:23-46 Mark 12:1-12 Luke 20:9-19 Read and discover Reading the confrontation faithfully Explore and study Hearers confronting the question of judgment Jesus' listeners answer His question about what the vineyard owner will do. Their response recognizes that those entrusted with the vineyard must answer for how they have treated its owner and his messengers. Matthew 21:40-41 The story must not become collective blame against Jewish people. Jesus, His disciples, and the scriptural world of the passage are Jewish; the confrontation is with particular leaders and their response. Careful study preserves that setting instead of extending hostility beyond the text. For personal reflection, the vineyard can prompt questions about entrusted responsibility. What changes when a role, relationship, or opportunity is received as a stewardship rather than possessed as an unquestionable right? Listening to correction may be part of honoring the One to whom the vineyard belongs. Pause and consider What has been entrusted to your care? How do you receive correction from a rightful source? Matthew 21:23-46 Mark 12:1-12 Luke 20:9-19 Related studies The Two Sons One son changes his mind; another never turns agreement into action. Jesus makes the difference between a response and its appearance clear. Open study → The Wedding of the King's Son The wedding invitation is refused, widened, and finally answered. Matthew's account asks readers to take both the welcome and their response seriously. Open study → Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship Continue through the connected teachings in this collection and compare their distinct settings. Open study → Sources for further study Matthew 21:23-46 Mark 12:1-12 Luke 20:9-19 Bible Dictionary: Parables

records.title: The Wise and Foolish Builders
records.text: Read and discover A life built on His words Explore and study Digging toward a firm foundation A worker bends over the rocky ground, giving the foundation his attention before the house is finished. Luke describes a builder who digs deeply and lays his foundation on rock. Jesus connects that care with hearing His words and doing them. Luke 6:47–49 Jesus ends His sermon by moving from listening to living. The people have heard about mercy, prayer, integrity, and love for enemies. Now He asks what will hold that teaching in place. A house becomes His picture of the life a person builds through daily choices. Matthew 7:21-29 Matthew 7:21-29 Luke 6:46-49 Read and discover Two foundations beneath the houses Explore and study A house before the storm The house looks sound while the weather is calm. Jesus places the foolish builder's house on sand, then describes the storm that reveals its weakness. The warning concerns hearing His words without doing them; a reassuring appearance cannot replace a faithful foundation. Matthew 7:26–27 The difference between the builders appears beneath the houses. One builds on rock; the other builds on sand. Luke describes the first man digging deeply before laying a foundation. Both houses meet a flood. The storm reveals the consequence of the earlier work; it does not create the difference. Luke 6:46-49 Jesus identifies the secure foundation with hearing His words and doing them. Knowing the sermon, admiring its beauty, or calling Him Lord cannot substitute for that response. The builder's work invites us to look at the quiet decisions through which a teaching becomes part of our conduct. Matthew 7:21-29 Luke 6:46-49 Read and discover When hearing becomes action Explore and study Two foundations in the storm The same storm surrounds both houses, but their foundations differ. One remains on rock while the other has fallen beside washed-out sand. Jesus uses this contrast to distinguish hearing and doing His sayings from hearing without acting, inviting a response that endures beyond the easier days. Matthew 7:24–27 This is not a promise that disciples avoid grief, disaster, or difficult questions. The faithful house is also struck by the storm. You might choose one teaching from the sermon and consider what practicing it would require this week, allowing steady obedience to grow beneath what others can see. Pause and consider Which teaching needs action rather than agreement? What quiet practice could deepen your foundation? records.title: Sorrow Turning to Joy
records.text: Read and discover Sorrow in the farewell discourse Explore and study Supported through the pain A woman in labor receives steady support through her pain. Jesus acknowledges the anguish of childbirth in the comparison He gives His disciples before speaking of joy. John 16:21 In His farewell discourse, Jesus tells the disciples that they will weep and be sorrowful while the world rejoices, but that their sorrow will turn to joy. He gives the image of a woman in labor to describe a real anguish followed by a changed moment. John 16:16-24 John 16:16-24 Read and discover The promised change and reunion The woman's sorrow is not dismissed as imaginary. The birth brings joy that changes her relation to the pain she has endured. Jesus then returns directly to the disciples, saying He will see them again and that their hearts will rejoice. Explore and study Joy after the birth The mother holds her child close, her tired face softened with joy. Jesus uses the change from anguish to joy to speak to His disciples about seeing Him again. John 16:21 This is a comparison within a particular promise to His followers as His death and their reunion approach. It is not a general prediction that every pregnancy ends safely or that every grief will soon feel resolved. Those conclusions would exceed what the passage says. John 16:16-24 Read and discover Hope that does not erase pain You may reflect on how hope can remain present without requiring denial of sorrow. The disciples are not told that they will never weep. The image allows the present pain to be named while directing attention toward the reunion Jesus promises them. Pause and consider How does the image acknowledge real sorrow? How can hope accompany pain? John 16:16-24 Related studies Birds and Lilies Jesus draws attention to creatures and flowers while speaking of daily needs. The invitation is to seek the kingdom with trust in the Father's care. Open study → A Parent's Good Gifts A child's request for food becomes a way to think about prayer. records.title: Sorrow in the farewell discourse
records.text: Read and discover Sorrow in the farewell discourse Explore and study Supported through the pain A woman in labor receives steady support through her pain. Jesus acknowledges the anguish of childbirth in the comparison He gives His disciples before speaking of joy. John 16:21 In His farewell discourse, Jesus tells the disciples that they will weep and be sorrowful while the world rejoices, but that their sorrow will turn to joy. He gives the image of a woman in labor to describe a real anguish followed by a changed moment. John 16:16-24 John 16:16-24

records.title: The promised change and reunion
records.text: Read and discover The promised change and reunion The woman's sorrow is not dismissed as imaginary. The birth brings joy that changes her relation to the pain she has endured. Jesus then returns directly to the disciples, saying He will see them again and that their hearts will rejoice. Explore and study Joy after the birth The mother holds her child close, her tired face softened with joy. Jesus uses the change from anguish to joy to speak to His disciples about seeing Him again. John 16:21 This is a comparison within a particular promise to His followers as His death and their reunion approach. It is not a general prediction that every pregnancy ends safely or that every grief will soon feel resolved. Those conclusions would exceed what the passage says. John 16:16-24

records.title: Hope that does not erase pain
records.text: Read and discover Hope that does not erase pain You may reflect on how hope can remain present without requiring denial of sorrow. The disciples are not told that they will never weep. The image allows the present pain to be named while directing attention toward the reunion Jesus promises them. Pause and consider How does the image acknowledge real sorrow? How can hope accompany pain? John 16:16-24

records.title: The Redeemer and Risen Lord
records.text: Read and discover A gift at Bethany Explore and study Mary's gift at Bethany Ointment falls from Mary's small vessel onto the Savior's feet. He meets her gaze with quiet attention while Martha serves nearby, and Mary's gift fills the house with fragrance. John 12:1–3 At a meal in Bethany, Martha serves and Lazarus is among those at the table. In John 12:1–8 , Mary anoints Jesus’s feet with costly ointment and wipes them with her hair. When the gift is criticized, Jesus receives it in connection with His approaching burial. John lets a household act of devotion stand beside the gathering weight of what is coming. This Mary belongs to the household of Martha and Lazarus. Her gift takes place among people whose lives have already been touched by Jesus, and John preserves its fragrance, cost and reception. Love becomes a concrete act at a time when the meaning of His approaching death is not yet fully understood. The scene invites us to consider the care we can offer now, while a person is still before us, instead of waiting until every feeling can be perfectly explained. Pause and consider What does this gift reveal that an abstract statement of devotion might not express? John 12:1–8 Read and discover Remembering Him in bread and cup At the Passover meal, Jesus speaks of His desire to eat with His apostles before His suffering. In Luke 22:14–20 , He gives thanks, breaks bread and connects bread and cup with His body and blood. The actions take place before His arrest, giving the disciples a way to remember the sacrifice toward which He is moving. Explore and study The morsel at the table Jesus holds out the morsel, His troubled gaze meeting Judas across the table. The disciples nearby do not yet understand the departure that will follow. John 13:21–30 The sacrament turns remembrance into something a community receives and practices. In Latter-day Saint worship, that remembrance continues with covenant promises and renewed attention to the Savior. The meal is not merely a farewell gathering; it belongs to His deliberate preparation of His followers. Reading it slowly can help us approach our own worship with greater awareness of whom we remember and why. At the same meal, John 13:21–30 records Jesus speaking of betrayal and giving Judas a morsel. The disciples do not understand why Judas leaves. The small gesture belongs to an evening in which the Savior shares the table with His friends while facing the suffering ahead. Pause and consider What part of His life or character would you like to remember more deliberately during the sacrament? Luke 22:14–20 John 13:21–30 Read and discover His will offered to the Father On the Mount of Olives, Jesus withdraws from His disciples and kneels in prayer. In Luke 22:39–46 , He speaks openly of the cup before Him and submits His will to the Father. Luke records an angel strengthening Him and describes His agony, while His disciples sleep in sorrow. The scene gives us prayer within suffering, rather than a picture of suffering as effortless. Explore and study Could ye not watch with me? Jesus returns from prayer and finds the disciples asleep. Peter looks up as the Savior calls him to watch and pray. Matthew 26:36–41 In Doctrine and Covenants 19:16–19 , the Savior’s own words connect His suffering with the invitation to repent. Together the passages help us approach the Atonement with gratitude and reverence. We need not imagine that we can measure everything He endured to receive the help He offers. Nor should His submission be used to tell a hurting person to hide honest anguish: His prayer itself holds both the plea and the willing response. Matthew 26:36–41 also records His return to the sleeping disciples. Their weakness and His invitation to watch and pray remain beside His solitary anguish, giving the garden account a deeply human setting. Pause and consider What can His prayer teach you about bringing a difficult desire honestly before the Father? Luke 22:39–46 Doctrine and Covenants 19:16–19 Matthew 26:36–41 Read and discover A kingdom beyond coercion Explore and study My kingdom is not of this world Pilate leans forward with a question, and Jesus meets him with quiet resolve. Their exchange turns to His kingdom and the truth He came to bear witness of. John 18:33–38 Pilate questions Jesus about kingship. In John 18:33–38 , Jesus distinguishes His kingdom from the world’s familiar contest for power and speaks about bearing witness to truth. Pilate’s questions take place within a trial whose consequences are deadly, so the exchange should not be detached from the vulnerability of the prisoner standing before him. Jesus’s words turn attention from whether He can defeat an opponent by force to the nature of His mission. He does not abandon truth because political authority questions Him. This account also calls for care in how the Passion is told: responsibility belongs to the people and institutions described, never to Jewish people collectively. The Savior’s own Jewish life and the Gospel’s specific voices must remain visible. Pause and consider What does Jesus’s answer suggest about the kind of power His disciples should seek? John 18:33–38 Read and discover Someone bears the cross after Him As Jesus is led away, Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross behind Him. Luke 23:26–31 also describes people and women following in lamentation, and Jesus speaking to the women about what lies ahead. The road to the place of execution includes both forced participation and the grief of witnesses. Luke leaves Simon’s inner response unrecorded, but gives his service a visible place on the road. A person arriving from the country suddenly bears a burden within the Savior’s suffering. As reflection, the encounter can help us examine how we respond when another person’s pain becomes impossible to keep at a distance. Compassion often begins with the concrete task before us, even when we have no complete explanation for what has happened. Explore and study Bearing the cross behind Jesus Simon bends beneath the beam and follows Jesus along the road. Behind them, women mourn as the Savior continues toward Calvary. Luke 23:26–27 Pause and consider When another person’s burden enters your day unexpectedly, what helps you respond with care? Luke 23:26–31 Read and discover Care for His mother at the cross John places Jesus’s mother and other women near the cross, with the disciple Jesus loves. In John 19:25–30 , Jesus entrusts His mother and that disciple to one another. The passage then records His thirst, the completion of His work and His death. Human care remains present within the account of His sacrifice. This moment does not lessen the suffering of the Crucifixion; it lets us see the Savior attending to a relationship within it. The Christian proclamation of His Atonement concerns His willing gift for the world, and the scene also keeps a mother and a disciple from disappearing into that broad statement. Reverent study can hold the universal reach of His redemption alongside the particular people at the cross. Pause and consider How does this act of care deepen your understanding of the One who gives His life? John 19:25–30 Read and discover The care of Joseph and Nicodemus Explore and study Laid in a garden tomb Joseph and Nicodemus draw the linen gently over Jesus's body. Their careful hands offer a final service of love as they prepare Him for burial in the nearby garden tomb. John 19:38–42 Joseph of Arimathea asks Pilate for Jesus’s body. Nicodemus brings myrrh and aloes, and together they prepare the body with linen and spices. John 19:38–42 places the burial in a new tomb within a garden near the place of Crucifixion. These details give the hours after His death a quiet, concrete gravity. Joseph of Arimathea is a different person from Joseph in the Nativity accounts. Nicodemus is identified here with the earlier nighttime visitor to Jesus. Their actions do not yet read like a triumphant Easter announcement; they perform the care that can be given to a body after death. Before moving to Resurrection, it is worth allowing this part of the story its silence and the faithful work of those present. Pause and consider What do these practical acts teach about showing love when words are difficult? John 19:38–42 Read and discover The risen Lord stands among them Explore and study He eats before them The risen Jesus eats before His disciples in Luke's account. This imagined indoor scene gives their astonished joy a personal focus, distinct from the shore breakfast in John 21. Luke 24:36–43 The disciples are startled when Jesus stands among them. In Luke 24:36–49 , He invites them to see His hands and feet, speaks of flesh and bones, and eats food before them. He then opens their understanding of the scriptures and connects His suffering and rising with the message they are to carry. Luke’s witness joins a real risen body with a renewed understanding of God’s purposes. Resurrection is more than the survival of an idea or the disciples keeping His memory alive. The same Jesus who died lives, and His followers are to become witnesses of repentance and forgiveness in His name. Their astonishment is part of the account; understanding grows as He teaches them what His victory means. Pause and consider Why do you think the account includes both the food He eats and the scriptures He explains? Luke 24:36–49 Read and discover Witnesses sent into the world Explore and study A cloud receives Him The disciples watch as Jesus is taken up and a cloud receives Him. Their upturned faces bring us into the parting Acts describes. Acts 1:9–11 · Luke 24:50–51 Before His Ascension, the disciples ask about the restoration of the kingdom to Israel. In Acts 1:4–11 , Jesus turns them from a timetable to the power and witness they are to receive. They will testify near home and outward to the ends of the earth. A cloud receives Him, and heavenly messengers speak of His return. The Ascension does not leave the disciples with only the task of watching the sky. The account places hope in His return beside a present commission. That combination still matters: we can await the Savior while attending to the people, responsibilities and opportunities for witness already before us. His promise does not authorize a predicted date; His instruction gives His followers useful work to do now. Pause and consider What present act of discipleship could express your hope in the living Savior? records.title: Jesus Christ in the Restoration and Today
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ in the Restoration and Today
records.text: Read and discover The Father introduces His Son The First Vision Joseph kneels among the trees. Explore his account of the Father and the Son appearing in answer to his prayer. Open study → Joseph Smith’s published history describes his attempt to pray in the woods on a clear spring morning in 1820. In Joseph Smith—History 1:14–20 , a struggle precedes the appearance of two Personages, and one introduces the other as His beloved Son. Joseph’s question about religious belonging becomes part of a much larger encounter with God. Latter-day Saints receive this account as foundational testimony of the Father and the Son and of the opening of the Restoration. Joseph’s written witness allows us to follow the question he brought and the answer he understood himself to receive. Our own seeking may unfold very differently. Reading his account directly can encourage patient prayer and careful attention to the sources, while leaving each reader room to consider the testimony honestly. Pause and consider What question does Joseph bring, and how does the account enlarge the subject beyond that question? Joseph Smith—History 1:14–20 Read and discover Joseph and Sidney testify that He lives Explore and study We saw Him Joseph and Sidney look up from their work as the vision opens before them. Their testimony reaches beyond the room: they have seen the living Son of God. Doctrine and Covenants 76:19–24 While Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon meditate on scripture, the vision recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 76:19–24 opens their understanding. They testify of seeing the Son at the Father’s right hand and hearing the witness of His divine identity. The testimony also connects Christ with the creation of worlds and the relationship of their inhabitants to God. This is a joint witness, not a scene with Joseph alone. It contributes to the Restoration’s insistence that the risen Savior is living and active, while linking back to the scriptural witness of His creative work. The surrounding revelation explores a much larger vision of salvation. Beginning with these verses helps keep Christ Himself at the center of that study rather than treating the revelation only as a map of the life to come. Pause and consider How does this testimony connect the Savior’s present life with His identity before Bethlehem? Doctrine and Covenants 76:19–24 Read and discover The Lord accepts His house Explore and study The Lord in His house Joseph and Oliver lift their eyes toward the Savior in the temple. His words assure them that He has accepted the house built to His name. Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10 On April 3, 1836, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery pray in the Kirtland Temple after participating in the day’s worship. Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10 records their vision of the Lord standing upon the pulpit breastwork. He identifies Himself as the living One who was slain, speaks of forgiveness and accepts the house built to His name. The account connects divine glory with words of mercy and rejoicing. The Savior who appears with a radiant countenance speaks forgiveness and calls His people to lift their hearts. His acceptance of the temple leads toward the continuing covenant work described in the rest of the section. The building matters because of the One whose name it bears and the blessings He intends to extend through the work entrusted to His people. Pause and consider Which words of the Lord’s message would have made this encounter more than a striking visual experience? Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10 Read and discover The Savior’s words reach a prisoner The opening of Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 gives voice to Joseph Smith’s anguish while imprisoned at Liberty. His questions concern absence, suffering and the plight of the Saints. The response speaks of peace, endurance and the limits of his affliction. In Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 , the Savior’s descent beneath suffering becomes part of the reassurance and instruction he receives. Explore and study Listening with patience At a shared worktable, one person listens while another explains a concern. Patient attention can give practical shape to persuasion, gentleness and love. Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–44 These are words of revelation in a painful historical setting; the passages do not record a visible appearance of Christ in the cell. Nor should they be used to tell someone that every harm was divinely desired or that distress must be hidden. Joseph’s questions remain in scripture beside the answer. Their presence gives readers a way to bring anguish honestly into prayer while continuing to seek help, justice and faithful action. Later in the same revelation, D&C121:41–44 speaks of persuasion, gentleness, kindness and love in the use of influence. Words that emerge from imprisonment can shape how a person with responsibility treats others today. Pause and consider What does it mean to you that the pleading questions were preserved together with the response? Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–44 Read and discover His work reaches beyond death Explore and study Messengers prepared to serve The Savior addresses the righteous spirits and sends messengers to carry the gospel onward. Doctrine and Covenants 138 places this ministry between His death and Resurrection. Doctrine and Covenants 138:18–20 · Doctrine and Covenants 138:29–37 In 1918, Joseph F. Smith records a vision concerning the redemption of the dead. Doctrine and Covenants 138:11–24 describes the righteous assembled in the spirit world and Christ declaring redemption. Doctrine and Covenants 138:27–37 explains how His message reaches others: He organizes faithful messengers and commissions them to carry the gospel to those in darkness. The date of the vision and the time of the ministry it reveals are different. The passage explicitly places Christ’s described visit between His Crucifixion and Resurrection. It also says He did not personally go among the wicked. Those distinctions help us read the revelation carefully while receiving its broad hope that death does not place people beyond the reach of His redemptive work. Pause and consider How does the presence of commissioned messengers enlarge your understanding of service in Christ’s name? Doctrine and Covenants 138:11–24 Doctrine and Covenants 138:27–37 Read and discover A testimony that gathers the whole journey The Living Christ, issued on January 1, 2000, gathers the testimony of the First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve Apostles around the Savior’s identity and mission. It connects Jehovah, creation, mortal ministry, Atonement, Resurrection, Restoration and His promised return. Its scriptural witnesses include the creative role described in John 1:1–3 and the testimony recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 76:22–24 . Explore and study A testimony sung together Voices join in a quiet room as singers follow their leader. Shared song can become an offering of faith and praise. Moroni 6:9 · Doctrine and Covenants 25:12 Read the full testimony through the source link below, then return to one of the original passages it cites. That movement keeps a broad declaration connected to the scriptural accounts on which it draws. The testimony gathers the whole life and mission of Christ without limiting Him to one season or episode. It can become a useful companion as you move between the branches of this journey, remembering how each encounter belongs to the same living Savior. Testimony also finds expression in worship. Moroni6:9 includes prayer and song in the life of the gathered Church, while D&C25:12 gives the song of the heart a place before God. Singing can help a community attend together to the Savior it confesses. Pause and consider Which part of the testimony would you like to explore through its original scripture source? John 1:1–3 Doctrine and Covenants 76:22–24 Moroni 6:9 Doctrine and Covenants 25:12 Read and discover His love in an ordinary day Explore and study Listening before offering help At the entrance to the home, a resident explains what would help while the others listen. Useful care begins with attention to the person who will receive it. Moroni 7:45–48 Mormon’s teaching preserved in Moroni 7:45–48 describes charity through patience, kindness, humility and endurance, then connects it with the pure love of Christ. He invites hearers to pray to the Father to be filled with that love. The passage presents charity as something received and cultivated, with consequences for how a person lives. Making time, keeping a promise, bringing useful help or listening patiently to someone who is grieving can give charity a place in an ordinary day. We offer that care freely, allowing others their own feelings and response. As we pray for the pure love of Christ, we can also notice the person who needs our attention now. Pause and consider What specific act of patient love could you offer without expecting recognition or a particular response? Moroni 7:45–48 Read and discover Remembering Him together Explore and study Preparing the table Quiet preparation makes the table ready for worship. Ordinary hands attend to the bread, water and cloth before the congregation gathers. records.title: The Father introduces His Son
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ in the Restoration and Today
records.text: Read and discover The Father introduces His Son The First Vision Joseph kneels among the trees. Explore his account of the Father and the Son appearing in answer to his prayer. Open study → Joseph Smith’s published history describes his attempt to pray in the woods on a clear spring morning in 1820. In Joseph Smith—History 1:14–20 , a struggle precedes the appearance of two Personages, and one introduces the other as His beloved Son. Joseph’s question about religious belonging becomes part of a much larger encounter with God. Latter-day Saints receive this account as foundational testimony of the Father and the Son and of the opening of the Restoration. Joseph’s written witness allows us to follow the question he brought and the answer he understood himself to receive. Our own seeking may unfold very differently. Reading his account directly can encourage patient prayer and careful attention to the sources, while leaving each reader room to consider the testimony honestly. Pause and consider What question does Joseph bring, and how does the account enlarge the subject beyond that question? Joseph Smith—History 1:14–20

records.title: Joseph and Sidney testify that He lives
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ in the Restoration and Today
records.text: Read and discover Joseph and Sidney testify that He lives Explore and study We saw Him Joseph and Sidney look up from their work as the vision opens before them. Their testimony reaches beyond the room: they have seen the living Son of God. Doctrine and Covenants 76:19–24 While Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon meditate on scripture, the vision recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 76:19–24 opens their understanding. They testify of seeing the Son at the Father’s right hand and hearing the witness of His divine identity. The testimony also connects Christ with the creation of worlds and the relationship of their inhabitants to God. This is a joint witness, not a scene with Joseph alone. It contributes to the Restoration’s insistence that the risen Savior is living and active, while linking back to the scriptural witness of His creative work. The surrounding revelation explores a much larger vision of salvation. Beginning with these verses helps keep Christ Himself at the center of that study rather than treating the revelation only as a map of the life to come. Pause and consider How does this testimony connect the Savior’s present life with His identity before Bethlehem? Doctrine and Covenants 76:19–24

records.title: The Lord accepts His house
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ in the Restoration and Today
records.text: Read and discover The Lord accepts His house Explore and study The Lord in His house Joseph and Oliver lift their eyes toward the Savior in the temple. His words assure them that He has accepted the house built to His name. Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10 On April 3, 1836, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery pray in the Kirtland Temple after participating in the day’s worship. Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10 records their vision of the Lord standing upon the pulpit breastwork. He identifies Himself as the living One who was slain, speaks of forgiveness and accepts the house built to His name. The account connects divine glory with words of mercy and rejoicing. The Savior who appears with a radiant countenance speaks forgiveness and calls His people to lift their hearts. His acceptance of the temple leads toward the continuing covenant work described in the rest of the section. The building matters because of the One whose name it bears and the blessings He intends to extend through the work entrusted to His people. Pause and consider Which words of the Lord’s message would have made this encounter more than a striking visual experience? Doctrine and Covenants 110:1–10

records.title: The Savior’s words reach a prisoner
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ in the Restoration and Today
records.text: Read and discover The Savior’s words reach a prisoner The opening of Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 gives voice to Joseph Smith’s anguish while imprisoned at Liberty. His questions concern absence, suffering and the plight of the Saints. The response speaks of peace, endurance and the limits of his affliction. In Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 , the Savior’s descent beneath suffering becomes part of the reassurance and instruction he receives. Explore and study Listening with patience At a shared worktable, one person listens while another explains a concern. Patient attention can give practical shape to persuasion, gentleness and love. Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–44 These are words of revelation in a painful historical setting; the passages do not record a visible appearance of Christ in the cell. Nor should they be used to tell someone that every harm was divinely desired or that distress must be hidden. Joseph’s questions remain in scripture beside the answer. Their presence gives readers a way to bring anguish honestly into prayer while continuing to seek help, justice and faithful action. Later in the same revelation, D&C121:41–44 speaks of persuasion, gentleness, kindness and love in the use of influence. Words that emerge from imprisonment can shape how a person with responsibility treats others today. Pause and consider What does it mean to you that the pleading questions were preserved together with the response? Doctrine and Covenants 121:1–9 Doctrine and Covenants 122:7–9 Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–44

records.title: His work reaches beyond death
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ in the Restoration and Today
records.text: Read and discover His work reaches beyond death Explore and study Messengers prepared to serve The Savior addresses the righteous spirits and sends messengers to carry the gospel onward. Doctrine and Covenants 138 places this ministry between His death and Resurrection. Doctrine and Covenants 138:18–20 · Doctrine and Covenants 138:29–37 In 1918, Joseph F. Smith records a vision concerning the redemption of the dead. Doctrine and Covenants 138:11–24 describes the righteous assembled in the spirit world and Christ declaring redemption. Doctrine and Covenants 138:27–37 explains how His message reaches others: He organizes faithful messengers and commissions them to carry the gospel to those in darkness. The date of the vision and the time of the ministry it reveals are different. The passage explicitly places Christ’s described visit between His Crucifixion and Resurrection. It also says He did not personally go among the wicked. Those distinctions help us read the revelation carefully while receiving its broad hope that death does not place people beyond the reach of His redemptive work. Pause and consider How does the presence of commissioned messengers enlarge your understanding of service in Christ’s name? Doctrine and Covenants 138:11–24 Doctrine and Covenants 138:27–37

records.title: A testimony that gathers the whole journey
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ in the Restoration and Today
records.text: Read and discover A testimony that gathers the whole journey The Living Christ, issued on January 1, 2000, gathers the testimony of the First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve Apostles around the Savior’s identity and mission. It connects Jehovah, creation, mortal ministry, Atonement, Resurrection, Restoration and His promised return. Its scriptural witnesses include the creative role described in John 1:1–3 and the testimony recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 76:22–24 . Explore and study A testimony sung together Voices join in a quiet room as singers follow their leader. Shared song can become an offering of faith and praise. Moroni 6:9 · Doctrine and Covenants 25:12 Read the full testimony through the source link below, then return to one of the original passages it cites. That movement keeps a broad declaration connected to the scriptural accounts on which it draws. The testimony gathers the whole life and mission of Christ without limiting Him to one season or episode. It can become a useful companion as you move between the branches of this journey, remembering how each encounter belongs to the same living Savior. Testimony also finds expression in worship. Moroni6:9 includes prayer and song in the life of the gathered Church, while D&C25:12 gives the song of the heart a place before God. Singing can help a community attend together to the Savior it confesses. Pause and consider Which part of the testimony would you like to explore through its original scripture source? John 1:1–3 Doctrine and Covenants 76:22–24 Moroni 6:9 Doctrine and Covenants 25:12

records.title: His love in an ordinary day
records.pageTitle: Jesus Christ in the Restoration and Today
records.text: Read and discover His love in an ordinary day Explore and study Listening before offering help At the entrance to the home, a resident explains what would help while the others listen. Useful care begins with attention to the person who will receive it. Moroni 7:45–48 Mormon’s teaching preserved in Moroni 7:45–48 describes charity through patience, kindness, humility and endurance, then connects it with the pure love of Christ. He invites hearers to pray to the Father to be filled with that love. The passage presents charity as something received and cultivated, with consequences for how a person lives. Making time, keeping a promise, bringing useful help or listening patiently to someone who is grieving can give charity a place in an ordinary day. We offer that care freely, allowing others their own feelings and response. As we pray for the pure love of Christ, we can also notice the person who needs our attention now. Pause and consider What specific act of patient love could you offer without expecting recognition or a particular response? Moroni 7:45–48

records.title: The Risen Savior in the Book of Mormon
records.pageTitle: The Risen Savior in the Book of Mormon
records.keywords: risen savior in the book of mormon
records.text: Read and discover They learn to hear the voice Explore and study They turn to listen Faces turn upward as the people listen again. This time they understand the voice directing them to the Beloved Son. 3 Nephi 11:1–7 A multitude has gathered around the temple in Bountiful, speaking about the changes in the land and about Jesus Christ. In 3 Nephi 11:1–7 , they hear a voice but do not understand it at first. On the third hearing they open their ears and look toward heaven. The Father introduces His beloved Son and directs them to hear Him. The introduction leads into the personal witness recorded in 3 Nephi 11:8–17 , when the risen Savior descends and invites the people to come to Him. Reading the two passages together preserves the movement from hearing to recognition. The Book of Mormon presents this as another witness of the same Jesus whose Resurrection the New Testament records, while giving these people their own encounter, place and testimony. Pause and consider What does the repeated listening add to the opening of this account? 3 Nephi 11:1–7 3 Nephi 11:8–17 Read and discover He gives them time to understand After teaching, Jesus tells the people that they cannot yet understand all He has been commanded to say. In 3 Nephi 17:1–6 , He invites them to go home, ponder, pray to the Father in His name and prepare for His return. Then He sees their tears and their desire for Him to remain, and responds with compassion. Explore and study Words carried home The people make their way home after Jesus departs. His invitation goes with them: ponder what they have heard, pray to the Father and prepare for His return. 3 Nephi 19:1 The invitation to ponder is not followed by an immediate departure. The healing and blessings in the rest of the chapter grow from His attention to the people before Him. This is a generous model of learning: a listener may need time, prayer and another meeting with a passage. We do not have to confuse the amount we have read with the depth of what we have understood. The actual return home comes after His later departure. Third Nephi 19:1 records the people dispersing to their households. The invitation to ponder can now be carried into the life of a home. Pause and consider Which teaching would benefit from another quiet reading at home before you move on? 3 Nephi 17:1–6 3 Nephi 19:1 Read and discover Make room for those who come Jesus instructs the people to meet together often and allow others to come among them. In 3 Nephi 18:22–25 , He tells them to pray for those who join them and to hold up the light of His own example. His invitation to the multitude becomes a pattern for how they are to receive others. Explore and study Room for the gathered people People find their places as the gathering forms twelve groups. The disciples prepare to teach those who have come to hear. 3 Nephi 19:4–8 The passage connects worship with welcome. A community that remembers Christ is asked to consider the experience of the person entering it. Its light is not simply a claim to possess truth; it is the Savior’s example made visible in its conduct. A present-day application might be as ordinary as learning a visitor’s name, helping someone follow the study or making space for a person who does not yet feel at home. When the people gather the next morning, the disciples organize them into twelve groups and teach the words Jesus has given them. Third Nephi 19:4–8 shows welcome taking practical form through attention to those who need to hear. Pause and consider What might someone new to your community learn about Christ from the way you receive them? 3 Nephi 18:22–25 3 Nephi 19:4–8 Read and discover He entrusts a ministry to the disciples Explore and study Overshadowed as He departs A cloud hides Jesus from the multitude as He departs. The disciples bear witness that He ascends into heaven. 3 Nephi 18:38–39 At the close of this part of the visit, Jesus touches the chosen disciples one by one and speaks to them. 3 Nephi 18:36–39 distinguishes what the multitude witnesses from what the disciples report: the people do not hear the words, while the disciples bear record of receiving power to give the Holy Ghost. A cloud then overshadows the people as He departs. The distinction between witnesses is useful. The record does not ask us to pretend that every person saw and heard everything. It identifies how testimony reaches the community and shows that Christ prepares others to continue ministering. His departure therefore belongs to a story of entrusted service as well as an extraordinary appearance. Pause and consider How does the account’s care about who heard and saw each detail strengthen your reading of it? 3 Nephi 18:36–39 Read and discover The people gather again Explore and study The news travels through the night News of the Savior's visit reaches a household in the night. Attentive faces receive the message as others prepare to gather the next day. 3 Nephi 19:2–3 News of the Savior’s visit spreads before dark and through the night. In 3 Nephi 19:1–14 , many labor to reach the place where He is expected the next day. The disciples arrange the multitude into twelve groups, repeat what Jesus taught and pray with them. Nephi is baptized and then baptizes the others Jesus has chosen. These preparations receive more space in the record than a simple statement that the people were excited. They travel, gather, listen, pray and receive ordinances. The disciples’ care to teach the same words underscores whose ministry this is. Their example can prompt us to consider how preparation changes the way we receive worship or scripture, without assuming every gathering will reproduce their extraordinary signs. Explore and study Into the water Water runs from the young disciple's robe as Nephi steadies him. After receiving baptism himself, Nephi baptizes those Jesus has chosen. 3 Nephi 19:10–12 Pause and consider What preparation could help you participate more thoughtfully in your next opportunity to worship? 3 Nephi 19:1–14 Read and discover Children of the covenant Jesus connects the people before Him with the prophets, the house of Israel and the covenant made with Abraham. In 3 Nephi 20:25–31 , He describes blessing in terms of turning people from iniquity and speaks of the covenant reaching beyond the immediate gathering. Their encounter with Him belongs within a purpose extending across peoples and generations. Explore and study Encircled as if by fire Still in their wet clothing, the disciples look up to receive the angels' ministry. The light around them recalls the heavenly fire witnessed by the multitude after their baptism. 3 Nephi 19:13–14 This covenant language can be unfamiliar, but its reach is important. It joins the Old Testament promise to Abraham with the risen Savior’s ministry and the invitation to live differently. The passage is not a license for pride over ancestry or contempt for another people. It invites readers to see divine blessing as a responsibility and a gift that is intended to reach outward. Earlier in the visit’s second day, 3Nephi19:13–14 records the disciples receiving the Holy Ghost after baptism. The covenant teaching is heard among people who have already begun responding through prayer and ordinances. Pause and consider How does the connection between blessing and turning from iniquity shape your understanding of covenant? 3 Nephi 20:25–31 3 Nephi 19:13–14 Read and discover He opens the scriptures to future generations Explore and study He helps them understand Jesus gives the listeners His attention as He explains the scriptures. His teaching opens their understanding and prepares words of hope for generations still to come. 3 Nephi 26:1–6 Jesus gives the people words associated with Malachi and then explains them. Read 3 Nephi 24:1–6 and 3 Nephi 25:1–6 alongside the explanation in 3 Nephi 26:1–5 . He says these scriptures had not been in their possession and were given for the benefit of future generations. The act of teaching includes preserving words that later readers will need. The sequence helps explain why this record is concerned with both immediate listeners and people who come after them. The Savior’s teaching reaches from creation toward judgment, placing particular prophetic words within a larger purpose. We can follow that example by reading the supplied passages in context instead of reducing them to isolated phrases about the future. Pause and consider What changes when you read a passage as a gift intended for people beyond its first audience? 3 Nephi 24:1–6 3 Nephi 25:1–6 3 Nephi 26:1–5 Read and discover Children have something to give In 3 Nephi 26:14–16 , Jesus ministers to the children and enables them to speak marvelous things to their parents. The record then describes another gathering on the following day, after His departure, when even infants speak. It explicitly says that the marvelous words were not to be written. The account gives us the event while withholding its content. Explore and study A man restored to life A man who had died stands alive before the Savior. Third Nephi records this miracle briefly, leaving us to consider the life restored to him. 3 Nephi 26:15 This scene differs from the blessing of the children in 3 Nephi 17. Keeping the moments distinct helps us appreciate the range of their place in His ministry: children receive His care, and they also have something the adults are asked to hear. Our reflection can begin with attentive listening to children today, without inventing the unrecorded teachings or making claims about what a particular child must know. The brief summary in 3Nephi26:15 also records a man being raised from the dead. No extended account is supplied, but the detail adds another witness of the Savior’s power within these days of ministry. Pause and consider When could you give a child enough time and attention to hear what they are trying to express? 3 Nephi 26:14–16 Read and discover The life He asks His disciples to follow Jesus explains His gospel through His coming to do the Father’s will, His being lifted upon the cross and His drawing people to judgment. In 3 Nephi 27:13–21 , repentance, baptism, faithfulness and sanctification belong within the response to His redeeming work. The teaching begins with what He has done and then calls people into a life shaped by that gift. Explore and study Care becomes a way of life The people minister to one another and hold things in common. Shared necessities give an imagined everyday form to the mutual care recorded after the Savior's ministry. 3 Nephi 26:19–20 In 3 Nephi 27:27 , He directs the disciples to His own example as the pattern for what they should become. That question reaches beyond outward resemblance or occasional acts of kindness. It asks how His honesty, mercy, obedience and willing service can shape a person over time. The record’s broad invitation is therefore deeply personal: learn who He is, receive His gospel and let His example work its way into the choices before you. Third Nephi 26:19–20 describes a community changed in its ordinary relationships. The people minister to one another, share what they have and deal justly. His gospel becomes visible in their common life. Pause and consider Which feature of His example would you like to practice in one specific relationship? 3 Nephi 27:13–21 3 Nephi 27:27 3 Nephi 26:19–20 Continue with Jesus Christ Next study in the journey Jesus Christ in the Restoration and today Explore restored witnesses of the living Savior, daily discipleship, and hope in His promised return.
