Attentive faces receive the message as others prepare to gather the next day. 3 Nephi 19:2–3 News of the Savior’s visit spreads before dark and through the night. In 3 Nephi 19:1–14 , many labor to reach the place where He is expected the next day. The disciples arrange the multitude into twelve groups, repeat what Jesus taught and pray with them. Nephi is baptized and then baptizes the others Jesus has chosen. These preparations receive more space in the record than a simple statement that the people were excited. They travel, gather, listen, pray and receive ordinances. The disciples’ care to teach the same words underscores whose ministry this is. Their example can prompt us to consider how preparation changes the way we receive worship or scripture, without assuming every gathering will reproduce their extraordinary signs. Explore and study Into the water Water runs from the young disciple's robe as Nephi steadies him. After receiving baptism himself, Nephi baptizes those Jesus has chosen. 3 Nephi 19:10–12 Pause and consider What preparation could help you participate more thoughtfully in your next opportunity to worship? 3 Nephi 19:1–14

records.title: Children of the covenant
records.pageTitle: The Risen Savior in the Book of Mormon
records.text: Read and discover Children of the covenant Jesus connects the people before Him with the prophets, the house of Israel and the covenant made with Abraham. In 3 Nephi 20:25–31 , He describes blessing in terms of turning people from iniquity and speaks of the covenant reaching beyond the immediate gathering. Their encounter with Him belongs within a purpose extending across peoples and generations. Explore and study Encircled as if by fire Still in their wet clothing, the disciples look up to receive the angels' ministry. The light around them recalls the heavenly fire witnessed by the multitude after their baptism. 3 Nephi 19:13–14 This covenant language can be unfamiliar, but its reach is important. It joins the Old Testament promise to Abraham with the risen Savior’s ministry and the invitation to live differently. The passage is not a license for pride over ancestry or contempt for another people. It invites readers to see divine blessing as a responsibility and a gift that is intended to reach outward. Earlier in the visit’s second day, 3Nephi19:13–14 records the disciples receiving the Holy Ghost after baptism. The covenant teaching is heard among people who have already begun responding through prayer and ordinances. Pause and consider How does the connection between blessing and turning from iniquity shape your understanding of covenant? 3 Nephi 20:25–31 3 Nephi 19:13–14

records.title: He opens the scriptures to future generations
records.pageTitle: The Risen Savior in the Book of Mormon
records.text: Read and discover He opens the scriptures to future generations Explore and study He helps them understand Jesus gives the listeners His attention as He explains the scriptures. His teaching opens their understanding and prepares words of hope for generations still to come. 3 Nephi 26:1–6 Jesus gives the people words associated with Malachi and then explains them. Read 3 Nephi 24:1–6 and 3 Nephi 25:1–6 alongside the explanation in 3 Nephi 26:1–5 . He says these scriptures had not been in their possession and were given for the benefit of future generations. The act of teaching includes preserving words that later readers will need. The sequence helps explain why this record is concerned with both immediate listeners and people who come after them. The Savior’s teaching reaches from creation toward judgment, placing particular prophetic words within a larger purpose. We can follow that example by reading the supplied passages in context instead of reducing them to isolated phrases about the future. Pause and consider What changes when you read a passage as a gift intended for people beyond its first audience? 3 Nephi 24:1–6 3 Nephi 25:1–6 3 Nephi 26:1–5

records.title: Children have something to give
records.pageTitle: The Risen Savior in the Book of Mormon
records.text: Read and discover Children have something to give In 3 Nephi 26:14–16 , Jesus ministers to the children and enables them to speak marvelous things to their parents. The record then describes another gathering on the following day, after His departure, when even infants speak. It explicitly says that the marvelous words were not to be written. The account gives us the event while withholding its content. Explore and study A man restored to life A man who had died stands alive before the Savior. Third Nephi records this miracle briefly, leaving us to consider the life restored to him. 3 Nephi 26:15 This scene differs from the blessing of the children in 3 Nephi 17. Keeping the moments distinct helps us appreciate the range of their place in His ministry: children receive His care, and they also have something the adults are asked to hear. Our reflection can begin with attentive listening to children today, without inventing the unrecorded teachings or making claims about what a particular child must know. The brief summary in 3Nephi26:15 also records a man being raised from the dead. No extended account is supplied, but the detail adds another witness of the Savior’s power within these days of ministry. Pause and consider When could you give a child enough time and attention to hear what they are trying to express? 3 Nephi 26:14–16

records.title: The life He asks His disciples to follow
records.pageTitle: The Risen Savior in the Book of Mormon
records.text: Read and discover The life He asks His disciples to follow Jesus explains His gospel through His coming to do the Father’s will, His being lifted upon the cross and His drawing people to judgment. In 3 Nephi 27:13–21 , repentance, baptism, faithfulness and sanctification belong within the response to His redeeming work. The teaching begins with what He has done and then calls people into a life shaped by that gift. Explore and study Care becomes a way of life The people minister to one another and hold things in common. Shared necessities give an imagined everyday form to the mutual care recorded after the Savior's ministry. 3 Nephi 26:19–20 In 3 Nephi 27:27 , He directs the disciples to His own example as the pattern for what they should become. That question reaches beyond outward resemblance or occasional acts of kindness. It asks how His honesty, mercy, obedience and willing service can shape a person over time. The record’s broad invitation is therefore deeply personal: learn who He is, receive His gospel and let His example work its way into the choices before you. Third Nephi 26:19–20 describes a community changed in its ordinary relationships. The people minister to one another, share what they have and deal justly. His gospel becomes visible in their common life. Pause and consider Which feature of His example would you like to practice in one specific relationship? 3 Nephi 27:13–21 3 Nephi 27:27 3 Nephi 26:19–20

records.title: The Teachings and Parables of Jesus Christ
records.pageTitle: The Teachings and Parables of Jesus Christ
records.text: Six paths through His teaching Explore the parables of Jesus Mercy, Repentance, and the Joy of Returning Jesus teaches mercy through searches, debts, patient care, and the welcome of a father. These studies invite us to receive His compassion, respond honestly, and make room for another person's return. Open study → Loving Our Neighbor The neighbor in Jesus' teaching is someone whose need calls for attention. Explore the difference between noticing, welcoming, and following through with care. Open study → Hearing and Living His Word Jesus' teaching asks for more than recognition. Follow the movement from listening and understanding to patience, discernment, and action. Open study → The Kingdom of God Jesus teaches the kingdom through growth, discovery, invitation, and judgment. Each image contributes something particular; none needs to carry the whole meaning by itself. Open study → Faithful Stewardship and the Cost of Discipleship Jesus asks how people use what has been entrusted to them. These studies explore responsibility, generosity, honest preparation, and the freedom to serve without comparison. Open study → Prayer, Readiness, and His Return Jesus joins prayer with humility, readiness with service, and hope with honest attention to uncertainty. These studies invite steady faithfulness without pretending to know the time or outcome. Open study → Jesus teaches through stories and comparisons drawn from ordinary life. These six paths help you explore their settings, notice their questions, and consider how to receive His word. Read each teaching in its Gospel context; the themes are study aids. The library includes 47 main parables and judgment pictures, together with 16 related comparisons and allegories. Counts vary according to how short comparisons are grouped. These labels describe this study library, not an official fixed count. Read and discover The life He calls blessed Matthew introduces the Sermon on the Mount with Jesus seated and His disciples coming to Him. In Matthew 5:1–12 , He speaks of people who are poor in spirit, who mourn, who are meek, merciful or pure in heart, and who hunger for righteousness. His words place blessing beside circumstances and qualities that are not always honored by the world. Explore and study A city that cannot be hidden A hillside town remains visible above the valley. The imagined setting illustrates Jesus' comparison of His disciples to a city on a hill, within His teaching about good works that glorify the Father. Matthew 5:13–16 These sayings deserve more than a quick list of desirable traits. Each joins a human condition or response to a promise within God’s kingdom. Mourning is not called pleasant, and persecution is not something to seek for its own sake. Jesus addresses lives that may be difficult while teaching what His kingdom values. Choose one saying to read slowly, noticing both the person described and the promise attached to it. Immediately after the Beatitudes, Matthew 5:13–16 turns to salt and light. These ordinary images ask what a disciple’s life contributes to the people around it. Pause and consider Which Beatitude brings a person you know to mind, and how could you respond with greater care? Matthew 5:1–12 Matthew 5:13–16 Read and discover Pray to your Father In Matthew 6:5–15 , Jesus speaks about the purpose of prayer before giving a model for it. He contrasts prayer aimed at public recognition with prayer addressed sincerely to the Father. The pattern He gives includes reverence, the Father’s will, daily need, forgiveness and help in the face of temptation. Explore and study They neither toil nor spin A woman spins wool into thread. This ordinary work of making clothing gives context to Jesus' contrast with the lilies, which neither toil nor spin, as He teaches about the Father's care. Matthew 6:25–30 The order widens prayer beyond a list of requests. We bring real needs, but also learn to desire God’s purposes and to consider our relationships with others. The warning against empty repetition is not a ban on returning to the same honest concern. It calls us to speak as people seeking God, rather than treating words as a performance or a mechanism that obliges Him to respond on our timetable. Jesus continues in Matthew 6:25–30 by pointing to birds and flowers. Attention to the ordinary living world becomes part of His teaching about trust and the Father’s care. Pause and consider Which part of the prayer Jesus teaches could help you express something you have struggled to say? Matthew 6:5–15 Matthew 6:25–30 Read and discover Love God and your neighbor Explore and study A thoughtful answer Jesus gives the scribe His attention as they speak about loving God and neighbor. Mark records a sincere question, a thoughtful answer and the Savior's recognition of the man's understanding. Mark 12:28–34 A scribe who has heard Jesus answer well asks about the foremost commandment. In Mark 12:28–34 , Jesus answers from Israel’s scriptures, joining love for God with love for one’s neighbor. The scribe responds thoughtfully, and Jesus recognizes the understanding in his answer. This is a conversation worth hearing with its mutual attention intact. The exchange gathers religious life around love that involves heart, soul, mind and strength. Love of neighbor is not an unrelated second subject; it belongs beside devotion to God. The account also resists a flat picture of every religious teacher as hostile to Jesus. Here a sincere question opens into recognition, inviting us to listen for understanding even across a difference of position or background. Pause and consider What would loving with your mind and strength add to an act of kindness this week? Mark 12:28–34 Read and discover He notices two small coins The widow’s two coins Jesus draws His disciples' attention to the widow's small gift and the sacrifice behind it. He sees what the size of an offering alone cannot tell them. Open study → Jesus sits opposite the treasury and watches people give. In Mark 12:41–44 , a poor widow places two small coins among the offerings. He calls His disciples’ attention to her because the size of her gift cannot be understood apart from what she has to live on. An amount that looks small to an observer carries great cost for her. The scene asks us to look beyond visible totals when considering devotion. It should not become a way to pressure a person in need to give money they cannot safely spare. Jesus sees the widow’s circumstances, and readers should not overlook them. Her story can deepen gratitude for quiet sacrifice and make us more attentive to the people whose contributions are easily dismissed. Pause and consider What contribution might you value differently if you understood the giver’s circumstances? Mark 12:41–44 Read and discover Listening within a busy home Martha welcomes Jesus into her home, while her sister Mary sits at His feet and listens. In Luke 10:38–42 , Martha asks Him to tell Mary to help with the work. Jesus responds to Martha’s troubled attention and affirms Mary’s choice to receive His words. Both the hospitality and the conversation belong to this particular household moment. Explore and study Peter notices the withered tree Peter stops beside the dry branches and turns to Jesus. What he has noticed on the road opens a teaching about faith, prayer and forgiveness. Mark 11:20–25 Martha’s service is real, and Jesus addresses her with personal concern. The question is what is drawing her attention at that moment. Even worthwhile responsibilities can become entangled with resentment or worry; time with the Savior’s words may help us return to those responsibilities with a different heart. Mary’s place at His feet also makes her a receiving disciple, someone whose attention and learning are welcomed within this home. Listening continues outside a home as well. In Mark 11:20–25 , Peter notices the withered fig tree and Jesus teaches about faith, prayer and forgiveness. A moment on the road becomes an invitation to bring both trust and relationships before the Father. Room to hear His words Martha brings her concern to Jesus while Mary listens at His feet. His answer calls Martha by name and draws her attention to the good part Mary has chosen. Open study → Pause and consider Where might you need to pause and receive before continuing to give? Luke 10:38–42 Mark 11:20–25 Read and discover An invitation spoken with love A man runs to Jesus, kneels and asks about eternal life. In Mark 10:17–27 , Jesus speaks of commandments and then looks on him with love before inviting him to sell his possessions, help the poor and follow Him. The man goes away grieving. Mark allows both Jesus’s love and the difficulty of the invitation to remain visible. Explore and study A promise to make things right Zacchaeus stands before Jesus with open hands and a promise: to share with the poor and repay those he has wronged. The Savior listens as welcome becomes a changed way of living. Luke 19:5–10 This is a recorded encounter, not a parable. Its challenge should not be softened into the idea that possessions never shape discipleship, nor flattened into the claim that wealth automatically measures a person’s spiritual worth. The disciples are astonished by what follows, and Jesus directs them to what is possible with God. The story asks what we find hardest to release when His invitation reaches beyond our familiar obedience. Another wealthy man responds differently in Luke 19:5–10 . Zacchaeus speaks of giving and restitution, and Jesus speaks of salvation coming to his house. Set beside the grieving rich man, his response invites reflection on the practical changes that welcome can make possible. Jesus looked on him with love Jesus looks on the man with love and invites him to follow. Before the sorrowful departure, Mark gives us this moment of personal love and a searching invitation. Open study → Pause and consider What does Mark’s note that Jesus loved the man change about how you hear the invitation? Mark 10:17–27 Luke 19:5–10 Read and discover A coin and a deeper allegiance Some Pharisees and Herodians approach Jesus with a question intended to trap Him over tribute to Caesar. In Mark 12:13–17 , He asks for a coin and draws attention to its image and inscription. His answer distinguishes what is owed to Caesar from what belongs to God, and the questioners marvel. Explore and study He stoops to the ground Jesus bends to write on the ground while the woman stands before Him. We are not told what He writes. As the accusers leave, His words join mercy with a call to leave sin behind. John 8:3–11 The exchange does not provide a complete rulebook for every later political dispute. It exposes an attempt to force Jesus into a narrow choice and turns the discussion toward obligation and allegiance. A reader can begin by asking what belongs to God in a life that also includes civic duties. That question reaches into honesty, conduct and the way we treat people, rather than remaining only a debate about what others should do. John 8:3–11 records another question intended to test Him, this time at the expense of a woman brought before Him. Jesus’s response interrupts the accusation and joins mercy with an invitation to leave sin. The text records His writing on the ground without revealing the words. Whose image is on the coin? Jesus responds to a question about tribute by asking His listeners to consider the image on a coin and their duty to God. Open study → Pause and consider Which ordinary responsibility could you approach more faithfully because your life belongs to God? Mark 12:13–17 John 8:3–11 Read and discover The Teacher takes the towel John frames the washing of the disciples’ feet with Jesus’s knowledge of His relationship to the Father. In John 13:3–17 , He rises from supper, takes a towel and basin, and begins to wash their feet. Peter’s resistance brings a conversation about receiving what Jesus offers. The Teacher then explains the example He has given them. Explore and study Following the sign Jesus gave The water jar rests securely in the man's arms as Peter and John follow him through the lane. Jesus's simple instruction leads them toward the place where they will prepare the Passover. Luke 22:7–13 His authority is expressed through willing service. Yet the passage begins with disciples needing to receive His care, not simply deciding to become useful themselves. Both movements belong in discipleship: allowing Christ to cleanse and teach us, and extending humble service to others. The basin and towel give that teaching a concrete form that cannot be reduced to kind feelings alone. Before the meal, Luke 22:7–13 describes Peter and John preparing a place according to Jesus’s instructions. Their ordinary work gives another form to service before the Teacher takes the towel. As I have done to you Jesus kneels with a basin and towel. He asks His disciples to follow His example of service. Open study → Pause and consider Is it harder for you to offer help humbly or to receive it humbly, and why? John 13:3–17 Luke 22:7–13 Read and discover A life that remains in Him Explore and study Branches apart from the vine Detached branches lie withered beside a living vine. John 15:6 gives this sober counterpart to the fruitful branches as Jesus teaches His disciples to remain in Him. John 15:1–6 In John 15:1–17 , Jesus describes Himself as a vine, His Father as the gardener and His disciples as branches. The image develops into teaching about remaining in Him, bearing fruit, keeping His commandments and loving one another. The passage is an extended comparison, and its value grows as its connected parts are read together. The image points toward dependence and a continuing relationship. A branch does not create its own source of life, yet it truly bears fruit. Jesus’s teaching likewise joins what His disciples receive from Him with what they become and do. His parables often invite this kind of attentive reading: notice the picture, listen for His explanation and allow the teaching to challenge your life without inventing a fixed meaning for every small detail. Pause and consider What practice helps you remain connected to Christ when life becomes hurried? John 15:1–17 Continue with Jesus Christ Next study in the journey The Redeemer and risen Lord Follow the final days of His mortal ministry, His sacrifice, and the witnesses of His Resurrection. Open study → Related studies The Teacher in His Ministry Return to the people and settings in which His invitations were heard. Open study → The Compassion He Practiced See how His actions give weight to His teaching about love. Open study → His Love and His Sacrifice Follow the service of the upper room toward the Atonement. Open study → His Teaching among the Nephites Compare related teachings while respecting the different setting and audience. Open study → Sources for further study Bible Dictionary: Parables Guide to the Scriptures: Parable Official Bible videos: Teachings

The Teacher then explains the example He has given them. Explore and study Following the sign Jesus gave The water jar rests securely in the man's arms as Peter and John follow him through the lane. Jesus's simple instruction leads them toward the place where they will prepare the Passover. Luke 22:7–13 His authority is expressed through willing service. Yet the passage begins with disciples needing to receive His care, not simply deciding to become useful themselves. Both movements belong in discipleship: allowing Christ to cleanse and teach us, and extending humble service to others. The basin and towel give that teaching a concrete form that cannot be reduced to kind feelings alone. Before the meal, Luke 22:7–13 describes Peter and John preparing a place according to Jesus’s instructions. Their ordinary work gives another form to service before the Teacher takes the towel. As I have done to you Jesus kneels with a basin and towel. He asks His disciples to follow His example of service. Open study → Pause and consider Is it harder for you to offer help humbly or to receive it humbly, and why? John 13:3–17 Luke 22:7–13

records.title: A life that remains in Him
records.pageTitle: The Teachings and Parables of Jesus Christ
records.text: Read and discover A life that remains in Him Explore and study Branches apart from the vine Detached branches lie withered beside a living vine. John 15:6 gives this sober counterpart to the fruitful branches as Jesus teaches His disciples to remain in Him. John 15:1–6 In John 15:1–17 , Jesus describes Himself as a vine, His Father as the gardener and His disciples as branches. The image develops into teaching about remaining in Him, bearing fruit, keeping His commandments and loving one another. The passage is an extended comparison, and its value grows as its connected parts are read together. The image points toward dependence and a continuing relationship. A branch does not create its own source of life, yet it truly bears fruit. Jesus’s teaching likewise joins what His disciples receive from Him with what they become and do. His parables often invite this kind of attentive reading: notice the picture, listen for His explanation and allow the teaching to challenge your life without inventing a fixed meaning for every small detail. Pause and consider What practice helps you remain connected to Christ when life becomes hurried? John 15:1–17

records.title: Joseph Smith: The Face Behind the History
records.pageTitle: Joseph Smith: The Face Behind the History
records.text: 01 · A person before a portrait History has a human face A familiar face can make a distant life feel closer. This journey follows the surviving evidence and the choices behind the likeness used in our new Joseph Smith artwork. Creative interpretation · Explore the picture A moment of warmth A relaxed gaze and a slight smile bring warmth to this imagined moment. The face follows our adopted portrait; the setting and expression are creative choices, not a record of a particular encounter. Read descriptions of Joseph Smith The scenes and reconstructed portraits on this page are artistic interpretations. The museum photographs show historical artifacts. 02 · What the plaster preserves The death masks Historical artifact photograph Joseph on the left. Hyrum on the right. These are the Dibble masks in the Church History Museum collection. Their worn surfaces are part of the objects’ history. Image: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Open the museum collection account ↗ The museum dates George Cannon’s molds to June 29, 1844, after the brothers’ deaths. The date when the surviving casts were made is unknown. Their forms offer important evidence of facial proportions, while repairs and copying complicate individual details. Follow the masks’ history. Explore the evidence: casts, copies, and 3D models The museum distinguishes the Dibble masks from the Pedestal masks, whose history is less certain. Some details differ because of repair or finishing. Treat each object as a source with its own history. Church History specialists later used photographs from many angles to create detailed 3D models of the surviving masks. You can examine those artifacts through the official downloads. A model of a cast does not supply a living expression, eye color, or hair. View the masks and model downloads See how the 3D models were made Joseph beside his own death mask Joseph: our adopted portrait Joseph’s open eyes and living expression invite a comparison with his own mask. This is the exact portrait adopted for focusChrist; hair, skin, color and expression remain artistic choices. Explore the museum mask collection Joseph: the historical cast The plaster preserves a closed-eyed, postmortem impression of Joseph’s face. Examine the nose, brow and chin while remembering the effects of casting, repairs and copying. Photograph courtesy of the Museum of Church History and Art, reproduced in BYU Studies, Figure 18, page 30 . Explore the museum mask collection Hyrum beside his own death mask Hyrum: an artistic reconstruction This reconstruction presents Hyrum at age 44, drawing on his own death-mask references and historical profile. The masks cannot establish hair, eye or skin color; open eyes, expression and living soft tissue require interpretation. Read Hyrum’s biographical record Hyrum: the historical cast Hyrum’s own mask offers a distinct face to study. A repair obscures the cleft in the Dibble mask’s chin; the museum notes that the Pedestal version retains it. Its damaged and repaired surface should not be mistaken for an undisturbed view of his living features. Photograph courtesy of the Museum of Church History and Art, reproduced in BYU Studies, Figure 18, page 30 . Explore the museum mask collection Creative interpretation · Explore the picture Beside my brother Joseph rests an arm around Hyrum’s shoulders, and the brothers smile at each other in shirts with rolled sleeves and suspenders. This imagined moment places the brothers together in 1844; the garden, clothing and exchange are artistic choices. Joseph’s recorded affection for Hyrum gives this scene its historical starting point. Read about Joseph and Hyrum’s bond Pause and look: what can this source tell you? Choose one feature you can see in the mask. What can you observe directly? What would you need a portrait, written description, or another source to explore? 03 · A moment held by an artist Joseph sat for a portrait Creative interpretation · Explore the picture Sitting in the light Joseph waits in the window light as an artist works nearby. This imagined sitting introduces a real question: what can a portrait made from life preserve, and what does the artist’s style contribute? Open the June 25, 1842 journal entry Joseph’s journal records a sitting for a profile on June 25, 1842. The Joseph Smith Papers identifies the artist as Sutcliffe Maudsley. A portrait made from life is valuable evidence, but its line, angle, and style still deserve attention. Read the entry and its annotation. Explore the evidence: the surviving portraits The museum traces Maudsley’s Nauvoo portraits and their influence on later images. Compare the historical examples with the creative scene above; that scene does not reconstruct a documented room or identify the unseen artist. Explore the Nauvoo portrait artist and his work Try a comparison: what changes from one view to another? Look at the historical profile and the museum mask. Notice how viewpoint changes the nose, jaw, and eye area. Which differences might come from angle or artistic technique? 04 · From references to a consistent likeness How we developed the focusChrist portrait Creative interpretation · Explore the picture A quiet page Joseph looks down at the open page, intent on his work. The pose changes the way his face catches the light. No particular letter, revelation, or journal entry is being depicted. Explore Joseph Smith’s journal Our portrait was developed using the Church History Museum’s death-mask references. Joseph’s masks informed the facial proportions; Hyrum’s were considered for comparison. We adopted the resulting artistic portrait as the reference for new scenes, keeping the same recognizable face as pose and expression change. Explore our process: evidence, interpretation, and review Begin with the references. The masks inform structure. Historical portraits and descriptions help readers examine appearance from other perspectives. Make the creative choices visible. Living eyes, skin, hair, expression, clothing, and light require interpretation. The adopted portrait is not an authenticated photograph or a forensic identification. Keep the person recognizable. New scenes use the adopted portrait as their image reference. We compare faces, hands, expression, clothing, and the full composition, including how the picture reads on a phone. This page’s artwork follows that process. Our project record establishes how we developed and adopted the image; it does not establish historical certainty about every feature. Return to the adopted portrait Revisit the historical mask references 05 · More than a fixed expression A face changes when a person speaks Creative interpretation · Explore the picture Across the table An open hand and attentive eyes give this imagined conversation its movement. The listeners are unnamed, and the encounter is not tied to a recorded event. The portrait supplies a consistent face; the human moment is an artistic choice. Compare remembered descriptions Written descriptions can add movement, voice, and personal impressions to the visual record. They also differ. The Church’s survey of Joseph’s appearance brings several accounts together and shows why no single description gives a complete picture. Explore the descriptions. Reflect: what does an expression add? Compare the attentive face at the desk with the outdoor portrait. What changes in your response? Which part comes from the historical evidence, and which part comes from the artist’s choices? 06 · Follow the life as well as the likeness Keep exploring Joseph Smith Let the pictures lead you back to the person’s words, work, and historical setting. Who was Joseph Smith? Explore his life, testimony, and the foundational questions. Return to Church History Follow the people, places, and records of the Restoration. Explore Book of Mormon Evidences Study the translation, witnesses, and surviving record. Ask a question about this study Open the source shelf Church History Museum: Joseph and Hyrum Death Masks Church History Library: Imaging the Death Masks Joseph Smith Papers: journal, June 25, 1842 Church History Museum: Nauvoo Portrait Artist Church Magazines: What Did Joseph Smith Really Look Like? The mask photographs are historical source material. The scenes and reconstructed portraits are creative interpretations; Joseph’s appearance follows the adopted focusChrist portrait. The project’s portrait-development record supplies the account of our own process.

records.title: Missionary Work
records.text: His work throughout the world Invite Others to Come Unto Christ Discover how love, service, and the restored gospel invite people to Christ. “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.” Mark 16:15 Meet with Missionaries Explore Ways to Serve Christ's commission A call to teach, baptize, and help people follow Him After His Resurrection, Jesus Christ sent His disciples to teach all nations, baptize in His name, and help people live what He taught. Latter-day Saint missionary work continues from that commission. “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations.” Matthew 28:19 Read the Savior's commission Jesus teaches His Apostles as they walk together. Their calling begins with following Him. Select the image to learn more and choose the full-size view. Restoration and early missionaries From a Book of Mormon in hand to a worldwide witness Missionary work began before the Church was formally organized and gathered momentum during Joseph Smith's lifetime. 1829–1830 The message begins to travel Early believers shared the Book of Mormon and testified of the Restoration even before the Church's organization. June 1830 Samuel Smith is called Joseph Smith's brother Samuel became the first missionary called after the Church was organized, carrying copies of the Book of Mormon through communities near Palmyra, New York. 1830s–1840s Missions cross borders and oceans Missionaries traveled through the United States and Canada and then to England and the Pacific, often serving at great personal sacrifice. Today Local disciples build a global Church Missionaries serve among many cultures and languages while local members and leaders nurture faith in their own communities. Carrying the message Samuel Smith began with a few books, a willing heart, and faith that the message would find those prepared to receive it. Crossing oceans Early missionaries left familiar homes and carried their witness into new nations, languages, and communities. Study Early Missionaries Explore the Growth of the Work One Savior, one invitation, carried with love throughout the world. The missionary purpose Help people draw closer to the Savior Missionaries do more than deliver a message. They help people build faith in Jesus Christ, turn toward Him, prepare for baptism, receive the gift of the Holy Ghost, and continue along the covenant path. That work is personal. It happens through prayer, scripture study, sincere conversation, patient listening, invitations to act in faith, and continued friendship. Read the Missionary Purpose Faith expressed through action What Missionaries Do Every assignment is different, but the work remains centered on Jesus Christ and the needs of God's children. 01 Teach of Jesus Christ Missionaries study the scriptures, share the restored gospel, answer questions, and testify of the Savior. 02 Listen and Invite They seek to understand each person, then offer simple invitations that help faith become personal action. 03 Serve with Love Missionaries lift burdens through practical service, community work, disaster cleanup, and everyday kindness. 04 Strengthen Communities They work with local members and leaders, support new friends, and help build belonging that continues after a visit. A pattern for every disciple Love, Share, Invite Sharing the gospel is not limited to full-time missionaries. It can grow naturally from Christlike love, honest friendship, and respect for each person's agency. Love See the person first Pray for people, listen without an agenda, and serve because they are children of God, not because you expect a particular response. Share Speak naturally of goodness Share what gives you hope in Jesus Christ through ordinary conversation, personal experience, scripture, and quiet example. Invite Open a door without pressure Offer a simple invitation to learn, worship, serve, or meet missionaries, then honor the answer with warmth and friendship. Explore Love, Share, Invite Every nation, kindred, tongue, and people A Worldwide Work, Lived One Person at a Time Missionaries serve across languages, cultures, cities, villages, and local communities. The setting changes, but the pattern remains: love people, respect their agency, teach clearly, and point them toward Jesus Christ. Scriptures that shape the work Study the invitation to serve and gather Matthew 28:19–20 Teach all nations The risen Lord commissions His disciples to teach, baptize, and trust His continuing presence. Doctrine and Covenants 4:3 Desires to serve The Lord connects a willing desire with a call to participate in His work. Doctrine and Covenants 18:15–16 Joy in helping souls return Missionary service finds its deepest joy in helping even one person come unto Jesus Christ. Mosiah 18:8–9 Bear one another's burdens Disciples witness of God through compassion, comfort, and a willingness to mourn with others. Called to serve Different Assignments, the Same Savior Missionary calls and assignments are suited to the missionary and to the needs of God's children. Listening before teaching Missionary lessons begin with people, their questions, and a sincere desire to help them draw closer to Jesus Christ. Serving side by side Young adults and senior couples offer different gifts while sharing the same purpose of loving and lifting God's children. Young adults Teaching Missionaries Young elders and sisters serve away from home, learn to teach the gospel, and invite people to come closer to Jesus Christ. Learn about teaching missions Local service Service Missionaries Young service missionaries live at home and serve God and His children through assignments shaped around local needs and individual capacity. Explore service missions Experience offered Senior Missionaries Senior couples and individuals may teach, support Church operations, strengthen local leaders, serve charities, and use a lifetime of experience to bless others. Discover senior opportunities A simple first conversation What Happens When You Meet Missionaries? You can meet at home, online, at church, or in another comfortable public place. Missionaries will listen to your questions, pray with you, read scripture with you, and discuss the teachings of Jesus Christ. Missionary visits are free. Choose a time and place. Meet in the setting that feels comfortable to you. Bring your questions. The conversation should begin with what matters to you. Decide your next step. You choose whether and how the conversation continues. Request a Missionary Visit Know What to Expect Continue the journey Choose a path to learn or serve Follow a trusted source, deepen your study, or begin a real conversation. Study Preach My Gospel Learn the doctrine, skills, and Christlike purpose that guide missionary service. Explore Church History Continue into source-grounded stories of the Restoration and the Church's worldwide growth. Discover Global Stories Use the official Church History collection to learn how faith took root in many places. Meet Missionaries Ask questions and learn about Jesus Christ in a free conversation arranged around you. Independent website. focusChrist is not an official website of, sponsored by, or endorsed by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Missionary information and next steps link to current official Church resources. Official Missionary Resources Ask a Gospel Question Watch, read, and reflect Faith shared through words and service These messages join personal testimony with sincere care for another person. Church video What Do Missionaries Do? See how missionaries seek to follow Jesus Christ by teaching His gospel and serving people. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church video Missionary Work: Sharing What Is in Your Heart Explore simple, respectful ways disciples can love, share, and invite. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Continue with sharing and service Study before a conversation, or continue afterward Meeting missionaries can bring both curiosity and uncertainty. You can prepare by reading a short passage and bringing your own questions. You may ask what a term means, request the source of a teaching, or say that you need more time. A respectful conversation makes room for your background and your choices. In Matthew 28:18-20 , the risen Jesus commissions His disciples to teach and baptize, and promises His presence. Read the commission with its focus on Him. It explains the Christian invitation to discipleship; it does not remove another person's freedom to consider, ask, or decline an invitation. Start with Jesus Christ Learn what Latter-day Saints mean by His Atonement and Resurrection. Bring a question about how those beliefs shape daily discipleship. Read a passage before discussing the book Explore its purpose and try a focused reading. Separate questions about its teachings from questions about its origin. Consider the invitation to pray Study prayer and discernment without assuming everyone receives an answer in the same way or at the same speed. After a conversation, return to the original passage and write down what was explained, what you understood differently, and what remains open. You do not need to resolve every question in one visit.

records.text: You can meet at home, online, at church, or in another comfortable public place. Missionaries will listen to your questions, pray with you, read scripture with you, and discuss the teachings of Jesus Christ. Missionary visits are free.

records.title: Choose a path to learn or serve
records.text: Follow a trusted source, deepen your study, or begin a real conversation. Study Preach My Gospel Learn the doctrine, skills, and Christlike purpose that guide missionary service. Explore Church History Continue into source-grounded stories of the Restoration and the Church's worldwide growth. Discover Global Stories Use the official Church History collection to learn how faith took root in many places. Meet Missionaries Ask questions and learn about Jesus Christ in a free conversation arranged around you.

records.title: Faith shared through words and service
records.text: These messages join personal testimony with sincere care for another person. Church video What Do Missionaries Do? See how missionaries seek to follow Jesus Christ by teaching His gospel and serving people. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Church video Missionary Work: Sharing What Is in Your Heart Explore simple, respectful ways disciples can love, share, and invite. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Continue with sharing and service

records.title: Study before a conversation, or continue afterward
records.text: Meeting missionaries can bring both curiosity and uncertainty. You can prepare by reading a short passage and bringing your own questions. You may ask what a term means, request the source of a teaching, or say that you need more time. A respectful conversation makes room for your background and your choices. In Matthew 28:18-20 , the risen Jesus commissions His disciples to teach and baptize, and promises His presence. Read the commission with its focus on Him. It explains the Christian invitation to discipleship; it does not remove another person's freedom to consider, ask, or decline an invitation. Start with Jesus Christ Learn what Latter-day Saints mean by His Atonement and Resurrection. Bring a question about how those beliefs shape daily discipleship. Read a passage before discussing the book Explore its purpose and try a focused reading. Separate questions about its teachings from questions about its origin. Consider the invitation to pray Study prayer and discernment without assuming everyone receives an answer in the same way or at the same speed. After a conversation, return to the original passage and write down what was explained, what you understood differently, and what remains open. You do not need to resolve every question in one visit.

records.title: Latter-day Saint Pioneer Stories
records.text: Faith across the journey Pioneer Faith & History Explore pioneer faith and history through stories, sources, and questions. What would you like to understand? Ask about pioneer lives, journeys, and faith. Follow historical sources and related focusChrist studies beneath each answer. AI-assisted answers are study aids and may contain errors. Unreviewed questions and limited recent context may be sent to external AI providers for research and verification. Please do not submit sensitive personal information. PIONEER TOPICS The gathering begins From Nauvoo to Winter Quarters The westward story began with families leaving homes they had built, crossing the Mississippi River, and enduring the difficult first season in temporary settlements along the Missouri River. Leaving Nauvoo, 1846 Families crossed the Mississippi and began an uncertain journey west. Winter Quarters, 1846 to 1847 Temporary homes became places of preparation, worship, grief, and endurance. 1846–1847 Leaving home, preparing a way The pioneer story begins before the handcart companies. Families leaving Nauvoo crossed Iowa, endured a winter beside the Missouri and prepared for the mountains. Their road passed through Indigenous homelands, not an empty continent. The pictures are historical illustrations created for this study, not photographs of the events. Named figures draw on historical portraits; clothing, settings and unrecorded faces are artistic interpretations. Open a picture for its account, source and full-size view. February 1846 · Open picture study Crossing the Mississippi The departure from Nauvoo began with wagons ferried across the Mississippi on February 4, 1846. Families gathered at Sugar Creek in Iowa, carrying provisions and belongings into an uncertain future. When the camp moved west on March 1, the journey was only beginning: the Missouri River, not the Salt Lake Valley, would become that year’s stopping place. Leaving home is more than a line on a map. Consider what a family could carry, what it had to leave, and the help it would need from its neighbors. National Park Service: the departure Spring 1846 · Open picture study The slow miles across Iowa Rain, flooded streams and deep mud slowed the companies across Iowa. A wagon could carry a household’s necessities and still become a burden in a difficult crossing. Reaching the Missouri River took months; the hoped-for journey west unfolded through delays, illness and repeated work. Faith did not make the mud disappear. This scene invites us to notice patient effort and the ordinary hands that keep another family moving. National Park Service: the 1846 trek Garden Grove and Mount Pisgah · 1846 · Open picture study Planting for people still to come At Garden Grove and Mount Pisgah, pioneers established farms and stopping places to help later travelers. Some stayed to plant while others continued. Their service reached beyond their own immediate company: shelter and food prepared today could sustain a family arriving later. At Winter Quarters, the revelation now recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 136 joined the practical organization of travel with care for people in need. Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:8–9 and consider whose journey your preparation might lighten. National Park Service: the 1846 trek Revelations in Context: the covenant Read Revelations in Context: the covenant alongside Doctrine and Covenants 136:8–9 . The gospel purpose of a company included responsibility for those who needed help. 1846–1896 · Journey timeline · 9 milestones THE JOURNEY The Exodus Begins - February 1846 The first wagons left Nauvoo, Illinois, on February 4, 1846, beginning the westward exodus. The National Park Service estimates that nearly 70,000 Latter-day Saint emigrants followed the trail to the Great Salt Lake Valley from 1847 through 1868. Winter Quarters - 1846-1847 After crossing Iowa, the Saints established Winter Quarters on the west bank of the Missouri River in present-day Omaha, Nebraska. Other settlements and outfitting camps were established across the river in Iowa. Entering the Valley - July 21-24, 1847 Members of the advance company entered the Salt Lake Valley before Brigham Young, who was ill and traveling behind them. Young's carriage entered the camp on July 24, 1847. Pioneer Day - July 24, 1847 The arrival is celebrated. Today, Pioneer Day is a Utah state holiday commemorating this historic journey. 1850s-1900s Temple Square Development Temple Square evolves from a muddy lot to a spiritual center. The Tabernacle and other buildings transform the heart of Salt Lake City. 1853-1893 Salt Lake Temple Construction Construction of the Salt Lake Temple began in 1853. The temple was dedicated in 1893, forty years after the cornerstone ceremony. Handcart Companies - 1856-1860 Over 3,000 pioneers pull handcarts across the plains. The Martin and Willie handcart companies face tragic rescues in 1856. 1869 Transcontinental Railroad The golden spike was driven at Promontory Summit on May 10, 1869. The completed transcontinental railroad reduced a journey of months to days and brought the organized overland pioneer era to a close. January 4, 1896 Utah Statehood Utah became the 45th state on January 4, 1896, after a long and contested path from territory to statehood. Life between landmarks The trail was lived one day at a time Beyond the dates and destinations, the journey was made through ordinary work, long stretches beside the Platte River, and difficult crossings that required the strength of the entire company. Daily Life on the Trail Repairs, meals, animals, and family responsibilities continued with every mile. Westward Beside the Platte Companies followed the broad river corridor across the plains in natural traveling groups. Crossing the Rivers People, animals, and wagons worked together against current, rock, and cold water. A new wave of gathering · 1856 Across an ocean, then the plains The handcart story began in homes and ports far from the American plains. Preparation, limited resources and the season of departure shaped what followed. British emigration · 1856 · Open picture study The journey began across an ocean For Elizabeth Crook Panting, the plains came after an Atlantic crossing. She sailed on the Thornton with Christopher and Jane. Her brother Samuel Lane Crook was also aboard; Peter Madsen’s diary records his marriage to Sarah Haines during the voyage. Samuel and Sarah stayed in the East and did not make the Willie company’s overland journey with Elizabeth. The family also remembered a fire aboard ship: Elizabeth alerted the captain and prayed with her children. This episode comes through the family history gathered in Tell My Story, Too , rather than a ship’s log examined for this page. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 Summer 1856 · Open picture study Making ready at Iowa City The Willie company journal records making tents, building carts, preparing wagons and weighing luggage. Its July entries also record births, deaths, worship and ordinary tasks such as washing clothing. Emigration was already demanding before the company began its passage across the plains on July 15. The same journal makes daily travel tangible: an early bugle, breakfast, prayers, greasing carts, packing tents and another stretch of road. These were people meeting practical needs while caring for one another. Read the Willie company journal Florence · August 1856 · Open picture study A late departure and a long road Handcarts offered a less expensive way to reach Utah, with emigrants pulling limited belongings in wooden carts. Ten companies traveled this way from 1856 through 1860. Most did not suffer the catastrophe of the late Willie and Martin companies. Their experience should not be confused with every handcart journey. At Florence, the question of continuing so late in the season was serious. The dated rescue overview below includes Levi Savage’s warning and the companies’ separate departures. Families listen together beside a waiting cart in this interpretation of a camp discussion. Church History: handcart companies Read the official 1856 timeline Nauvoo to the valley · Trail guide · 13 landmarks THE TRAIL These landmarks trace the route; the general route labels do not give an arrival date for every company. The Church History Pioneer Sketches exhibit documents William Clayton’s June 21, 1847 visit to Independence Rock and places the surviving drawings in the wider trail landscape. 1846 Nauvoo, Illinois The organized exodus began here in February 1846 after violence, legal conflict, and pressure against the Latter-day Saints in Illinois. Wagons crossed the Mississippi River into Iowa Territory. 1846 Garden Grove, Iowa The pioneers established Garden Grove as an Iowa way station, where they planted crops and built shelters to help companies that followed. Winter 1846 Missouri River Settlements Winter Quarters stood in present-day Omaha, Nebraska, with additional camps and settlements across the river in Iowa. This Missouri River area became the principal staging and outfitting region for westward companies. 1847 route Chimney Rock, Nebraska Famous natural landmark on the trail. This distinctive rock formation served as a beacon for weary travelers crossing the plains. Summer 1847 Fort Laramie, Wyoming This established trading post on the North Platte River was an important landmark and resupply point on several western emigrant trails. June 21, 1847 Independence Rock, Wyoming This prominent granite landmark became known for the names and dates carved or painted by travelers on the western emigrant trails. William Clayton reached it with the vanguard company on June 21, 1847. 1847 route Sweetwater River, Wyoming The trail followed and repeatedly crossed the Sweetwater River. Devil's Gate, a narrow gorge cut by the river, became one of the route's best-known landmarks. 1847 route South Pass, Wyoming Crossing the Continental Divide. This gentle pass through the Rocky Mountains opened the way to the Great Basin. July 1847 Fort Bridger, Wyoming Fort Bridger was a trading post and landmark on the final portion of the route toward the Great Salt Lake Valley. July 1847 Echo Canyon, Utah The trail passed through this narrow canyon during the final mountain approach toward the Salt Lake Valley. July 1847 Emigration Canyon, Utah Steep canyon descent into the valley. Pioneers guide their wagons through narrow passages before emerging into Salt Lake Valley. July 21-24, 1847 Salt Lake Valley, Utah Members of the advance company entered the valley before Brigham Young arrived on July 24. The company began planting crops and digging irrigation ditches soon after arrival. 1857 Mountain Meadows, Utah The 1857 Mountain Meadows Massacre occurred far south of the main 1846-1847 pioneer route. It is included here only as a separate and painful episode in territorial Utah history; follow the official Church History topic for a sourced account. A mother’s faith · The Willie company Elizabeth Crook Panting and her children A mother, a little boy and a baby stand at the heart of this account. We can honor their testimony by telling what the family preserved, identifying how it comes to us and leaving unknown details unfilled. The Willie company · 1856 · Open picture study Elizabeth, Christopher and Jane Elizabeth Crook Panting began the overland journey with Christopher, five, and Jane, one. Christopher turned six on the way west; Elizabeth turned twenty-nine in October. Their names give the migration an intimate scale: a mother, a young boy and a baby, traveling toward a hoped-for home. The Church’s historical database records all three in the Willie company. Christopher later recalled that his father, Frederick, opposed Elizabeth’s Church participation, threatened her and hid her shoes. He remembered her borrowing shoes for worship and leaving with the children; on a train, another woman exchanged clothing with her to help her avoid recognition. These details survive as his family recollection. Elizabeth in the Church History database Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 Elizabeth’s family account · Open picture study Fuel for a hungry camp As food dwindled on the trail, the family account remembers Elizabeth going out to gather buffalo chips for fuel. She had nearly filled her apron when an unfamiliar man approached and asked about her situation. She told him of the hunger in camp. He offered help and led her over a small hill. The remembered encounter begins with ordinary work for a family’s survival. Neither an exact date nor a securely identified cave location is supplied by the principal family account. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 The account Elizabeth’s family preserved · Open picture study The gift in the cave Elizabeth followed the man to a cave where dried buffalo meat was hanging. He filled her apron with meat and instructed her to share it with others in need. After showing her the direction back to camp, he was gone. When she turned to thank him, she could no longer find either the man or the cave. The meat remained in her apron. This is the miracle as the family remembered it. The illustration leaves the stranger unidentified, as we do here. The account does not establish that he was Christ, an angel or a particular scriptural person. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 Relief among the Willie company · Open picture study A gift meant to be shared Elizabeth returned and distributed the meat to people who needed food. In the family’s telling, the blessing reached beyond her own children. Jennie Edith Bell Mason’s later biography, preserved in the Church History Library, also records the cave, the dried meat and her return to the company. Her journey still required endurance. The family remembered Jane becoming dangerously ill in the handcart. Mason’s biography describes the children sheltered in a rescue wagon during the Rocky Ridge ordeal while Elizabeth walked. Mother and children reached Salt Lake City with the Willie company on November 9. Read the family biography in the Church History Library Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 More of Elizabeth’s story and how it was preserved The family remembered Elizabeth trusting a blessing that she and her children would reach the valley safely. Her son Wilford Woodruff Cranney later spoke of that trust and her continuing faith. The surviving compilation associates the blessing with Wilford Woodruff; its exact setting has not been independently established here. The cave account comes through later family histories, including Mason’s biography and the recollections collected by Jolene S. Allphin. Allphin cites Peter Madsen’s diary, family histories, and interviews with June Cranney Monson. A family diary is mentioned in that source chain, but its location was unknown; this page does not claim to quote an inspected original diary. Elizabeth Crook Panting is a different person from Eliza Crook. Allphin’s Eliza Crook sketch corrects an earlier misattribution of the meat account. Elizabeth’s cave must also remain distinct from Martin’s Cove and from Hanks’s later buffalo provision. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 · Read the family biography in the Church History Library Read the individual records for Christopher and Jane . The children’s ages here follow their recorded birth dates. Faith under strain Handcarts, hardship, and rescue Most handcart companies reached the valley safely. The late departure of the Willie and Martin companies in 1856 placed them in severe autumn storms, where relief parties carried food, clothing, blankets, and hope east from Utah. The Handcart Journey, 1856 Families carried only what their carts and their own strength could bear. Rescue Wagons Arrive Relief parties met the companies with supplies, teams, shelter, and human care. October–November 1856 Go out and bring them in Willie and Martin were separate companies with different crisis points and arrival dates. Relief grew from Brigham Young’s urgent appeal into weeks of travel, giving, nursing and difficult choices. Brigham Young · October 5, 1856 · Open picture study Send help now On October 5, Brigham Young called for teams, wagons, flour and men to bring in the emigrants still on the plains. Wilford Woodruff’s journal records the concrete scale of the appeal: sixty teams, twelve tons of flour and forty additional teamsters. Concern for distant travelers became an assignment requiring immediate preparation and sacrifice. The call invites a direct question for disciples of Jesus Christ: what does another person need from me now? Read Matthew 25:35–40 beside this appeal for food, clothing and willing hands. Wilford Woodruff’s journal: October 5, 1856 Preparing the relief wagons · Open picture study The rescue began at home Women gathered bedding, clothing and other supplies while rescuers traveled east. Lucy Meserve Smith remembered the work of women in Provo to comfort those in need. Their service continued as survivors arrived; one delivery of food could not meet every need. Salt Lake City was still warm when the first appeal was made. The first relief company left on October 7, before the storm caught the emigrants on October 19. Further appeals and supplies sustained the rescue over the following weeks. Read about women’s relief efforts Church historic sites: how the rescue began Willie company · October 23, 1856 · Open picture study The hard climb at Rocky Ridge Relief did not instantly restore exhausted bodies. Daniel W. Jones later remembered rescuers bringing fuel, distributing provisions and encouraging the Willie emigrants. Some were already beyond recovery. The company still faced Rocky Ridge, a long, exposed crossing remembered for terrible suffering and loss. The dated overview records the crossing and the burials at Rock Creek. Remembering rescue also means remembering those who did not survive. Alma 7:11–12 directs our faith toward a Savior who knows suffering, rather than treating survival as a measure of anyone’s righteousness. Daniel W. Jones: later firsthand recollection Read the official 1856 timeline North Platte · October 19, 1856 · Open picture study The Martin company in the storm The Martin company crossed the North Platte as the October 19 storm struck. It would be October 28 before express riders reached them, and October 31 before supply wagons arrived. In November they sheltered in the cove near Devil’s Gate, still suffering hunger, cold and exhaustion. Jones identified Joseph A. Young, Abel Garr and himself as the riders sent to find the remaining companies. He also remembered helping pull exhausted families into camp. Later, baggage was stored at Fort Seminoe so wagons could carry people; Jones and others stayed to guard that property through winter. Read the official 1856 timeline Daniel W. Jones: later firsthand recollection With the Martin company · November 1856 · Open picture study Ephraim Hanks brings food and care In a reminiscence recorded in 1891, Ephraim Hanks described a repeated nighttime call to help the handcart travelers. When a later appeal for volunteers came, he recalled answering, “I am ready now!” He was thirty in 1856 and joined the later rescue effort; he was not one of the riders who first reached Martin on October 28. Hanks remembered praying for a buffalo, finding one, and killing another the next day. He loaded his horses with meat and brought it to hungry families. He also recalled caring for the sick and administering priesthood blessings, including a healing near Fort Bridger. His testimony includes miraculous help alongside the lasting effects of frostbite. Tell My Story, Too: Ephraim Hanks’s recollection Ephraim Hanks: life and company record 1856 at a glance: the companies and the rescue Separate companies, one sustained rescue effort Date in 1856 Event May 4 / May 25 Thornton / Horizon sail from England. July 15 / July 22–25 Willie / Martin depart Iowa City. August 13 Levi Savage advises Willie to wait until spring. August 16 / August 25 Willie / Martin leave Florence. October 4 Franklin D. Richards reports the late companies. October 5 / October 7 Brigham’s appeal / first relief company departs. October 19 Storm; riders reach Willie; Martin crosses North Platte. October 21 Supply wagons reach Willie. October 23–24 Willie crosses Rocky Ridge; thirteen buried at Rock Creek. October 27 Hanks departs with later rescuers. October 28 / October 31 Riders / supply wagons reach Martin. November 4–9 Martin shelters in the cove. November 9 Willie arrives in Salt Lake City. November 10 Hanks brings buffalo meat to Martin. November 30 Martin arrives in Salt Lake City. December 15 Final Hunt and Hodgetts arrivals. Read the official 1856 timeline More witnesses to the rescue Elizabeth Horrocks Kingsford’s later autobiography remembers her children among the hungry Martin emigrants who received Hanks’s buffalo meat. Her account offers the perspective of a family that was fed. She is a different Elizabeth from Elizabeth Crook Panting, who traveled with Willie. Elizabeth H. Kingsford’s recollection Hanks’s experiences come through a later reminiscence, not an 1856 diary. His account of providing fresh meat is separate from Elizabeth’s account of dried meat in a cave. Both deserve to be told in their own words and setting, without borrowing details from a film reconstruction. Tell My Story, Too: Ephraim Hanks’s recollection · Daniel W. Jones: later firsthand recollection · Church historic sites: how the rescue began The handcart rescue included many people. Avoid reducing the Sweetwater crossing to the embellished claim that only three young men carried everyone across and died because of it. The Church’s history topic explains the difference between the rescue and later retellings. 1856 · Willie and Martin · 7 study topics Willie & Martin Companies July 1856 The Companies Depart Late The Willie and Martin handcart companies depart from Iowa City later than planned. The delay sets off a chain of events that will test faith and endurance to the limit. August-October 1856 Hardships Begin The late departure left the companies on the plains as food diminished and severe autumn weather approached. Snowstorms in October intensified the crisis. October 1856 Stranded in Wyoming Severe October snowstorms caught both companies in present-day Wyoming. Cold, hunger, exhaustion, and illness caused many deaths while rescuers traveled east from Utah. October 1856 The Rescue After learning that the companies were still on the trail, Brigham Young called for rescuers, wagons, food, clothing, and teams. Relief parties traveled east from the Salt Lake Valley and assisted the emigrants. November 4-9, 1856 Martin's Cove The Martin Company camped in the area now called Martin's Cove from November 4 to 9. The cove offered some shelter, but the emigrants continued to suffer from cold, hunger, illness, and exhaustion. November 1856 Arrival in Salt Lake The Willie Company reached Salt Lake City on November 9, and the Martin Company arrived on November 30. Residents received the survivors and helped provide food, clothing, and shelter. November 1856 The Faith and Legacy The Willie and Martin experience is remembered for suffering, rescue, faith, and the consequences of delayed departure and inadequate provisions. Read accounts of miracles and individual experiences with their sources identified, distinguishing records made during the journey from later firsthand recollections and family testimony. A destination becomes a home Arrival was the beginning of another work Entering the valley ended the overland journey, but it began years of planting, building, worship, and community life. The same faith that carried pioneers west shaped what they built after arriving. First View of the Valley, 1847 The mountain passage opened onto the place where the advance company would begin planting. Building a New Community Irrigation, shelter, food, and shared labor turned arrival into settlement. Building the Salt Lake Temple, 1853 to 1893 Four decades of work made the temple a lasting expression of covenant and sacrifice. The journey’s end—and what remained Home, remembrance and a second witness Arrival ended the miles, but recovery and remembrance continued. The witnesses who lived on carried both gratitude and grief into their homes and families. Salt Lake City · November 1856 · Open picture study The rescue continued inside the home As the Martin company approached Salt Lake City on November 30, Brigham Young asked residents to receive the newcomers into comfortable family homes and provide careful nursing and nourishment. The rescue was not complete at the city boundary. Its next work belonged in kitchens, sickrooms and households willing to share what they had. The Willie company had arrived on November 9. For Elizabeth and her children, the overland journey ended with all three alive. We remember their arrival alongside the grief of neighbors whose families had been broken by death. Brigham Young’s November 30 discourse Elizabeth in the Church History database A later Mother’s Day meeting in Pocatello · Open picture study Jane hears a second witness Years later, Jane was visiting a daughter in Pocatello when she attended a Mother’s Day church meeting. An elderly man recalled being a hungry boy in the Willie company. He remembered a woman sharing dried meat that she had received miraculously. Jane wept and told him that woman was her mother. Jane later told her niece, June Cranney Monson, about this encounter. For Jane, whose mother’s account had sometimes been ridiculed, his recollection was a treasured second witness. Jane had been a baby on the trek; this is her later encounter with a recipient of the food, not a claim that she witnessed the cave herself. The surviving account does not name the man or date the meeting. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 The railroad connection · 1869 · Open picture study The overland era gives way to rail On May 10, 1869, the transcontinental lines met at Promontory Summit. Railroad travel changed the journey west that wagons and handcarts had once made over many months. The waiting family and passenger train bring that change in travel into view. Elizabeth’s later life continued in Logan. The family history records marriages to William Wilkes and Hiram K. Cranney and remembers her enduring trust in God. She died on March 15, 1891, aged sixty-three. Jane and Christopher carried the family’s memories into another generation. National Park Service: Golden Spike history Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 Elizabeth in the Church History database As you finish, read Mosiah 18:8–9 and Galatians 6:2 . Whose burden can you help carry? The object of this remembrance is deeper discipleship in Jesus Christ. Music for the journey Songs of courage and redeeming love Pause with the music that carries faith from one heart to another. Hear the pioneers’ enduring hymn, then turn toward the Savior with a personal song of gratitude. Come, Come, Ye Saints William Clayton’s words have helped generations give voice to courage, grief, and trust in God. Listen to The Tabernacle Choir and Orchestra at Temple Square, then open these two picture studies. Open picture study A song shared at the end of the day A child looks up as the adults sing. Worn clothing and muddy ground tell of a difficult day; their gathered voices offer companionship before another morning on the trail. William Clayton wrote the hymn in April 1846 during the exodus from Nauvoo. Its courage belongs beside the real hardship of the journey. This imagined camp scene honors that shared faith without identifying the singers as a particular family. Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:28–29 . The Lord’s counsel at Winter Quarters gives a place to singing in joy and praying in sorrow. What song helps you turn toward Him? Open picture study Hope for the road ahead A mother and child share a glance as their family walks beside the wagon. The road still stretches ahead. This scene imagines the hymn’s hope in the daily work of continuing together. In Ether 12:4 , faith in God opens a hope that steadies the soul. As you listen, remember both the people who reached a new home and those whose journeys ended along the way. Consider one small way to strengthen someone who is still in the middle of a hard journey. Continue with faith in trials and Elizabeth’s story . Listen: Come, Come, Ye Saints ↗ Read the hymn The story behind the song Open picture study A prayer of gratitude Savior, Redeemer of My Soul Cold water surges around the handcart as weary travelers climb toward the bank. The Savior bends to help push, His attention on the man beside Him; heavenly helpers share the effort. This devotional scene gives visible form to faith in His redeeming love. The Martin and Hodgetts companies crossed the North Platte on October 19, 1856, as the first winter storm struck. Read the official timeline beside this picture. Christ and the angels are a devotional interpretation, rather than a recorded appearance at the crossing. Dallyn Vail Bayles sings Orson F. Whitney’s hymn text in Rob Gardner’s musical setting, with violinist Jenny Oaks Baker and the Lyceum Philharmonic. The published hymn pairs Whitney’s words with a different tune by Harry A. Dean. This recording is offered here as a devotional companion to the pioneer stories. Read Matthew 25:35–40 , the Savior’s teaching about feeding, clothing, and welcoming people in need. Then read Mosiah 24:14–15 , where He strengthens a people to bear their burdens. As you listen, consider where you need the Savior’s healing and how gratitude might shape your next act of kindness. Continue in the Atonement of Jesus Christ study . Listen: Dallyn Vail Bayles ↗ Read Matthew 25:35–40 Open each picture to follow its scripture connections and view it in full. These scenes invite reflection on the hymns; the river study distinguishes the historical crossing from its portrayal of heavenly help. PRIMARY-SOURCE JOURNALS Hear brief, verified voices from the trail, then open the Church History record to read the transcript in context. The Ask experience above also uses Tell My Story, Too to identify a pioneer before corroborating the selected person through authoritative records. October 5, 1856 Wilford Woodruff Woodruff recorded Brigham Young's call for sixty teams, twelve tons of flour and forty additional teamsters to bring in the emigrants. Summary of a contemporary diary entry, page 154. Read the diary July 8, 1856 Willie Company Journal With the tents finished, company members washed clothing, built handcarts and prepared wagons for the journey ahead. Summary of the company's contemporary camp journal at Iowa City. Read the journal The rescue, October 1856 Daniel W. Jones “There were two of us and hundreds needing help.” Jones's 1890 recollection of helping exhausted handcart travelers into camp at Avenue Hill. Read the recollection Watch, read, and reflect Carry the story into your own discipleship Hear Elder Ronald A. Rasband connect pioneer faith with the legacy we are building today. Church video Ronald A. Rasband | Special Witness of Christ Elder Ronald A. Rasband reflects on handcart pioneers and invites us to build a heritage of faith in Jesus Christ for those who follow. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Continue with Restoration and covenant study Read a life, then consider what it asks of us The trail becomes more understandable when a named person's record is read alongside the wider setting. Choose a journal or company record from this page. Note the author, the dates covered, and whether the words were recorded during the journey or remembered later. One person's experience matters, but it does not stand for every pioneer. Keep historical questions and devotional applications visible. “What happened, where, and when?” requires records and context. “How might I respond to a neighbor in need?” is a personal application. An image of rescue can invite compassion without supplying evidence for every detail of the historical scene. Accounts of endurance deserve care. Suffering is not proof that someone was more faithful, and survival is not a measure of divine favor. Remember those who died as people with relationships and unfinished lives, not merely examples in someone else's lesson. Compare evidence and accounts Use a worked historical inquiry before drawing conclusions from a single recollection. Explore faith and practical support Continue the theme of endurance with scripture that makes room for lament and help from others. When pioneer loss touches your own grief Find a quieter study that does not require turning bereavement into an inspiring story. For an optional response, consider one practical act of care you could offer today and ask whether it would be welcome. For geography, use named historical sites such as Fort Bridger State Historic Site in present-day Wyoming alongside the route rather than assuming historical territorial names match modern state boundaries. Pause, pray, and respond Faith for the next step After following the journeys and reading a record, pause with the counsel given at Winter Quarters in Doctrine and Covenants 136. These questions invite a personal response; they do not ask you to compare your suffering with another person’s. Who needs a place in our plans? Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:6–9 . Notice the preparations for people who would remain behind and the care required for vulnerable travelers. Whose needs might be overlooked in a plan you are making? Ask what would actually help before offering it. What can I make right? Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:23–26 . The counsel includes everyday speech, borrowed property, and returning what was lost. Is there a promise to keep, something to return, or a conversation to repair? Choose a small, honest next step. Bring joy and sorrow to the Lord Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:28–29 . The passage gives a place both to praise and to prayer in sorrow. Which invitation meets you today? You might choose a hymn, offer a quiet prayer, or sit with someone who needs company.
