records.title: From Nauvoo to Winter Quarters
records.text: The westward story began with families leaving homes they had built, crossing the Mississippi River, and enduring the difficult first season in temporary settlements along the Missouri River.

records.title: Leaving home, preparing a way
records.text: The pioneer story begins before the handcart companies. Families leaving Nauvoo crossed Iowa, endured a winter beside the Missouri and prepared for the mountains. Their road passed through Indigenous homelands, not an empty continent.

records.title: Crossing the Mississippi
records.text: February 1846 · Open picture study Crossing the Mississippi The departure from Nauvoo began with wagons ferried across the Mississippi on February 4, 1846. Families gathered at Sugar Creek in Iowa, carrying provisions and belongings into an uncertain future. When the camp moved west on March 1, the journey was only beginning: the Missouri River, not the Salt Lake Valley, would become that year’s stopping place. Leaving home is more than a line on a map. Consider what a family could carry, what it had to leave, and the help it would need from its neighbors. National Park Service: the departure

records.title: The slow miles across Iowa
records.text: Spring 1846 · Open picture study The slow miles across Iowa Rain, flooded streams and deep mud slowed the companies across Iowa. A wagon could carry a household’s necessities and still become a burden in a difficult crossing. Reaching the Missouri River took months; the hoped-for journey west unfolded through delays, illness and repeated work. Faith did not make the mud disappear. This scene invites us to notice patient effort and the ordinary hands that keep another family moving. National Park Service: the 1846 trek

records.title: Planting for people still to come
records.text: Garden Grove and Mount Pisgah · 1846 · Open picture study Planting for people still to come At Garden Grove and Mount Pisgah, pioneers established farms and stopping places to help later travelers. Some stayed to plant while others continued. Their service reached beyond their own immediate company: shelter and food prepared today could sustain a family arriving later. At Winter Quarters, the revelation now recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 136 joined the practical organization of travel with care for people in need. Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:8–9 and consider whose journey your preparation might lighten. National Park Service: the 1846 trek Revelations in Context: the covenant

records.title: The trail was lived one day at a time
records.text: Beyond the dates and destinations, the journey was made through ordinary work, long stretches beside the Platte River, and difficult crossings that required the strength of the entire company.

records.title: Across an ocean, then the plains
records.text: The handcart story began in homes and ports far from the American plains. Preparation, limited resources and the season of departure shaped what followed.

records.title: The journey began across an ocean
records.text: British emigration · 1856 · Open picture study The journey began across an ocean For Elizabeth Crook Panting, the plains came after an Atlantic crossing. She sailed on the Thornton with Christopher and Jane. Her brother Samuel Lane Crook was also aboard; Peter Madsen’s diary records his marriage to Sarah Haines during the voyage. Samuel and Sarah stayed in the East and did not make the Willie company’s overland journey with Elizabeth. The family also remembered a fire aboard ship: Elizabeth alerted the captain and prayed with her children. This episode comes through the family history gathered in Tell My Story, Too , rather than a ship’s log examined for this page. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102

records.title: Making ready at Iowa City
records.text: Summer 1856 · Open picture study Making ready at Iowa City The Willie company journal records making tents, building carts, preparing wagons and weighing luggage. Its July entries also record births, deaths, worship and ordinary tasks such as washing clothing. Emigration was already demanding before the company began its passage across the plains on July 15. The same journal makes daily travel tangible: an early bugle, breakfast, prayers, greasing carts, packing tents and another stretch of road. These were people meeting practical needs while caring for one another. Read the Willie company journal

records.title: A late departure and a long road
records.text: Florence · August 1856 · Open picture study A late departure and a long road Handcarts offered a less expensive way to reach Utah, with emigrants pulling limited belongings in wooden carts. Ten companies traveled this way from 1856 through 1860. Most did not suffer the catastrophe of the late Willie and Martin companies. Their experience should not be confused with every handcart journey. At Florence, the question of continuing so late in the season was serious. The dated rescue overview below includes Levi Savage’s warning and the companies’ separate departures. Families listen together beside a waiting cart in this interpretation of a camp discussion. Church History: handcart companies Read the official 1856 timeline

records.title: Elizabeth Crook Panting and her children
records.text: A mother, a little boy and a baby stand at the heart of this account. We can honor their testimony by telling what the family preserved, identifying how it comes to us and leaving unknown details unfilled.

records.title: Elizabeth, Christopher and Jane
records.text: The Willie company · 1856 · Open picture study Elizabeth, Christopher and Jane Elizabeth Crook Panting began the overland journey with Christopher, five, and Jane, one. Christopher turned six on the way west; Elizabeth turned twenty-nine in October. Their names give the migration an intimate scale: a mother, a young boy and a baby, traveling toward a hoped-for home. The Church’s historical database records all three in the Willie company. Christopher later recalled that his father, Frederick, opposed Elizabeth’s Church participation, threatened her and hid her shoes. He remembered her borrowing shoes for worship and leaving with the children; on a train, another woman exchanged clothing with her to help her avoid recognition. These details survive as his family recollection. Elizabeth in the Church History database Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102

records.title: Fuel for a hungry camp
records.text: Elizabeth’s family account · Open picture study Fuel for a hungry camp As food dwindled on the trail, the family account remembers Elizabeth going out to gather buffalo chips for fuel. She had nearly filled her apron when an unfamiliar man approached and asked about her situation. She told him of the hunger in camp. He offered help and led her over a small hill. The remembered encounter begins with ordinary work for a family’s survival. Neither an exact date nor a securely identified cave location is supplied by the principal family account. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102

records.title: The gift in the cave
records.text: The account Elizabeth’s family preserved · Open picture study The gift in the cave Elizabeth followed the man to a cave where dried buffalo meat was hanging. He filled her apron with meat and instructed her to share it with others in need. After showing her the direction back to camp, he was gone. When she turned to thank him, she could no longer find either the man or the cave. The meat remained in her apron. This is the miracle as the family remembered it. The illustration leaves the stranger unidentified, as we do here. The account does not establish that he was Christ, an angel or a particular scriptural person. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102

records.title: A gift meant to be shared
records.text: Relief among the Willie company · Open picture study A gift meant to be shared Elizabeth returned and distributed the meat to people who needed food. In the family’s telling, the blessing reached beyond her own children. Jennie Edith Bell Mason’s later biography, preserved in the Church History Library, also records the cave, the dried meat and her return to the company. Her journey still required endurance. The family remembered Jane becoming dangerously ill in the handcart. Mason’s biography describes the children sheltered in a rescue wagon during the Rocky Ridge ordeal while Elizabeth walked. Mother and children reached Salt Lake City with the Willie company on November 9. Read the family biography in the Church History Library Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102

records.title: Handcarts, hardship, and rescue
records.text: Most handcart companies reached the valley safely. The late departure of the Willie and Martin companies in 1856 placed them in severe autumn storms, where relief parties carried food, clothing, blankets, and hope east from Utah.

records.title: Go out and bring them in
records.text: Willie and Martin were separate companies with different crisis points and arrival dates. Relief grew from Brigham Young’s urgent appeal into weeks of travel, giving, nursing and difficult choices.

records.title: Send help now
records.text: Brigham Young · October 5, 1856 · Open picture study Send help now On October 5, Brigham Young called for teams, wagons, flour and men to bring in the emigrants still on the plains. Wilford Woodruff’s journal records the concrete scale of the appeal: sixty teams, twelve tons of flour and forty additional teamsters. Concern for distant travelers became an assignment requiring immediate preparation and sacrifice. The call invites a direct question for disciples of Jesus Christ: what does another person need from me now? Read Matthew 25:35–40 beside this appeal for food, clothing and willing hands. Wilford Woodruff’s journal: October 5, 1856

records.title: The rescue began at home
records.text: Preparing the relief wagons · Open picture study The rescue began at home Women gathered bedding, clothing and other supplies while rescuers traveled east. Lucy Meserve Smith remembered the work of women in Provo to comfort those in need. Their service continued as survivors arrived; one delivery of food could not meet every need. Salt Lake City was still warm when the first appeal was made. The first relief company left on October 7, before the storm caught the emigrants on October 19. Further appeals and supplies sustained the rescue over the following weeks. Read about women’s relief efforts Church historic sites: how the rescue began

records.title: The hard climb at Rocky Ridge
records.text: Willie company · October 23, 1856 · Open picture study The hard climb at Rocky Ridge Relief did not instantly restore exhausted bodies. Daniel W. Jones later remembered rescuers bringing fuel, distributing provisions and encouraging the Willie emigrants. Some were already beyond recovery. The company still faced Rocky Ridge, a long, exposed crossing remembered for terrible suffering and loss. The dated overview records the crossing and the burials at Rock Creek. Remembering rescue also means remembering those who did not survive. Alma 7:11–12 directs our faith toward a Savior who knows suffering, rather than treating survival as a measure of anyone’s righteousness. Daniel W. Jones: later firsthand recollection Read the official 1856 timeline

records.title: The Martin company in the storm
records.text: North Platte · October 19, 1856 · Open picture study The Martin company in the storm The Martin company crossed the North Platte as the October 19 storm struck. It would be October 28 before express riders reached them, and October 31 before supply wagons arrived. In November they sheltered in the cove near Devil’s Gate, still suffering hunger, cold and exhaustion. Jones identified Joseph A. Young, Abel Garr and himself as the riders sent to find the remaining companies. He also remembered helping pull exhausted families into camp. Later, baggage was stored at Fort Seminoe so wagons could carry people; Jones and others stayed to guard that property through winter. Read the official 1856 timeline Daniel W. Jones: later firsthand recollection

records.title: Ephraim Hanks brings food and care
records.text: With the Martin company · November 1856 · Open picture study Ephraim Hanks brings food and care In a reminiscence recorded in 1891, Ephraim Hanks described a repeated nighttime call to help the handcart travelers. When a later appeal for volunteers came, he recalled answering, “I am ready now!” He was thirty in 1856 and joined the later rescue effort; he was not one of the riders who first reached Martin on October 28. Hanks remembered praying for a buffalo, finding one, and killing another the next day. He loaded his horses with meat and brought it to hungry families. He also recalled caring for the sick and administering priesthood blessings, including a healing near Fort Bridger. His testimony includes miraculous help alongside the lasting effects of frostbite. Tell My Story, Too: Ephraim Hanks’s recollection Ephraim Hanks: life and company record

records.title: Arrival was the beginning of another work
records.text: Entering the valley ended the overland journey, but it began years of planting, building, worship, and community life. The same faith that carried pioneers west shaped what they built after arriving.

records.title: Home, remembrance and a second witness
records.text: Arrival ended the miles, but recovery and remembrance continued. The witnesses who lived on carried both gratitude and grief into their homes and families.

records.title: The rescue continued inside the home
records.text: Salt Lake City · November 1856 · Open picture study The rescue continued inside the home As the Martin company approached Salt Lake City on November 30, Brigham Young asked residents to receive the newcomers into comfortable family homes and provide careful nursing and nourishment. The rescue was not complete at the city boundary. Its next work belonged in kitchens, sickrooms and households willing to share what they had. The Willie company had arrived on November 9. For Elizabeth and her children, the overland journey ended with all three alive. We remember their arrival alongside the grief of neighbors whose families had been broken by death. Brigham Young’s November 30 discourse Elizabeth in the Church History database

records.title: Jane hears a second witness
records.text: A later Mother’s Day meeting in Pocatello · Open picture study Jane hears a second witness Years later, Jane was visiting a daughter in Pocatello when she attended a Mother’s Day church meeting. An elderly man recalled being a hungry boy in the Willie company. He remembered a woman sharing dried meat that she had received miraculously. Jane wept and told him that woman was her mother. Jane later told her niece, June Cranney Monson, about this encounter. For Jane, whose mother’s account had sometimes been ridiculed, his recollection was a treasured second witness. Jane had been a baby on the trek; this is her later encounter with a recipient of the food, not a claim that she witnessed the cave herself. The surviving account does not name the man or date the meeting. Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102

records.title: The overland era gives way to rail
records.text: The railroad connection · 1869 · Open picture study The overland era gives way to rail On May 10, 1869, the transcontinental lines met at Promontory Summit. Railroad travel changed the journey west that wagons and handcarts had once made over many months. The waiting family and passenger train bring that change in travel into view. Elizabeth’s later life continued in Logan. The family history records marriages to William Wilkes and Hiram K. Cranney and remembers her enduring trust in God. She died on March 15, 1891, aged sixty-three. Jane and Christopher carried the family’s memories into another generation. National Park Service: Golden Spike history Tell My Story, Too: Elizabeth and Jane, pp. 101–102 Elizabeth in the Church History database

records.title: Songs of courage and redeeming love
records.text: Pause with the music that carries faith from one heart to another. Hear the pioneers’ enduring hymn, then turn toward the Savior with a personal song of gratitude.

records.title: Come, Come, Ye Saints
records.text: Music for the journey Songs of courage and redeeming love Pause with the music that carries faith from one heart to another. Hear the pioneers’ enduring hymn, then turn toward the Savior with a personal song of gratitude. Come, Come, Ye Saints William Clayton’s words have helped generations give voice to courage, grief, and trust in God. Listen to The Tabernacle Choir and Orchestra at Temple Square, then open these two picture studies. Open picture study A song shared at the end of the day A child looks up as the adults sing. Worn clothing and muddy ground tell of a difficult day; their gathered voices offer companionship before another morning on the trail. William Clayton wrote the hymn in April 1846 during the exodus from Nauvoo. Its courage belongs beside the real hardship of the journey. This imagined camp scene honors that shared faith without identifying the singers as a particular family. Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:28–29 . The Lord’s counsel at Winter Quarters gives a place to singing in joy and praying in sorrow. What song helps you turn toward Him? Open picture study Hope for the road ahead A mother and child share a glance as their family walks beside the wagon. The road still stretches ahead. This scene imagines the hymn’s hope in the daily work of continuing together. In Ether 12:4 , faith in God opens a hope that steadies the soul. As you listen, remember both the people who reached a new home and those whose journeys ended along the way. Consider one small way to strengthen someone who is still in the middle of a hard journey. Continue with faith in trials and Elizabeth’s story . The Savior bends to help push, His attention on the man beside Him; heavenly helpers share the effort. This devotional scene gives visible form to faith in His redeeming love. The Martin and Hodgetts companies crossed the North Platte on October 19, 1856, as the first winter storm struck. Read the official timeline beside this picture. Christ and the angels are a devotional interpretation, rather than a recorded appearance at the crossing. Dallyn Vail Bayles sings Orson F. Whitney’s hymn text in Rob Gardner’s musical setting, with violinist Jenny Oaks Baker and the Lyceum Philharmonic. The published hymn pairs Whitney’s words with a different tune by Harry A. Dean. This recording is offered here as a devotional companion to the pioneer stories. Read Matthew 25:35–40 , the Savior’s teaching about feeding, clothing, and welcoming people in need. Then read Mosiah 24:14–15 , where He strengthens a people to bear their burdens. As you listen, consider where you need the Savior’s healing and how gratitude might shape your next act of kindness. Continue in the Atonement of Jesus Christ study . Listen: Dallyn Vail Bayles ↗ Read Matthew 25:35–40 Open each picture to follow its scripture connections and view it in full. These scenes invite reflection on the hymns; the river study distinguishes the historical crossing from its portrayal of heavenly help.

records.title: Read a life, then consider what it asks of us
records.text: The trail becomes more understandable when a named person's record is read alongside the wider setting. Choose a journal or company record from this page. Note the author, the dates covered, and whether the words were recorded during the journey or remembered later. One person's experience matters, but it does not stand for every pioneer. Keep historical questions and devotional applications visible. “What happened, where, and when?” requires records and context. “How might I respond to a neighbor in need?” is a personal application. An image of rescue can invite compassion without supplying evidence for every detail of the historical scene. Accounts of endurance deserve care. Suffering is not proof that someone was more faithful, and survival is not a measure of divine favor. Remember those who died as people with relationships and unfinished lives, not merely examples in someone else's lesson. Compare evidence and accounts Use a worked historical inquiry before drawing conclusions from a single recollection. Explore faith and practical support Continue the theme of endurance with scripture that makes room for lament and help from others. When pioneer loss touches your own grief Find a quieter study that does not require turning bereavement into an inspiring story. For an optional response, consider one practical act of care you could offer today and ask whether it would be welcome. For geography, use named historical sites such as Fort Bridger State Historic Site in present-day Wyoming alongside the route rather than assuming historical territorial names match modern state boundaries.

records.title: Faith for the next step
records.text: After following the journeys and reading a record, pause with the counsel given at Winter Quarters in Doctrine and Covenants 136. These questions invite a personal response; they do not ask you to compare your suffering with another person’s. Who needs a place in our plans? Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:6–9 . Notice the preparations for people who would remain behind and the care required for vulnerable travelers. Whose needs might be overlooked in a plan you are making? Ask what would actually help before offering it. What can I make right? Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:23–26 . The counsel includes everyday speech, borrowed property, and returning what was lost. Is there a promise to keep, something to return, or a conversation to repair? Choose a small, honest next step. Bring joy and sorrow to the Lord Read Doctrine and Covenants 136:28–29 . The passage gives a place both to praise and to prayer in sorrow. Which invitation meets you today? You might choose a hymn, offer a quiet prayer, or sit with someone who needs company.
